note: Nutrient deficiencies by crop (2026-10-16). Built by the scratchpad nd/build.py from the researchers' entries. One entry is one crop and one nutrient.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in rice
entries.hint: Lower leaves turn pale yellow green first and the whole field looks light green and short.
entries.symptoms: The oldest leaves turn yellowish green first, starting at the tip, while the young leaves stay greener. Leaves become narrow, short and stand very upright. Plants stay short with few tillers, and in a bad case the whole field looks yellow. Fewer grains form and the harvest drops.
entries.stage: Tillering up to panicle initiation, when the crop takes up the most nitrogen.
entries.causes: Too little fertilizer for a modern variety, or nitrogen given at the wrong time or in the wrong way. Soils very low in organic matter, acid sulfate, saline, poorly drained and calcareous soils supply little nitrogen or lose it fast.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency looks almost the same, but it yellows the young leaves first. Iron deficiency starts on the newest leaf, with yellow between green veins. Nitrogen deficiency always starts on the old leaves and spreads evenly over the field.
entries.confirm: Use the leaf color chart every 7 days from 14 days after transplanting (or 21 days after seeding) until early flowering. If more than 5 of 10 leaves read below 4, the crop needs nitrogen. A MOET kit or a lab test of soil and leaves confirms it.
entries.fix: When the leaf color chart reads below 4, PhilRice advises 1.5 bags of Urea 46 0 0 per hectare in the dry season or 1 bag in the wet season. If the crop also shows sulfur deficiency, use Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 instead: 3.5 bags in the dry season or 2 bags in the wet season. Keep water in the field after applying, but do not let it spill over the bunds right away.
entries.prevent: Split nitrogen into several doses timed by the leaf color chart, keep weeds down, and return straw, manure or compost. Fix phosphorus, potassium and zinc problems so the crop can use the nitrogen.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in rice
entries.hint: Dark green plants whose lower leaves dry yellow brown at the tips and edges.
entries.symptoms: Plants stay dark green, but the tips and edges of the older leaves turn yellowish brown and dark brown spots appear. The browning moves from the tip down to the base of the leaf. Upper leaves become short, droopy and dirty dark green. Panicles get rusty brown spots and many unfilled grains, and plants fall over easily.
entries.stage: Mostly from late tillering to grain filling, so it is often noticed late.
entries.causes: Sandy soils with small potassium reserves, highly weathered acid soils, poorly drained soils. Fields given plenty of nitrogen and phosphorus but no potash. Taking away or burning the straw removes most of the potassium.
entries.confuse: PhilRice notes the color looks like tungro, but potassium deficiency covers the field evenly while tungro shows in patches. Phosphorus deficiency also gives dark green plants, but without the brown leaf edges.
entries.confirm: Soil test for exchangeable potassium or a MOET kit test. A small strip given potash next to the rest of the field also shows the difference within a few weeks.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 to the soil following the soil test. For quick help, TNAU advises a 1 percent potassium chloride or potassium sulfate spray (10 g per liter) every 15 days until the symptoms stop.
entries.prevent: Plow the straw back in instead of burning or hauling it away, spread straw ash evenly. Give potash together with nitrogen every season.

sources.title: PhilRice PalayCheck System, Key Check 5: nutrient management

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in rice
entries.hint: Short, very upright, dirty dark green plants with very few tillers.
entries.symptoms: Plants stay short with thin stems and very few tillers. Leaves are narrow, short, very upright and dirty dark green. The older leaves turn brown and die while the young ones look healthy. Some varieties turn red or purple. Panicles and grains are fewer, and the crop can mature a week or more late.
entries.stage: Early growth and tillering. Mild cases are hard to see in the field.
entries.causes: Acid upland soils, sandy soils low in organic matter, degraded lowland soils, acid sulfate soils, volcanic soils and calcareous soils, which hold phosphorus tightly.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency also gives dark green plants, but with yellow brown leaf edges. Phosphorus deficiency often comes together with zinc deficiency or iron toxicity, so look for more than one problem.
entries.confirm: Run a MOET kit test or a soil test for available phosphorus before planting. A plot left without phosphorus beside a fertilized plot shows the gap in tillers.
entries.fix: Apply a phosphorus fertilizer such as 16 20 0, Complete 14 14 14 or Superphosphate 0 18 0 early, following the soil test. TNAU gives 15 to 30 kg of phosphorus (P) per hectare to the soil. For a quick boost, spray 2 percent DAP 18 46 0 (20 g per liter, soaked overnight and filtered) twice, 15 days apart.
entries.prevent: Replace the phosphorus each harvest removes with fertilizer, manure or compost, and plow straw back in. On acid uplands correct the acidity first.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in rice
entries.hint: Two to four weeks after transplanting, patches of short plants with dusty brown spots and pale midribs.
entries.symptoms: Two to four weeks after transplanting the crop grows unevenly and some hills stay short. Young leaves turn pale along the midrib near the base, and dusty brown spots and streaks appear and join on the leaves. Leaf blades are smaller and tillering drops. In severe cases seedlings rust and die, direct seeded rice fails to come up, and maturity is late.
entries.stage: Seedbed and the first 2 to 4 weeks after transplanting. Plants may recover once the field is drained, but yield is lost.
entries.causes: Neutral to alkaline and calcareous soils, fields that stay flooded all year (three crops a year), sodic, saline and peat soils, and soils high in phosphorus. PhilRice calls it the most widespread micronutrient problem of rice.
entries.confuse: Iron toxicity gives similar brown spotting, but on waterlogged acid soils with orange leaves. Iron deficiency yellows the newest leaves between the veins. Tungro and grassy stunt viruses also stunt plants. Ask your technician if the spots are not there.
entries.confirm: Drain a small part of the field. Zinc deficient plants often perk up after the soil dries. Confirm with a soil or leaf test or a MOET kit.
entries.fix: Broadcast 25 kg Zinc sulfate per hectare 10 to 14 days after transplanting. In the seedbed, apply 0.5 kg zinc sulfate per 400 square meters (2 kg if severe) 7 to 10 days after sowing, or dip seedlings in a 2 percent zinc oxide mix for 15 to 30 minutes. For direct seeding, add 1 kg zinc sulfate per 40 kg seed to the last soaking water. TNAU also gives a 0.5 percent zinc sulfate spray (5 g per liter) twice, 15 days apart.
entries.prevent: PhilRice advises 25 kg zinc sulfate per hectare at 14 days after transplanting once a year, in the dry season. Drain and dry fields that are always flooded now and then, and use ammonium sulfate for part of the nitrogen.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in rice
entries.hint: The whole plant is pale yellow, and the youngest leaves are the palest.
entries.symptoms: The whole plant turns pale green to yellow, but unlike nitrogen deficiency the young leaves yellow first and their tips may die. Plants are short with fewer tillers, yet not dark like phosphorus or potassium deficient plants. Seedlings in the seedbed turn yellow and many die after transplanting. Panicles are fewer and shorter, and maturity comes 1 to 2 weeks late.
entries.stage: Seedbed and vegetative growth. The loss is biggest when it starts early.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, soils low in organic matter, highly weathered soils, and fields given only sulfur free fertilizer such as urea for years. Burning or hauling away straw removes sulfur.
entries.confuse: It is easy to take for nitrogen deficiency. Nitrogen yellows the old leaves first, sulfur yellows the young leaves first. A leaf color chart reading alone cannot tell them apart.
entries.confirm: Check which leaves turned yellow first, then run a MOET kit test or a soil and leaf test.
entries.fix: Use Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 (24 percent sulfur) instead of urea for the next nitrogen doses: PhilRice gives 3.5 bags per hectare in the dry season or 2 bags in the wet season when the leaf color chart reads below 4. The sulfur in 14 14 14 12S at the PalayCheck rate is enough for the usual shortage. TNAU also gives a 0.5 percent wettable sulfur spray (5 g per liter) twice, 15 days apart.
entries.prevent: Use a sulfur bearing fertilizer such as 14 14 14 12S or ammonium sulfate each season. Plow straw in instead of burning it. Gypsum is a slow sulfur source where rain washes the soil.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in rice
entries.hint: The newest leaves turn yellow between the veins, then almost white, in dry upland or alkaline fields.
entries.symptoms: Yellowing starts between the veins of the newest leaves while the older leaves stay green. The whole leaf then turns pale yellow and nearly white. In severe cases the whole plant turns pale, grows little and can die.
entries.stage: Seedling and early growth, mostly in upland or dry seeded fields.
entries.causes: Rare in flooded rice. Seen on neutral, alkaline or calcareous upland soils, lowland soils low in organic matter or watered with alkaline water, and sandy soils from granite.
entries.confuse: Zinc deficiency also hits alkaline soils, but gives brown spots and pale midribs. Nitrogen deficiency starts on the old leaves. Do not mix it up with iron toxicity, the opposite problem on waterlogged acid soils, where lower leaves get tiny brown spots and turn orange.
entries.confirm: Check the soil pH (alkaline soil is the warning sign) and send soil and young leaf samples to a laboratory.
entries.fix: Use Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 instead of urea to make the root zone more acid, add manure or crop residues. Use fertilizers that carry iron as a trace element. For an iron product such as ferrous sulfate, follow the soil test and the label.
entries.prevent: Grow iron efficient varieties on alkaline uplands and keep the soil rich in organic matter.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in rice
entries.hint: Older leaves show orange yellow stripes between the veins, like a string of beads, and hang wavy.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn orange yellow between the veins, with green and yellow stripes along the leaf like a string of beads. Leaves become wavy and droopy because they bend wider away from the stem. As it gets worse the younger leaves pale too and the old leaves die. Height and tillers change little, but grains are fewer and lighter.
entries.stage: Middle of the season to grain filling. The flag leaf can show it.
entries.causes: Rare in irrigated rice, where the water brings magnesium. Seen in rainfed and upland rice on acid, sandy, leached soils and old acid sulfate soils that have been cropped for years without replacing it.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency starts at the leaf tips and edges, not between the veins. Iron toxicity gives orange leaves too, but with tiny brown spots on waterlogged soils.
entries.confirm: Soil test for exchangeable magnesium and a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU advises a 0.5 percent magnesium sulfate spray (5 g Epsom salt per liter) twice, 15 days apart. For the soil, a soluble source such as kieserite corrects it fast. Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Replace the magnesium taken away in grain and straw with fertilizer or manure. Use Dolomite on acid soils as the soil test advises.

sources.title: IRRI Rice Doctor fact sheet: Magnesium deficiency

entries.name: Manganese deficiency in rice
entries.hint: Young leaves turn greyish green between the veins from the tip down, then get brown spots.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves turn pale greyish green between the veins, starting at the tip and moving to the base. Brown dead spots follow and the leaf can turn dark brown. New leaves come out short, narrow and light green, and plants stay short with small roots, though tillering is not much affected.
entries.stage: Tillering, mostly in upland rice.
entries.causes: Common in upland rice but rare in flooded fields, where manganese dissolves easily. Acid upland soils, alkaline or calcareous soils low in organic matter, leached sandy soils and old degraded paddies.
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency also yellows young leaves between the veins, but without the grey tone and brown spots. Manganese deficient plants also catch brown spot disease more easily.
entries.confirm: Leaf test and soil test, and note whether the field is upland or alkaline.
entries.fix: TNAU advises a 0.2 percent manganese sulfate spray (2 g per liter) twice, 15 days apart. For the soil, manganese sulfate can be banded along the rows at 5 to 20 kg of manganese per hectare. Use ammonium sulfate instead of urea and add manure or straw.
entries.prevent: Keep organic matter up with manure or straw and choose acid forming nitrogen such as ammonium sulfate on alkaline uplands.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in rice
entries.hint: Tips of the youngest leaves turn white and roll, and plants are short.
entries.symptoms: The tips of the young leaves turn white and roll, and plants stay short. In severe cases the growing point dies, though new tillers keep coming. If it strikes at panicle initiation the plant may not form panicles at all.
entries.stage: Vegetative growth up to panicle initiation.
entries.causes: Rare, especially in irrigated rice. Highly weathered acid soils, sandy soils, acid soils from igneous rock, and fields where water drains through the soil fast.
entries.confuse: Calcium deficiency gives the same white rolled leaf tips. Only a leaf or soil test tells them apart.
entries.confirm: Send soil and plant samples to a laboratory.
entries.fix: TNAU advises a 0.3 percent boric acid spray (3 g per liter) twice, 15 days apart. Borax can also go to the soil, but follow the soil test, because a little too much boron burns rice.
entries.prevent: Avoid heavy leaching and over drainage, and never apply boron without a test.

entries.name: Copper deficiency in rice
entries.hint: New leaves stay rolled into needles at the tip, plants are bluish green, and many grains are empty.
entries.symptoms: Leaves turn bluish green with pale streaks on both sides of the midrib. Dark brown dead patches form on the leaf tips. New leaves stay rolled, with a needle like upper part, while the lower part looks normal. Tillering drops and pollen is poor, so many grains stay empty.
entries.stage: Tillering to flowering.
entries.causes: Rare. Peat and other soils very high in organic matter, highly weathered red soils, sandy soils and calcareous soils.
entries.confuse: Boron and calcium deficiency also roll the young leaf tips, but the tips turn white. Copper gives bluish green leaves with brown needle tips and streaks along the midrib.
entries.confirm: Send soil and plant samples to a laboratory.
entries.fix: TNAU advises a 0.2 percent copper sulfate spray (2 g per liter) twice, 15 days apart. Soil copper sulfate (TNAU gives 1 to 5 kg of copper per hectare) should only follow a soil test, since copper builds up in the soil.
entries.prevent: On peat soils, test for copper before planting and use a fertilizer with trace elements.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in rice
entries.hint: Tips of the youngest leaves turn white, split and roll, only on very acid or leached soils.
entries.symptoms: The tips of the youngest leaves turn white or bleached, then split, roll and curl. Dead tissue can form along the leaf edges, and old leaves later turn brown and die. In extreme cases the growing points stay short and die. It only shows when the shortage is severe.
entries.stage: Any stage, but only under severe shortage.
entries.causes: Very rare in lowland rice, since fertilizer and irrigation water bring calcium. Seen on acid, strongly leached, sandy soils, old acid sulfate soils and soils from serpentine rock.
entries.confuse: Boron deficiency gives the same white rolled tips. Calcium deficient plants also suffer more from iron toxicity on acid soils.
entries.confirm: Send soil and plant samples to a laboratory. A soil pH test also helps.
entries.fix: TNAU advises a 1 percent calcium chloride spray (10 g per liter) for quick relief. About 500 kg Gypsum per hectare on calcium poor high pH soils. Superphosphate also carries calcium. On acid soils use Agricultural lime as the soil test advises.
entries.prevent: Return straw or manure to the field, and correct strong acidity before planting.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in yellow corn
entries.hint: Lower leaves turn yellow in a V from the tip down the midrib, and plants are pale and thin.
entries.symptoms: The lowest leaves turn pale, then yellow in a V shape that starts at the leaf tip and runs down the midrib. The yellowing climbs the plant if nothing is done, and the old leaves dry from the tip. Stalks stay thin and plants short, and ears come out small with poorly filled tips.
entries.stage: Knee high to silking. The crop takes up the most nitrogen in the month before tasseling.
entries.causes: Too little fertilizer, nitrogen washed out by heavy rain or irrigation, nitrogen lost from dry or hard soil, sandy soil. Fields flooded in hot weather. Plowing in a lot of dry crop residue also ties up nitrogen.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency also yellows the plant but starts on the young upper leaves. Potassium deficiency browns the leaf edges, not the midrib. Drought can dry the lower leaves too, so check soil moisture.
entries.confirm: Check that the yellowing started on the bottom leaves, in a V along the midrib. Compare with a few rows given extra urea, and have the soil tested before the next planting.
entries.fix: Sidedress Urea 46 0 0 or Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 beside the row and cover it with soil, then irrigate or wait for rain. Follow the soil test for the rate. For quick help, TNAU gives a 1 percent urea spray (10 g per liter) twice, 15 days apart. Nitrogen given after the ears start filling helps much less.
entries.prevent: Test the soil before planting, split nitrogen between planting and knee high, and avoid packing the soil hard.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in yellow corn
entries.hint: Young plants are short and dark green, with purple red edges on the lower leaves.
entries.symptoms: Young plants grow slowly and stay small and thin, with dark green leaves. The edges and tips of the older leaves turn reddish purple. The color can spread over the whole blade, while new leaves stay green. Later the crop matures late and ears are small, twisted or poorly formed.
entries.stage: Seedling to knee high. The purple usually fades once plants pass about 1 meter, but the yield loss stays.
entries.causes: Acid soils and very alkaline soils that hold phosphorus tightly, cold wet soil, hard packed soil. Roots hurt by insects or fertilizer. Acid uplands such as parts of Bukidnon need phosphorus, and some Isabela farms need lime first.
entries.confuse: Some hybrids show purple leaves when young even with enough phosphorus, so compare with other plants and the soil test. Magnesium deficiency also gives purple tints, but with yellow stripes between the veins.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus before planting. A real shortage shows on many plants in the same soil patch, not on one hybrid only.
entries.fix: Phosphorus works best at planting. For the standing crop, TNAU gives a 2 percent DAP 18 46 0 spray (20 g per liter). For the next crop, put 16 20 0, Complete 14 14 14 or DAP in the furrow at planting, following the soil test.
entries.prevent: Band phosphorus near the seed at planting, and lime very acid soils as the soil test advises.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in yellow corn
entries.hint: Lower leaves dry brown along the edges while the middle stays green, and stalks break and fall.
entries.symptoms: The edges and tips of the lower leaves turn yellow, then brown and dry, while the middle of the leaf stays green. It moves up the plant if the shortage goes on. Stalks get weak and plants fall over late in the season, and ears are small and pointed with empty tips.
entries.stage: Shows about 4 to 6 weeks after planting (around the 6 leaf stage) and again at grain filling.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, highly weathered acid soils, hard, dry or waterlogged soils that limit roots. Fields where earlier crops took away a lot of potassium.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen yellowing runs down the midrib in a V, while potassium burns the leaf edges. Drought scorch hits many leaves at once.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium, and look for brown edges starting on the bottom leaves. A leaf tissue test of the ear leaf confirms it.
entries.fix: Sidedress Muriate of potash 0 0 60 beside the row early, following the soil test. TNAU gives a 1 percent potassium chloride or potassium sulfate spray (10 g per liter) twice, 15 days apart.
entries.prevent: Return stalks and leaves to the field, and give potash at planting when the soil test is low.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in yellow corn
entries.hint: Wide white or pale yellow bands on both sides of the midrib from the leaf base, on short plants with bunched leaves.
entries.symptoms: Pale yellow to white bands appear between the veins, starting at the base of the leaf and running toward the tip. While the edges, tip and midrib stay green. Internodes stay short, so plants look stunted with bunched leaves. In severe cases the new leaves come out almost white (white bud), and leaf edges and stems turn reddish.
entries.stage: Seedling to knee high. Plants often outgrow mild cases.
entries.causes: High pH soils (DA Caraga warns at pH 7.5 and up), low organic matter, cool wet soil. Heavy phosphorus on soils already low in zinc. UPLB studies found zinc needs on corn farms in Cagayan.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency stripes the old leaves, not a band at the base of young leaves. Iron deficiency stripes the full length of the young leaf. Nitrogen deficiency yellows the midrib, the part that stays green with zinc.
entries.confirm: Soil test for zinc and pH, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Spray 0.5 percent Zinc sulfate (5 g per liter) twice, 15 days apart (TNAU). For the soil, TNAU gives 20 to 25 kg zinc sulfate per hectare. The University of Kentucky bands about 19 kg zinc sulfate per hectare (17 pounds per acre) near the row.
entries.prevent: On high pH or zinc poor soils, add zinc sulfate to the basal fertilizer. A broadcast dose lasts several seasons.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in yellow corn
entries.hint: The young upper leaves are the palest, while the lower leaves stay greener.
entries.symptoms: The whole plant looks pale like nitrogen deficiency. But the young upper leaves are the palest, and up close they show faint yellow stripes between the veins. Plants stay short and upright, and maturity comes late.
entries.stage: Early growth. It may fade as roots go deeper and the soil warms.
entries.causes: Acid sandy soils, low organic matter, waterlogged soils, and heavy rain soon after planting (DA Caraga). Years of urea and other sulfur free fertilizers make it more likely.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency starts on the old lower leaves. Zinc deficiency gives a white band at the leaf base.
entries.confirm: Note which leaves yellowed first, then test soil and leaves for sulfur.
entries.fix: Use Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 for the next nitrogen sidedress, and place a sulfur bearing fertilizer near the row (DA Caraga). Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Include ammonium sulfate or another sulfur source in the program on sandy or low organic matter soils.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in yellow corn
entries.hint: Lower leaves get yellow to white stripes between the veins, later turning reddish purple.
entries.symptoms: Yellow to white stripes appear between the veins of the lower leaves, sometimes with small dead spots that look like a string of beads. The old leaves then turn reddish purple, and the tips and edges may die. Growth stays normal unless it is severe.
entries.stage: Early growth to the middle of the season.
entries.causes: Very acid, sandy soils in rainy areas, fields that were never limed, and heavy potash on soils already low in magnesium.
entries.confuse: Iron and manganese deficiency give similar stripes but on the young leaves. Zinc gives a band near the base of young leaves. Phosphorus gives purple without stripes.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium and pH, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: Apply magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) to the soil or as a leaf spray (DA Caraga). TNAU gives a 2 percent spray (20 g per liter). On acid soils use Dolomite following the soil test.
entries.prevent: Lime acid fields with dolomite, and do not overdo potash.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in yellow corn
entries.hint: Tips of the young leaves stick together like a ladder, on very acid soil.
entries.symptoms: The tips of new leaves stick to the leaf below, so the whorl looks like a ladder or a row of hooks. Young leaves are light green with whitish streaks and brittle, brown, sticky edges. Plants can be badly stunted.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Rare. It needs very acid soils (below pH 5), unlimed weathered uplands, or soils where magnesium and potassium crowd out calcium. On such soils aluminum and manganese damage usually show first.
entries.confuse: Boron deficiency also hurts the growing tip but gives white spots and short upper internodes. Acid soil damage from aluminum stunts the roots.
entries.confirm: Soil pH and calcium test.
entries.fix: Apply Agricultural lime or Dolomite following the soil test. UPLB worked out 3.6 tons of lime per hectare for one extremely acid farm in Isabela. Gypsum adds calcium without raising the pH.
entries.prevent: Lime acid uplands before planting, ahead of the rains.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in yellow corn
entries.hint: Upper leaves have white spots and waxy brown streaks, and tassels and ears fail to come out.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves get small white or yellow spots and raised, waxy brown streaks, and turn brittle. Upper internodes stay short. Tassels and ear shoots are small and may not come out, so few kernels set.
entries.stage: Before tasseling up to silking.
entries.causes: Rare. Sandy soils low in organic matter, high pH soils and drought.
entries.confuse: Drought also delays ear shoots and spoils pollination, so both can happen together. Zinc gives bands, not spots.
entries.confirm: Test leaves and soil for boron before treating.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 0.5 percent borax spray (5 g per liter) every 15 days. Corn is very sensitive to too much boron. So never go above the advised rate and do not put boron in the seed row.
entries.prevent: Keep organic matter up, and irrigate at tasseling during dry spells.

entries.name: Copper deficiency in yellow corn
entries.hint: The youngest leaves come out yellow, and their tips brown, roll and break.
entries.symptoms: The youngest leaves are yellow as they come out of the whorl, and their tips turn brown, roll and break. Leaves can get streaks like iron deficiency, the stalk is soft and limp, and the edges of older leaves may die.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Rare. Seen on peat and other high organic matter soils and soils above pH 7.5. UPLB found copper needs on some Cagayan corn farms.
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency gives similar streaks. Nitrogen plus sulfur shortage in cool weather can look like mild copper deficiency.
entries.confirm: Soil and leaf test for copper.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 0.2 percent copper sulfate spray (2 g per liter). UPLB advised about 1 kg of copper per hectare on one Cagayan soil, so follow the soil test.
entries.prevent: Test for copper before planting on peat or alkaline soils.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in yellow corn
entries.hint: Upper leaves turn pale yellow to white between the veins along their whole length.
entries.symptoms: Long pale green to nearly white stripes run between the veins of the upper leaves, while the veins stay green. As it worsens the veins pale too, the crop looks bleached, and plants are stunted.
entries.stage: Seedling and early growth.
entries.causes: Rare in corn. Only on high pH, calcareous soils, worse when the soil is cold, wet and poorly aerated.
entries.confuse: Magnesium also stripes leaves, but the old ones. Zinc gives a band at the base of the leaf, not stripes the full length.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test (calcareous soil is the warning sign) and a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU gives 20 to 25 kg ferrous sulfate per hectare to the soil, or a 1 percent ferrous sulfate spray (10 g per liter) every week until new leaves come out green.
entries.prevent: Add manure and use an acid forming fertilizer such as ammonium sulfate on calcareous soil.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in sweet corn
entries.local: Kakulangan sa nitrogen ng mais na matamis
entries.hint: Lower leaves turn yellow in a V from the tip, and ears come out small with bare tips.
entries.symptoms: The lowest leaves turn pale, then yellow in a V shape that starts at the leaf tip and runs down the midrib. The yellowing climbs the plant if nothing is done, and the old leaves dry from the tip. Stalks stay thin and plants short, and ears come out small with poorly filled tips. In sweet corn this means short ears with bare tips that sell poorly.
entries.stage: Knee high to silking. The crop takes up the most nitrogen in the month before tasseling.
entries.causes: Too little fertilizer, nitrogen washed out by heavy rain or irrigation, nitrogen lost from dry or hard soil, sandy soil. Fields flooded in hot weather. Plowing in a lot of dry crop residue also ties up nitrogen.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency also yellows the plant but starts on the young upper leaves. Potassium deficiency browns the leaf edges, not the midrib. Drought can dry the lower leaves too, so check soil moisture.
entries.confirm: Check that the yellowing started on the bottom leaves, in a V along the midrib. Compare with a few rows given extra urea, and have the soil tested before the next planting.
entries.fix: Sweet corn is a heavy feeder: the University of Kentucky gives about 170 kg of nitrogen per hectare (150 pounds per acre), with 90 to 110 kg before planting and the rest when plants are knee high. Sidedress Urea 46 0 0 or Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 beside the row now and water it in. TNAU gives a 1 percent urea spray (10 g per liter) twice, 15 days apart, for quick help.
entries.prevent: Test the soil before planting, split nitrogen between planting and knee high, and avoid packing the soil hard.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in sweet corn
entries.local: Kakulangan sa potassium ng mais na matamis
entries.hint: Lower leaf edges dry brown, and ears are short and pointed with unfilled tips.
entries.symptoms: The edges and tips of the lower leaves turn yellow, then brown and dry, while the middle of the leaf stays green. It moves up the plant if the shortage goes on. Stalks get weak and plants fall over late in the season, and ears are small and pointed with empty tips. Sweet corn ears with bare, pointed tips are hard to sell.
entries.stage: Shows about 4 to 6 weeks after planting (around the 6 leaf stage) and again at grain filling.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, highly weathered acid soils, hard, dry or waterlogged soils that limit roots. Fields where earlier crops took away a lot of potassium.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen yellowing runs down the midrib in a V, while potassium burns the leaf edges. Drought scorch hits many leaves at once.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium, and look for brown edges starting on the bottom leaves. A leaf tissue test of the ear leaf confirms it.
entries.fix: Sidedress Muriate of potash 0 0 60 beside the row early, following the soil test. TNAU gives a 1 percent potassium chloride or potassium sulfate spray (10 g per liter) twice, 15 days apart.
entries.prevent: Return stalks and leaves to the field, and give potash at planting when the soil test is low.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in sweet corn
entries.local: Kakulangan sa phosphorus ng mais na matamis
entries.hint: Young plants are short and dark green, with purple red edges on the lower leaves.
entries.symptoms: Young plants grow slowly and stay small and thin, with dark green leaves. The edges and tips of the older leaves turn reddish purple. In sweet corn the purple often shows again around ear development. Ears are small, twisted or have missing kernels.
entries.stage: Seedling to knee high. The purple usually fades once plants pass about 1 meter, but the yield loss stays.
entries.causes: Acid soils below pH 6 (the University of Kentucky notes phosphorus gets locked up there), very alkaline soils, cold wet soil and hard packed soil.
entries.confuse: Some hybrids show purple leaves when young even with enough phosphorus, so compare with other plants and the soil test. Magnesium deficiency also gives purple tints, but with yellow stripes between the veins.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus before planting. A real shortage shows on many plants in the same soil patch, not on one hybrid only.
entries.fix: For sweet corn all the phosphorus normally goes in before planting, following the soil test (University of Kentucky). For the standing crop, TNAU gives a 2 percent DAP 18 46 0 spray (20 g per liter). Next time put 16 20 0, Complete 14 14 14 or DAP in the furrow at planting.
entries.prevent: Band phosphorus near the seed at planting, and lime very acid soils as the soil test advises.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in sweet corn
entries.local: Kakulangan sa zinc ng mais na matamis
entries.hint: Wide white or pale yellow bands on both sides of the midrib from the leaf base, on short plants with bunched leaves.
entries.symptoms: Pale yellow to white bands appear between the veins, starting at the base of the leaf and running toward the tip. While the edges, tip and midrib stay green. Internodes stay short, so plants look stunted with bunched leaves. In severe cases the new leaves come out almost white (white bud), and leaf edges and stems turn reddish.
entries.stage: Seedling to knee high. Plants often outgrow mild cases.
entries.causes: High pH soils (the University of Kentucky sees it most above pH 6.5), very early plantings in cool soil, low organic matter. Heavy phosphorus on soils already low in zinc.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency stripes the old leaves, not a band at the base of young leaves. Iron deficiency stripes the full length of the young leaf. Nitrogen deficiency yellows the midrib, the part that stays green with zinc.
entries.confirm: Soil test for zinc and pH, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Spray 0.5 percent Zinc sulfate (5 g per liter) twice, 15 days apart (TNAU). The University of Kentucky bands about 19 kg zinc sulfate per hectare (17 pounds per acre) or broadcasts up to about 100 kg per hectare (90 pounds per acre), which lasts several years. TNAU gives 20 to 25 kg zinc sulfate per hectare to the soil.
entries.prevent: On high pH or zinc poor soils, add zinc sulfate to the basal fertilizer. A broadcast dose lasts several seasons.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in sweet corn
entries.local: Kakulangan sa sulfur ng mais na matamis
entries.hint: The young upper leaves are the palest, while the lower leaves stay greener.
entries.symptoms: The whole plant looks pale like nitrogen deficiency. But the young upper leaves are the palest, and up close they show faint yellow stripes between the veins. Plants stay short and upright, and maturity comes late.
entries.stage: Early growth. It may fade as roots go deeper and the soil warms.
entries.causes: Acid sandy soils, low organic matter, waterlogged soils, and heavy rain soon after planting (DA Caraga). Years of urea and other sulfur free fertilizers make it more likely.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency starts on the old lower leaves. Zinc deficiency gives a white band at the leaf base.
entries.confirm: Note which leaves yellowed first, then test soil and leaves for sulfur.
entries.fix: Use Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 for the next nitrogen sidedress, and place a sulfur bearing fertilizer near the row (DA Caraga). Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Include ammonium sulfate or another sulfur source in the program on sandy or low organic matter soils.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in sweet corn
entries.local: Kakulangan sa magnesium ng mais na matamis
entries.hint: Lower leaves get yellow to white stripes between the veins, later turning reddish purple.
entries.symptoms: Yellow to white stripes appear between the veins of the lower leaves, sometimes with small dead spots that look like a string of beads. The old leaves then turn reddish purple, and the tips and edges may die. Growth stays normal unless it is severe.
entries.stage: Early growth to the middle of the season.
entries.causes: Very acid, sandy soils in rainy areas, fields that were never limed, and heavy potash on soils already low in magnesium.
entries.confuse: Iron and manganese deficiency give similar stripes but on the young leaves. Zinc gives a band near the base of young leaves. Phosphorus gives purple without stripes.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium and pH, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: Apply magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) to the soil or as a leaf spray (DA Caraga). TNAU gives a 2 percent spray (20 g per liter). On acid soils use Dolomite following the soil test.
entries.prevent: Lime acid fields with dolomite, and do not overdo potash.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in sweet corn
entries.local: Kakulangan sa boron ng mais na matamis
entries.hint: Upper leaves have white spots and waxy brown streaks, and tassels and ears fail to come out.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves get small white or yellow spots and raised, waxy brown streaks, and turn brittle. Upper internodes stay short. Tassels and ear shoots are small and may not come out, so few kernels set. In sweet corn this shows as ears with gaps and missing kernels.
entries.stage: Before tasseling up to silking.
entries.causes: Rare. Sandy soils low in organic matter, high pH soils and drought.
entries.confuse: Drought also delays ear shoots and spoils pollination, so both can happen together. Zinc gives bands, not spots.
entries.confirm: Test leaves and soil for boron before treating.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 0.5 percent borax spray (5 g per liter) every 15 days. Corn is very sensitive to too much boron. So never go above the advised rate and do not put boron in the seed row.
entries.prevent: Keep organic matter up, and irrigate at tasseling during dry spells.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in sweet corn
entries.local: Kakulangan sa calcium ng mais na matamis
entries.hint: Tips of the young leaves stick together like a ladder, on very acid soil.
entries.symptoms: The tips of new leaves stick to the leaf below, so the whorl looks like a ladder or a row of hooks. Young leaves are light green with whitish streaks and brittle, brown, sticky edges. Plants can be badly stunted.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Rare. It needs very acid soils (below pH 5), unlimed weathered uplands, or soils where magnesium and potassium crowd out calcium. On such soils aluminum and manganese damage usually show first.
entries.confuse: Boron deficiency also hurts the growing tip but gives white spots and short upper internodes. Acid soil damage from aluminum stunts the roots.
entries.confirm: Soil pH and calcium test.
entries.fix: Apply Agricultural lime or Dolomite following the soil test. UPLB worked out 3.6 tons of lime per hectare for one extremely acid farm in Isabela. Gypsum adds calcium without raising the pH.
entries.prevent: Lime acid uplands before planting, ahead of the rains.

entries.stage: Knee high to silking. The crop takes up the most nitrogen in the month before tasseling.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in sorghum
entries.hint: Pale, thin plants whose lower leaves yellow from the tip down the midrib.
entries.symptoms: Plants are stunted, thin and pale yellow green. The older leaves turn yellow from the tip, along the midrib and edges toward the base, then dry. Heads come out small with fewer seeds.
entries.stage: From the 5 leaf stage to boot, when the crop grows fastest.
entries.causes: Little or no fertilizer, sandy soils, low organic matter, nitrogen washed away by heavy rain. Ratoon crops that were not fed again after the first harvest.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency gives an even pale yellow on the young leaves without dead tissue. Iron deficiency stripes the young leaves between the veins.
entries.confirm: Check that yellowing started on the lowest leaves at the tip and runs down the midrib. Compare with a few rows given urea, and test the soil before the next crop.
entries.fix: Sidedress Urea 46 0 0 or Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 beside the rows, following the soil test. Work it in or water it. For quick help, TNAU gives a 1 percent urea spray (10 g per liter) or a 2 percent DAP 18 46 0 spray (20 g per liter).
entries.prevent: Split nitrogen between planting and about 30 days after, and feed a ratoon crop again after cutting.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in sorghum
entries.hint: Short, stiff, dark green plants with red or purple leaves and sheaths.
entries.symptoms: Plants are stunted and thin, with dark green, stiff and upright leaves that take on a dark red or purple color, also on the leaf sheaths. Roots stay small and turn dark brown to black. Grain filling is poor.
entries.stage: Seedling to early growth, with the loss showing later as poor heads.
entries.causes: Acid soils, calcareous soils, soils low in organic matter, and cold or dry spells that slow the roots.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency also brings red color but with dead patches on the leaf edges and tips. Magnesium gives stripes between the veins.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus before planting, and look at the roots for small, dark root systems.
entries.fix: For the standing crop, TNAU gives 2 to 3 sprays of 2 percent DAP 18 46 0 (20 g per liter). For the next crop, place 16 20 0, Complete 14 14 14 or DAP in the furrow at planting, following the soil test.
entries.prevent: Apply phosphorus at planting near the seed, and lime acid soils as the soil test says.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in sorghum
entries.hint: On limey, high pH soil, young leaves turn yellow to white between green veins, in patches of the field.
entries.symptoms: The newest leaves turn pale yellow between the veins, which stay green, so the leaf looks striped along its whole length. In bad cases the leaves turn yellow to white and the crop looks bleached and dries. It shows in uneven patches that follow the soil, and it delays maturity.
entries.stage: The first 30 to 60 days. Plants often grow out of it in good weather.
entries.causes: Sorghum is very prone to it on high pH, calcareous soils with free lime and low organic matter, worse in drought or waterlogging.
entries.confuse: Zinc deficiency gives bands in the lower half of the leaf, not full length stripes. Sulfur deficiency is an even pale yellow with no green veins standing out.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test and a check for lime (fizzing with vinegar is a field hint). A leaf test for iron.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 1 percent ferrous sulfate spray (10 g per liter) every week until new leaves are green, or 20 to 25 kg ferrous sulfate per hectare to the soil. In Kansas trials a chelated iron product (Fe EDDHA) placed in the furrow at about 3.4 kg product per hectare (3 pounds per acre), or split at planting and 2 weeks later, cut the yellowing and raised yield.
entries.prevent: Choose tolerant hybrids for limey fields, add manure, and treat the first 30 days, which are the critical period.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in sorghum
entries.hint: The young upper leaves turn evenly pale yellow, with no dead spots.
entries.symptoms: The new upper leaves come out pale yellow, evenly over the leaf, and the veins do not stand out. There are no dead patches. Plants grow slowly.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in organic matter, heavy rain that washes sulfate down, and years of sulfur free fertilizer.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency starts on the old leaves and dries the tips. Iron deficiency leaves green veins on the young leaves.
entries.confirm: Note that the youngest leaves are the palest. Test soil and leaves for sulfur.
entries.fix: Use Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 for the sidedress nitrogen, or add Gypsum, following the soil test.
entries.prevent: Include a sulfur source such as ammonium sulfate in the fertilizer plan on sandy soils.

sources.title: TNAU Agritech Portal: Sorghum, sulphur deficiency
University of Nebraska CropWatch: Key to nutrient deficiencies of corn and sorghum

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in sorghum
entries.hint: Older leaves turn dark yellow between the veins, then deep red and rusty brown.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn dark yellow between the veins, then develop rusty brown dead spots, mostly at the tips and edges. Leaves can turn deep red, become brittle and die.
entries.stage: Mid growth.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy soils in rainy areas and heavy potash on soils already low in magnesium.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency browns the edges first, not between the veins. Iron deficiency hits young leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium and pH, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 2 percent magnesium sulfate spray (20 g Epsom salt per liter). On acid soils apply Dolomite following the soil test.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soils with dolomite and keep potash balanced.

sources.title: TNAU Agritech Portal: Sorghum, magnesium deficiency
University of Nebraska CropWatch: Key to nutrient deficiencies of corn and sorghum

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in mungbean
entries.hint: Pale, thin plants with few branches whose lower leaves yellow and drop. The roots often have few or dead nodules.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn pale and then yellow and fall early, while the rest of the plant stays pale green. Stems are thin and weak, with fewer leaves and branches. In mungbean this usually means the root nodules are not working, so the plant cannot make its own nitrogen.
entries.stage: Two to five weeks after emergence, when nodules should be fixing nitrogen.
entries.causes: In a legume this usually means poor nodulation: no inoculant in a field new to the crop, inoculant killed by sun or heat, very acid soil, waterlogging, hot dry soil, or too much nitrogen fertilizer near the seed, which stops nodules from forming.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency also yellows the whole plant, but the young leaves first. Iron deficiency yellows the young leaves between green veins. Waterlogging gives the same pale look, so check drainage.
entries.confirm: Dig, do not pull, a few plants 3 to 6 weeks after planting, wash the roots and cut some nodules open. Pink to red inside means they are working, white means not active yet, and brown, grey or mushy means dead. Yellow plants with few or dead nodules point to a nodulation failure, not a lack of fertilizer.
entries.fix: Nodules cannot be added to a standing crop, so feed it. TNAU gives 10 to 20 kg of nitrogen per hectare, or a 2 percent DAP 18 46 0 spray (20 g per liter) every week. Urea 46 0 0 beside the rows also works.
entries.prevent: Coat the seed with a mungbean Rhizobium inoculant just before planting and keep it out of the sun (DA). Give only a small starter, about 20 kg of nitrogen per hectare from 150 kg of 14 14 14, because more nitrogen holds back nodules.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in mungbean
entries.hint: Plants stay small and dark green with few pods, often without clear leaf marks.
entries.symptoms: Plants grow slowly and stay short with dark, sometimes bluish green leaves, but there are often no clear marks on the leaves. Roots and nodules are few, branching is poor, and pods are few and late.
entries.stage: Seedling to flowering.
entries.causes: Acid upland soils and soils low in phosphorus. Each harvest takes phosphorus away, so fields cropped for years without fertilizer run low (DA).
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency makes plants pale, not dark. Drought also stunts plants, but leaves wilt in the heat of the day.
entries.confirm: Soil test for phosphorus before planting, or compare with a strip given 14 14 14.
entries.fix: DA advises 30 to 45 kg each of phosphorus and potassium per hectare before planting on poor soils, or, without a soil test, 3 bags of Complete 14 14 14 per hectare on heavy soils and 4 bags on light soils as a basal dose. For a standing crop, TNAU gives a 2 percent DAP 18 46 0 spray (20 g per liter) every 15 days for pulses.
entries.prevent: Apply phosphorus at planting every season and add compost or manure.

sources.title: DA High Value Crops Development Program: Mungbean production guide

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in mungbean
entries.hint: Yellow patches on the edges of the lower leaves join up, with dark spots and curled edges.
entries.symptoms: Yellow patches form on the edges of the lower leaves and join, until the leaf turns yellow. Dark spots appear on the yellow parts, leaf tips go black to brown and the leaf curls. Upper leaves stay green for a while.
entries.stage: Flowering and pod filling.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, soils cropped for years without potash, and fields where straw and crop residues are always removed.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency yellows between the veins, not from the edges. Leaf spot diseases give round spots with rings, scattered over the leaf.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium, and check that the yellow edges start on the lowest leaves.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 to the soil following the soil test. DA gives 30 to 45 kg of potassium per hectare on potassium poor soils. TNAU also gives a 1 percent potash spray (10 g Muriate of potash per liter) at flowering.
entries.prevent: Use Complete 14 14 14 at planting and return crop residues to the field.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in mungbean
entries.hint: The young leaves turn pale yellow first, then the whole plant is evenly pale.
entries.symptoms: The newest leaves turn pale yellow first, and over time the whole plant becomes evenly pale yellow. Growth slows and nodules work less well.
entries.stage: Early growth to flowering.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in organic matter and years of sulfur free fertilizer. Legumes need a lot of sulfur, so they show it before cereals do (UW).
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency starts on the old leaves. Iron deficiency keeps the veins green on yellow young leaves.
entries.confirm: Note that the youngest leaves are the palest, then test soil and leaves for sulfur.
entries.fix: Add a sulfur source such as Gypsum, which suits a legume because it adds no nitrogen. The University of Wisconsin finds about 11 kg of sulfur per hectare (10 pounds per acre) enough for row crops on sulfur poor soil.
entries.prevent: Use a fertilizer with sulfur, or gypsum, every few seasons on sandy soils.

sources.title: TNAU Agritech Portal: Greengram (mungbean), sulphur deficiency
University of Wisconsin Extension A2525: Soil and applied sulfur

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in mungbean
entries.hint: About a month after sowing, leaves turn small and yellow between green veins and the plants stop growing.
entries.symptoms: About a month after germination the leaves turn yellow between the veins, which stay green, and the yellow parts die early. New leaves come out small and yellowish, and plants grow little.
entries.stage: About 30 days after sowing.
entries.causes: High pH and calcareous soils, sandy soils, and heavy phosphorus on soils low in zinc.
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency also yellows young leaves between the veins but turns the whole leaf yellow to white. Manganese deficiency is hard to tell apart. A leaf test settles it.
entries.confirm: Soil test for zinc and pH, or a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU gives 25 kg Zinc sulfate per hectare as a basal dose. A 0.5 percent zinc sulfate spray (5 g per liter) at 20, 30 and 40 days after sowing.
entries.prevent: On high pH soils, mix zinc sulfate into the basal fertilizer.

sources.title: TNAU Agritech Portal: Greengram (mungbean), zinc deficiency
University of Wisconsin Extension A2528: Soil and applied zinc

entries.name: Iron deficiency in mungbean
entries.hint: New leaves turn yellow green with green veins, then fully yellow, on limey or high pH soil.
entries.symptoms: Newly opened leaves turn yellowish green while the veins stay green. In time the whole leaf turns yellow to almost white and growth slows.
entries.stage: Seedling and early growth.
entries.causes: High pH soils with free lime, and wet, cold or poorly aerated soil.
entries.confuse: Zinc deficiency also gives small leaves and dead spots. Nitrogen deficiency starts on the old leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test and a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 1 percent ferrous sulfate spray (10 g per liter) three times, 10 days apart. 25 kg ferrous sulfate per hectare as a basal dose.
entries.prevent: Add compost and choose fields that are not limey for mungbean.

sources.title: TNAU Agritech Portal: Greengram (mungbean), iron deficiency

entries.name: Boron deficiency in mungbean
entries.hint: The top of the plant bunches into a rosette and the upper leaves turn yellow or reddish at the tips.
entries.symptoms: The upper internodes stay short, so the top of the plant bunches into a rosette. Leaves near the growing point turn yellow and sometimes red, worst at the tips while the leaf bases stay green.
entries.stage: Flowering and pod setting.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in organic matter, high pH soils and dry spells.
entries.confuse: Zinc deficiency also gives short internodes, but with yellow between the veins.
entries.confirm: Leaf or soil test for boron before treating.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 0.2 percent borax spray (2 g per liter) every 15 days. Do not put boron fertilizer in the seed row. The University of Wisconsin warns a band of boron is toxic to bean seed.
entries.prevent: Keep organic matter up and water during flowering in dry spells.

sources.title: TNAU Agritech Portal: Greengram (mungbean), boron deficiency
University of Wisconsin Extension A2522: Soil and applied boron

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in peanut
entries.hint: The plants look fine, but many pods are empty (pops) or the kernels are shrunken and dark.
entries.symptoms: Leaves rarely show it. Pods form but stay empty (pops), kernels are shrunken or misshapen with a dark germ, and more pods rot. Seed from such pods sprouts poorly. In bad cases the buds at branch tips blacken and the leaves there are small and twisted.
entries.stage: Pegging and pod filling, about 20 to 80 days after the pegs enter the soil.
entries.causes: Pods take calcium straight from the soil around them, not through the roots. So a dry or calcium poor pegging zone causes it. Acid sandy soil, heavy potash and dry spells at pod fill make it worse.
entries.confuse: Boron deficiency gives hollow, discolored hearts in the kernels and stubby branches. Drought and poor pollination also leave empty pods.
entries.confirm: Crack open pods from a test row: many pops point to calcium. Test the top 8 cm of soil next to the row soon after emergence (UF IFAS).
entries.fix: Spread Gypsum over the rows at early flowering, 30 to 45 days after planting. TNAU gives 200 kg gypsum per hectare at 45 days. UF IFAS gives about 1,100 kg per hectare (1,000 pounds per acre) for seed crops and low testing soils. Gypsum after 100 days is too late.
entries.prevent: Lime soils below pH 5.8 a few months before planting to reach pH 6.2 to 6.5. Do not plow deep after liming. Keep the soil moist during pod fill.

sources.title: UF IFAS: Calcium fertilization in peanuts, importance, sources and considerations
TNAU Agritech Portal: Groundnut, calcium deficiency

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in peanut
entries.hint: Pale yellow, stunted plants, sometimes with reddish stems, and few nodules on the roots.
entries.symptoms: Leaves turn pale yellow and plants stay short. Stems may turn reddish. Peanut makes its own nitrogen through root nodules, so pale plants usually mean the nodules failed. Yellow rows next to green rows often mark a missed inoculant row.
entries.stage: Five to six weeks after planting, when nodules should be well formed.
entries.causes: In a legume this usually means poor nodulation: no inoculant in a field new to the crop, inoculant killed by sun or heat, very acid soil, waterlogging, hot dry soil, or too much nitrogen fertilizer near the seed, which stops nodules from forming.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency also gives evenly pale plants. Check the nodules first. Iron deficiency yellows the young leaves between green veins on limey soils.
entries.confirm: Dig, do not pull, a few plants 3 to 6 weeks after planting, wash the roots and cut some nodules open. Pink to red inside means they are working, white means not active yet, and brown, grey or mushy means dead. Yellow plants with few or dead nodules point to a nodulation failure, not a lack of fertilizer. For peanut, more than 20 nodules per plant early in the season is excellent and 5 or fewer is poor (Texas AandM).
entries.fix: Feed the crop, since new nodules cannot be added now. TNAU gives a 1 to 2 percent urea spray (10 to 20 g per liter) every 15 days. A light sidedress of Urea 46 0 0 also helps when nodules are poor.
entries.prevent: Inoculate seed with a peanut Rhizobium inoculant at planting, keep it out of the sun, and avoid heavy nitrogen near the seed.

Texas AandM AgriLife: Mid season assessment of Rhizobium nodulation in Texas peanuts and other legumes

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in peanut
entries.hint: Lower leaves pale slightly between the veins, then the leaf edges turn yellow and dry.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves first show a slight yellowing between the veins, then the edges of the leaflets turn yellow and later brown and dry. It starts on the lowest leaves and climbs the plant as pods fill.
entries.stage: Mid growth to pod filling.
entries.causes: Sandy soils and soils cropped for years without potash. Note that too much potash in the pegging zone blocks calcium from reaching the pods (UF IFAS).
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also yellows between the veins of old leaves, but without the scorched edges.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium. Keep the calcium to potassium balance in mind.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 1 to 2 percent potassium chloride spray (10 to 20 g Muriate of potash per liter) every 15 days. Give soil potash only as the soil test advises, because too much crowds calcium out of the pods.
entries.prevent: Balance potash with gypsum or lime so pods still get enough calcium.

sources.title: TNAU Agritech Portal: Groundnut, potassium deficiency
UF IFAS: Calcium fertilization in peanuts, importance, sources and considerations

entries.name: Boron deficiency in peanut
entries.hint: Young leaves stay small in a rosette, and kernels have a hollow, dark heart.
entries.symptoms: Growth of young leaves is held back, giving a rosette look, with small leaves and stubby branches. Stems may split. Pods form poorly and many are pops, and kernels show a hollow, discolored heart.
entries.stage: Flowering to pod filling.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in organic matter, high pH soils and drought.
entries.confuse: Calcium deficiency also gives pops, but kernels are shrunken with a dark germ rather than hollow. Check both in a soil test.
entries.confirm: Split kernels to look for the hollow heart. Test soil and leaves for boron.
entries.fix: TNAU gives 10 kg Borax per hectare together with 200 kg Gypsum per hectare at 45 days after sowing. Spread it evenly and never more, because too much boron burns the crop.
entries.prevent: Test for boron on sandy soils before planting peanut.

sources.title: TNAU Agritech Portal: Groundnut, boron deficiency
University of Wisconsin Extension A2522: Soil and applied boron

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in peanut
entries.hint: The whole plant is evenly light green, thin stemmed and spindly.
entries.symptoms: Plants look light green all over, young leaves included, rather than yellowing from the bottom up. They stay short and thin stemmed and look spindly.
entries.stage: Early growth to flowering.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in organic matter and fields fed for years with sulfur free fertilizer. Legumes need more sulfur than cereals (UW).
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency also gives pale plants. Check the nodules and whether the old leaves yellowed first.
entries.confirm: Soil and leaf test for sulfur.
entries.fix: TNAU gives 200 kg Gypsum per hectare to the soil, which also feeds the pods calcium.
entries.prevent: Gypsum at flowering covers both sulfur and calcium needs.

University of Wisconsin Extension A2525: Soil and applied sulfur

entries.name: Iron deficiency in peanut
entries.hint: Young leaves suddenly turn yellow between green veins and stay small, on limey soil.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves come out small and suddenly turn yellow between the veins. Growth of both tops and roots slows and plants are stunted.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: High pH soils with free lime, and wet or poorly aerated soils.
entries.confuse: Manganese deficiency also yellows between the veins but is usually milder. Sulfur deficiency yellows the whole leaf evenly.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test and a young leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 1 percent ferrous sulfate spray (10 g per liter) at 30, 40 and 50 days after sowing.
entries.prevent: Avoid over liming, and add compost to limey fields.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in peanut
entries.hint: Light yellow stripes along the veins of the leaves, and the bud at the top stops growing.
entries.symptoms: Leaves show light yellow stripes along the veins. In severe cases the yellowing spreads between the veins and the growing bud at the top stops. Older leaves may pale slightly.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: High pH and calcareous soils and heavy phosphorus fertilizer on zinc poor soils.
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency starts on the youngest leaves with green veins and no stripes along the veins.
entries.confirm: Soil test for zinc and pH, or a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU gives 25 kg Zinc sulfate per hectare as a basal dose, or a 1 percent zinc sulfate spray (10 g per liter) every 15 days.
entries.prevent: Add zinc sulfate with the basal fertilizer on high pH soils.

entries.name: Manganese deficiency in peanut
entries.hint: Leaves pale between the veins and plants stay short, often after heavy liming.
entries.symptoms: Leaves turn pale yellow between the veins while the veins stay green. Plants stay short and grow unevenly across the field.
entries.stage: Early to mid growth.
entries.causes: High pH soils, sandy soils that were limed too much, and soils high in organic matter (UW).
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency gives a stronger yellow on the newest leaves. Magnesium deficiency starts on the older leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf test for manganese and a soil pH test.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 0.5 percent manganese sulfate spray (5 g per liter) every 15 days, or 5 to 10 kg manganese sulfate per hectare to the soil.
entries.prevent: Do not lime above the target pH of 6.2 to 6.5.

University of Wisconsin Extension A2526: Soil and applied manganese

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in soybean
entries.hint: Light green, stunted plants, often in patches or rows, with few or white nodules on the roots.
entries.symptoms: Plants are stunted with very pale green leaves, starting on the older leaves. TNAU notes this happens because the roots did not nodulate or the nodules do not work, from poor soil fertility or too little molybdenum. Yellow strips in the field often mark where the inoculant was missed.
entries.stage: Two to six weeks after emergence.
entries.causes: In a legume this usually means poor nodulation: no inoculant in a field new to the crop, inoculant killed by sun or heat, very acid soil, waterlogging, hot dry soil, or too much nitrogen fertilizer near the seed, which stops nodules from forming.
entries.confuse: Molybdenum deficiency looks exactly the same, because the nodules need molybdenum to work. It shows on very acid soils. Potassium deficiency yellows the leaf edges first.
entries.confirm: Dig, do not pull, a few plants 3 to 6 weeks after planting, wash the roots and cut some nodules open. Pink to red inside means they are working, white means not active yet, and brown, grey or mushy means dead. Yellow plants with few or dead nodules point to a nodulation failure, not a lack of fertilizer. A healthy soybean has 5 to 7 nodules on the taproot two weeks after emergence (Penn State).
entries.fix: If nodules are poor and plants are yellow, Penn State advises up to about 56 kg of nitrogen per hectare (50 pounds per acre) before full bloom. TNAU also gives a 1 percent urea spray (10 g per liter) every 15 days.
entries.prevent: Before planting, coat 10 kg of seed with a 100 g pack of soybean inoculant after wetting the seed with a glass of water, keep it in the shade and sow at once (DA). Lime very acid soils.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in soybean
entries.hint: Short, dark bluish green plants with few pods.
entries.symptoms: Plants stay small and dark bluish green, sometimes with purple or bronze tints. Growth is slow, nodules are few and pods are fewer.
entries.stage: Early growth to flowering.
entries.causes: Acid upland soils and soils low in phosphorus, and fields cropped for years without fertilizer.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen and molybdenum deficiency make plants pale, not dark.
entries.confirm: Soil test for phosphorus before planting.
entries.fix: DA Region 2 advises 2 bags of Complete 14 14 14 per hectare along the furrows before sowing when there is no soil test. Soybean also uses phosphorus left by the corn or rice before it, so feeding that crop well helps.
entries.prevent: Fertilize the rotation, not only the soybean, and add organic matter.

sources.title: DA Regional Field Office 02: Soybean production handbook
University of Wisconsin Extension A2520: Soil and applied phosphorus

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in soybean
entries.hint: Older leaves yellow in blotches from the edges inward.
entries.symptoms: Irregular yellow mottling appears around the edges of the leaves, joins into a yellow band and then moves toward the center of the leaf, followed by dead brown tissue. It starts on the lower leaves. In severe cases all but the newest leaves show it.
entries.stage: Early growth to pod filling.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, highly weathered soils and fields cropped without potash.
entries.confuse: Manganese and iron deficiency start on young leaves. Nitrogen deficiency pales the whole leaf, not the edges.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium, and check that edges of the old leaves yellow first.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 following the soil test. TNAU gives a 1 percent potassium chloride spray (10 g per liter) every 15 days.
entries.prevent: Return crop residues and include potash in the rotation.

sources.title: Iowa State University Extension IPM42: Nutrient deficiencies and application injuries in field crops
TNAU Agritech Portal: Soybean, potassium deficiency

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in soybean
entries.hint: The newest leaves turn pale first, then the whole plant is evenly yellow green.
entries.symptoms: New leaves are the first to turn pale, then the whole plant becomes evenly pale yellow. It looks like nitrogen deficiency but is not centred on the old leaves.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in organic matter, and sulfur free fertilizer over many years. Legumes need more sulfur than grasses (UW).
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency starts on the older leaves. Iron deficiency keeps the veins green.
entries.confirm: Soil and leaf test for sulfur.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 0.5 to 1 percent calcium sulfate spray (5 to 10 g per liter). For the soil, Gypsum adds sulfur without nitrogen. The University of Wisconsin finds about 11 kg of sulfur per hectare enough for row crops.
entries.prevent: Use gypsum or a sulfur bearing fertilizer every few seasons.

sources.title: TNAU Agritech Portal: Soybean, sulphur deficiency
University of Wisconsin Extension A2525: Soil and applied sulfur

entries.name: Molybdenum deficiency in soybean
entries.hint: Light green plants that look nitrogen starved, on very acid soil, even with nodules present.
entries.symptoms: Plants are light green and small, just like nitrogen deficiency, because the nodules need molybdenum to fix nitrogen. Nodules may be present but work poorly.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Very acid, sandy or highly weathered soils, where iron and aluminum hold molybdenum tightly.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency from missed inoculation looks the same. Check soil pH. Sulfur deficiency starts on the newest leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test (below about 5.5 is a warning) and a look at the nodules.
entries.fix: Liming to pH 6.0 or above often fixes it alone (UW). Otherwise treat seed with about 35 g of molybdenum per hectare (half an ounce per acre), or spray about 140 to 210 g of sodium or ammonium molybdate per hectare (2 to 3 ounces per acre) on the growing crop.
entries.prevent: Lime acid fields before planting and use a molybdenum seed treatment where the pH is low (Penn State).

sources.title: Iowa State University Extension IPM42: Nutrient deficiencies and application injuries in field crops
University of Wisconsin Extension A3555: Soil and applied molybdenum
Penn State Extension: Evaluating nodulation in soybeans

entries.name: Iron deficiency in soybean
entries.hint: Youngest leaves turn yellow with green veins, then almost white, on limey soil.
entries.symptoms: Young upper leaves turn yellow between the veins first, then the veins yellow too. In severe cases the leaves become almost white. Older leaves stay green, and the patches follow spots of limey soil.
entries.stage: Seedling and early growth.
entries.causes: High pH soils with plenty of free lime.
entries.confuse: Manganese deficiency also yellows between the veins, but the veins stay green and brown spots form. Nitrogen deficiency starts on the old leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test and a young leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 1 percent ferrous sulfate spray (10 g per liter) every 15 days, or 5 to 10 kg ferrous sulfate per hectare to the soil.
entries.prevent: Avoid planting soybean on limey patches or choose tolerant varieties.

sources.title: Iowa State University Extension IPM42: Nutrient deficiencies and application injuries in field crops
TNAU Agritech Portal: Soybean, iron deficiency

entries.name: Manganese deficiency in soybean
entries.hint: Leaves pale green to yellow between green veins, later with brown spots, often after liming.
entries.symptoms: Leaves turn pale green to pale yellow between the veins while the veins stay green. As it gets worse, brown spots and dead patches form. New leaves can grow out normal later in the season.
entries.stage: Early to mid growth.
entries.causes: High pH, sandy soils, over limed fields and soils high in organic matter. Soybean and beans need much manganese (UW).
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency turns the veins yellow too. Magnesium deficiency starts on the old leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf test for manganese and a soil pH test.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 0.5 percent manganese sulfate spray (5 g per liter) every 15 days, or 20 to 25 kg manganese sulfate per hectare to the soil. The University of Wisconsin uses about 5.6 kg of manganese per hectare to the soil or 1.1 kg as a spray. Warns that chelated manganese in the soil can make it worse.
entries.prevent: Do not lime above about pH 6.5 on sandy soils.

sources.title: TNAU Agritech Portal: Soybean, manganese deficiency
University of Wisconsin Extension A2526: Soil and applied manganese

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in soybean
entries.hint: Leaves pale evenly between green veins, then turn rusty brown.
entries.symptoms: Leaves become pale between the veins, which stay green, and then turn rusty brown. The pale color is even over the leaf, not starting at the edges as with potassium. It is not common.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: High pH soils, heavy phosphorus and sandy soils low in organic matter.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency starts at the leaf edges. Manganese deficiency is hard to tell apart without a leaf test.
entries.confirm: Leaf test for zinc.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in winged bean
entries.hint: Vines stay short and weak on red, acid soil, with few pods and small roots.
entries.symptoms: Vines grow slowly and stay short, leaves are dark green, and pods and tubers are few. Nodules form poorly and fix little nitrogen.
entries.stage: Early growth to flowering.
entries.causes: Red, acid, phosphorus poor soils. Okinawa trials found poor growth there came from phosphorus shortage, not from acidity, and lime alone did not help.

entries.fix: Apply a phosphorus fertilizer such as 16 20 0, Complete 14 14 14 or Superphosphate 0 18 0 at planting, following the soil test. Phosphorus fed vines grew much better than limed ones in the Okinawa trials.
entries.prevent: Put phosphorus in the planting rows each season. Lime only if the soil test calls for it.

entries.hint: Pale, slow vines whose roots have few pink nodules.
entries.symptoms: Lower leaves pale and yellow and the vine stays light green and slow. Winged bean gets its nitrogen from root nodules, so pale vines usually mean the nodules are few or not working. Low phosphorus and potassium also cut nodule activity.
entries.stage: Three to six weeks after planting.
entries.causes: In a legume this usually means poor nodulation: no inoculant in a field new to the crop, inoculant killed by sun or heat, very acid soil, waterlogging, hot dry soil, or too much nitrogen fertilizer near the seed, which stops nodules from forming. In winged bean, low phosphorus and potassium also reduce nitrogen fixation.
entries.confuse: Phosphorus shortage stunts the vine but keeps leaves dark. Sulfur deficiency yellows the young leaves first.
entries.confirm: Dig, do not pull, a few plants 3 to 6 weeks after planting, wash the roots and cut some nodules open. Pink to red inside means they are working, white means not active yet, and brown, grey or mushy means dead. Yellow plants with few or dead nodules point to a nodulation failure, not a lack of fertilizer.
entries.fix: Feed the vines with a light sidedress of Urea 46 0 0 or Complete 14 14 14, following the soil test. Correct phosphorus and potassium so the nodules can work.

entries.name: Molybdenum deficiency in winged bean
entries.hint: Pale, nitrogen starved vines on very acid soil even when nodules are present.
entries.symptoms: Vines are pale and small, just like nitrogen deficiency, because nodules need molybdenum to fix nitrogen. In some vegetables the leaf edges brown and cup upward.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy and highly weathered soils, where molybdenum is held tightly.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency from poor inoculation looks the same. Check the soil pH.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test and a look at the nodules.
entries.fix: Liming to pH 6.0 or above often fixes it (UW). Otherwise treat seed with about 35 g of molybdenum per hectare, or spray about 140 to 210 g of sodium or ammonium molybdate per hectare.
entries.prevent: Lime very acid soils before planting legumes.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in pigeon pea
entries.hint: Narrow, pale leaves that yellow between the veins from the tip, leaving only the midrib green.
entries.symptoms: Plants are stunted and the leaves narrow and pale green or yellow. Yellow starts between the veins at the tip of the leaflets and spreads until only the midrib stays green.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: High pH and calcareous soils, and heavy phosphorus.
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency yellows between the veins but keeps the veins and nearby tissue dark green.
entries.confirm: Soil test for zinc and pH, or a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 0.5 percent zinc sulfate spray (5 g per liter) every 15 days, or 10 to 15 kg zinc sulfate per hectare to the soil.
entries.prevent: Add zinc sulfate to the basal fertilizer on high pH soils.

sources.title: TNAU Agritech Portal: Redgram (pigeon pea), zinc deficiency

entries.name: Iron deficiency in pigeon pea
entries.hint: Young leaves turn light green between dark green veins, on limey soil.
entries.symptoms: The spaces between the veins of young leaves turn light green. While the veins and the tissue next to them stay dark green. Older leaves look normal, since the shortage shows in new growth.
entries.stage: Seedling and early growth.
entries.causes: High pH, calcareous soils and waterlogged patches.
entries.confuse: Zinc deficiency narrows the leaves and starts at the leaflet tip.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test and a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 0.5 percent ferrous sulfate spray (5 g per liter) every week.
entries.prevent: Avoid limey, poorly drained spots.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in pigeon pea
entries.hint: Mild yellow between dark green veins that turns rusty brown in streaks.
entries.symptoms: Leaves pale slightly between the veins while the veins stay dark green. The pale areas then turn rusty brown or bronze, and narrow streaks of dead tissue form between the veins. Edges of young leaves often roll in.
entries.stage: Mid growth.
entries.causes: Acid sandy soils and heavy potash.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency starts at leaf tips and edges.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium and pH.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a spray of 2 percent magnesium sulfate (20 g Epsom salt per liter) with 1 percent urea (10 g per liter). Use Dolomite on acid soils as the soil test advises.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soils with dolomite.

sources.title: TNAU Agritech Portal: Redgram (pigeon pea), magnesium deficiency

entries.name: Boron deficiency in pigeon pea
entries.hint: The top bunches into a rosette and upper leaves yellow or redden at the tips.
entries.symptoms: Upper internodes stay short and the top bunches into a rosette. Leaves near the growing point turn yellow and sometimes red, worst at the tips while the bases stay green.
entries.stage: Flowering.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in organic matter and dry spells.
entries.confuse: Zinc deficiency also shortens internodes but yellows between the veins.
entries.confirm: Leaf or soil test for boron.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 0.2 percent boron spray (2 g borax per liter) every two weeks.
entries.prevent: Add compost. Never overdo boron.
