entries.name: Potassium deficiency in sweet potato
entries.hint: Older leaves yellow and scorch at the edges and roll up, and roots stay small.
entries.symptoms: Yellowing starts at the edges of the older leaves and turns into brown, scorched margins. Leaves may curl or roll upward at the edges, age early and drop, so the vine covers less ground. Vines wilt even in moist soil, and fewer and smaller storage roots form.
entries.stage: Mid season, when storage roots bulk up.
entries.causes: Sandy and highly weathered soils, and fields planted to root crops for years, since roots carry away a lot of potassium. Acid soils hold less potassium.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency yellows between the veins of old leaves rather than burning the edges. Drought scorch shows on many leaves at once and recovers after rain.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium, and a leaf test. Look for edge scorch starting on the oldest leaves.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 following the soil test, best split between planting and early vine growth (KAU). For quick help spray potassium sulfate at 10 g per liter in the morning (KAU), or 1 percent potassium chloride every 15 days (TNAU).
entries.prevent: Add organic matter and wood ash, keep the soil pH above 6 with lime or dolomite, and give potash every season.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in sweet potato
entries.hint: Pale green vines that spread slowly, with the oldest leaves yellowing and drying.
entries.symptoms: Leaves turn an even light green, starting on the older, lower leaves. Vines grow slowly with fewer leaves, so the ground stays bare longer. The oldest leaves yellow, wilt and dry, and young leaves may show purple veins.
entries.stage: First two months, while the vines spread.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, soils low in organic matter, and rain that washes nitrogen out.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency yellows the young leaves too and veins do not stay green. Magnesium deficiency shows yellow between green veins.
entries.confirm: Check that yellowing started on the oldest leaves, then test the soil.
entries.fix: Apply Urea 46 0 0 following the soil test. KAU also gives a urea spray of 10 g per liter every 15 days. Do not overdo nitrogen. It grows vines at the cost of roots.
entries.prevent: Use compost or manure before planting and a balanced fertilizer such as 14 14 14.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in sweet potato
entries.hint: Small, stunted vines with dark old leaves and purple red color under the leaves.
entries.symptoms: Plants stay small and stunted with a poor root system. Older leaves turn dark green, and a purple red color shows mostly on the underside of the leaves. Yellow patches then spread unevenly and the oldest leaves die.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Acid soils and volcanic soils that hold phosphorus tightly, and soils low in organic matter.
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency can be confused with the dark old leaves, but it yellows the young leaves. Cold or wet weather also gives purple tints for a short time.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus.
entries.fix: KAU advises single superphosphate for a quick fix, or bone meal and rock phosphate for the long term, following the soil test. Phosphorus is taken up best at pH 6.5 to 7.5.
entries.prevent: Add organic manure with phosphorus fertilizer and correct strong acidity.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in sweet potato
entries.hint: Older leaves yellow between the veins, sometimes with red or purple on top, and cup.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves yellow between the veins and age early, and may curl or cup. Red or purple color can appear on the upper side of old leaves, and the yellow parts turn brown and dead. Roots may come out small and misshapen.
entries.stage: Mid season.
entries.causes: Sandy and acid soils, and heavy potash, which blocks magnesium.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency burns the leaf edges first. Nitrogen deficiency yellows the whole leaf evenly.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium.
entries.fix: KAU gives about 80 kg magnesium sulfate per hectare (32 kg per acre) in bands near the plants. Apply magnesium and potash at different times.
entries.prevent: Use Dolomite over the long run on acid soils.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in sweet potato
entries.hint: Young leaves are distorted and brittle, and storage roots have hollow or brown spots inside.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves become distorted and pale, stems are brittle, and leaf tips and edges yellow and die in spots. Storage roots develop poorly and can have hollow areas in the flesh, which ruins their sale.
entries.stage: Root bulking.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in organic matter, high pH soils, and dry spells.
entries.confuse: Calcium deficiency also hits the growing tips, but gives small, soft roots. Weevil damage leaves tunnels, not hollows.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron. Cut roots to look inside.
entries.fix: KAU gives about 10 kg Borax per hectare (4 kg per acre) to the soil, or a borax spray of 1 g per liter. Do not apply boron together with calcium or ammonium fertilizers.
entries.prevent: Test for boron on sandy fields before planting.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in sweet potato
entries.hint: Leaf tips die back and storage roots come out soft, small and misshapen, on very acid soil.
entries.symptoms: Growing points and young leaves show dead spots and tip dieback, with some yellowing between the veins. Root growth is poor, and storage roots can be soft, very small and misshapen.
entries.stage: Early growth to root bulking.
entries.causes: Very acid soils, and soils very high in phosphorus.
entries.confuse: Boron deficiency also damages the tips, with brittle stems and hollows in the roots.
entries.confirm: Soil pH and calcium test.
entries.fix: On acid soils, KAU limes about 250 kg per hectare where the pH is 5.5 to 6. About 840 kg per hectare in two splits where it is 3.5 to 4.5. On alkaline soils use Gypsum instead.
entries.prevent: Test the pH every few seasons and lime ahead of planting.

sources.title: Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech Portal: Sweet potato nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in sweet potato
entries.hint: Leaves yellow from the tip to the base, veins included, and vines stay short with few branches.
entries.symptoms: Yellowing starts at the leaf tip and moves to the base, and the veins turn yellow too. Plants are badly stunted with small leaves and few branches, and leaves may curl or cup. Roots can be misshapen.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Soils low in organic matter, and burning crop waste, which drives off sulfur.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency starts on the old leaves. Iron deficiency keeps the veins green.
entries.confirm: Soil and leaf test for sulfur.
entries.fix: Use a sulfur bearing fertilizer such as Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 or single superphosphate. KAU gives about 25 kg sulfur dust per hectare (10 kg per acre) on sulfur poor soils, or Gypsum on alkaline soils.
entries.prevent: Add organic matter and stop burning crop waste.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in sweet potato
entries.hint: Short internodes, small pale young leaves, and purple shoot tips.
entries.symptoms: Internodes stay short and young leaves show vein clearing and paling. Shoot tips may turn purple.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Soils outside pH 5 to 7.5, and heavy phosphorus.
entries.confuse: Phosphorus deficiency gives purple older leaves, not purple tips. Iron deficiency yellows young leaves between green veins.
entries.confirm: Soil test for zinc.
entries.fix: KAU gives about 20 kg Zinc sulfate per hectare (8 kg per acre) to the soil. In severe cases spray 2 g zinc sulfate with 2.5 g lime (calcium carbonate) per liter in the morning. Do not apply zinc and phosphate together.
entries.prevent: Keep the soil pH between 5 and 7.5.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in cassava
entries.local: Kakulangan sa potassium ng kamoteng kahoy
entries.hint: Older leaves yellow between the veins and scorch at the edges. Plants branch a lot and sprawl.
entries.symptoms: Yellowing between the veins starts on older leaves and moves up. Leaf edges die and turn brown, and the dead area spreads inward. Plants branch too much and sprawl, leaves are smaller and narrower, and roots carry less starch.
entries.stage: From about 3 months after planting, as roots bulk.
entries.causes: Fields planted to cassava year after year, since roots take away a lot of potassium, and sandy, acid soils. A Philippine study noted cassava takes up more potassium than nitrogen or phosphorus.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also yellows between veins but without edge scorch. Mite damage gives speckled, bronzed leaves, with mites under the leaf.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium. Check the oldest leaves for edge scorch.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 following the soil test, split in parts (KAU). In Philippine trials, one third of the N and K went in at planting and the rest at 2.5 and 5 months. KAU gives a potassium sulfate spray of 10 g per liter in the morning for quick help.
entries.prevent: The national recommendation is 8 bags of Complete 14 14 14 per hectare. Philippine trials found a site particular rate of 180 70 250 kg N, P2O5 and K2O per hectare yielded more. Return leaves and stems to the field.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in cassava
entries.local: Kakulangan sa nitrogen ng kamoteng kahoy
entries.hint: Pale green plants with short stems and small leaves, yellowing from the bottom up.
entries.symptoms: The whole plant turns pale to light green, starting on the older, lower leaves and moving up. Stems are short and leaves small, and new leaves come slowly. Roots are fewer and smaller, with less starch.
entries.stage: First 3 to 4 months.
entries.causes: Soils low in organic matter, sandy soils, and fields cropped for years without fertilizer.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency burns the leaf edges. Sulfur deficiency yellows the young upper leaves first.
entries.confirm: Check that yellowing starts at the bottom of the plant. Soil test.
entries.fix: Apply Urea 46 0 0 following the soil test, split with the potash. KAU also gives a urea spray of 10 g per liter every 15 days.
entries.prevent: Use compost or manure and a balanced fertilizer at planting.

sources.title: Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech Portal: Tapioca (cassava) nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in cassava
entries.local: Kakulangan sa phosphorus ng kamoteng kahoy
entries.hint: Stunted plants with a few yellow lower leaves and purple under the leaves, and late harvest.
entries.symptoms: Plants are stunted with a small root system. A few lower leaves turn yellow while the upper leaves stay green, and the underside of leaves may turn purple. Maturity is late and roots are small with less starch.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Acid upland soils. In Philippine omission trials, plots without phosphorus yielded about half as much as fully fed plots.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency also yellows lower leaves but scorches the edges.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus.
entries.fix: Apply all the phosphorus at planting, as in the Philippine trials, using Superphosphate, 16 20 0 or 14 14 14 following the soil test. KAU uses single superphosphate for a quick fix and rock phosphate for the long term.
entries.prevent: Apply phosphorus each crop and add organic manure.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in cassava
entries.local: Kakulangan sa zinc ng kamoteng kahoy
entries.hint: Young leaves have narrow, pale lobes that curl up, on short internodes.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves turn yellow between the veins and the leaf lobes become narrow, pale and curl upward. Leaf tips die, internodes stay short and leaves are deformed. Maturity is delayed.
entries.stage: Early growth, from the first weeks after planting.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in zinc, soils outside pH 5 to 7.5, and heavy phosphorus. Zinc deficiency is a known cause of low yield on sandy soils in Northeast Thailand.
entries.confuse: Mite damage also distorts young leaves but with speckling. Mosaic virus gives a yellow and green mosaic with twisted leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for zinc and pH, or a leaf test.
entries.fix: KAU gives about 20 kg Zinc sulfate per hectare (8 kg per acre) to the soil, or in severe cases a spray of 2 g zinc sulfate with 2.5 g lime per liter in the morning. A Thai field trial got the best yield and return from 18.75 kg zinc sulfate per hectare worked into the soil with the NPK.
entries.prevent: Add zinc sulfate with the basal fertilizer on sandy fields, and do not apply it together with phosphate.

entries.local: Kakulangan sa magnesium ng kamoteng kahoy
entries.hint: Lower leaves turn yellow between green veins and cup inward.
entries.symptoms: Yellowing between the veins starts on older leaves and moves to younger ones while the veins stay green. Leaves curl or cup inward, and in extreme cases turn whitish and die. Plants are stunted.
entries.stage: Mid season.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, acid soils and heavy potash.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency scorches the leaf edges. Zinc deficiency narrows the young leaf lobes.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium.
entries.fix: KAU gives about 80 kg magnesium sulfate per hectare (32 kg per acre) in bands near the plants. Do not apply magnesium and potash at the same time.
entries.prevent: Use Dolomite over the long run on acid soils.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in cassava
entries.local: Kakulangan sa calcium ng kamoteng kahoy
entries.hint: Upper leaves curl and get brown to black spots at the tips and edges, on very acid soil.
entries.symptoms: Upper leaves curl and twist, and dead spots form at the tips and edges that grow brown to black. Stems are short and brittle, leaves small, and roots shallow.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Very acid soils, soils high in phosphorus, and boron shortage, which calcium needs to work.
entries.confuse: Boron deficiency also deforms young leaves, with gummy brown spots on the leaf stalks.
entries.confirm: Soil pH and calcium test.
entries.fix: On acid soils, KAU limes about 250 kg per hectare where the pH is 5.5 to 6. About 840 kg per hectare in two splits where it is 3.5 to 4.5. On alkaline soils use Gypsum.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soils ahead of planting.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in cassava
entries.local: Kakulangan sa sulfur ng kamoteng kahoy
entries.hint: The young upper leaves yellow first, and stems are thin and weak.
entries.symptoms: Yellowing appears first on the upper, younger leaves and moves down. Shoots and roots grow less, stems are thin and weak, maturity is late and root yield drops.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Soils low in organic matter and burning of crop waste.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency starts on the lower leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil and leaf test for sulfur.
entries.fix: Use Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 or single superphosphate in the program. KAU gives about 25 kg sulfur dust per hectare on sulfur poor soils, or Gypsum on alkaline soils.
entries.prevent: Add organic matter and stop burning crop waste.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in cassava
entries.local: Kakulangan sa boron ng kamoteng kahoy
entries.hint: Small deformed young leaves on short stalks with brown gummy spots on the stalks and stem tips.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves come out small and deformed on short leaf stalks, with abnormal edges. Brown, gummy spots form on the leaf stalks and the growing part of the stem, stems turn brittle and root growth drops.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in organic matter and dry spells.
entries.confuse: Calcium deficiency also curls young leaves but without gummy spots. Zinc deficiency narrows the leaf lobes.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron.
entries.fix: KAU gives about 10 kg Borax per hectare (4 kg per acre) to the soil, or a borax spray of 1 g per liter. Keep boron and calcium applications apart.
entries.prevent: Test sandy fields before planting.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in taro
entries.hint: Older leaf blades yellow first, then all of them, with stunted plants and few suckers.
entries.symptoms: Roots, main shoot and suckers stay stunted. Yellowing starts on the oldest leaf blades and, as it gets worse, all the blades turn yellow. Old leaves die early, so fewer leaves are working and the corm yield drops.
entries.stage: From 2 months after planting through corm bulking.
entries.causes: Flooded (wetland) taro loses nitrogen to the air when the soil has no oxygen. Taro grows best when soil nitrogen is mostly in the nitrate form.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency yellows the young leaves evenly. Magnesium deficiency yellows between the veins of old leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of leaf number 2 (the second fully opened leaf below the newest one): below 4.0 percent nitrogen is deficient (CTAHR).
entries.fix: Apply nitrogen following the soil test, for example Urea 46 0 0 or Complete 14 14 14 in split doses. KAU also gives a urea spray of 10 g per liter every 15 days. Do not overdo it: too much nitrogen promotes taro leaf blight (CTAHR).
entries.prevent: Split nitrogen through the season and add compost or manure.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in taro
entries.hint: Slow plants that wilt easily, with scorched edges or brown spots in the middle of older leaves.
entries.symptoms: Growth slows, plants wilt easily and leaf blades are smaller. Older leaves get a burnt look between the veins or along the edges. In some varieties irregular brown spots form in the center of older blades and join until the whole leaf yellows or browns. Corms stay small.
entries.stage: Corm bulking.
entries.causes: Sandy and leached soils, and fields where taro and other root crops have been grown for years.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency yellows between veins first, then browns the margins. Taro leaf blight gives water soaked spots that ooze, mainly in wet weather.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of leaf number 2. Soil test for potassium.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 following the soil test, split in parts (KAU). KAU gives a potassium sulfate spray of 10 g per liter as a quick fix.
entries.prevent: Return crop waste and add wood ash or compost.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in taro
entries.hint: Stunted plants with darker green old leaves dotted with light spots.
entries.symptoms: Root and shoot growth are stunted. Older leaf blades can look darker green, and in some varieties many light colored dots form between the veins. Later the leaf edges yellow and turn brown.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Acid upland soils and volcanic soils that hold phosphorus. In flooded fields phosphorus becomes more available.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency gives brown spots and scorched edges, not light dots on dark leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf test (0.3 to 0.5 percent phosphorus is sufficient, CTAHR) and a soil test.
entries.fix: Use single superphosphate for a quick fix and rock phosphate for the long term, following the soil test (KAU).
entries.prevent: Apply phosphorus at planting and add organic manure.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in taro
entries.hint: The youngest leaf yellows between the veins and cups, with brown edges, and roots die back.
entries.symptoms: Root and shoot growth drop and roots look stunted. The youngest leaf blade first yellows between the veins. In severe cases blades cup, with brown edges, then fail to unfurl and the shoot dies. Dying roots let soil diseases in.
entries.stage: Early growth, on acid upland soils.
entries.causes: Very acid soils. At pH 4 aluminum also poisons the roots (CTAHR).
entries.confuse: Manganese toxicity in older leaves can look like calcium deficiency with cupped blades. Calcium deficiency starts on the youngest leaf.
entries.confirm: Leaf test (below 0.7 percent calcium is deficient, CTAHR) and a soil pH test.
entries.fix: On acid soils, KAU limes about 250 kg per hectare where the pH is 5.5 to 6. About 840 kg per hectare in two splits where it is 3.5 to 4.5. CTAHR found dolomite protected taro roots on aluminum toxic soil.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soils ahead of planting.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in taro
entries.hint: Younger leaves are small and evenly yellow, and roots stay short.
entries.symptoms: Roots and shoots grow less, leaf blades are smaller, and the younger leaves turn evenly yellow. The yellow is uniform across the blade, without a pattern of green veins.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Soils low in organic matter and burning crop waste.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency yellows the old leaves first.
entries.confirm: Leaf test (below 0.2 percent sulfur is deficient, CTAHR).

entries.prevent: Add organic matter.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in taro
entries.hint: Young leaves yellow between the veins, then bleach evenly, in dry upland fields.
entries.symptoms: Younger leaf blades first yellow between the veins, then turn evenly bleached. Fewer side roots form.
entries.stage: Early growth, in upland taro.
entries.causes: Upland (not flooded) soils with high pH. Flooding makes iron more available. Too much manganese can also block iron.
entries.confuse: Manganese toxicity on older leaves looks like iron deficiency but starts on the old blades. Manganese deficiency also starts on young leaves. A leaf test separates them.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of leaf number 2 (below 100 ppm iron is deficient, CTAHR).
entries.fix: KAU gives about 15 kg ferrous sulfate per hectare (6 kg per acre) to the soil, following a soil test.
entries.prevent: Keep organic matter high in upland taro fields.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in taro
entries.hint: Plants are just stunted with small leaves. There are few other signs.
entries.symptoms: Taro short of zinc is stunted in roots and shoots, but CTAHR saw no other clear signs. KAU notes smaller, distorted young leaves in a rosette and slow leaf growth.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Soils outside pH 5 to 7.5 and heavy phosphorus.
entries.confuse: Many problems stunt taro. Only a leaf test confirms zinc.
entries.confirm: Leaf test (20 to 40 ppm zinc is sufficient, CTAHR).
entries.fix: KAU gives about 20 kg Zinc sulfate per hectare (8 kg per acre) to the soil, or a spray of 2 g zinc sulfate with 2.5 g lime per liter in severe cases. Keep zinc and phosphate applications apart.
entries.prevent: Test before adding zinc. Too much is toxic to taro.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in purple yam
entries.hint: Dull, light green vines with small leaves and short internodes.
entries.symptoms: The foliage turns a dull light green, often slightly darker along the main veins. Mature leaves are smaller, the vine tip grows slowly with short internodes and few branches. The oldest leaves may yellow and drop early. In severe cases the paleness increases toward the youngest leaves.
entries.stage: Rapid vine growth, 2 to 4 months after planting.
entries.causes: Intensive cropping with short fallows and burning of fallow vegetation, which loses nitrogen. Pale yam crops are almost universal where land is cropped hard.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency looks similar. Potassium shortage also makes the crop pale. A test strip tells them apart.
entries.confirm: Put urea on one or two rows and ammonium sulfate on another, at about 50 kg N per hectare (5 g N per mound at 1 by 1 meter). If both green up it is nitrogen. If only ammonium sulfate works it is sulfur (ACIAR).
entries.fix: Common rates are 50 to 200 kg N per hectare, half after the crop is established and half during rapid vine growth, buried in a shallow furrow or spread just before rain (ACIAR). Use Urea 46 0 0, Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 or a complete fertilizer.
entries.prevent: Do not burn fallow vegetation, grow legumes in the rotation, and mulch with legume tree prunings such as kakawate (Gliricidia).

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in purple yam
entries.hint: Lighter green crop with fine yellow between the veins of young mature leaves. Lower leaves brown from the tips at tuber filling.
entries.symptoms: The crop is a lighter green, with fine yellowing between a network of greener veins, clearest on young mature leaves. The vine tip slows and internodes shorten. At tuber filling the lowest leaves quickly brown from the tips and edges, often with a yellow strip ahead of the dead area. Plants wilt more in dry weather.
entries.stage: Tuber filling.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, leached soils, and gardens cropped with root crops for many years. In Papua New Guinea surveys, potassium deficiency was the most common and severe problem of yam.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also yellows between veins but with a light brown stain on old leaves. Nitrogen deficiency makes the whole crop dull green with small leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of blades from the fifth and sixth youngest nodes (2.1 to 3.9 percent potassium is the critical range for ubi, ACIAR) and a soil test.
entries.fix: Apply 80 to 200 kg potassium per hectare, mostly as Muriate of potash 0 0 60. On sandy soils put half in the planting hole and broadcast half during rapid vine growth. On clay soils one dose at planting is enough (ACIAR).
entries.prevent: Mulch with plant material and return crop waste. Do not overdo potash, which can cause magnesium and calcium shortage.

sources.title: O'Sullivan, ACIAR Monograph 144 (2010): Yam nutrition, nutrient disorders and soil fertility management

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in purple yam
entries.hint: Growth slows with no clear marks, then young leaves get small, stiff and curl down at the tip.
entries.symptoms: Moderate shortage slows growth without visible signs, and leaves can be even darker green. When severe, internodes shorten and young leaves become thick, stiff and curl down toward the tip, with bleached zones between the main veins, then die from the tip. Tubers stay small.
entries.stage: Vine growth.
entries.causes: Volcanic ash soils, acid soils and calcareous soils that hold phosphorus. In Tonga, phosphorus raised yam yields 20 to 100 percent on volcanic ash soils.
entries.confuse: Unlike most crops, yam shows phosphorus shortage on young leaves. Boron deficiency also deforms young leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf test (0.21 to 0.37 percent phosphorus is the critical range for ubi, ACIAR) and a soil test.
entries.fix: Band or spot place single superphosphate, ammonium phosphate or an NPK fertilizer in the mound. On phosphorus binding soils 50 to 100 kg P per hectare placed in a band may be needed (ACIAR).
entries.prevent: Add manure or compost, which feeds the soil fungi that help yam take up phosphorus.

sources.title: O'Sullivan, ACIAR Monograph 144 (2010): Yam nutrition, nutrient disorders and soil fertility management

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in purple yam
entries.hint: Light green crop with yellow between the veins of young mature leaves and light brown stains on old leaves.
entries.symptoms: The crop is light green with yellow between the veins, strongest on young mature leaves, while vine tips look healthy. Leaves in full sun are paler. Older leaves develop tan dead patches with dark edges, and their surface often gets a light brown stain between the veins.
entries.stage: Mid season.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, volcanic soils high in potassium, some calcareous soils, and too much potash fertilizer.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency browns the lowest leaves from tips and edges. Iron deficiency hits the youngest leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf test (0.10 to 0.14 percent magnesium is the critical range, ACIAR).
entries.fix: Mix Dolomite or magnesium oxide into acid soils at 20 to 50 kg magnesium per hectare, or band kieserite or magnesium sulfate at 10 to 40 kg magnesium per hectare. For a standing crop magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) can be sprayed on the leaves (ACIAR).
entries.prevent: Keep the potassium to magnesium balance and use dolomite on acid soils.

sources.title: O'Sullivan, ACIAR Monograph 144 (2010): Yam nutrition, nutrient disorders and soil fertility management

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in purple yam
entries.hint: Smaller, narrow, curled or wavy leaves on short internodes, and cracked tubers.
entries.symptoms: Leaves are smaller than normal and curled or wavy. Mid vine leaves show mild yellowing between a network of green veins, older leaves may get purple mottling. Young leaves become narrow, twisted and pale or bronzed on short internodes. Side shoots show it worst. Tubers often have long cracks.
entries.stage: Vine growth.
entries.causes: Sandy, acid to neutral soils low in zinc, alkaline soils, and fields limed heavily or given much phosphorus.
entries.confuse: Manganese and iron deficiency also hit young leaves on limey soils, often together with zinc.
entries.confirm: Paint half of a pale leaf with 0.5 percent zinc sulfate plus 0.25 percent hydrated lime. Regreening after a few days confirms it (ACIAR). A leaf test also works.
entries.fix: Spray a 1 percent zinc sulfate mix at about 8 kg zinc sulfate per hectare (2 kg zinc), which cleared symptoms in Papua New Guinea (ACIAR). On neutral and acid soils apply zinc to the soil at or before planting.
entries.prevent: Avoid over liming and heavy phosphorus on zinc poor soils.

sources.title: O'Sullivan, ACIAR Monograph 144 (2010): Yam nutrition, nutrient disorders and soil fertility management

entries.name: Manganese deficiency in purple yam
entries.hint: Young leaves show fine pale, sunken spots between the veins that turn into dead spots, on limey soil.
entries.symptoms: Young expanding leaves get a fine yellowing between the minor veins, with pale, see through spots that may be sunken. These turn into dead spots, also on the stem wings. Older leaves get dark dead spots, and roots and tubers grow less.
entries.stage: Vine growth, worse in dry spells.
entries.causes: Alkaline soils such as coral soils, and limed soils. It can come and go as the soil dries and wets.
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency bleaches young leaves without the sunken spots. Zinc deficiency makes small, twisted leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf test (10 to 15 mg per kg manganese is the critical range, ACIAR). Painting a leaf with manganese sulfate causes regreening.
entries.fix: On alkaline soils, soil manganese gets locked up, so spray 0.1 percent manganese sulfate on the leaves (ACIAR). Build up soil organic matter.
entries.prevent: Do not over lime, and keep organic matter high on coral soils.

sources.title: O'Sullivan, ACIAR Monograph 144 (2010): Yam nutrition, nutrient disorders and soil fertility management

entries.name: Iron deficiency in purple yam
entries.hint: Young leaves turn pale with a fine network of green veins, then bleach white, on coral or limey soil.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves turn yellowish green with darker veins. Young mature leaves show a fine network of green veins on a pale blade. In severe cases young leaves bleach white and die from the edges, while the stem stays alive.
entries.stage: Vine growth.
entries.causes: High pH soils on coral or limestone, heavy lime or phosphorus, and sandy or organic soils. Often found together with manganese, copper and zinc shortage.
entries.confuse: Manganese deficiency gives sunken spots. Nitrogen deficiency pales the whole vine.
entries.confirm: Paint half of a pale leaf with 1 percent ferric ammonium sulfate. Regreening in 4 to 7 days confirms it (ACIAR).
entries.fix: Soil iron does not work on limey soils. Spray chelated iron or a 1 to 2 percent ammonium ferric sulfate mix (ACIAR). Burying scrap iron such as old cans in the mound, away from the tubers, also helps.
entries.prevent: Build up organic matter with compost, the traditional fix on coral soils.

sources.title: O'Sullivan, ACIAR Monograph 144 (2010): Yam nutrition, nutrient disorders and soil fertility management

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in potato
entries.hint: Whole leaves, veins included, turn evenly pale yellow, starting low on the plant.
entries.symptoms: Leaves turn evenly yellow, veins and all, starting on the older leaves. When nitrogen is given, young leaves green up but the old ones stay yellow. Severe shortage makes leaves cup upward, and the crop stops early with small tubers.
entries.stage: Before and during tuber set.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain that washes nitrogen out, and too little fertilizer in highland fields cropped every season.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency also yellows the whole plant but includes the young leaves and gives a reddish tint to veins. Magnesium deficiency yellows between green veins.
entries.confirm: Check that the yellowing started on the old leaves, then test the soil. A leaf tissue test confirms it.
entries.fix: Apply Urea 46 0 0 or Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 following the soil test, hilled in beside the rows. KAU gives a urea spray of 10 g per liter every 15 days for quick help.
entries.prevent: Split nitrogen between planting and hilling, and add compost.

sources.title: Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech Portal: Potato nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in potato
entries.hint: Leaflets crinkle, tips burn and dead patches form between green veins, turning the leaf scorched and dark.
entries.symptoms: Leaflets crinkle, the tips burn and dead tissue spreads between the veins while the veins stay green. Leaves curl and look scorched, with dark edges. The yellowing does not reverse even after potash is given, and tubers stay small.
entries.stage: Tuber bulking.
entries.causes: Sandy and acid soils, and fields cropped for years without potash. Potato needs a higher soil potassium level than most field crops (UW).
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency can look much the same when advanced, but starts as mottled yellow between veins. Early blight gives round spots with rings.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium (aim higher than for field crops) and a leaf test.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 following the soil test, split between planting and hilling (KAU). For quick help spray potassium sulfate at 10 g per liter in the morning (KAU).
entries.prevent: Keep the soil pH above 6 with lime or dolomite, add organic matter and wood ash, and give potash every crop.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in potato
entries.hint: Short, dark plants with purple stems and leaf undersides, and leaflets curled upward.
entries.symptoms: Plants grow slowly and stay stunted and darker than normal. Stems, leaf stalks and the undersides of leaves turn purple, and the lower leaf surface looks grey green. Older leaves get dead spots and leaflets curl upward.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Acid and volcanic soils that lock up phosphorus, and cold soil early in the season.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency also curls leaflets but burns the tips and edges. Purple top viruses give purple and rolled top leaves, not dark plants.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus (potato needs a higher level than field crops, UW).
entries.fix: KAU uses single superphosphate for a quick fix and bone meal or rock phosphate for the long term, following the soil test. Phosphorus is taken up best at pH 6.2 to 7.0. Band it near the seed pieces at planting.
entries.prevent: Apply phosphorus at planting each crop and lime acid soils.

sources.title: Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech Portal: Potato nutrient deficiencies
University of Wisconsin Extension A2520: Soil and applied phosphorus

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in potato
entries.hint: Mottled yellow between the veins of young mature leaves, then dead scorched patches.
entries.symptoms: Mottled yellow areas form between the veins, first on young mature leaves. In advanced cases dead tissue between the veins gives a scorched look that can resemble potassium deficiency.
entries.stage: Mid season.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy soils in rainy highlands, and heavy potash.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency starts with burned tips and crinkled leaflets.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium and pH, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: KAU gives about 80 kg magnesium sulfate per hectare (32 kg per acre) in bands near the plants. Apply it apart from potash. Use Dolomite on acid soils over the long run.
entries.prevent: Lime acid fields with dolomite instead of plain lime.

sources.title: Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech Portal: Potato nutrient deficiencies
University of Wisconsin Extension A2524: Soil and applied magnesium

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in potato
entries.hint: Young leaves small, pale and curled, sprout tips black, and rusty spots inside the tubers.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves and leaflet tips turn pale, stay small and curl slightly. Severe cases stunt the plant. Sprout tips can turn black and die, and tubers show rusty brown spots inside.
entries.stage: Tuber bulking, and in stored seed potatoes as they sprout.
entries.causes: Very acid soils, and also higher pH sandy soils, where potatoes may respond well to added calcium (UW). High phosphorus and boron shortage make it worse.
entries.confuse: Boron deficiency also kills the growing point and gives brittle leaves. A leaf test does not show tuber calcium, since calcium may reach the leaves but not the tubers (UW).
entries.confirm: Soil pH and calcium test. Cut tubers to look for internal spots.
entries.fix: On acid soils, KAU limes about 250 kg per hectare where the pH is 5.5 to 6. About 840 kg per hectare in two splits where it is 3.5 to 4.5. On alkaline soils, or to add calcium without raising pH, use Gypsum.
entries.prevent: Test the soil before each crop and keep the soil evenly moist so calcium can move into the tubers.

sources.title: Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech Portal: Potato nutrient deficiencies
University of Wisconsin Extension A2523: Soil and applied calcium

entries.name: Boron deficiency in potato
entries.hint: The growing tip dies and the plant turns bushy. Young leaves wilt even with enough water.
entries.symptoms: Leaves pale slightly. The growing tip dies, so the plant loses its main shoot and grows in a bushy rosette. Leaves turn brittle and break easily, and young leaves wilt even when the soil is moist.
entries.stage: Mid season.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in organic matter, high pH soils and dry spells.
entries.confuse: Calcium deficiency looks very similar. A soil or leaf test separates them.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron.
entries.fix: KAU gives about 10 kg Borax per hectare (4 kg per acre) to the soil, or a borax spray of 1 g per liter. Keep boron apart from calcium and ammonium fertilizers.
entries.prevent: Test for boron before planting on sandy fields.

sources.title: Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech Portal: Potato nutrient deficiencies
University of Wisconsin Extension A2522: Soil and applied boron

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in potato
entries.hint: The whole plant, young leaves included, yellows evenly, with reddish veins and leaf stalks.
entries.symptoms: The whole plant yellows evenly, young leaves included, with a reddish tint in the veins, leaf stalks and leaf undersides. In advanced cases leaves stand upright, twist and turn brittle.
entries.stage: Early to mid growth.
entries.causes: Soils low in organic matter, sulfur free fertilizer for years, and burning crop waste.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency starts on the old leaves and has no red veins.
entries.confirm: Soil and leaf test for sulfur.
entries.fix: Use a sulfur bearing fertilizer such as Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 or single superphosphate. KAU gives about 25 kg sulfur dust per hectare (10 kg per acre) on sulfur poor soils, or Gypsum on alkaline soils.
entries.prevent: Add organic matter and use a fertilizer that carries sulfur.

sources.title: Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech Portal: Potato nutrient deficiencies
University of Wisconsin Extension A2525: Soil and applied sulfur

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in potato
entries.hint: Young leaves yellow and mature leaves get pitted, dead spots between green veins.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves yellow and mature leaves show small pits on the upper surface between the veins. Dead patches between the veins spread while the main veins stay green.
entries.stage: Early to mid growth.
entries.causes: High pH soils, heavy phosphorus, and soils low in zinc. Potato has a medium zinc need (UW).
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency yellows between veins on older leaves without pitting.
entries.confirm: Soil and leaf test for zinc.
entries.fix: KAU gives about 20 kg Zinc sulfate per hectare (8 kg per acre) to the soil, or in severe cases a morning spray of 2 g zinc sulfate with 2.5 g lime per liter. Keep zinc and phosphate applications apart.
entries.prevent: Keep soil pH between 5 and 7.5 and test for zinc.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in carrot
entries.hint: Fewer, smaller tops that turn yellow green from the oldest leaves, and thin, stiff roots.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn yellowish green, sometimes with red tints, then die or drop. Leaves are fewer and smaller and plants stunted. Roots grow thin, stiff and fibrous.
entries.stage: First 6 to 8 weeks.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain and too little fertilizer.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency scorches the leaf edges. Sulfur deficiency yellows the young leaves first.
entries.confirm: Check that the oldest leaves yellowed first. Test the soil.
entries.fix: Apply Urea 46 0 0 or Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 beside the rows following the soil test. TNAU gives a 1 percent urea spray (10 g per liter). KAU repeats it every 15 days.
entries.prevent: Use compost and a balanced basal fertilizer. Split nitrogen.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in carrot
entries.hint: Older leaves pale and scorch at the edges, which cup backward, and roots show violet streaks.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn pale yellow, then brown and scorched along the edges, and the margins cup backward. Leaves can turn reddish, growth slows, and violet streaks appear on the roots.
entries.stage: Root bulking.
entries.causes: Sandy soils and fields cropped for years without potash. Carrot needs a higher soil potassium level than field crops (UW).
entries.confuse: Leaf blight diseases give spots with yellow halos, scattered on the leaf. Nitrogen deficiency yellows the whole old leaf without scorching.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 following the soil test, split in parts (KAU). TNAU gives a 1 percent potassium chloride spray (10 g per liter). KAU uses potassium sulfate at 10 g per liter.
entries.prevent: Give potash at planting and keep the pH above 6.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in carrot
entries.hint: Short plants with small, distorted leaves tinged pink or purple, and late root formation.
entries.symptoms: Plants are shorter with smaller, distorted leaves, and a pink or purple tinge appears along the margins and veins. Older leaves die early, and the storage root forms late and stays small.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Acid and volcanic soils, and cold, wet soils. Carrot needs a higher soil phosphorus level than field crops (UW).
entries.confuse: Cold weather can tint leaves purple for a short time. Phosphorus deficiency stays and stunts the plant.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus.
entries.fix: Apply the recommended phosphorus dose to the soil (TNAU), such as single superphosphate for a quick fix or rock phosphate for the long term (KAU), following the soil test. Uptake is best at pH 6.2 to 7.0.
entries.prevent: Mix phosphorus into the beds before sowing.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in carrot
entries.hint: Crinkled young leaves, a dead growing point, orange tinted old leaves and small carrots.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves crinkle and the growing point may die, giving a rosette of leaves. Older leaves can turn orange. Seeds come up poorly and carrots stay small.
entries.stage: From sowing to root bulking.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in organic matter, soils at pH 7 or above, over limed soils and dry spells.
entries.confuse: Calcium deficiency also damages the growing tips but gives ragged, brittle leaf edges.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a 0.5 percent borax spray (5 g per liter). For the soil, KAU gives about 10 kg Borax per hectare. The University of Wisconsin treats carrot as a medium boron crop and gives about 1 to 2 kg of boron per hectare (about 10 to 20 kg borax) on soils testing low.
entries.prevent: Test for boron on sandy fields and do not over lime.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in radish
entries.hint: Small, pale tops that yellow from the oldest leaves, with thin, fibrous roots.
entries.symptoms: Leaves turn pale then yellow from the oldest leaves, often with red tints, then die. Leaves are fewer and smaller, plants stunted, and roots thin, stiff and fibrous.
entries.stage: From the first true leaves to harvest. Radish grows fast, so any shortage shows quickly.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain and too little fertilizer. Repeated crops on the same beds run low.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency yellows young leaves first. Manganese deficiency gives a general yellowing midway through the season on high pH soils.
entries.confirm: Check that the oldest leaves yellowed first. Test the soil.
entries.fix: Michigan State gives about 45 kg of nitrogen per hectare (40 pounds per acre) before the first crop of the season. For a standing crop TNAU gives a 1 percent urea spray (10 g per liter). Too much nitrogen and potash makes radish brittle and prone to cracking.
entries.prevent: Add compost and feed the beds again before the last crop of the year.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in radish
entries.hint: Roots crack and develop poorly, and the growing point may die.
entries.symptoms: Roots develop poorly and crack, and may show brown, broken down flesh inside. The growing point can die and young leaves bunch into a rosette, while older leaves turn orange and pale.
entries.stage: Root swelling.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in organic matter, soils at pH 7 or above, over limed beds and dry spells.
entries.confuse: Cracking also comes from uneven watering and too much nitrogen and potash. Black root disease turns roots black inside and out.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron. Cut roots to look for brown centers.
entries.fix: Michigan State includes about 1.1 kg of boron (about 11 kg Borax) per hectare in the broadcast fertilizer, or sprays about 0.2 kg of boron per hectare about 15 days after seeding. KAU gives about 10 kg borax per hectare to the soil or a borax spray of 1 g per liter.
entries.prevent: Add boron to the basal fertilizer on sandy beds and water evenly.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in ginger
entries.hint: Lower leaves turn pale yellow, leaves are small and the clump grows weak.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn pale or yellow, starting low and moving up. Reddish tints can creep from the leaf edges toward the midrib. Leaves stay small, plants are stunted and roots weak, and the rhizome yield drops.
entries.stage: From 2 to 5 months after planting, during tillering.
entries.causes: Sandy or worn out soils, heavy rain washing nitrogen away, and little or no fertilizer. Ginger takes up large amounts of nutrients (DA CAR).
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency yellows veins and all on the young leaves too. Bacterial wilt yellows leaves quickly with rotting, foul smelling rhizomes.
entries.confirm: Check that the old leaves yellowed first. Soil test.
entries.fix: The DA CAR technoguide gives a general need of 180 kg N, 180 kg P2O5 and 255 kg K2O per hectare. Split the nitrogen through the season. For quick help TNAU gives a 1 percent urea spray (10 g per liter). KAU repeats it every 15 days.
entries.prevent: Mix decomposed organic matter into the furrows before planting, and mulch with rice straw or coconut leaves (DA CAR).

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in turmeric
entries.local: Kakulangan sa phosphorus ng luyang dilaw
entries.hint: Slow plants with deeper color or purple browning, thin stems and lost lower leaves.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in pechay
entries.hint: Outer leaves turn pale yellow and the plants stay small and slow.
entries.symptoms: The outer, older leaves turn pale green and then yellow, and the yellowing spreads to the whole plant. Leaves stay small and growth slows, so plants are light at harvest. Old leaves may get reddish tints and die early.
entries.stage: From transplanting to harvest. Pechay is harvested only three to four weeks after transplanting, so any shortage shows fast.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain or daily watering that leaches nitrogen, low organic matter, and missed weekly drenches.
entries.confuse: Sulfur shortage starts on the young centre leaves. Root damage from clubroot or waterlogging also yellows plants. Pull a plant and check the roots.
entries.confirm: Old leaves yellow first. A soil test for organic matter and nitrogen, and a quick test drench on a few plants.
entries.fix: The DA guide from ATI Region 7 drenches urea dissolved in 16 liters of water at 150 ml per hill, using 75 grams of urea in the first week, 150 grams in the second, 225 grams in the third and 300 grams in the fourth. KAU gives a urea leaf spray at 10 grams per liter of water for cole crops. Water after feeding.
entries.prevent: Mix chicken manure or compost into the beds before planting, as the DA guide does, and keep up the weekly drench.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in pechay (tip burn)
entries.local: Pagkasunog ng dulo ng dahon ng petsay
entries.hint: The tips and edges of the young centre leaves turn brown and dry, and soft rot can follow.
entries.symptoms: The tips and edges of young, fast growing leaves die and turn brown, and the damage spreads inward. Young leaves can be cupped or claw shaped. Soft rot bacteria often enter the burnt tissue, so the heart of the plant turns slimy.
entries.stage: Fast growth in hot, dry weather, close to harvest.
entries.causes: Poor calcium movement into fast growing leaves, mainly from uneven watering, plus acid sandy soils, high nitrogen, potassium or ammonium, and high humidity.
entries.confuse: Bacterial soft rot starts as a wet, smelly rot. With tip burn the edges die first and rot comes later. Black rot makes V shaped yellow lesions from the outer leaf edges.
entries.confirm: Look at the youngest leaves for burnt tips. Soil test for calcium and pH.
entries.fix: Water evenly every day as the DA guide advises, and do not let beds dry out. On acid soil, KAU suggests lime at about 250 kg per hectare when pH is 5.5 to 6, or about 840 kg per hectare in two doses when pH is 3.5 to 4.5. Gypsum on soil that is not acid.
entries.prevent: Lime acid beds before planting (pechay grows best at pH 5.5 to 6.5), keep watering steady, and avoid heavy ammonium fertilizer.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in pechay
entries.hint: Older leaves get a light brown, dry band along the edges that curls up.

entries.confuse: Fertilizer burn from a strong drench poured on the leaves also browns edges. It appears suddenly after feeding.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium.
entries.fix: Include potash in the basal fertilizer, such as complete 14 14 14, and apply muriate of potash based on the soil test. For a quick fix, KAU gives a morning spray of sulfate of potash at 10 grams per liter of water for cabbage, a close relative.
entries.prevent: Use complete fertilizer at bed preparation instead of urea alone.

entries.hint: Outer leaves yellow between the veins while the veins stay green.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn yellow between the veins, starting at the edges, while the veins stay green. Later the yellow areas can turn orange or die. Michigan State extension notes Chinese cabbage, a close relative of pechay, is especially prone to it.
entries.stage: Mid growth to harvest.
entries.causes: Low pH soils, soils high in potassium, heavy potash fertilizer, sandy soils and heavy rain.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage yellows the whole leaf evenly, veins included.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium, potassium and pH.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in pechay
entries.hint: New centre leaves come out small, thick and crinkled, and stalks may crack.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves stay small, curl and become deformed and brittle, with yellow mottling along the edges. Stalks and midribs can crack or turn corky, and in severe cases the growing point dies. Plants stay stunted and open.
entries.stage: Mid growth, after dry spells or on limed beds.
entries.causes: Sandy soils where boron leaches, alkaline or overlimed soils, low organic matter, high nitrogen and drought. Crucifers need more boron than most crops.
entries.confuse: Calcium tip burn kills leaf edges but does not make leaves thick and crinkled. Aphid feeding also curls young leaves. Look for insects under the leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: For cole crops, KAU gives borax at about 10 kg per hectare in the soil or a spray at 1 gram per liter of water. Do not mix borax with lime or ammonium fertilizer, and do not repeat without a test, because too much boron burns leaves.
entries.prevent: Add a small dose of borax to the basal fertilizer on sandy beds. Source note: there are no pechay particular boron trials in the sources found. Advice here follows cabbage and other crucifers.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in pechay
entries.hint: Young centre leaves turn pale with blue green veins and purple undersides.
entries.symptoms: Plants are small and spindly. Young and middle leaves turn pale between the veins, with the veins standing out in a blurred blue green pattern. The leaves cup and may become brittle. The undersides can turn purple or bronze.
entries.stage: Early growth on light soils after heavy rain.

entries.confirm: Teagasc notes a leaf tissue test is the most reliable check, since sulfate leaches and soil tests can mislead.
entries.fix: Use ammonium sulfate for part of the nitrogen. Teagasc advises about 20 kg of sulfur per hectare for brassicas on light soils, which is roughly 85 kg of ammonium sulfate per hectare. Leaf sprays may help but are not a sure cure.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in cabbage
entries.hint: Outer leaves turn yellow green with a red or orange tint and the head stays small or never forms.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn yellow green first, then the yellowing spreads over the whole plant. Some leaves get a reddish or orange tint and dry patches. Leaves keep their shape but stay smaller, growth slows and old leaves may die. In severe cases the plant forms a tiny head or none.
entries.stage: From transplanting to head formation.
entries.causes: Sandy or light soils, heavy rain or irrigation that leaches nitrogen, low organic matter, raw straw or manure that ties up nitrogen. Very low or high soil pH.
entries.confuse: Sulfur shortage starts on the young inner leaves. Phosphorus shortage slows growth but does not yellow the leaves.
entries.confirm: Old outer leaves yellow first. Confirm with a soil test and leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Side dress urea or ammonium sulfate based on the soil test, in split doses before heading. For a quick green up, KAU suggests a urea spray at 10 grams per liter of water once every 15 days.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in cabbage
entries.hint: Hollow, brown centre of the stem and light, loose heads.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves stay small, curl down and become deformed, with yellow mottling along the edges and between the veins and some dead patches. Heads are light and loose, plants look open and are stunted. The stem can turn hollow with a brown cavity, and heads taste bitter.
entries.stage: Head formation.
entries.causes: Sandy soils where boron leaches, especially in the tropics, alkaline or overlimed soils, low organic matter, high nitrogen or calcium, and drought. Cabbage and other crucifers need more boron than most crops.
entries.confuse: Hollow stem from very fast growth or too much nitrogen stays white and clean inside. Boron hollow stem is brown or discolored.

Do not mix borax with calcium or ammonium fertilizer.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in cabbage (tip burn)
entries.local: Pagkasunog ng dulo ng dahon ng repolyo
entries.hint: Brown, dry edges on the inner leaves of the head, seen only when you cut it open.
entries.symptoms: Dead brown lesions form on the tips and edges of young leaves and spread inward. Inside the head, the edges of inner leaves turn brown with a sharp border while the outer wrapper leaves look fine. So it shows only when the head is cut. It often gets worse near harvest and in storage, and soft rot can follow. Early, severe shortage stunts the plant so it may not head.
entries.stage: Head filling, especially during hot dry periods of fast growth.
entries.causes: Usually poor calcium movement into fast growing inner leaves rather than low soil calcium. Water stress (too dry or too wet), high ammonium, potassium or magnesium, acid sandy soils and large heads raise the risk. Boron shortage also adds to tip burn.
entries.confuse: Black rot (a bacterial disease) makes V shaped yellow lesions from the outer leaf edges with black veins. Thrips scars inside heads are small brown scratches, not dead leaf edges.
entries.confirm: Cut sample heads open to check inner leaves. Soil test for calcium and pH.
entries.fix: Keep soil moisture steady. On acid soil, KAU suggests lime at about 250 kg per hectare when pH is 5.5 to 6, or about 840 kg per hectare in two doses when pH is 3.5 to 4.5. Gypsum on soil that is not acid. Correct boron at the same time.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soil before planting, avoid heavy ammonium and potash, water evenly, and choose varieties less prone to tip burn.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in cabbage

entries.causes: Acid or sandy soils, heavy rain or irrigation, drought, low potassium reserves and soils rich in magnesium.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage yellows between the veins with orange or red tints rather than a brown edge band.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Apply muriate of potash based on the soil test, preferably in split doses. For an immediate remedy, KAU suggests a morning spray of sulfate of potash at 10 grams per liter of water with a sticker. Keep soil pH above 6 with lime or dolomite.
entries.prevent: Include potash in the basal fertilizer and one side dressing.

entries.confuse: Root problems such as clubroot or nematodes also stunt plants. Pull a few plants and check the roots.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: Apply phosphorus fertilizer near the roots based on the soil test. KAU lists single superphosphate for a quick correction and rock phosphate or bone meal for the long term, with best uptake near pH 6.2 to 7.0.
entries.prevent: Use a phosphorus starter at transplanting and add compost.
