KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cabbage nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in cabbage
entries.hint: Outer leaves yellow between the veins and turn orange or red, while big veins stay green.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn yellow green between the veins, starting at the edge and moving to the midrib, then orange or red. Small veins also yellow while large veins stay green, and the areas between veins curl upward. Severely affected plants may have normal sized leaves but fail to head.
entries.stage: Head formation.
entries.causes: Sandy or acid soils, soils rich in potassium, heavy potash fertilizer, and cold wet periods.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage yellows the whole leaf evenly. Potassium shortage gives a brown dead band on the edges.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium and potassium, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU suggests magnesium sulfate in a band near the plants at about 80 kg per hectare (32 kg per acre). A foliar spray of magnesium sulfate gives faster relief. Do not apply magnesium and potassium fertilizer together.
entries.prevent: Use dolomite on acid soil over the long term.

sources.title: Yara UK: Magnesium deficiency in cabbage
KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cabbage nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in cabbage
entries.hint: Young inner leaves turn pale yellow and the plant is slow to head.
entries.symptoms: Growth is slow and development delayed. Yellowing appears first on the younger leaves, which can become purplish, curl upward and turn brittle. Head formation is held back, and plants are more open to fungal attack.
entries.stage: Early growth and head formation.
entries.causes: Acid or sandy soils where sulfate leaches, low organic matter, waterlogged soils, and fertilizer programs with no sulfur. Crucifers need a lot of sulfur.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage also slows growth but starts on the older outer leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for sulfate and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Use ammonium sulfate as part of the nitrogen, or other sulfur fertilizer. KAU suggests sulfur dust at about 25 kg per hectare (10 kg per acre) on sulfur deficient soil, and gypsum on alkaline soil.
entries.prevent: Give some sulfur every crop and add organic matter.

sources.title: Yara UK: Sulfur deficiency in cabbage
KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cabbage nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Molybdenum deficiency in cabbage
entries.hint: On acid soil, faint yellow green plants with narrow, toothed leaves that bend down and loose heads.
entries.symptoms: Leaves show a faint yellow green color all over. Young plants have small leaves that bend down with edges more toothed than usual. Older plants have long leaves that bend down. Plants grow loose and head formation is held back. In patches of a field, leaf edges may scorch.
entries.stage: Seedling to early heading.
entries.causes: Acid soils, especially pH 5.5 or lower, sandy soils and low organic matter.
entries.confuse: Looks like nitrogen shortage, and patches in the field are typical. A test spray on a few plants tells them apart.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test and leaf tissue test. NSW DPI suggests spraying a few plants with sodium molybdate and watching for greener, normal growth.
entries.fix: NSW DPI suggests about 50 grams of sodium molybdate in 100 liters of water sprayed on the leaves, or 150 ml of that mix at the base of each plant. For the next crop, mix about 1 kg sodium molybdate per hectare with the fertilizer, or water the seedbed with 40 grams in 50 liters per 10 square meters one to two weeks before transplanting.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soils to about pH 6. Liming takes months to work, so plan ahead.

sources.title: Yara UK: Molybdenum deficiency in cabbage
NSW DPI Agfact AC.4: Molybdenum deficiency in plants

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in lettuce
entries.hint: Outer leaves turn light green to yellow and the head stays loose and small.
entries.symptoms: Older outer leaves turn light green first, then the whole head becomes yellow green. Growth is strongly held back and the crop is late. Older leaves may rot, red varieties can show a purple flush, and in severe cases no head forms. Roots grow long with few side roots.
entries.stage: From transplanting to heading.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain or watering that leaches nitrogen, low organic matter, and raw straw or manure.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage keeps the veins green. Sulfur shortage starts on younger leaves. Manganese shortage yellows leaves with green veins and brown spots on the edges but slows growth less.
entries.confirm: Old leaves yellow first. Soil test and leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Side dress or fertigate with urea based on the soil test. The BPI lettuce guide uses 1 tablespoon of urea in 1 gallon of water, given every two weeks, when urea is applied through the water.
entries.prevent: BPI advises 3 to 10 tonnes of organic fertilizer per hectare mixed into the plots before planting, plus basal and side dress fertilizer based on soil analysis.

sources.title: Yara UK: Nitrogen deficiency in lettuce
Bureau of Plant Industry: Lettuce production guide

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in lettuce (tip burn)
entries.hint: Brown or grey dead edges on the young inner leaves, worse in hot weather.
entries.symptoms: Brown or grey dead lesions appear first on the edges and tips of young leaves (tip burn). The leaves can look wavy and darker green. The damage spreads inward and later to older leaves, and brown veins may show near the burnt areas. Early, severe shortage stunts plants so they do not head. Roots are short, bushy and brown, with blackened tips.
entries.stage: Rapid growth and heading, especially in hot weather. BPI notes tip burn occurs at high temperatures.
entries.causes: Too little calcium reaching fast growing inner leaves because of heat, dry soil or uneven watering, plus acid sandy soils and high nitrogen or potassium.
entries.confuse: Boron shortage also starts on the youngest leaves, but stays at the growing point and does not spread as edge lesions. Bacterial leaf spot makes angular spots, not burnt edges.
entries.confirm: Check the inner leaves for brown edges after hot spells. Soil test for calcium and pH.
entries.fix: BPI advises enough irrigation and enough calcium in the soil. Water evenly, shade or plant in cooler months in the lowlands, lime acid soil based on the test, and use tolerant varieties.
entries.prevent: Grow head lettuce in cool months or highlands, lime acid soil to the pH 6 to 6.8 that BPI recommends, and avoid heavy nitrogen.

sources.title: Yara UK: Calcium and boron deficiency in lettuce
Bureau of Plant Industry: Lettuce production guide

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in lettuce
entries.hint: Older leaves get yellow spots on the edges that die and scorch, and heads stay loose.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves show yellow spots on the tips and edges that grow and then die, and the scorched edges distort the leaves. Severe cases have mottled dark green leaves that wilt. Leaves may be smoother and rounder than normal, and plants are stunted with loose heads or none. Roots are long with few side roots and may be yellowish and slimy.
entries.stage: Mid growth to heading.
entries.causes: Acid or sandy soils, heavy rain or irrigation, drought, low potassium reserves and soils rich in magnesium.
entries.confuse: High salt in the soil gives similar edge burn but usually with brown veins.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium and salinity, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Apply muriate of potash or sulfate of potash based on the soil test, in split doses. Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Include potash in the basal fertilizer.

sources.title: Yara UK: Potassium deficiency in lettuce

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in lettuce
entries.hint: Stunted, dull dark green plants that are late to head.
entries.symptoms: Growth is stunted and heading is late or fails, leaving a rosette. Leaves are dull dark green and may crinkle or show reddish color. Red varieties flush purple. Older leaves get papery dead patches and die, and side roots are few and may be reddish.
entries.stage: Seedling and early growth, especially in cool weather.
entries.causes: Low temperatures, acid or calcareous soils, iron rich soils, low organic matter and weak roots.
entries.confuse: Too much nitrogen also makes plants dark green, but those leaves are rounder and the undersides are not purple.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: Apply phosphorus near the roots based on the soil test, and lime very acid soil. Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Use a phosphorus starter at transplanting and add compost.

sources.title: Yara UK: Phosphorus deficiency in lettuce

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in lettuce
entries.hint: Older leaves get yellow to orange edges and yellow between green veins.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves show it first: the edges turn yellow to orange and the areas between the veins yellow, while the veins stay green. With time the yellow areas die, and the areas between veins curl upward. Growth is only a little slower when the shortage is moderate but badly held back when severe.
entries.stage: Mid growth to heading.
entries.causes: Sandy or acid soils, soils rich in potassium, heavy potash fertilizer, and cold wet periods.
entries.confuse: Manganese shortage looks similar but its yellow is greenish yellow, not orange yellow. Nitrogen shortage yellows the whole leaf.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium and potassium, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Spray magnesium sulfate on the leaves for quick relief and correct the soil with dolomite or magnesium sulfate based on the soil test.
entries.prevent: Use dolomite on acid soil and do not overuse potash.

sources.title: Yara UK: Magnesium deficiency in lettuce

entries.name: Boron deficiency in lettuce
entries.hint: Damage sits at the growing point of the youngest leaves, with poor, stubby roots.
entries.symptoms: Like calcium shortage it starts on the youngest leaves. But the damage stays at the growing point instead of spreading as edge lesions. Roots are poorly developed, with many very short, branched side roots that brown and die back in severe cases.
entries.stage: Mid growth.
entries.causes: Sandy soils where boron leaches, alkaline or overlimed soils, low organic matter and drought.
entries.confuse: Calcium tip burn spreads along the leaf edges. Boron damage stays at the growing point.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron and a leaf tissue test before treating, since boron has a narrow safe range.
entries.fix: Apply boron only after a test confirms the need, at a light rate. Follow the soil test. Do not repeat doses, as too much boron burns leaves.
entries.prevent: Keep organic matter up and avoid overliming.

sources.title: Yara UK: Calcium and boron deficiency in lettuce

entries.name: Molybdenum deficiency in lettuce
entries.hint: On acid soil, pale stunted plants whose leaf edges wilt and die back, with clear spots between veins.
entries.symptoms: Plants are pale green with clearly stunted growth. Leaves wilt from the tips and edges and the tissue dies back to brown or yellow, most often on young plants. Clear, see through spots appear between the veins, then die and join into bigger dead patches.
entries.stage: Young plants, on acid soils.
entries.causes: Acid soils and low pH, and low organic matter.
entries.confuse: Calcium shortage makes the youngest leaves crinkled and darker green. The see through spots are not insect damage. No larvae are found in them.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test and leaf tissue test. A trial spray of sodium molybdate on a few plants.
entries.fix: For vegetable crops NSW DPI suggests about 50 grams of sodium molybdate in 100 liters of water sprayed on the leaves, or about 1 kg per hectare mixed with fertilizer for the next crop. Lime acid soils.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soil to about pH 6 well ahead of planting.

sources.title: Yara UK: Molybdenum deficiency in lettuce
NSW DPI Agfact AC.4: Molybdenum deficiency in plants

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in kangkong
entries.hint: Lower leaves turn pale yellow and shoots stay thin and short.
entries.symptoms: Older, lower leaves fade to yellowish green and then yellow, and in bad cases the whole plant turns pale. Shoots are thin and hard and grow slowly, so bundles are light at harvest. In a hydroponic study on kangkong, plants grown without nitrogen reached only about 14 cm against about 33 cm for plants given a full nutrient mix, and had less leaf chlorophyll.
entries.stage: From planting to harvest, which comes only three to four weeks after planting, and again after each cutting.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, daily watering or heavy rain that washes nitrogen away, low organic matter, and missed weekly feeding. Each harvest removes a lot of nitrogen with the shoots.
entries.confuse: Iron shortage yellows the youngest tips with green veins instead. Too much water or root rot also makes plants pale.
entries.confirm: Lower leaves yellow first. A soil test for organic matter and a test drench on a few plants.
entries.fix: The DA guide from ATI Region 7 drenches urea dissolved in 16 liters of water at 150 ml per hill, using 75 grams of urea in the first week, 150 in the second, 225 in the third and 300 in the fourth. Repeat a light feeding after each cutting.
entries.prevent: Mix chicken manure or compost into the beds before planting and keep up the weekly drench.

sources.title: ATI Region 7 (DA): Kangkong production guide
Jurnal Biologi Tropis: Chlorophyll levels of water kale (kangkong) under nutrient deficiencies
PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in kangkong
entries.hint: Plants stay short with dark green leaves and thin, woody stems.
entries.symptoms: Growth is held back without yellowing. Stems are slender and woody, leaves are small and darker green, and some leaves show a reddish purple tint underneath. In the hydroponic kangkong study, leaving out phosphorus also lowered leaf chlorophyll.
entries.stage: Early growth after sowing or planting cuttings.
entries.causes: Acid soils (the DA guide gives pH 5.5 to 6.5 as best), iron rich soils, low organic matter, and feeding urea only.
entries.confuse: Purple stem varieties are naturally colored. Root knot nematodes also stunt upland kangkong.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: Use complete 14 14 14 in the beds as the DA guide does, adjusted to the soil test, and lime very acid soil. Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Apply complete fertilizer and manure at bed preparation.

sources.title: ATI Region 7 (DA): Kangkong production guide
Jurnal Biologi Tropis: Chlorophyll levels of water kale (kangkong) under nutrient deficiencies
PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in kangkong
entries.hint: Older leaves look greyish, then bronze, with brown edges.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn ashy grey green, then bronze or yellowish brown, and the edges brown and cup down. Stems are slender and weak and roots are poor. In the hydroponic kangkong study, leaving out potassium lowered leaf chlorophyll.
entries.stage: Later growth and regrowth after repeated cuttings.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy watering, and repeated harvests fed with urea only.
entries.confuse: Leaf spot diseases make round spots across the leaf rather than edge burn.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium.
entries.fix: Use complete 14 14 14 or muriate of potash based on the soil test. Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Use complete fertilizer at planting and after every few cuttings.

sources.title: PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops
Jurnal Biologi Tropis: Chlorophyll levels of water kale (kangkong) under nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in kangkong
entries.hint: Older leaves yellow between the veins while the veins stay green.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn yellow between the veins while the veins stay green, and the leaves become brittle with edges curling. In the hydroponic kangkong study, plants grown without magnesium had clearly less leaf chlorophyll than plants given a full nutrient mix.
entries.stage: Mid growth.
entries.causes: Acid soils, heavy potash fertilizer, and heavy liming with plain lime only.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage yellows the whole leaf, veins included.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium, potassium and pH.
entries.fix: Spray magnesium sulfate on the leaves for quick relief and correct acid soil with dolomite. Follow the soil test for rates.
entries.prevent: Use dolomite instead of plain lime on acid beds.

sources.title: Jurnal Biologi Tropis: Chlorophyll levels of water kale (kangkong) under nutrient deficiencies
PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops

entries.name: Iron deficiency in kangkong
entries.hint: The newest shoot tips turn pale yellow between green veins, then fully yellow.
entries.symptoms: New leaves at the shoot tips turn light yellow, first between the veins, then over the whole leaf, usually without dead spots. In the hydroponic kangkong study, plants grown without iron had clearly less leaf chlorophyll than plants given a full nutrient mix.
entries.stage: Any stage, mostly on limed or alkaline soil and in nutrient mixes without iron.
entries.causes: Alkaline or overlimed soils, and soilless or hydroponic setups with too little iron. On ordinary acid Philippine soils iron shortage is uncommon.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage yellows the older leaves first.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test, and a check of the nutrient recipe in hydroponic setups.
entries.fix: Stop liming, and spray ferrous sulfate or iron chelate on the leaves, or add iron chelate to the nutrient mix. Follow the product label.
entries.prevent: Do not overlime beds, and include iron in hydroponic mixes.

sources.title: Jurnal Biologi Tropis: Chlorophyll levels of water kale (kangkong) under nutrient deficiencies
PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in mustard
entries.hint: Lower leaves turn pale yellow, sometimes with red tints, and leaves stay small.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn yellow green first, then the whole plant pales. Some leaves get reddish or orange tints and dry patches. Leaves keep their shape but stay small, growth slows and plants may bolt early.
entries.stage: From transplanting to harvest.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain or watering, low organic matter and too little nitrogen for a fast leafy crop.
entries.confuse: Sulfur shortage, very common in mustard, starts on the young leaves instead. Purple color in some mustard varieties is normal.
entries.confirm: Old leaves yellow first. Soil test and leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Side dress or drench with urea or ammonium sulfate in small weekly doses based on the soil test. KAU gives a urea leaf spray at 10 grams per liter of water for cole crops.
entries.prevent: Add manure or compost at bed preparation and feed weekly. Mustard is a short leafy crop.

sources.title: Yara UK: Nitrogen deficiency in cabbage
KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cabbage nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in mustard
entries.hint: Young leaves turn pale between blue green veins, cup, and get purple undersides.
entries.symptoms: Plants are small and spindly. Young and middle leaves turn pale between the veins while the veins stand out blue green, the leaves cup and become brittle. The undersides turn purple or bronze. Symptoms develop slowly.
entries.stage: Early growth on light soils after heavy rain.
entries.causes: Light, sandy soils with low organic matter, wet weather that leaches sulfate, and fertilizer programs of urea and muriate of potash only. Mustard and other brassicas need a lot of sulfur.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage starts on the older, lower leaves.
entries.confirm: A leaf tissue test is the most reliable check, since sulfate leaches and soil tests can mislead.
entries.fix: Use ammonium sulfate or gypsum. Teagasc advises about 20 kg of sulfur per hectare for brassica vegetables on light soils (roughly 85 kg ammonium sulfate per hectare). In a field trial on Indian mustard grown for seed, gypsum gave better yields than single superphosphate as the sulfur source.
entries.prevent: Use some sulfur fertilizer every crop.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in mustard
entries.hint: Older leaves get light brown, dry edges that curl up.
entries.symptoms: The edges of older leaves yellow and then turn light brown and dry, and the dead band spreads inward. Leaf edges curl upward and growth slows.
entries.stage: Mid growth to harvest.
entries.causes: Sandy or acid soils, heavy rain or watering, and fertilizing with urea only.
entries.confuse: Fertilizer burn appears suddenly after a strong feed. Potassium shortage builds slowly on the old leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium.
entries.fix: Apply complete fertilizer or muriate of potash based on the soil test. For a quick fix, KAU gives a morning spray of sulfate of potash at 10 grams per liter of water for cabbage, a close relative.
entries.prevent: Use complete fertilizer at bed preparation.

KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cabbage nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in mustard
entries.hint: Small, slow plants with reddish or purple older leaves.
entries.symptoms: Plants grow slowly and stay small. Older leaves can turn dark, then reddish or purple from the edges, often on the undersides.
entries.stage: Seedling and early growth, in cold or dry soil.
entries.causes: Acid or iron rich soils, low organic matter, cold, wet or dry soil, and no phosphorus at planting.
entries.confuse: Some mustard varieties are naturally purple. Nitrogen shortage gives pale rather than dark leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: Apply complete 14 14 14 or 16 20 0 at planting based on the soil test. KAU lists single superphosphate for a quick correction in cole crops.
entries.prevent: Use a phosphorus fertilizer and manure at bed preparation.

sources.title: Yara UK: Phosphorus deficiency in broccoli

entries.name: Boron deficiency in mustard
entries.hint: New leaves come out small, crinkled and brittle, and stalks may crack.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves stay small, curl and become deformed, with yellow mottling along the edges. Leaf stalks and midribs can crack or turn corky, and in severe cases the growing point dies.
entries.stage: Mid growth.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, overlimed or alkaline soils, low organic matter and drought. Brassicas need more boron than most crops.
entries.confuse: Aphids also curl young leaves. Look for insects. Calcium tip burn only kills leaf edges.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: For cole crops, KAU gives borax at about 10 kg per hectare in the soil or a spray at 1 gram per liter of water. Do not repeat without a test.
entries.prevent: Add a small dose of borax to the basal fertilizer on sandy beds. Source note: advice follows cabbage and other crucifers, as no mustasa particular boron work was found.

entries.hint: Older leaves yellow between green veins, starting from the edge.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves yellow between the veins, starting at the edges and moving toward the midrib, while the veins stay green. Yellow areas may later turn orange, red or brown.
entries.stage: Mid growth to harvest.
entries.causes: Acid sandy soils, soils high in potassium, heavy potash fertilizer and heavy rain.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage yellows the whole leaf.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium, potassium and pH.
entries.fix: Spray magnesium sulfate for quick relief. For cole crops KAU gives magnesium sulfate in a band at about 80 kg per hectare (32 kg per acre). Do not apply it together with potash.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in mustard (tip burn)
entries.local: Pagkasunog ng dulo ng dahon ng mustasa
entries.hint: Brown, dead tips on the youngest leaves in hot, dry weather.
entries.symptoms: The tips and edges of young, fast growing leaves die and turn brown, and the damage spreads inward. Rot can enter the damaged tissue.
entries.stage: Fast growth in hot, dry spells.
entries.causes: Uneven watering and fast growth, acid sandy soils, and heavy ammonium or potash.
entries.confuse: Bacterial rots start wet. Tip burn starts as dry dead edges.
entries.confirm: Soil test for calcium and pH.
entries.fix: Water evenly. On acid soil, KAU suggests lime at about 250 kg per hectare when pH is 5.5 to 6, or about 840 kg per hectare in two doses when pH is 3.5 to 4.5. Gypsum on soil that is not acid.
entries.prevent: Lime acid beds before planting and keep watering steady.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in broccoli
entries.hint: Pale plants with orange to red edges on old leaves, and small, loose heads.
entries.symptoms: Leaves and heads turn evenly pale, starting on older leaves. Mature leaves yellow with orange to red color along the edges. Heads are small and loose, or do not form at all in severe cases. Plants are stunted and slow, with a higher risk of early bolting.
entries.stage: Early leaf growth and again as the florets form. Broccoli needs nitrogen early, then a moderate supply at heading.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain or irrigation, low organic matter, raw straw or manure. A single unsplit dose that runs out before heading.
entries.confuse: Red leaf edges can also come from phosphorus shortage. Phosphorus leaves are dark or bluish, nitrogen leaves are pale.
entries.confirm: Soil test and leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Side dress urea or ammonium sulfate in split doses based on the soil test. For a quick green up, KAU suggests a urea spray at 10 grams per liter of water every 15 days for cole crops such as cabbage.
entries.prevent: Give nitrogen early after transplanting and a second dose before heading.

KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cabbage nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Boron deficiency in broccoli (hollow stem)
entries.hint: The stem is hollow with brown tissue inside, and new leaves look crinkled.
entries.symptoms: Watery tissue forms inside the stem and slowly turns brown or black, then dries out and leaves a hollow with brown patches. New leaves look crinkled and mottled, and plants are stunted with short spaces between leaves. Light brown spots can show on the head, and soft rot bacteria may enter the hollow stem.
entries.stage: Head formation.
entries.causes: High soil pH, sandy soils where boron leaches, low organic matter, high nitrogen or calcium, drought or cold wet weather. Crucifers need more boron than most crops.
entries.confuse: Hollowness from excess nitrogen or heat stays bright inside instead of browning.
entries.confirm: Cut stems lengthwise. Soil test and leaf tissue test for boron.
entries.fix: Delaware extension advises about 3 pounds of boron per acre in the fertilizer before planting for broccoli, or a spray of 1.0 to 1.5 pounds of Solubor per acre in plenty of water before heading if no boron went in the soil. For cole crops, KAU gives borax at about 10 kg per hectare in the soil or a 1 gram per liter spray. Do not overdo it. Too much boron burns leaf edges.
entries.prevent: Include boron in the basal fertilizer on sandy or limed soils.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in broccoli (tip burn)
entries.local: Pagkasunog ng dulo ng dahon ng brokoli
entries.hint: Burnt, dead tips and edges on the youngest leaves.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves are hit first, with dead lesions on the tips and edges that spread inward. Growth is restricted.
entries.stage: Fast growth before and during heading.
entries.causes: Restricted uptake more than low soil calcium: water stress, high ammonium, potassium, magnesium or sodium, and acid sandy soils.

entries.fix: Keep the soil evenly moist. On acid soil, KAU suggests lime at about 250 kg per hectare when pH is 5.5 to 6, or about 840 kg per hectare in two doses when pH is 3.5 to 4.5. Gypsum on soil that is not acid.
entries.prevent: Lime before planting, water evenly and avoid heavy ammonium and potash.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in broccoli

entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn yellow, then brown and dead, with a sharp border between dead and living tissue. The damage spreads from the edges inward, and in severe cases growth is badly stunted. Heads are smaller and of lower quality.
entries.stage: Head formation and head enlargement, when broccoli needs the most potassium.
entries.causes: Acid or sandy soils, heavy rain or irrigation, drought, low potassium reserves and soils rich in magnesium.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage yellows between the veins first. Potassium burns the edges.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Apply muriate of potash based on the soil test, in split doses before and at heading. For an immediate remedy on cole crops, KAU suggests a morning spray of sulfate of potash at 10 grams per liter of water with a sticker.
entries.prevent: Give potash before head formation.

entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn reddish starting at the edges, with a yellow green band between the red and the green. Early on leaf size is normal. In severe cases leaves and the whole plant stay small.

entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in broccoli
entries.hint: Older leaves get a mottled yellow look between green veins, from the edges inward.
entries.symptoms: Yellowing starts on older leaves and spreads between the veins from the edges inward. While the veins stay green and the leaf looks mottled. Severe cases get dead spots between the veins and along the edges, and growth is stunted.
entries.stage: Head formation.
entries.causes: Excess potassium, ammonium or calcium, sandy or acid soils, heavy potash fertilizer, and cold wet periods.
entries.confuse: Potassium shortage can look similar. Magnesium usually yellows the whole area between veins before dead spots appear. A leaf test settles it.
entries.confirm: Leaf tissue test plus soil test for magnesium and potassium.
entries.fix: For cole crops KAU suggests magnesium sulfate in a band near the plants at about 80 kg per hectare (32 kg per acre). A foliar spray of magnesium sulfate gives faster relief.
entries.prevent: Use dolomite on acid soil.

sources.title: Yara UK: Magnesium deficiency in broccoli
KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cabbage nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in broccoli
entries.hint: Young leaves turn pale, stiff and purplish, with narrow spoon shaped leaves on long stalks.
entries.symptoms: Yellowing starts in the youngest leaves, first between the veins and later evenly pale. Stems, leaf stalks and leaves may turn purple. Leaves become stiff, curl inward and grow narrow and spoon shaped on long stalks. Severe cases are badly stunted.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Acid or sandy soils, low organic matter, waterlogged soils, and very high nitrogen, which can hold back sulfur uptake.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage starts on old leaves. Magnesium shortage also yellows between veins but on old leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for sulfate and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Use ammonium sulfate as part of the nitrogen. For cole crops, KAU suggests sulfur dust at about 25 kg per hectare (10 kg per acre) on sulfur deficient soil.
entries.prevent: Give some sulfur every crop.

sources.title: Yara UK: Sulfur deficiency in broccoli
KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cabbage nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Molybdenum deficiency in broccoli
entries.hint: On acid soil, narrow, cupped young leaves with yellow, scorched edges in patches of the field.
entries.symptoms: Leaves stay pale and the plant is stunted, with yellow green color between the veins and along the edges. Young leaves are narrow and distorted with edges that cup up or scorch, similar to whiptail in cauliflower. Affected plants usually come in patches.
entries.stage: Seedling and young plant stage.
entries.causes: Acid soils, mostly pH 5.5 or lower, and low organic matter.
entries.confuse: Boron shortage also distorts young leaves. Nitrogen shortage gives pale plants without distorted leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test. NSW DPI suggests a trial spray of sodium molybdate on a few plants and checking for greener, normal new growth.
entries.fix: NSW DPI suggests about 50 grams of sodium molybdate in 100 liters of water sprayed on the leaves, or 150 ml of that mix at the base of each plant. For the next crop, mix about 1 kg sodium molybdate per hectare with the fertilizer, or treat the seedbed with 40 grams in 50 liters per 10 square meters one to two weeks before transplanting.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soils to about pH 6 ahead of planting.

sources.title: NSW DPI Agfact AC.4: Molybdenum deficiency in plants
Yara UK: Molybdenum deficiency in cauliflower

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in cauliflower
entries.hint: Older leaves yellow with red edges, and small button curds form too early.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn yellow and get red color starting at the edges, then die or drop. Growth is stunted and roots are weak. A shortage of nitrogen on young plants is one cause of buttoning, where tiny curds form early and the plant stops growing leaves.
entries.stage: From transplanting to curd formation.
entries.causes: Sandy or light soils, heavy rain or irrigation, low organic matter, raw straw or manure. Too little nitrogen early in the season.
entries.confuse: Phosphorus shortage also reddens leaves, but phosphorus leaves are dull bluish green while nitrogen leaves are light green. Buttoning also comes from overaged seedlings or heat.
entries.confirm: Soil test and leaf tissue test. Note whether the old leaves yellow first.
entries.fix: Side dress urea or ammonium sulfate based on the soil test. For a quick green up, KAU suggests a urea spray at 10 grams per liter of water every 15 days.
entries.prevent: Give enough nitrogen and water for fast leaf growth in the first weeks after transplanting, and use young, healthy seedlings.

sources.title: Yara UK: Nitrogen deficiency in cauliflower
National Horticulture Board India: Cauliflower disorders
KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cauliflower nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Boron deficiency in cauliflower (browning and hollow stem)
entries.local: Pangingitim ng bulaklak at hungkag na tangkay ng koliplor
entries.hint: Brown or pink patches on the curd and a hollow, water soaked stem.
entries.symptoms: After the curd forms, water soaked areas appear on the stem and curd. The stem becomes hollow, with water soaked tissue inside that later turns brown or black. Brown or pink patches form on the curd surface (brown rot or browning), and the curd tastes bitter. Young leaves stay small, stiff and light green with reddish or brown edges, and in severe cases the growing point dies.
entries.stage: Curd formation and development.
entries.causes: High soil pH and alkaline or overlimed soils, sandy soils where boron leaches, low organic matter, high nitrogen or calcium. Dry or cold wet spells. Cauliflower is the most sensitive of the cole crops.
entries.confuse: Hollow stem from fast growth or too much nitrogen stays bright inside. Boron hollow stem browns. Molybdenum shortage gives strap like leaves rather than brown curds.
entries.confirm: Cut stems to check for brown cavities. Soil test and leaf tissue test for boron.
entries.fix: The National Horticulture Board of India suggests borax at 10 to 15 kg per hectare in acid soils, more in neutral or alkaline soils. KAU gives a borax spray at 1 gram per liter of water. Delaware extension advises about 3 pounds of boron per acre before planting, or a spray of 1.0 to 1.5 pounds of Solubor per acre before heading if none went in the soil. Do not mix borax with calcium or ammonium fertilizer.
entries.prevent: Add boron in the basal fertilizer for every cauliflower crop on light soils, and treat the nursery too.

sources.title: National Horticulture Board India: Cauliflower disorders
Yara UK: Boron deficiency in cauliflower
University of Delaware Weekly Crop Update: Boron and molybdenum in vegetable crops
KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cauliflower nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Molybdenum deficiency in cauliflower (whiptail)
entries.hint: New leaves are narrow and strap like, sometimes only the midrib, and no proper curd forms.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves yellow at the edges, and the leaf blade fails to grow, in bad cases leaving only the midrib (whiptail). Leaves are thick, distorted and cupped. The growing point is deformed, so the curd does not develop, or late shortage gives loose curds with small leaves pushing through. Affected plants often come in patches.
entries.stage: Seedling and young plant stage, and at curd formation if it comes late.
entries.causes: Acid soils, mostly below pH 5.5, where molybdenum is locked up. Low organic matter makes it worse.
entries.confuse: Boron shortage also deforms young plants, so check both. Nitrogen shortage yellows old leaves but does not make strap leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test and a leaf tissue test. A trial spray of sodium molybdate on a few plants should bring normal new growth.
entries.fix: NSW DPI suggests about 50 grams of sodium molybdate in 100 liters of water sprayed on the leaves, or 150 ml of that mix at the base of each plant. For the next crop, mix about 1 kg sodium molybdate per hectare with the fertilizer, or water the seedbed with 40 grams in 50 liters per 10 square meters one to two weeks before transplanting. KAU gives a 1 gram per liter foliar spray. Lime acid soils.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soils to about pH 6 well before planting, and add molybdenum to the nursery. TNAU mixes 50 grams sodium molybdate and 100 grams borax into each 100 square meters of cabbage nursery, a practice that suits cauliflower seedlings too.

sources.title: NSW DPI Agfact AC.4: Molybdenum deficiency in plants
Yara UK: Molybdenum deficiency in cauliflower
National Horticulture Board India: Cauliflower disorders
KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cauliflower nutrient deficiencies
TNAU Agritech Portal: Cabbage

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in cauliflower (tip burn)
entries.local: Pagkasunog ng dulo ng dahon ng koliplor
entries.hint: Young leaves get dead, burnt tips and claw like curling. Curd segments turn brown and glassy.
entries.symptoms: Dead lesions form on the tips and edges of young leaves and spread inward with a yellow border (tip burn). The youngest leaves become claw shaped, cupped and brittle, and the leaf edges can look glassy. Curd segments can turn brown and glassy and parts of the curd die.
entries.stage: Rapid leaf growth and curd development.
entries.causes: Restricted calcium uptake rather than low soil calcium: water stress (dry or waterlogged), high ammonium, potassium, magnesium or sodium, and acid sandy soils. Low boron also limits calcium use.
entries.confuse: Boron shortage also damages the growing point but gives hollow stems and brown curds. Downy mildew and black rot are diseases with spots or V shaped lesions.
entries.confirm: Soil test for calcium, pH and boron.
entries.fix: Keep soil moisture even. On acid soil, KAU suggests lime at about 250 kg per hectare when pH is 5.5 to 6, or about 840 kg per hectare in two doses when pH is 3.5 to 4.5. Gypsum on soil that is not acid. Check boron too.
entries.prevent: Lime before planting, water evenly, and avoid heavy ammonium and potash.

sources.title: Yara UK: Calcium deficiency in cauliflower
KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cauliflower nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in cauliflower
entries.hint: Older leaf edges turn yellow, then light to dark brown, and curl up.
entries.symptoms: Leaf edges turn yellow, then light brown and later dark brown, and curl upward. Leaves lose their waxy coating. The dead tissue spreads from the edges toward the middle, and stems become weak.
entries.stage: Curd formation.
entries.causes: Acid or sandy soils, heavy rain or irrigation, drought, low potassium reserves, and soils rich in magnesium.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage yellows between the veins. Potassium shortage burns the edges first.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Apply muriate of potash based on the soil test, in split doses. For an immediate remedy, KAU suggests a morning spray of sulfate of potash at 10 grams per liter of water with a sticker. Keep soil pH above 6.
entries.prevent: Include potash in the basal fertilizer and side dressing.

sources.title: Yara UK: Potassium deficiency in cauliflower
KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cauliflower nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in cauliflower
entries.hint: Older leaves turn dull bluish green with purple color and red undersides.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn a pale bluish green with purple color, especially along the veins, and the undersides often turn red. Plants are stunted with short, thin shoots, and vigour and yield drop.
entries.stage: Seedling and early growth, in cold or wet soil.
entries.causes: Acid or calcareous soils, iron rich soils, low organic matter, cold or wet weather and weak roots.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage can also redden leaves, but those leaves stay light green, not bluish.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: Apply phosphorus near the roots based on the soil test. KAU lists single superphosphate for a quick correction and rock phosphate or bone meal for the long term, with best uptake near pH 6.2 to 7.0.
entries.prevent: Use a phosphorus starter at transplanting.

sources.title: Yara UK: Phosphorus deficiency in cauliflower
KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cauliflower nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in cauliflower
entries.hint: Older leaves yellow from the edges toward the midrib while the veins stay green.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves yellow between the veins, starting at the edges and moving toward the midrib, while the veins stay green. In severe cases dead spots form between the veins, and old leaves become stiff and drop early.
entries.stage: Curd formation.
entries.causes: Sandy or acid soils, soils rich in potassium, heavy potash fertilizer, and cold wet periods. Cauliflower is one of the crucifers most prone to it.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage yellows the whole leaf, veins included.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium and potassium, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU suggests magnesium sulfate in a band near the plants at about 80 kg per hectare (32 kg per acre). A foliar spray of magnesium sulfate gives faster relief. Do not apply magnesium and potassium together.
entries.prevent: Use dolomitic lime on acid soils.

sources.title: Yara UK: Magnesium deficiency in cauliflower
Michigan State University Extension: Disorders of cole crops (archive bulletin E1668)
KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cauliflower nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in cauliflower
entries.hint: Young leaves turn evenly pale, stiff and reddish, with thin leaf stalks.
entries.symptoms: Yellowing starts in the young leaves and moves to older ones. Leaves turn uniformly light green or yellow and feel stiff, may show red color, and later curl inward. Often only thin leaf stalks form, and in severe cases seedlings die.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Acid or sandy soils where sulfate leaches, low organic matter, waterlogged soils, and no sulfur in the fertilizer.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage starts on old leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for sulfate and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Use ammonium sulfate as part of the nitrogen. KAU suggests sulfur dust at about 25 kg per hectare (10 kg per acre) on sulfur deficient soil, and gypsum on alkaline soil.
entries.prevent: Give some sulfur every crop.

sources.title: Yara UK: Sulfur deficiency in cauliflower
KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Cauliflower nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in alugbati
entries.hint: Older leaves fade to pale yellow and new shoots come thin and slow after cutting.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves fade to yellowish green and then yellow, and new shoots are thin, hard and slow to regrow after each harvest. Leaves stay small and the plant flowers early.
entries.stage: Mid growth and the regrowth after each harvest.
entries.causes: Repeated harvests that remove nitrogen with the shoots, sandy soils, heavy watering and low organic matter.
entries.confuse: Root knot nematodes, which alugbati is weak against, also stunt and yellow plants. Check the roots for galls.
entries.confirm: Soil test for organic matter and nitrogen. The PCARRD and BPI guides both recommend a soil test for N, P and K.
entries.fix: The PCARRD guide top dresses urea at half to one bag (25 to 50 kg) per hectare after each harvest. Both guides also side dress manure or compost once a month at 20 to 30 bags per hectare, or drench diluted manure tea (1 part to 20 parts water).
entries.prevent: Apply compost or manure at 3 to 5 tonnes per hectare when preparing the plots, as both guides advise.

sources.title: PCARRD (UPLB IPB): Alugbati production guide, Information Bulletin 269/2009
Bureau of Plant Industry: Alugbati production guide
PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in alugbati
entries.hint: Older leaves get bronze, brown edges that curl down.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn greyish green then bronze or yellowish brown, and the edges brown and cup down with specks along the veins. Stems are slender and roots weak.
entries.stage: Later harvests.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy watering that leaches nutrients (the BPI guide warns against over irrigation for this reason), and feeding with urea only.
entries.confuse: Leaf spot from Cercospora or Colletotrichum makes round spots across the leaf, not edge burn.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium.
entries.fix: Use complete 14 14 14 or muriate of potash based on the soil test. The PCARRD cost table budgets 6 bags of 14 14 14 per hectare. Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Feed complete fertilizer, not only urea, and keep adding compost.

sources.title: PCARRD (UPLB IPB): Alugbati production guide, Information Bulletin 269/2009
Bureau of Plant Industry: Alugbati production guide
PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in alugbati
entries.hint: Cuttings root and grow slowly, with small, dark green leaves.
entries.symptoms: Growth is held back without yellowing. Stems are slender and leaves are small and darker green, and some leaves show a reddish purple tint underneath. Cuttings are slow to establish.
entries.stage: Establishment of cuttings or seedlings.
entries.causes: Acid or iron rich soils, low organic matter, and no phosphorus at planting.
entries.confuse: The red stemmed alugbati is naturally purplish. Judge by growth, not color alone.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: Use complete 14 14 14 at planting based on the soil test, and add compost. Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Apply compost or manure at 3 to 5 tonnes per hectare during plot preparation, as the PCARRD guide advises.

sources.title: PCARRD (UPLB IPB): Alugbati production guide, Information Bulletin 269/2009
PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in alugbati
entries.hint: Older leaves yellow between the veins, sometimes with a reddish purple tint.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn yellow between the veins while the veins stay green. Leaves become brittle with upturned edges, and some plants show reddish purple color instead of yellow.
entries.stage: After several harvests.
entries.causes: Acid soils, heavy potash, and liming with plain lime only.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage yellows the whole leaf.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium, potassium and pH.
entries.fix: Spray magnesium sulfate on the leaves and correct acid soil with dolomite. Follow the soil test for rates.
entries.prevent: Use dolomite on acid beds.

sources.title: PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops

entries.name: Iron deficiency in alugbati
entries.hint: On limed or alkaline soil, the newest leaves turn pale yellow between green veins.
entries.symptoms: New leaves turn light yellow between the veins, then over the whole leaf, usually without dead spots, while older leaves stay green.
entries.stage: Any stage on alkaline or heavily limed soil.
entries.causes: Alugbati is grown on soils up to pH 8. The PNW handbook notes iron shortage is mostly a problem of alkaline or overlimed soils. Waterlogging can also bring it on.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage starts on the older leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test.
entries.fix: Stop liming and spray ferrous sulfate or iron chelate on the leaves. Follow the product label.
entries.prevent: Do not overlime, and add compost, which helps keep iron available.

sources.title: Bureau of Plant Industry: Alugbati production guide
PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in saluyot
entries.hint: Lower leaves turn pale yellow and plants grow thin, hard stems with few tender tops.
entries.symptoms: Older, lower leaves fade to yellowish green and yellow, and the yellowing moves up the plant. Stems are slender, hard and fibrous, leaves are small, and plants flower early with few tender tops to pick.
entries.stage: From about two weeks after sowing to the last picking.
entries.causes: Low organic matter, sandy soils, heavy rain, and repeated pickings without feeding.
entries.confuse: Root knot nematodes, which stunt saluyot, also yellow plants. Check the roots. Drought also yellows and wilts saluyot, which is sensitive to dry soil.
entries.confirm: Lower leaves yellow first. The DA guide recommends a soil test for N, P and K.
entries.fix: The DA guide notes saluyot responds well to organic fertilizer, with rates set by soil fertility and a soil test. A light side dressing of urea or ammonium sulfate after picking speeds regrowth. Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Work compost or manure into the soil before sowing.

sources.title: Department of Agriculture: Mga Katutubong Gulay (Indigenous Vegetables) guide
PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in saluyot
entries.hint: Seedlings stay small and dark green with thin, woody stems.
entries.symptoms: Growth is slow without yellowing. Stems are slender and woody, leaves small and darker green, and some leaves show a reddish purple tint underneath.
entries.stage: Seedling and early growth. Saluyot seedlings are already slow and weak against weeds.
entries.causes: Strongly acid or iron rich soils, low organic matter and cold or waterlogged soils.
entries.confuse: The red stemmed Pula variety is naturally purplish.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: Use complete 14 14 14 at sowing based on the soil test, and add compost. Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Prepare the soil well with organic matter before sowing, as the DA guide advises.

sources.title: PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops
Department of Agriculture: Mga Katutubong Gulay (Indigenous Vegetables) guide

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in saluyot
entries.hint: Older leaves bronze and brown at the edges and curl down.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn greyish green then bronze or yellowish brown, with brown edges that cup down. Stems are slender and roots are poor.
entries.stage: After several pickings.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain, and feeding with urea only.
entries.confuse: Spider mite feeding bronzes leaves too, but with fine speckling and webbing under the leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium.
entries.fix: Use complete 14 14 14 or muriate of potash based on the soil test. Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Use complete fertilizer and compost rather than urea alone.

sources.title: PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops

entries.name: Iron deficiency in saluyot
entries.hint: On limed or alkaline soil, the newest top leaves turn pale yellow between green veins.
entries.symptoms: New leaves at the top turn light yellow between the veins, then over the whole leaf, while older leaves stay green. In a greenhouse study on white jute (a close relative of saluyot), iron was the first micronutrient to show symptoms when left out and one of the most limiting for growth.
entries.stage: Seedling and early growth on alkaline soil.
entries.causes: The DA guide says saluyot tolerates pH 4.5 to 8.0 and that going beyond that range reduces iron in the soil for the plant. Overliming and waterlogging add to it.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage starts on the older leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test.
entries.fix: Stop liming and spray ferrous sulfate or iron chelate on the leaves. Follow the product label.
entries.prevent: Keep soil pH within the 4.5 to 8.0 range the DA guide gives, and add compost.

sources.title: Department of Agriculture: Mga Katutubong Gulay (Indigenous Vegetables) guide
Bioscience Journal: Growth and symptoms of deficiency of micronutrients in young plants of jute

entries.name: Boron deficiency in saluyot
entries.hint: New leaves and tips are small, brittle and deformed, and roots stay short.
entries.symptoms: New leaves and leaf stalks are light, brittle and deformed, internodes are short and the shoot tips rosette, and roots grow poorly. In the white jute study, boron was one of the two micronutrients that most limited growth and its absence cut root growth.
entries.stage: Early growth, especially on sandy soil in dry spells.
entries.causes: Sandy, leached soils, overliming, low organic matter and drought.
entries.confuse: Mite damage also distorts young leaves. Look for mites under the leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron.
entries.fix: Apply boron only after a soil test, at a light rate. Follow the soil test. Do not repeat doses.
entries.prevent: Keep organic matter up. Source note: boron advice here rests on a jute study, not saluyot field trials.

sources.title: Bioscience Journal: Growth and symptoms of deficiency of micronutrients in young plants of jute
PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in celery
entries.hint: Oldest outer stalks turn evenly yellow and then almost white.
entries.symptoms: The oldest leaves turn an even yellow first and eventually white, and the yellowing moves up to younger leaves. Growth slows, stalks stay thin and fibrous, and the plant is small at harvest.
entries.stage: From about three weeks after transplanting to harvest. Celery has a high nitrogen need.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain or watering, low organic matter, and too few top dressings for a long, hungry crop.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage keeps the veins green on old leaves. Root damage from carrot fly larvae or root rot also yellows plants. Check the roots.
entries.confirm: Soil test and leaf tissue test. Hill Labs samples the youngest mature leaf with its stalk when plants are half grown.
entries.fix: Top dress nitrogen in split doses. Teagasc tops up celery with up to 200 kg nitrogen per hectare in two or more doses, about three weeks after transplanting and again three weeks later. Advises calcium nitrate rather than ammonium forms to help prevent blackheart.
entries.prevent: Apply basal nitrogen based on the soil test (Teagasc gives 50 to 100 kg per hectare depending on the soil index) and add manure or compost.

sources.title: Hill Laboratories: Crop guide celery
Teagasc: Celery technical note 2020

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in celery (blackheart)
entries.hint: The young heart leaves in the centre turn brown to black and rot.
entries.symptoms: The young leaves in the centre of the plant turn brown, then black, and the growing tip dies and decays. It can hit scattered plants or a whole field.
entries.stage: Fast growth in hot or dry weather, often after a heavy watering of a dry field.
entries.causes: Calcium does not move well inside the plant. So dry soil, irregular watering, and excess potassium or sodium stop it reaching the heart. Heavy nitrogen, especially ammonium, makes it worse.
entries.confuse: Bacterial soft rot of the heart smells and is slimy from the start. Blackheart begins with browning of the young leaf tips.
entries.confirm: Look at the heart leaves of several plants. Soil test for calcium, potassium and pH.
entries.fix: At the first signs, Teagasc sprays calcium nitrate at 10 to 20 kg in 1,000 liters of water per hectare (10 to 20 grams per liter). Smaller regular sprays prevent it. Keep watering steady.
entries.prevent: Never let the crop go dry, use calcium nitrate for top dressing instead of ammonium nitrogen. Lime acid soil (celery grows best near pH 6.5 to 6.8).

sources.title: Teagasc: Celery technical note 2020
Hill Laboratories: Crop guide celery

entries.name: Boron deficiency in celery (cracked stem)
entries.hint: Stalks crack across or split along the veins, like claw marks.
entries.symptoms: The skin of the leaf stalks splits along the veins (called cat's claw) or cracks across, and the cracks turn brown. New leaves and stalks are light, brittle and deformed, with short spaces between them and rosetting at the tips.
entries.stage: Mid growth to harvest.
entries.causes: Low soil boron, sandy or overlimed soils, dry spells. Celery is prone to both boron shortage and boron excess, and some varieties are more sensitive.
entries.confuse: Growth cracks from sudden heavy watering are fewer and clean. Boron cracks are many and browned. Too much boron burns leaf edges instead.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Teagasc advises a couple of foliar boron sprays after planting on top of a boron containing basal fertilizer. Follow the product label for the rate, and do not overdo it, because celery is also hurt by excess boron.
entries.prevent: Use a basal fertilizer that contains boron on sandy or limed fields and choose less sensitive varieties.

sources.title: Teagasc: Celery technical note 2020
PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops
Hill Laboratories: Crop guide celery

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in celery
entries.hint: Older leaves look ashy grey green, then bronze, with brown, downturned edges.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves look ashy grey green, then bronze or yellowish brown, with brown edges that cup down and small specks along the veins. Stalks are slender and woody and roots are poor.
entries.stage: Mid growth to harvest. Celery needs a lot of potassium.
entries.causes: Sandy or acid soils, heavy rain, and low potash rates for a crop with a very high potassium need.
entries.confuse: Too much potassium is also a problem, since it brings on blackheart. Balance matters.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Apply potash based on the soil test. Teagasc gives 175 to 375 kg of potassium per hectare for celery depending on the soil test index, usually through a compound fertilizer that also carries boron.
entries.prevent: Base potash on a soil test and avoid going far above it, to limit blackheart.

sources.title: Teagasc: Celery technical note 2020
PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in celery
entries.hint: Older leaves yellow between the veins while the veins stay green.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn yellow between the veins while the veins stay green. Leaves become brittle and their edges curl up, and in some plants the yellow areas take a reddish purple tint.
entries.stage: Mid growth to harvest.
entries.causes: Acid soils, heavy potash fertilizer, and heavy liming with calcium lime only.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage yellows the whole leaf. Manganese shortage starts on new leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium and potassium, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Spray magnesium sulfate on the leaves and correct the soil with dolomite or magnesium sulfate. Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Use dolomite rather than plain lime on acid soil, and keep potash balanced.

sources.title: PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Key nutrient deficiencies in vegetable crops
TNAU Agritech Portal: Celery nutrient deficiency photos

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in celery
entries.hint: Plants stay small with slender stalks and dark green leaves.
entries.symptoms: Growth is held back without yellowing. Stalks are slender and woody, leaves are small and darker green, and some plants show a reddish purple cast on leaf undersides.
entries.stage: Seedling and early growth.
entries.causes: Acid or iron rich soils, cold or waterlogged soils, and low phosphorus at planting. Celery has a high phosphorus need.
entries.confuse: Root damage also stunts plants. Check the roots.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: Apply phosphorus at planting based on the soil test. Teagasc gives 28 to 88 kg of phosphorus per hectare for celery depending on the soil index.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soil and band phosphorus near the transplants.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in tomato
entries.hint: Lower leaves turn pale yellow first and the plant looks thin and spindly.
entries.symptoms: The oldest, lowest leaves turn pale green and then yellow, and the yellowing climbs up the plant as the shortage gets worse. Leaflets stay small and stand upright, and the veins on the underside can look pink or purple. Shoots are thin, flower buds may yellow and drop, and the fruits that set stay small. In bad cases the old leaves turn fully yellow or brown and fall off.
entries.stage: Any time, but most often from early growth to fruit set when the plant is growing fast.
entries.causes: Sandy or light soils, heavy rain or heavy watering that washes nitrogen down, low organic matter. Fresh straw or raw manure that ties up nitrogen while it rots. Very low or very high soil pH also makes it worse.
entries.confuse: Sulfur shortage also makes the plant pale. But it starts on the young top leaves, while nitrogen starts on the old bottom leaves. Magnesium shortage leaves the veins green on the old leaves. With nitrogen the whole leaf, veins included, turns pale.
entries.confirm: Look at where the yellowing starts (bottom leaves first). A soil test for organic matter and a leaf tissue test give a firm answer. A quick check is to spray a few plants with urea and see if new leaves green up within a week.
entries.fix: Side dress with urea or ammonium sulfate based on your soil test, split into small doses. For a fast green up, spray urea at 10 grams per liter of water. KAU suggests repeating every 15 days and TNAU gives two sprays one week apart. Water after side dressing so the fertilizer reaches the roots.
entries.prevent: Mix compost or well rotted manure into the beds and split nitrogen into several side dressings instead of one big dose. Do not bury fresh straw or raw manure just before planting.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in tomato
entries.hint: Old leaves get scorched, curled edges and the fruit ripens in green or yellow blotches.
entries.symptoms: The edges of the older leaves turn yellow, then brown and dry, and the scorch moves in between the veins. Small whitish dead spots can appear inside the yellow areas, and the leaf edges curl. On the fruit, patches near the stem stay green or yellow when the rest turns red. The flesh under them is firm and tasteless. Fruit can also be soft, hollow or poorly colored.
entries.stage: Most often from fruit set to harvest, when the fruits pull a lot of potassium out of the leaves.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, acid soils, heavy rain or irrigation that leaches potassium, soils with low potassium reserves, and soils rich in magnesium. Drought and cool cloudy weather make blotchy ripening worse.
entries.confuse: Salt damage also burns leaf edges. A salty soil or irrigation water test tells them apart. Magnesium shortage yellows between the veins of old leaves but the edges usually stay alive longer. Blotchy ripening can also come from heat or cloudy weather, so check the leaves too.
entries.confirm: A soil test for exchangeable potassium and a leaf tissue test. The University of Kentucky notes that a leaf test, or a handheld potassium meter on leaf sap, shows the plant's potassium status.
entries.fix: Apply muriate of potash or sulfate of potash based on your soil test, split into two or three side dressings. For a quick fix, spray sulfate of potash at 10 grams per liter of water with a sticker in the morning. TNAU gives three sprays one week apart. On acid soil, lime or dolomite helps the plant hold and use potassium.
entries.prevent: Give potassium before flowering and again during fruiting, add organic matter, and keep soil pH above 6.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in tomato (blossom end rot)
entries.local: Bulok sa puwitan ng bunga ng kamatis
entries.hint: A dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom end of the fruit, opposite the stem.
entries.symptoms: A small light brown or water soaked spot appears at the blossom end of young green fruit. It grows into a sunken, dark brown to black, leathery patch with a sharp border, and the fruit often ripens early. Some fruits have hard brown tissue inside with no outside mark. In severe cases the top leaves curl, their edges die and the growing tip dies.
entries.stage: Early fruit growth, usually on the first fruit clusters and in hot, dry spells.
entries.causes: Usually not a lack of calcium in the soil but uneven watering: when the soil dries out or stays waterlogged, too little calcium moves with water into the fruit. Sandy and acid soils, salty soil, too much nitrogen or potassium, root damage and large fruited or elongated varieties raise the risk.
entries.confuse: Sunscald makes a pale or white patch on the side facing the sun, not at the bottom end. Fruit rots from disease are soft and often show mould from the start. Blossom end rot starts dry and leathery and only gets mouldy later.
entries.confirm: Check the pattern first: bottom end of the fruit, early fruits, after a dry spell. A soil test for calcium and pH tells you if lime or gypsum is needed. Keep a watering record to see if the soil has been drying out between waterings.
entries.fix: Water deeply and regularly so the root zone never dries out or stays soggy, and mulch to hold moisture. TNAU suggests a calcium chloride spray at 5 grams per liter of water, three times two weeks apart. On acid soil, KAU suggests lime at about 250 kg per hectare when pH is 5.5 to 6, or about 840 kg per hectare split in two doses when pH is 3.5 to 4.5. Use gypsum on soil that is not acid. Remove damaged fruits. They will not recover.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soil before planting, mulch, water on a steady schedule, and avoid heavy nitrogen or ammonium fertilizer. Calcium nitrate as part of the side dressing supplies both nitrogen and calcium.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in tomato
entries.hint: Small, stiff, dark bluish green plants with purple undersides on the lower leaves.
entries.symptoms: Plants stay small with thin stems and few side branches, and the leaves turn dark blue green. The undersides of the older leaves and their veins turn purple or reddish, starting at the edges, and leaflets curl down. Later the old leaves get brown dead patches, yellow and drop early. Roots are small and brownish, and flowering and fruit set are delayed.
entries.stage: Seedling and early growth after transplanting, especially in cool weather.
entries.causes: Strongly acid soils and iron rich soils that lock up phosphorus, very alkaline soils, low organic matter, cold or waterlogged soil, and weak or damaged roots.
entries.confuse: Cold nights alone can turn seedlings purple for a while even when soil phosphorus is fine. The color fades once it warms up. Nitrogen shortage makes leaves pale, not dark green.
entries.confirm: A soil test for available phosphorus and pH, plus a leaf tissue test if the soil looks fine.
entries.fix: Apply phosphorus at planting based on your soil test, placed in the hole or band near the roots, not broadcast on top. For a quick boost, TNAU suggests spraying DAP at 10 grams per liter of water, twice two weeks apart. Correct very acid soil with lime so phosphorus stays available.
entries.prevent: Use a starter of 16 20 0 or 14 14 14 at transplanting, keep the soil near pH 6 to 7, and add compost or manure.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in tomato
entries.hint: Lower leaves turn yellow between green veins, starting from the leaf edge, while fruits are filling.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn yellow or yellow orange between the veins while the main veins stay green. The yellowing starts at the leaf edges and moves inward. Small whitish to light brown dead spots form in the yellow areas. The problem moves from the bottom of the plant upward, and in bad cases whole lower leaves die and yield drops.
entries.stage: Fruit set and fruit filling, when the plant moves magnesium from old leaves to the fruits.
entries.causes: Sandy and acid soils, heavy rain, and heavy use of potash or ammonium fertilizer, which push magnesium out of the root zone and block its uptake.
entries.confuse: Iron and manganese shortage also yellow between the veins but on the young top leaves. Nitrogen shortage yellows the whole leaf, veins too. Potassium shortage scorches the leaf edges brown before the areas between veins turn yellow.
entries.confirm: Leaf tissue test and a soil test for magnesium and potassium. A high potassium to magnesium balance points to magnesium shortage.
entries.fix: Spray magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) at 20 grams per liter of water, twice two weeks apart (TNAU). For the soil, KAU suggests magnesium sulfate in a band near the plants at about 80 kg per hectare. TNAU suggests dolomite at about 2 tonnes per hectare on acid soil. Do not apply potash and magnesium fertilizer at the same time.
entries.prevent: Use dolomite instead of plain lime on acid soil and keep potash rates in line with the soil test.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in tomato
entries.hint: Brittle leaf stalks that snap, a dying tip, and fruits with rough, cracked or corky skin.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves stay small, curl inward and become misshapen, with yellow to orange spots between the veins. Leaf stalks become brittle and snap easily. The growing tips of the main shoot and side shoots can die, and stems become thick, stiff and short. Fruits ripen unevenly and show rough, cracked skin or corky pits, and some fruits are hollow.
entries.stage: Flowering and fruit set, and after dry spells.
entries.causes: Sandy soils where boron washes out, soils low in organic matter, overliming or alkaline soil, heavy nitrogen or calcium, and drought.
entries.confuse: Calcium shortage also kills the growing tip but brings blossom end rot and dead leaf edges. Fruit cracking also comes from sudden heavy watering after a dry spell. Boron cracking comes with brittle stalks and deformed tops.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available boron and a leaf tissue test. Boron has a narrow safe range, so confirm before applying more than one dose.
entries.fix: Spray borax at 1 gram per liter of water (KAU), or up to 3 grams per liter twice two weeks apart (TNAU). For the soil, KAU gives borax at about 10 kg per hectare. Do not mix borax with calcium or ammonium fertilizers in one application, and never double the dose. Too much boron burns leaf edges.
entries.prevent: Include boron in the basal fertilizer on sandy or heavily limed fields and keep organic matter up.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in tomato
entries.hint: Short, bunched shoots with small, stiff, leathery leaves that curl down.
entries.symptoms: Leaves are small, thick and leathery, and the leaflet edges curl down. Yellowing shows between the veins and along the midrib, which can turn white in bad cases. The spaces between leaves on the stem become short, so the plant looks bunched and stiff. Growth and fruiting both drop.
entries.stage: Early vegetative growth, especially after a cold or waterlogged spell.
entries.causes: High pH or overlimed soil, soils very high in phosphorus or heavily fertilized with phosphorus, waterlogged soil, and organic or peaty soils.
entries.confuse: Herbicide drift also twists and narrows leaves. Zinc shortage shows yellowing between the veins and short internodes over a whole patch. Iron shortage yellows young leaves but they keep their normal size and shape.
entries.confirm: Soil test for zinc and pH, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU suggests a morning spray of zinc sulfate at 2 grams plus calcium carbonate (or lime) at 2.5 grams per liter of water. Soil zinc sulfate at about 20 kg per hectare on deficient fields. TNAU gives zinc sulfate sprays twice two weeks apart. Do not apply zinc and phosphate fertilizer at the same time.
entries.prevent: Avoid heavy phosphorus beyond the soil test, keep pH between 5 and 7.5. Add zinc sulfate to the basal fertilizer where tests show low zinc.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in tomato
entries.hint: Young top leaves turn pale yellow green, stiff and curled down, with purple stems.
entries.symptoms: It looks like nitrogen shortage but starts on the young leaves at the top. Leaves turn light green to yellow, often more between the veins, and become stiff and curl downward. Stems, veins and leaf stalks can turn purple, and stems become hard and woody. Old leaves may get dead tips and edges with small purple spots.
entries.stage: Early growth on light soils, and after long rainy periods.
entries.causes: Sandy soils where sulfate washes out, low organic matter, acid soils, waterlogged soils. Long use of fertilizers with no sulfur such as urea and muriate of potash alone.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage starts on the old bottom leaves. Sulfur starts on the young top leaves. Iron shortage keeps the veins sharply green on young leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for sulfate and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Switch part of the nitrogen to ammonium sulfate, or use sulfate of potash for the potassium. TNAU suggests gypsum at 50 kg per hectare in the soil, or a spray of calcium sulfate at 10 grams per liter twice two weeks apart. KAU gives sulfur dust at about 25 kg per hectare on sulfur deficient soil.
entries.prevent: Use some sulfur containing fertilizer every season and keep organic matter up.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in tomato
entries.hint: New top leaves turn yellow with a fine net of green veins, but keep their normal shape.
entries.symptoms: The young leaves at the shoot tips turn yellow between the veins while the veins stay green, giving a net pattern. The leaves are small but not deformed. As it gets worse, the whole tip turns yellow and the leaves can become almost white, veins included.
entries.stage: Any stage, often after heavy watering or on limed soil.
entries.causes: High pH, calcareous or overlimed soil, waterlogged soil, and soil high in copper, manganese or zinc. Many Philippine soils are acid and rich in iron, so true iron shortage is uncommon there. Check pH first.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage looks similar but starts on old lower leaves. Manganese shortage also hits young leaves, but more veins stay green and small dead spots appear. Waterlogged or damaged roots can give the same yellow tips.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test first, then a soil or leaf test for iron. KAU warns that low potassium can also bring on iron yellowing.
entries.fix: TNAU suggests spraying ferrous sulfate at 5 grams per liter of water on the leaves. KAU gives ferrous sulfate at about 15 kg per hectare in the soil only where a test shows iron is low. Improve drainage and stop liming.
entries.prevent: Do not overlime, and keep beds well drained.

entries.name: Manganese deficiency in tomato
entries.hint: Young leaves get orange yellow mottling between green veins with tiny dark brown dots.
entries.symptoms: Orange yellow mottling starts between the veins near the leaflet tip and spreads over the leaflet while the veins stay green. Very young leaves show many small dark brown dead spots. Leaves are smaller, sometimes narrow and long, and roots are smaller than normal.
entries.stage: Vegetative growth and early flowering.
entries.causes: High pH or overlimed soil, sandy soil, organic soil, and cold, wet spells.
entries.confuse: Iron shortage gives a cleaner yellow with no dead dots. Magnesium shortage starts on old leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil pH and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Spray manganese sulfate at 2 grams per liter of water (KAU). TNAU uses a stronger 5 grams per liter, twice two weeks apart. Avoid more lime until the pH is checked.
entries.prevent: Keep soil pH near 6 to 6.5 and do not overlime.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in eggplant
entries.hint: Bottom leaves turn pale yellow, plants stay thin, and fruits come small and pale.
entries.symptoms: Yellowing starts on the older, lower leaves and moves up the plant. Plants are stunted and spindly with small leaves. Fewer flowers open and fewer fruits set, and the fruits that form are small and pale.
entries.stage: From early growth through the long harvest period, when the plant keeps flowering and fruiting.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain or watering that leaches nitrogen, low organic matter, and too long a gap between side dressings during harvest.
entries.confuse: Sulfur shortage yellows the young top leaves first and turns veins reddish. Magnesium shortage keeps the veins green on the old leaves.
entries.confirm: Note that the bottom leaves yellow first. Confirm with a soil test and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Side dress with urea or ammonium sulfate based on your soil test, in small split doses through the harvest season. For a quick green up, KAU suggests a urea spray at 10 grams per liter of water, once every 15 days.
entries.prevent: Add compost or manure at bed preparation and side dress regularly once harvesting starts, since every picking removes nitrogen.
