entries.name: Potassium deficiency in eggplant
entries.hint: Older leaves get scorched, crinkled edges and stems feel weak.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves show dead tissue along the edges and between the veins, then curl, crinkle and look scorched. The plant makes fewer leaves, the stems are weak, and roots and fruits develop poorly.
entries.stage: Fruiting and harvest, when the fruits draw potassium from the leaves.
entries.causes: Sandy or acid soils, heavy rain that leaches potassium, and long harvest seasons with no potash side dressing.
entries.confuse: Salt burn also scorches leaf edges. Test the water or soil salt if fertilizer was heavy. Magnesium shortage yellows between the veins of old leaves without first browning the edges.
entries.confirm: Soil test for exchangeable potassium and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Apply muriate of potash based on your soil test, preferably in split doses. For an immediate remedy, KAU suggests a morning spray of sulfate of potash at 10 grams per liter of water with a sticker. Keep soil pH above 6 with lime or dolomite.
entries.prevent: Include potash in the basal fertilizer and in side dressings during harvest. Add organic matter.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in eggplant
entries.hint: Stems, leaf stalks and the undersides of old leaves turn purplish and the plant stays short.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves are affected first. Stems, leaf stalks and leaf undersides, especially along the veins, turn purplish. Plants stay stunted, leaf tips and edges can scorch, and roots and fruits develop poorly.
entries.stage: Seedling and early growth after transplanting.
entries.causes: Strongly acid or iron rich soils that hold phosphorus tightly, low organic matter, cold or waterlogged soil.
entries.confuse: Purple color on young seedlings in cool weather can fade on its own. Nitrogen shortage gives pale leaves rather than purple ones.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: Apply the recommended phosphorus fertilizer near the roots based on your soil test. KAU lists single superphosphate for a quick correction and rock phosphate or bone meal for the long term. Phosphorus is best taken up near pH 6.2 to 7.0, so lime very acid soil.
entries.prevent: Use a phosphorus starter at transplanting and add manure or compost.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in eggplant
entries.hint: Mature leaves turn yellow in the middle between green veins, with spotted dead patches.
entries.symptoms: Fully grown leaves turn yellow between the veins while the veins and often the leaf edges stay green. Small dead spots appear in the yellow areas, leaf stalks can show purple mottling, and leaves become deformed and drop early. Yield falls.
entries.stage: Fruiting and the long harvest period.
entries.causes: Sandy acid soils, heavy rain, and heavy potash or ammonium fertilizer that block magnesium uptake.
entries.confuse: Iron and zinc shortage start on the young top leaves. Nitrogen shortage yellows the whole leaf.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium and potassium, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU suggests magnesium sulfate in a band near the plants at about 80 kg per hectare (32 kg per acre). A foliar spray of magnesium sulfate gives faster relief. Do not apply magnesium and potassium fertilizer together.
entries.prevent: Use dolomite on acid soils over the long term.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in eggplant (blossom end rot)
entries.local: Bulok sa puwitan ng bunga ng talong
entries.hint: Brown to black leathery spots at the bottom end of the fruit and curled, hard young leaves.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves are affected first: they crinkle, curl upward and feel hard, and growing tips can die back. The classic sign is blossom end rot, with brown to black leathery spots on the underside or tip of the fruit.
entries.stage: Fruit development, especially in dry spells or with uneven watering.
entries.causes: Uneven or too little watering, fast growth, acid soils low in calcium, high phosphorus. Boron shortage, which the plant needs to use calcium.
entries.confuse: Fruit rots from disease spread fast and grow mould. Blossom end rot starts as a dry, firm patch at the blossom end.
entries.confirm: Soil test for calcium and pH, plus a record of watering. Look for curled hard young leaves together with the fruit spots.
entries.fix: Water evenly and mulch. KAU suggests lime at about 250 kg per hectare when soil pH is 5.5 to 6, or about 840 kg per hectare in two doses when pH is 3.5 to 4.5. Gypsum on soil that is not acid. Check and correct boron too.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soil before planting, keep watering steady, and avoid very heavy phosphorus.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in eggplant
entries.hint: New leaves come out wrinkled and brittle, tips die, and the plant stops branching and flowering.
entries.symptoms: New leaves are misshapen and brittle, with wrinkled bases. Growing tips die, the spaces between leaves are short, and the plant is stunted. Branching and flowering fail, so few fruits set.
entries.stage: Flowering and early fruiting.
entries.causes: Sandy soils where boron leaches, alkaline or heavily limed soils, low organic matter and drought.
entries.confuse: Calcium shortage also hits young tissue but brings blossom end rot. Virus diseases also distort new leaves. Boron problems affect whole patches on the same soil.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU suggests borax in the soil at about 10 kg per hectare (4 kg per acre) or a borax spray at 1 gram per liter of water. Delaware extension lists eggplant among crops with a medium boron need, about 2 pounds of boron per acre before planting. Do not mix borax with calcium or ammonium fertilizer in one application.
entries.prevent: Add boron to the basal fertilizer on sandy or limed fields, but do not repeat doses without a test.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in eggplant
entries.hint: Small, bunched rosettes of yellowish new leaves and flowers that drop without fruiting.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves yellow between the veins, which can turn whitish. Leaves are small, few and distorted or bunched in rosettes, and the spaces between leaves are short. Growth and fruiting slow down and flowers fail to set fruit.
entries.stage: Vegetative growth and flowering.
entries.causes: High pH or overlimed soil, heavy phosphorus fertilizer, and waterlogged soil.
entries.confuse: Iron shortage keeps normal leaf size. Virus diseases also make small mottled leaves. Zinc shortage follows soil patches, not insects.
entries.confirm: Soil test for zinc and pH, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU suggests zinc sulfate in the soil at about 20 kg per hectare (8 kg per acre). In severe cases a morning spray of zinc sulfate at 2 grams plus calcium carbonate at 2.5 grams per liter of water. Do not apply zinc with phosphate fertilizer.
entries.prevent: Keep soil pH between 5 and 7.5 and avoid phosphorus beyond what the soil test calls for.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in eggplant
entries.hint: Young leaves turn evenly yellow, stay narrow and pointed, and veins look reddish.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves turn pale, then yellow overall. Veins and leaf stalks turn reddish, leaves are narrow, pointed and small and curl downward, and growth is held back.
entries.stage: Early growth on light soils.
entries.causes: Sandy, low organic matter soils and long use of fertilizers with no sulfur.

entries.confirm: Soil test for sulfate and a leaf tissue test.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in ampalaya
entries.hint: Lower leaves turn pale yellow and drop, and fruits come small, pale and thick.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn pale green to yellow and may die and drop. Vines are stunted, and fruits are pale, small and thick.
entries.stage: Vine growth and the long harvest period.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain, low organic matter, and missed side dressings. BPI advises side dressing every two weeks in the rainy season because nitrogen washes out faster.

entries.prevent: BPI applies 2 tonnes of processed chicken manure or vermicompost per hectare two weeks before planting and 10 to 15 grams of complete 14 14 14 per hill at planting.

entries.symptoms: Young leaves show yellow stripes along the midrib, crinkle, scorch and become distorted, and new leaves are hooked and curled. The growing tip dies back, plants are stunted, and fruit set is poor or fails.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in chili
entries.hint: Brittle, twisted new leaves and fruits that crack or drop.
entries.symptoms: New leaves are pale, misshapen, brittle and small, and the plant loses its main tip and grows bushy. Fruits stay small and light, crack, and drop before they mature.
entries.stage: Flowering and fruit set.
entries.causes: Sandy soils where boron leaches, heavily limed or alkaline soils, low organic matter and drought.
entries.confuse: Virus diseases also twist new leaves. Check for insects such as thrips and mites, and whether the pattern follows soil patches.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU suggests borax in the soil at about 10 kg per hectare (4 kg per acre) or a borax spray at 1 gram per liter of water. Peppers need only a little boron, so do not repeat doses without a test. Do not mix borax with calcium or ammonium fertilizer.
entries.prevent: Use boron only where tests show low levels, and keep organic matter up.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in chili
entries.hint: Young leaves are small, stiff and mottled yellow, and the plant is short jointed.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves yellow between the veins and can turn whitish. Leaves are small, stiff and brittle, stems are thin, and the space between leaves is short. The crop matures unevenly.
entries.stage: Vegetative growth and early flowering.
entries.causes: High pH or overlimed soil, heavy phosphorus fertilizer, waterlogged soil.
entries.confuse: Leaf curl virus also makes small, crinkled leaves, but it comes with whiteflies on the plants. Zinc shortage shows yellowing between the veins over a whole soil patch.
entries.confirm: Soil test for zinc and pH, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU suggests zinc sulfate in the soil at about 20 kg per hectare (8 kg per acre). In severe cases a morning spray of zinc sulfate at 2 grams plus calcium carbonate at 2.5 grams per liter of water. Do not apply zinc and phosphate together.
entries.prevent: Keep soil pH between 5 and 7.5 and avoid excess phosphorus.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in chili
entries.hint: Young top leaves turn evenly pale and curl down, with reddish veins.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves turn pale then yellow overall, with reddish veins and leaf stalks. Leaves are small, brittle and twisted and curl downward, and growth is held back.
entries.stage: Early growth on light soils.
entries.causes: Sandy, low organic matter soils and fertilizer programs with no sulfur.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage starts at the bottom leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for sulfate and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Use ammonium sulfate or other sulfur containing fertilizer. KAU suggests sulfur dust at about 25 kg per hectare (10 kg per acre) on sulfur deficient soil, and gypsum on alkaline soil.
entries.prevent: Include ammonium sulfate in the program and add organic matter. Do not burn crop residues.

entries.name: Manganese deficiency in chili
entries.hint: Young leaves are mottled yellow with a fine net of green veins and dark spots along the veins.
entries.symptoms: Leaves that are nearly full size show mottled yellowing between the veins, leaving a fine net of green veins on a light green leaf. Young leaves yellow at the edges and dark dead areas form along the veins. Fruits may show raised dark brown to black spots.
entries.stage: Vegetative growth and fruiting.
entries.causes: High pH or overlimed soils, sandy soils, and cold wet spells.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage starts on old leaves. Iron shortage gives a clean yellow without dark spots.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU suggests a manganese sulfate spray at 2 grams per liter of water after a soil test confirms the need.
entries.prevent: Do not overlime. Keep soil pH near 6 to 6.5.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in bell pepper
entries.hint: Lower leaves yellow and fall early, and the whole plant looks pale and small.
entries.symptoms: Growth is badly held back. Lower leaves turn yellow and die early, and the rest of the leaves stay small and pale yellow green. Fewer fruits set and fruit size drops.
entries.stage: From transplanting through fruiting.
entries.causes: Sandy or light soils, heavy rain or irrigation, low organic matter, and raw straw or manure that ties up nitrogen.
entries.confuse: Sulfur shortage starts on the youngest leaves at the top. Magnesium shortage keeps the main veins green on older leaves.
entries.confirm: Bottom leaves yellow first. Confirm with a soil test and leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Side dress urea or ammonium sulfate based on the soil test, in split doses. For a quick green up, KAU gives a urea spray at 10 grams per liter of water every 15 days for chilli, which is the same species.
entries.prevent: Add compost to the beds and split nitrogen through the season.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in bell pepper (blossom end rot)
entries.local: Bulok sa puwitan ng bunga ng atsal
entries.hint: Large sunken, water soaked patches near the bottom of the fruit that turn black and leathery.
entries.symptoms: Large sunken, water soaked spots form near the blossom end of the fruit. They start soft, then dry, harden and turn black, and mould may grow on them. Several spots can form on one fruit, and on young fruit the whole end may rot and the fruit drop. Upper leaves may yellow between the veins with dark brown dead spots on the edges of the youngest leaves.
entries.stage: Early fruit growth. It can appear suddenly and spread over a field in hot dry weather.
entries.causes: Too little calcium reaching the fruit, usually because of uneven watering or dry soil. Acid sandy soils, salty soil, high nitrogen or potassium, and large fruits raise the risk.
entries.confuse: Sunscald makes pale, papery patches on the side facing the sun. Bacterial soft rot is wet and smelly from the start.
entries.confirm: Spots at the blossom end of young fruit after dry spells. Then a soil test for calcium and pH.
entries.fix: Keep the soil evenly moist and mulch. On acid soil, KAU suggests lime at about 250 kg per hectare when pH is 5.5 to 6, or about 840 kg per hectare in two doses when pH is 3.5 to 4.5. Gypsum on soil that is not acid. Remove damaged fruits.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soil before planting, water on a steady schedule, use calcium nitrate as part of the nitrogen, and avoid heavy ammonium fertilizer.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in bell pepper
entries.hint: Dark green leaves droop and wilt, with small sunken whitish spots and burnt edges.
entries.symptoms: Plants are short with small leaves that bend down and look limp and wilted while staying dark green. Leaf edges and the areas between veins yellow, and small sunken, sometimes whitish spots form on the edges. On older leaves these turn into dead patches that join until the leaf looks scorched.
entries.stage: Fruiting.
entries.causes: Sandy or acid soils, heavy rain or irrigation that leaches potassium, drought, and soils high in magnesium.
entries.confuse: Wilting from root disease or dry soil comes without the spotting and edge burn. Magnesium shortage yellows between the veins without wilting.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Apply muriate of potash or sulfate of potash based on the soil test, in split doses. For immediate relief, KAU gives a morning spray of sulfate of potash at 10 grams per liter of water with a sticker for chilli, the same species.
entries.prevent: Include potash at planting and in side dressings during fruiting.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in bell pepper
entries.hint: Small, wilting plants with mottled leaves and short, narrow fruits.
entries.symptoms: In severe cases the whole plant and its leaves are much smaller and the older leaves wilt. Leaves look mottled yellow with dark green patches. A narrow dead strip can form along the main vein near the leaf base. Larger yellow spots near the edge turn grey and die. Fruits are shorter and narrower than normal.
entries.stage: Seedling and early growth, and in cool or wet spells.
entries.causes: Acid or very alkaline soils, iron rich soils that hold phosphorus, low organic matter, cold or wet soils and poor roots.
entries.confuse: Root rot also causes wilting and small plants. Check the roots for rot.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: Apply phosphorus near the roots based on the soil test. KAU lists single superphosphate for a quick fix and rock phosphate or bone meal for the long term. Notes phosphorus is best taken up near pH 6.2 to 7.0.
entries.prevent: Use a phosphorus starter at transplanting and add compost.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in bell pepper
entries.hint: Older leaves go pale between the veins while a green band stays along each main vein.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn pale between the veins while the main veins and a band along them stay green. Sometimes it begins as a faint yellowing at the leaf edge that moves toward the centre. In advanced cases dead patches start at the edge and spread inward, and growth and yield drop.
entries.stage: Fruit set and fruit filling.
entries.causes: Sandy or acid soils, soils rich in potassium, heavy potash fertilizer, and cold wet periods.
entries.confuse: Manganese and iron shortage start on young leaves, where even the smallest veins stay green.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium and potassium, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU gives magnesium sulfate in a band near the plants at about 80 kg per hectare (32 kg per acre) for chilli, the same species. A foliar spray of magnesium sulfate gives faster relief. Do not apply magnesium and potassium fertilizer together.
entries.prevent: Use dolomite on acid soil and keep potash in line with the soil test.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in bell pepper
entries.hint: The youngest top leaves look evenly pale from a distance, with short jointed stems.
entries.symptoms: The youngest leaves at the top turn an even light green while the veins stay darker. Held against light, the green veins show. Some young leaves get a yellow green color between the veins that starts at the leaf base. Plants are stunted with short spaces between leaves.
entries.stage: Early growth on light soils.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy, low organic matter soils, waterlogged soils, and fertilizer programs with no sulfur.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage starts on the old lower leaves. Iron shortage gives a sharper yellow with very green veins on young leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for sulfate and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Use ammonium sulfate or sulfate of potash in the next side dressing. KAU gives sulfur dust at about 25 kg per hectare (10 kg per acre) on sulfur deficient soil for chilli, and gypsum on alkaline soil.
entries.prevent: Include some sulfur fertilizer every season.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in bell pepper
entries.hint: Short, stunted plants with small leaves crowded on short stems.
entries.symptoms: Plants are stunted with shortened spaces between leaves, and the leaves are smaller than normal. Young leaves may also yellow between the veins.
entries.stage: Vegetative growth.
entries.causes: High pH soils, soils rich in phosphorus or given heavy phosphorus, organic soils, and cold wet spells.
entries.confuse: Virus diseases also stunt plants and shrink leaves. They usually come with mosaic or curling and insects such as aphids, thrips or whiteflies.
entries.confirm: Soil test for zinc and pH, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU gives zinc sulfate in the soil at about 20 kg per hectare (8 kg per acre) for chilli. In severe cases a morning spray of zinc sulfate at 2 grams plus calcium carbonate at 2.5 grams per liter of water. Do not apply zinc together with phosphate fertilizer.
entries.prevent: Avoid phosphorus beyond the soil test and keep pH between 5 and 7.5.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in bell pepper
entries.hint: Newest leaves at the tip turn yellow green between dark green veins.
entries.symptoms: The newest leaves at the shoot tips turn yellow green between the veins while the veins stay dark green at first. If the shortage lasts, the veins also pale and the whole leaf turns light. Plants can be shorter with limp leaves.
entries.stage: Any stage, often after heavy watering or liming.
entries.causes: High pH, calcareous or overlimed soils, waterlogged soils, and soils high in copper, manganese or zinc. On acid Philippine soils true iron shortage is uncommon, so check the pH and drainage first.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage starts on old leaves. Manganese shortage also hits young leaves but leaves more small veins green.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test, then a soil or leaf test for iron.
entries.fix: Improve drainage and stop liming. KAU gives ferrous sulfate in the soil at about 15 kg per hectare (6 kg per acre) for chilli where a test confirms low iron. A foliar spray of ferrous sulfate or iron chelate greens leaves faster.
entries.prevent: Do not overlime and keep beds well drained.

entries.name: Manganese deficiency in bell pepper
entries.hint: Young leaves go pale between the veins while even the small veins stay dark green.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves turn pale between the veins while the small veins stay dark green, giving a fine net pattern. Small dark dead spots can form in the pale areas.
entries.stage: Vegetative growth and fruiting.
entries.causes: Organic or sandy soils, high pH, loose fluffy soils, and cold wet weather.
entries.confuse: Iron shortage looks similar on young leaves. Magnesium shortage starts on old leaves and leaves only the main veins green.
entries.confirm: Soil pH and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU gives a manganese sulfate spray at 2 grams per liter of water for chilli, after a soil test confirms the need.
entries.prevent: Do not overlime.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in patola
entries.hint: Older leaves turn yellow, vines grow slowly and fruits stay small and pale.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves on the vine turn pale and then yellow, and the yellowing climbs as the shortage grows. Vines grow slowly and set fewer, smaller and paler fruits.
entries.stage: Rapid vine growth and fruit set, when cucurbits most often run short.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain, low organic matter, and no side dressing before fruiting.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage leaves the veins green on old leaves. Downy mildew gives angular yellow patches between veins.
entries.confirm: Old leaves yellow first. Soil test and leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Side dress urea or ammonium sulfate in one or two doses before fruits form, based on the soil test, as the University of Kentucky advises for cucurbits. For bottle gourd, a related gourd, KAU gives a urea leaf spray at 10 grams per liter of water every 15 days.
entries.prevent: Add manure to the hills before planting and side dress before fruit set.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in patola
entries.hint: Oldest leaves yellow between the veins while fruits enlarge, and the yellow tissue falls out.
entries.symptoms: Yellowing between the veins starts on the oldest leaves and moves up the vine. The yellow tissue may brown, die and drop out, leaving holes.
entries.stage: Fast growth while fruits enlarge.
entries.causes: Sandy soils with low holding capacity, low pH, dry years, and heavy potash, lime or ammonium fertilizer.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage yellows the whole leaf. Manganese toxicity on very acid soil gives bronze spots.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium, potassium and pH.
entries.fix: The University of Kentucky advises keeping soil pH near 6.5 and feeding Epsom salt through drip lines if needed. Leaf sprays rarely fix a serious shortage. For bottle gourd, KAU gives magnesium sulfate in a band at about 80 kg per hectare (32 kg per acre).

entries.name: Boron deficiency in sayote
entries.hint: New leaves and tips come out brittle and deformed, with few female flowers and fruits.
entries.symptoms: New leaves and leaf stalks are light, brittle and deformed, internodes are short and tips rosette. Fruit set is poor.
entries.stage: Flowering and fruit set.
entries.causes: Slightly acid, leached soils where nutrients get fixed, as a TNAU study on sayote points out, plus low organic matter and dry spells.

The best mix gave longer vines, earlier flowers and the highest yield. Boron has a narrow safe range, so test first and do not go beyond the trial dose.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in watermelon
entries.hint: Old leaves pale and yellow up the runner, with small, misshapen fruits.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn pale, yellow and drop, and the yellowing moves up the runners. Vines are stunted, and fruits are pale, small, thick skinned or misshapen, so yield falls.
entries.stage: Vine growth and fruit set.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain or irrigation, low organic matter and no side dressing before fruit set.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage leaves the veins green. Fusarium wilt makes whole runners wilt and the stem turns brown inside.
entries.confirm: Old leaves yellow first. Soil test and leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Side dress urea or ammonium sulfate based on the soil test, before the fruits form. For a quick fix, KAU gives a urea leaf spray at 10 grams per liter of water every 15 days.
entries.prevent: Put part of the nitrogen in before planting and side dress the rest in one or two doses, as the University of Kentucky advises for cucurbits. Avoid heavy late nitrogen.

sources.title: KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Watermelon nutrient deficiencies
University of Kentucky Vegetable Scouting: Nitrogen deficiency of cucurbits

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in watermelon
entries.hint: Old leaves scorch and cup up, and fruits have poor flesh and weak flavour.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves yellow and scorch, then curl upward or cup, with sunken dark spots along the midrib. Browning spreads until leaves dry out. Shoots die back, stems weaken and fewer female flowers form. Fruits can have poor flesh texture, off flavour or spotted skin.
entries.stage: Fruit filling.
entries.causes: Sandy or acid soils, heavy rain or irrigation, and fertilizing with urea only.
entries.confuse: Gummy stem blight and anthracnose also brown the leaves, but as spreading spots that start anywhere on the leaf.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Apply muriate of potash based on the soil test, preferably in split doses. For immediate relief, KAU gives a morning spray of sulfate of potash at 10 grams per liter of water with a sticker. Keep soil pH above 6 with lime or dolomite.
entries.prevent: Give potash at planting and again as fruits enlarge.

sources.title: KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Watermelon nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in watermelon
entries.hint: Mature leaves yellow in the middle with green edges, and the yellow turns red and dies.
entries.symptoms: Mature leaves turn yellow in the middle with green edges and green veins. The yellow areas turn red and develop spotted dead patches, older leaves shrivel and drop early, and yield falls.
entries.stage: Fruit enlargement.
entries.causes: Sandy acid soils, dry years, and heavy potash, lime or ammonium fertilizer.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage yellows the whole leaf. Manganese toxicity on very acid soil gives bronze spots on old leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium, potassium and pH, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU suggests magnesium sulfate in a band near the plants at about 80 kg per hectare (32 kg per acre). The University of Kentucky advises keeping pH near 6.5, feeding Epsom salt through drip lines if needed. Notes leaf sprays rarely fix a serious shortage. Do not apply magnesium with potash.
entries.prevent: Use dolomite on acid soil before planting.

sources.title: KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Watermelon nutrient deficiencies
University of Kentucky Vegetable Scouting: Magnesium deficiency of cucurbit crops

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in watermelon (blossom end rot)
entries.local: Bulok sa puwitan ng bunga ng pakwan
entries.hint: A dark rot at the flower end of young fruits, opposite the stem.
entries.symptoms: Developing fruits rot at the blossom end, opposite the stem, starting as a sunken, leathery patch. Young leaves show yellow stripes along the midrib, crinkle and scorch at the edges, and new leaf tips hook. Growing points can die back, roots are stunted, and fruits may be small or tasteless.
entries.stage: Early fruit growth.
entries.causes: Uneven or too little watering, high humidity, poor root growth or anything else that slows water flow, which leaves the fruit short of calcium for a while. Heavy ammonium fertilizer, root injury and waterlogged soil make it worse.
entries.confuse: Poor pollination gives shrivelled, misshapen young fruits without a leathery rot. Fruit rots from fungi are soft and mouldy.
entries.confirm: Look for the rot on young fruits after dry spells. Soil test for calcium and pH.
entries.fix: Give steady, proper irrigation, avoid root injury and waterlogging, and avoid heavy ammonium fertilizer, as the University of Kentucky advises. On acid soil, KAU suggests lime at about 250 kg per hectare when pH is 5.5 to 6, or about 840 kg per hectare in two doses when pH is 3.5 to 4.5. Gypsum on soil that is not acid.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soil before planting and keep watering even.

sources.title: University of Kentucky Vegetable Scouting: Blossom end rot of cucurbits
KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Watermelon nutrient deficiencies
UC IPM: Blossom end rot

entries.name: Boron deficiency in watermelon
entries.hint: Young fruits drop, and fruits show yellow streaks, corky scurf and cracks.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves are malformed and buds die, making the plant bushy. Young fruits drop or abort, and fruits show mottled yellow streaks, corky scurf on the skin, cracks, small size and early fall.
entries.stage: Flowering and fruit set.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, overlimed soils, low organic matter and drought.
entries.confuse: Poor pollination also drops young fruits but leaves stay normal. Thrips scarring on fruit skin is silvery rather than corky streaks.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU suggests borax in the soil at about 10 kg per hectare (4 kg per acre) or a borax spray at 1 gram per liter of water. Do not mix borax with calcium or ammonium fertilizer.
entries.prevent: Add a small boron dose to the basal fertilizer on sandy fields.

sources.title: KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Watermelon nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in watermelon
entries.hint: Older leaves turn purple along the veins and young leaves are small, stiff and dark.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn purple, especially along the veins. Shoots are short and thin, young leaves are small, stiff and dark green, leaves look dull and shrivel, and vigour and yield drop.
entries.stage: Early vine growth.
entries.causes: Acid or iron rich soils, low organic matter, cold or waterlogged soil, and no phosphorus at planting.
entries.confuse: Root knot nematodes also stunt vines.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: Apply phosphorus in the hill based on the soil test. KAU lists single superphosphate for a quick fix and rock phosphate or bone meal for the long term, with best uptake near pH 6.2 to 7.0.
entries.prevent: Use complete fertilizer or 16 20 0 in the hill at planting.

sources.title: KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Watermelon nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in watermelon
entries.hint: Young leaves pale with green veins, small and bunched on short runners.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves yellow between the veins and can turn white. Leaves are pale with green veins and smaller, the spaces between leaves are short, and leaves form distorted rosettes.
entries.stage: Vine growth.
entries.causes: High pH or overlimed soils, heavy phosphorus and waterlogged soils.
entries.confuse: Mosaic viruses also give small, mottled leaves, often with aphids around.
entries.confirm: Soil test for zinc and pH, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU suggests zinc sulfate in the soil at about 20 kg per hectare (8 kg per acre). In severe cases a morning spray of zinc sulfate at 2 grams plus calcium carbonate at 2.5 grams per liter of water. Do not apply zinc and phosphate together.
entries.prevent: Keep soil pH between 5 and 7.5.

sources.title: KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Watermelon nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in melon
entries.hint: Old leaves pale and yellow up the vine, and fruits are small and misshapen.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn pale to light green, yellow and drop, and the yellowing moves up the shoot. Vines are stunted and fruits are pale, small and misshapen, so yield falls.
entries.stage: Vine growth and fruit set.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain or irrigation, low organic matter, and no side dressing before fruit set.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage, very common in melon, leaves the veins green on old leaves. Molybdenum shortage on acid soil shows pale crown leaves at vining.
entries.confirm: Old leaves yellow first. Soil test and leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Side dress urea or ammonium sulfate based on the soil test, before the fruits form. For a quick fix, KAU gives a urea leaf spray at 10 grams per liter of water every 15 days for Cucumis melo.
entries.prevent: Add manure and split nitrogen. Yara notes too much late nitrogen can lead to fruit blemishes and rots.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in melon
entries.hint: Old leaves scorch and cup up, and fruits are poorly flavoured and spotted.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves yellow and scorch, cup and curl upward, with sunken dead spots along the midrib. Vines die back, stems weaken and fewer female flowers form. Fruits can be spotted, off flavoured and less sweet.
entries.stage: Fruit filling. Melon uses more potassium than nitrogen and most of it moves from the leaves into the fruit.
entries.causes: Sandy or acid soils, heavy rain, and too little potash during fruit filling.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage yellows between the veins first. Potassium burns the edges first.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: Apply muriate of potash or sulfate of potash based on the soil test, in split doses. For immediate relief, KAU gives a morning spray of sulfate of potash at 10 grams per liter of water with a sticker.
entries.prevent: Give potash at planting and again at fruit set, and keep potassium, calcium and magnesium in balance.

sources.title: KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Oriental pickling melon nutrient deficiencies
Yara: Melon nutritional summary

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in melon
entries.hint: Oldest leaves yellow between the veins while fruits are swelling, and the yellow patches fall out.
entries.symptoms: Yellowing between the veins starts on the oldest leaves and moves up the vine. Yellow tissue may brown, die and drop out, leaving a shot hole look, or turn red with spotted dead patches. Older leaves drop early and yield falls. The University of Kentucky says muskmelon shows this more than other cucurbits.
entries.stage: Fast growth while the fruits enlarge.
entries.causes: Sandy soils with low holding capacity, low pH, dry years, and heavy potash, lime or ammonium fertilizer.
entries.confuse: Manganese toxicity on very acid soil can look like it, with water soaked areas under the leaves and yellow or bronze spots on top. A soil pH test tells them apart.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium, potassium and pH, and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: The University of Kentucky advises keeping pH near 6.5 and feeding Epsom salt through drip lines if needed. Leaf sprays rarely fix a serious shortage. KAU gives magnesium sulfate in a band near the plants at about 80 kg per hectare (32 kg per acre) for Cucumis melo. Do not apply magnesium with potash.
entries.prevent: Apply dolomitic lime before planting on acid soil and avoid heavy potassium, calcium or ammonium fertilizer.

sources.title: University of Kentucky Vegetable Scouting: Magnesium deficiency of cucurbit crops
KAU Agri Infotech Portal: Oriental pickling melon nutrient deficiencies
University of Kentucky Vegetable Scouting: Manganese toxicity of cucurbits

entries.name: Molybdenum deficiency in melon
entries.hint: On acid soil, crown leaves turn pale between the veins as vines start to run, then leaf edges burn.
entries.symptoms: Leaves near the crown turn pale green to slightly yellow between the veins around the time plants begin to vine. As it worsens, leaf edges and areas between veins burn and die, and growth stops. Other cucurbits on the same soil often show no signs.
entries.stage: Start of vining.
entries.causes: Heavy soils with pH below 6, and heavy ammonium fertilizer through drip lines, which acidifies the root zone and can also bring manganese toxicity.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage yellows old leaves evenly. Magnesium shortage starts on the oldest leaves and comes later, during fruiting.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test. NSW DPI suggests spraying a few plants with sodium molybdate and checking for normal, greener growth.
entries.fix: The University of Kentucky advises leaf sprays of sodium molybdate and keeping pH at 6.0 to 6.5. NSW DPI gives about 50 grams of sodium molybdate in 100 liters of water as a leaf spray, or about 1 kg per hectare mixed with fertilizer before the next crop.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soil to pH 6 to 6.5 ahead of planting and avoid heavy ammonium feeding.

sources.title: University of Kentucky Vegetable Scouting: Molybdenum deficiency of cucurbit crops
NSW DPI Agfact AC.4: Molybdenum deficiency in plants

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in melon
entries.hint: New leaves crinkle and hook, vine tips die, and fruits are small, soft or tasteless.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves show yellow stripes beside the midrib, crinkle, yellow at the edges and become brittle, and the spaces between leaves shorten. Growing tips die back and roots are stunted. Fruits may be small and tasteless or fail to form.
entries.stage: Vine growth and early fruiting.
entries.causes: Very acid soils, uneven watering, excess phosphorus and low boron. Only a small share of the plant's calcium reaches the fruit, so steady water matters.
entries.confuse: Boron shortage also deforms new growth and drops young fruit.
entries.confirm: Soil test for calcium, pH and boron.
entries.fix: KAU suggests lime at about 250 kg per hectare when soil pH is 5.5 to 6, or about 840 kg per hectare in two doses when pH is 3.5 to 4.5. Gypsum on soil that is not acid. Water evenly.
entries.prevent: Lime before planting and keep calcium, potassium and magnesium in balance.

entries.hint: Young fruits drop, and fruits show yellow streaks, corky marks and cracks.
entries.symptoms: New leaves are malformed and the plant becomes bushy as buds die. Young fruits drop or abort, and fruits show yellow streaks and corky skin marks. Mature fruits may be small, light or cracked.
entries.stage: Flowering and fruit set.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, overlimed soils, low organic matter and drought.
entries.confuse: Poor pollination also drops young fruits but leaves stay normal.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron and a leaf tissue test.
entries.fix: KAU suggests borax in the soil at about 10 kg per hectare (4 kg per acre) or a borax spray at 1 gram per liter of water. Delaware lists muskmelon among crops with a medium boron need, about 2 pounds of boron per acre before planting. Do not mix borax with calcium or ammonium fertilizer.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in melon
entries.hint: Purplish leaves along the veins, small stiff dark young leaves and weak vines.
entries.symptoms: Leaves turn purple, especially along the veins. Shoots are short and thin, young leaves are small, stiff and dark green, and leaves look dull and shrivelled. Vigour, fruit set and yield are poor.
entries.stage: Early growth, and from flowering to fruit fill, when melon needs the most phosphorus.
entries.causes: Acid or iron rich soils, low organic matter, cold or waterlogged soil, and no phosphorus at planting.
entries.confuse: Root knot nematodes also stunt vines.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: Apply phosphorus in the hill based on the soil test. KAU lists single superphosphate for a quick fix, with best uptake near pH 6.2 to 7.0.
entries.prevent: Use complete fertilizer or 16 20 0 in the hill at planting.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in strawberry
entries.hint: Mature leaves turn pale then evenly yellow, with reddish stalks and edges.
entries.symptoms: Mature leaves are hit first: they turn pale green, then evenly yellow, and stay small. As they age, the leaf edges and stalks turn reddish and whole blades can redden. In severe cases lower leaves turn yellow to red with dead blotches and growth is badly stunted.
entries.stage: Runner and leaf growth, and during long fruiting periods.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain or irrigation, low organic matter, raw manure or straw mulch tying up nitrogen. Very low or high pH.
entries.confuse: Sulfur or molybdenum shortage can give similar yellowing. A leaf test settles it. Red leaves on old foliage in cool weather can be normal ageing.
entries.confirm: Leaf tissue test and soil test.
entries.fix: Side dress or fertigate small, frequent doses of nitrogen based on the soil test. Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Add compost before planting and feed little and often rather than one big dose.

sources.title: Yara UK: Nitrogen deficiency in strawberry

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in strawberry
entries.hint: Mature leaves brown and dry along the edges, with sunken brown spots and dark leaf stalks.
entries.symptoms: The first sign is browning and drying along the edges of mature leaves, which spreads inward between the veins. Light and dark brown sunken spots can appear on the blade, with yellowing between the veins. The leaf base, midrib and stalk may darken and, in severe cases, die.
entries.stage: Fruiting.
entries.causes: Acid or sandy soils, heavy rain or irrigation, drought, low potassium reserves and soils rich in magnesium.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage and salt burn give similar edges. Potassium shortage usually also affects the leaf base.
entries.confirm: Leaf tissue test (Yara notes deficient leaves hold less than 0.5 percent potassium) and a soil test.
entries.fix: Apply sulfate of potash or potassium nitrate based on the soil test, in split doses. Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Keep potash in the fertilizer program through fruiting.

sources.title: Yara UK: Potassium deficiency in strawberry

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in strawberry (tip burn)
entries.local: Pagkasunog ng dulo ng dahon ng presa
entries.hint: Young leaves crinkle with dead tips, and berries are small, hard and seedy at the tip.
entries.symptoms: Young leaf blades crinkle and may get dead tips (tip burn), most often during fast leaf growth. Fruits are small, hard and sour, with a dense cluster of seeds at the tip or over the whole berry.
entries.stage: Fast leaf growth and fruiting.
entries.causes: Acid soils, sandy soils, drought, and high nitrogen or potassium. Yara notes deficient leaves hold less than 0.2 percent calcium.
entries.confuse: Boron shortage gives similar leaf symptoms, but its small fruits are bumpy and misshapen.
entries.confirm: Leaf tissue test for calcium and boron, and a soil pH test.
entries.fix: Keep watering even and lime acid soil based on the soil test. Calcium nitrate as part of the feed supplies calcium. Follow the soil test for rates.
entries.prevent: Lime acid beds before planting and avoid heavy nitrogen and potash.

sources.title: Yara UK: Calcium deficiency in strawberry

entries.name: Boron deficiency in strawberry
entries.hint: Misshapen, bumpy berries, aborted flowers and small young leaves with dark dead tips.
entries.symptoms: Leaves yellow between the veins from the edges, medium aged leaves get bronze veins near the edges. The youngest leaves have dark dead tips and stay very small. Flowers are damaged or abort, and poor fruit set gives misshapen, bumpy berries that are smaller and softer. Side roots are stubby and brown.
entries.stage: Flowering and fruit set.
entries.causes: High soil pH or sandy soils where boron leaches, low organic matter, high nitrogen or calcium, and drought.
entries.confuse: Poor pollination from too few bees or cold also gives misshapen berries, but leaves stay normal. Calcium shortage also kills leaf tips.
entries.confirm: Leaf tissue test for boron and calcium before treating.
entries.fix: Apply boron only after a test confirms it. Delaware lists strawberry among crops with a medium boron need, about 2 pounds of boron per acre (about 2.2 kg per hectare) before planting. Do not repeat doses.
entries.prevent: Keep organic matter up and avoid overliming.

sources.title: Yara UK: Boron deficiency in strawberry
University of Delaware Weekly Crop Update: Boron and molybdenum in vegetable crops

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in strawberry
entries.hint: Older leaves turn dull deep green with a metallic sheen and purple undersides.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves are dark green and slightly small, with a purple tint that deepens as they age. Upper surfaces can take a dark metallic sheen while undersides turn reddish purple. In severe cases edges yellow then brown from the tips, and flowers and fruits are smaller, sometimes with pale patches.
entries.stage: Early growth in cold or wet soil, and before flowering.
entries.causes: Cold, dry or wet conditions, strongly acid or alkaline soils, iron rich soils, low organic matter and weak roots.
entries.confuse: Cool weather alone can redden old strawberry leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf stalk tissue test and soil test for available phosphorus.
entries.fix: Apply phosphorus near the roots based on the soil test. Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Use a phosphorus fertilizer at planting and keep the soil near pH 5.5 to 6.5.

sources.title: Yara UK: Phosphorus deficiency in strawberry

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in strawberry
entries.hint: Older leaf edges yellow and scorch, then the leaf turns bright yellow while its base stays green.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves show it first: the edges turn yellow and scorch. Yellowing spreads inward between the veins until the leaf is bright yellow with dead tints. The leaf base stays green longest. Later the oldest leaves can turn fully brown while young centre leaves stay green.
entries.stage: Fruiting.
entries.causes: Sandy or acid soils, soils rich in potassium, heavy potash fertilizer and cold wet weather.
entries.confuse: Potassium shortage and salt damage look similar, but potassium shortage usually also darkens the leaf base.
entries.confirm: Leaf tissue test (Yara notes deficient leaves hold under 0.1 percent magnesium) and soil test.
entries.fix: Spray magnesium sulfate on the leaves for quick relief and correct the soil with dolomite or magnesium sulfate based on the soil test.
entries.prevent: Use dolomite on acid beds and keep potash balanced.

sources.title: Yara UK: Magnesium deficiency in strawberry

entries.name: Iron deficiency in strawberry
entries.hint: The youngest centre leaves turn pale yellow between the veins and can bleach.
entries.symptoms: Yellow or pale yellow color appears between the veins of the youngest leaves. If it lasts, the veins also yellow and leaves bleach, then dead areas spread from the edges, and growth is stunted. Fruits are rarely affected.
entries.stage: Any stage, often after heavy watering or liming.
entries.causes: Soil pH above 6.5, calcareous or overlimed soils, waterlogged soils, and high copper, manganese or zinc. Root damage, including from waterlogging, gives the same look.
entries.confuse: Magnesium and manganese shortage usually do not start on the youngest leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil pH test and leaf tissue test (Yara notes deficient leaves hold less than 40 ppm iron).
entries.fix: Improve drainage, stop liming, and spray iron chelate or ferrous sulfate on the leaves. Follow the product label.
entries.prevent: Keep beds raised and well drained and do not overlime.

sources.title: Yara UK: Iron deficiency in strawberry

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in onion
entries.hint: Pale, stiff, upright leaves that yellow and die back from the tips, and small bulbs.
entries.symptoms: Plants stay short with pale green to yellow leaves that stand stiff and upright and die back from the tips, starting on the older leaves. Bulbs stay small and mature early, and the neck tissue above the bulb turns soft at maturity.
entries.stage: From transplanting to the start of bulbing.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, heavy rain or irrigation that washes nitrogen out, and too little fertilizer.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency yellows the young leaves first. Potassium deficiency first makes leaves darker, with wilting tips.
entries.confirm: Soil test before planting. A tissue test of the tallest leaf before bulbing (Haifa). Check that the oldest leaves yellowed first.
entries.fix: Haifa gives 200 to 300 kg N per hectare for dry bulbs: a quarter or so before planting and the rest in splits every 10 to 14 days for 2 to 2.5 months. For quick help TNAU gives a 1 percent urea (10 g per liter) or 2 percent DAP spray twice, a week apart. A UPLB survey found most Nueva Ecija farmers already use more than 120 kg N per hectare. So check your rate before adding more.
entries.prevent: Split nitrogen and stop before bulbing ends. Late or heavy nitrogen delays maturity, gives soft bulbs and storage rot (Haifa).

sources.title: Haifa: Crop guide, onion nutrient requirements
Haifa: Onion fertilizer and crop guide, nutrition of the onion crop
TNAU Agritech Portal: Onion, nitrogen deficiency
Brown and others, UPLB IPM CRSP report (2008): Management of soil borne diseases of onions in rice and vegetable systems using mycorrhizae

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in onion
entries.hint: Young leaves turn evenly yellow, plants are thin and spindly, and bulbing is late.
entries.symptoms: The young leaves turn evenly yellow first, then the whole plant. Plants are thin, weak and spindly, and bulb formation and maturity are delayed. Bulbs are less pungent.
entries.stage: Before bulbing.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in organic matter, sulfur free fertilizers such as urea and 14 14 14 used for years, and burning crop waste.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency starts on the older leaves. Iron deficiency yellows the youngest leaves completely but is rare.
entries.confirm: Soil and leaf test for sulfur.
entries.fix: Haifa gives 45 to 70 kg of sulfur per hectare, half at planting or transplanting and half before bulbing. On sulfur poor soil, 40 kg of sulfur per hectare as Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 or single superphosphate with the usual NPK raised aggregatum onion yield by about a quarter (TNAU trial). KAU also uses sulfur dust, about 25 kg per hectare.
entries.prevent: Keep a sulfur source such as ammonium sulfate in every crop. Do not drop sulfur from the program even on rich soils (Haifa).

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in onion
entries.hint: Leaves first turn darker green, then the tips of older leaves wilt, droop and turn papery.
entries.symptoms: Foliage first turns darker green, then the tips of the older leaves wilt, especially on the upper side. Leaves droop, turn satiny and then papery, and yellow like nitrogen deficiency. Tip burn and early bolting are common, and bulbs stay small.
entries.stage: Bulb development.
entries.causes: Sandy soils, soils cropped for years without potash, and heavy nitrogen without potash.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency gives pale, not dark, leaves at first. Purple blotch disease gives purple spots with rings.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potassium. Tissue test of the tallest leaf.
entries.fix: Haifa advises putting 30 to 50 percent of the potash in before planting and the rest during bulb development, which increases bulb size. TNAU gives a 1 percent potassium sulfate spray (10 g per liter) twice, a week apart.
entries.prevent: Split potash and keep the soil pH above 6.

Haifa: Onion fertilizer and crop guide, nutrition of the onion crop

Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech Portal: Onion nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in onion
entries.hint: Slow, dull green plants whose leaf tips die back without yellowing, and many thick necked bulbs.
entries.symptoms: Growth is slow and maturity late. Leaves turn a dull green and die back from the tips without the yellowing seen in nitrogen or potassium shortage, and some tips turn reddish. Many bulbs have thick necks or fail to form.
entries.stage: Seedling to early bulbing.
entries.causes: Acid and volcanic soils, cold soils, and fields where the soil fungi that help onion take up phosphorus are few, such as after fumigation.
entries.confuse: Manganese deficiency also gives thick necks but with yellow between veins of older leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test: Haifa keeps available P at 25 ppm.
entries.fix: Haifa adds 1 kg of phosphorus per hectare for every 1 ppm the soil test is below 25 ppm. For a standing crop TNAU gives a 2 percent DAP 18 46 0 spray (20 g per liter) twice, 15 days apart.
entries.prevent: Apply phosphorus at planting, and add organic matter that feeds the root fungi.

sources.title: Haifa: Crop guide, onion nutrient requirements
Haifa: Onion fertilizer and crop guide, nutrition of the onion crop
TNAU Agritech Portal: Onion, phosphorus deficiency
Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech Portal: Onion nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in onion
entries.hint: Stunted plants with twisted, bent leaves and faint yellow stripes.
entries.symptoms: Growth is restricted and leaves twist and bend, with yellow streaks and faint yellowing between the veins. Onion is very sensitive to zinc shortage.
entries.stage: Early growth.
entries.causes: Soils above pH 6.5, over limed soils and heavy phosphorus. Onion is one of the crops with the highest zinc need (UW).
entries.confuse: Herbicide injury also twists onion leaves. Check spray records.
entries.confirm: Soil test for zinc and a leaf test.
entries.fix: Haifa gives 6 kg of zinc per hectare in the basal fertilizer only when a soil test confirms the shortage, since too much is toxic. For a standing crop TNAU gives a 0.5 percent zinc sulfate spray (5 g per liter) twice, 15 days apart.
entries.prevent: Test for zinc before planting on high pH soils.

sources.title: Haifa: Crop guide, onion nutrient requirements
TNAU Agritech Portal: Onion, zinc deficiency
University of Wisconsin Extension A2528: Soil and applied zinc

entries.name: Boron deficiency in onion
entries.hint: Brittle, bluish green, distorted leaves with yellow cross lines and cracks near the base.
entries.symptoms: Plants grow distorted and stunted. Leaves turn brittle and grey green to blue green, young leaves mottle yellow green. Older leaves die back from the tip with sunken areas. Yellow lines across the leaf near the base turn into cracks, and bulbs can crack or split.
entries.stage: Leaf growth to bulbing.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in organic matter, high pH soils and dry spells.
entries.confuse: Calcium deficiency also kills leaf tips but without the cross cracks.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron.

entries.name: Copper deficiency in onion

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in garlic

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in sugarcane
entries.hint: The whole field looks pale yellow green, the lower leaves dry early and the stalks stay thin.
entries.symptoms: The older, lower leaves turn pale first, then the whole stool becomes yellowish green. Old leaves dry from the tips and die early, and leaf sheaths pull away from the stalk too soon. Stalks are thin, internodes stay short and the cane grows slowly. Young leaves stay pale green instead of turning dark green.
entries.stage: Tillering and the grand growth period, when cane takes up nitrogen fastest. Ratoons that got no fertilizer after harvest show it early.
entries.causes: Soils low in organic matter, skipped or late side dressing, and heavy rain that washes nitrogen out of light soils. Urea left on the soil surface also loses nitrogen to the air.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency also makes cane pale, but it starts on the youngest top leaves and does not dry the tips of old leaves. Yellow leaf virus starts as a yellow midrib on the underside of leaves 3 to 6 from the top, not as a pale lower canopy. Drought yellows and rolls leaves too, but they open again after rain.
entries.confirm: Send the top visible dewlap leaf blade (the highest leaf with a visible collar) to a lab during the grand growth period. UF IFAS counts below 1.8 percent N as deficient and 2.0 to 2.6 percent as the target. Ask the SRA soils laboratory for a soil analysis before planting and before each ratoon. A test row given urea that greens up within one to two weeks confirms it.
entries.fix: Side dress Urea 46 0 0 or Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 now, placed beside the row and covered with soil so it is not lost to the air. Split the nitrogen into two or more doses through tillering and early grand growth rather than one big dose. Set the total from the SRA soil analysis, since the right rate depends on the field. For a quick boost, TNAU gives a 1 to 2 percent urea spray (10 to 20 g urea per liter of water) twice, one week apart.
entries.prevent: Fertilize every crop, including each ratoon, from a soil analysis. Return cane trash and add mill mud or compost to build organic matter.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in sugarcane
entries.hint: Old leaves turn yellow orange with scorched edges and red midribs, while the young leaves stay dark green.
entries.symptoms: Older, lower leaves show yellow to orange patches with many small spots that turn brown with dead centers. The edges and tips dry as if scorched. The upper side of the midrib turns red. Young leaves stay dark green, stalks are slender and growth slows. In long deficiency the top bunches into a fan shape and roots stay weak.
entries.stage: Grand growth and ripening, when the cane takes up the most potassium. It gets worse ratoon after ratoon when no potash is given.
entries.causes: Sandy or light soils, acid soils low in exchangeable potassium, and fields cropped for many ratoons without potash. A 100 ton cane crop takes about 150 to 200 kg of potassium out of each hectare.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also starts on old leaves but shows small rusty freckles, not scorched edges. Salt burn and some leaf diseases can also scorch tips or redden midribs, so confirm with a leaf test when in doubt.
entries.confirm: Send the top visible dewlap leaf blade to a lab: UF IFAS counts below 0.9 percent K as deficient and 1.0 to 1.6 percent as the target. A soil test for exchangeable potassium before planting shows how much potash the field needs.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 at the rate the soil test gives, split between planting and the side dressing. For a quick fix on a standing crop, TNAU gives a 1 percent potassium chloride spray (10 g per liter) twice, two weeks apart. Do not overdo it: cane takes up more potash than it needs. Extra potassium raises ash in the juice and lowers sugar recovery.
entries.prevent: Test the soil at every new planting and keep cane trash in the field instead of burning it.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in sugarcane
entries.hint: Leaves look dark bluish green with purple tips and edges, tillers are few and the stalks stay short.
entries.symptoms: Leaves turn dark green to bluish green and stay short and narrow, with red to purple tips and margins. Older leaves yellow and die back from the tip. The cane makes few tillers, roots are poor, and stalks are short and thin, tapering fast toward the top.
entries.stage: Germination to tillering. A shortage at planting is hard to make up later in the crop.
entries.causes: Acid soils that lock up phosphorus and fields that never got phosphate. Sugarcane farms in Bukidnon, for example, tested medium acid with very deficient phosphorus.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency makes leaves pale yellow, not dark bluish green. Potassium deficiency reddens the midrib rather than the leaf tips and edges, and it scorches the old leaves.
entries.confirm: Send the top visible dewlap leaf blade to a lab: UF IFAS counts below 0.19 percent P as deficient and 0.22 to 0.30 percent as the target. Soil test before planting. On acid soil the lab will also give a lime need.
entries.fix: Phosphorus works best placed in the planting furrow at planting, using Ammonium phosphate 16 20 0, Ammonium phosphate 18 46 0 or Superphosphate 0 18 0 at the soil test rate. On a standing crop, TNAU gives a 2 percent DAP spray (20 g of 18 46 0 per liter) twice, two weeks apart, to carry the cane until the next crop. Lime acid fields so the phosphate stays available.
entries.prevent: Lime acid fields to the soil test rate and put all the phosphate in the furrow at planting.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in sugarcane
entries.hint: The top young leaves turn yellow green with purple edges, while the old leaves stay greener.
entries.symptoms: The youngest leaves at the top turn pale yellowish green first. As it gets worse, purple bands show along both leaf margins. Leaves become shorter and narrower, and stalks are thin and bend easily at the tip.
entries.stage: Young cane and fast growth, often after several crops fed with urea only.
entries.causes: Soils low in organic matter, sandy leached soils, and years of urea and other fertilizers that carry no sulfur.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency starts on the old leaves and dries their tips. Sulfur deficiency starts at the top and does not dry the tips. Iron and manganese shortage also yellow young leaves, but in stripes between green veins.
entries.confirm: Send the top visible dewlap leaf blade to a lab: below 0.13 percent S is low in the UF IFAS table. Ask for sulfate sulfur on the soil test. A test row given ammonium sulfate should turn green again.
entries.fix: Use Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 for part of the nitrogen, since it carries sulfur as well. Gypsum or sulfur dust also add sulfur. KAU gives sulfur dust at about 25 kg per hectare (10 kg per acre). For a quick fix TNAU gives a 1 percent potassium sulfate spray (10 g per liter) twice, two weeks apart.
entries.prevent: Use ammonium sulfate for at least one nitrogen dose each crop and keep trash and organic matter in the field.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in sugarcane
entries.hint: Young leaves show a broad yellow band across the middle of the blade, while the midrib and edges stay green.
entries.symptoms: Young, newly opened leaves turn light green to yellow in broad bands. While the midrib and leaf edges stay green until it is severe. The yellow tissue can get red spots, then dries and collapses between the veins. Leaves are shorter and wider at the middle, internodes are short and the cane is stunted.
entries.stage: Young cane and early tillering.
entries.causes: Liming that raises the soil pH, land leveling that exposes low zinc subsoil, sandy soils, and heavy phosphate use.
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency stripes the whole length of the leaf from base to tip and can bleach it white. Manganese stripes start in the middle of the leaf and run to the tip, and the blades split in the wind. Zinc keeps the edges and midrib green with a yellow band between them.
entries.confirm: Send the top visible dewlap leaf blade to a lab: UF IFAS counts below 15 mg/kg Zn as deficient and 17 to 32 mg/kg as the target. Test soil zinc and pH. Spray zinc sulfate on a few stools and watch whether the new leaves come out green.
entries.fix: Spray Zinc sulfate at 0.5 percent (5 g per liter of water) on the leaves, as TNAU advises. Repeat if new leaves still show bands. For the next planting, mix Zinc sulfate into the soil. KAU gives about 20 kg per hectare (8 kg per acre). Do not put zinc in the same application as phosphate fertilizer.
entries.prevent: Lime only to the soil test, and add zinc sulfate at planting on fields that showed bands before.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in sugarcane
entries.hint: Older leaves look rusty, covered with small orange brown freckles.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves get small yellow spots that turn reddish brown, giving the leaf a rusty, freckled look. It can spread to all the leaves, and old leaves drop early. In severe cases stalks are stunted and the inside of the stalk turns brown.
entries.stage: Grand growth, mostly in ratoons on acid, sandy soils.
entries.causes: Acid sandy soils low in magnesium, and heavy potash that blocks magnesium uptake.
entries.confuse: Brown rust and orange rust also give orange brown spots. Rust spots are raised pustules that leave colored powder on your finger, while nutrient freckles do not. Potassium deficiency scorches the leaf edges and reddens the midrib instead.
entries.confirm: Send the top visible dewlap leaf blade to a lab: UF IFAS counts below 0.13 percent Mg as deficient and 0.15 to 0.32 percent as the target. A soil test shows exchangeable magnesium and the balance with potassium.
entries.fix: Apply magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt or kieserite) to the soil. TNAU gives 25 kg per hectare, or a 2 percent magnesium sulfate spray (20 g per liter) twice, two weeks apart. On acid soils, Dolomite raises the pH and adds magnesium. KAU advises not to apply magnesium and potassium fertilizers together.
entries.prevent: Use dolomite rather than plain lime when acid fields need liming. Do not apply much more potash than the soil test asks.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in sugarcane
entries.hint: Older leaves get tiny dead spots and a rusty look, and in bad cases the spindle tip dies.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves show mottling and tiny yellow spots with dead centers that turn dark reddish brown, giving a rusty look, and they die early. Plants are weak with thin, soft stalks. In acute cases the tips and edges of the spindle leaves die and young leaves come out twisted.
entries.stage: Any stage on very acid soils, most visible in young cane.
entries.causes: Very acid soils, below about pH 5.2, where aluminum is high and calcium is low. It is uncommon on soils that are limed.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also gives rusty spots on old leaves. A soil test for calcium, magnesium and pH tells them apart. Boron shortage also kills the spindle, but leaves become brittle with water soaked spots along the edges.
entries.confirm: Send the top visible dewlap leaf blade to a lab: below 0.20 percent Ca is low in the UF IFAS table. Test soil pH and exchangeable calcium. PH below 5.2 means the field needs lime.
entries.fix: Lime acid fields with Agricultural lime or Dolomite at the soil test rate, worked in before planting. On fields where the pH is fine, TNAU gives Gypsum at 100 kg per hectare. Lime needs vary a lot: one study on Bukidnon cane farms set 1.6 to 7 tons of lime per hectare. So always follow the soil test.
entries.prevent: Check soil pH at every planting and lime before it falls below about 5.2.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in sugarcane
entries.hint: Young leaves show pale stripes from base to tip and can turn almost white.
entries.symptoms: The youngest leaves show pale yellow stripes between the veins that run the full length of the leaf, from base to tip. In bad cases the whole leaf, even the veins and midrib, turns white. Roots stay short and the cane is stunted with short internodes. It often shows in patches beside healthy cane, and young plants may grow out of it as roots go deeper.
entries.stage: Young cane and ratoon regrowth.
entries.causes: High pH soils, limestone and other calcareous soils, and over liming. It is rare on the usual acid sugarcane soils.
entries.confuse: Manganese deficiency stripes start in the middle of the leaf and run to the tip, not from the base. Grassy shoot disease also gives white leaves, but the stool throws many thin, grassy tillers.
entries.confirm: Check soil pH first, since iron shortage is mostly a high pH problem. UF IFAS counts below 50 mg/kg Fe in the top visible dewlap leaf as low. A test spray on a few stools that turns the new leaves green confirms it.
entries.fix: Spray Ferrous sulfate at 2.5 to 5 g per liter (250 to 500 g per 100 liters), or 5 kg ferrous sulfate plus 2.5 kg urea in 500 liters per hectare. Repeat every 7 to 10 days until new leaves are green, as TNAU advises. TNAU also gives 25 kg ferrous sulfate per hectare to the soil, or 100 kg mixed with 12.5 tons of farm manure. Stop liming the field.
entries.prevent: Lime only to the soil test and add manure or mill mud on calcareous fields.

entries.name: Manganese deficiency in sugarcane
entries.hint: Pale stripes on the young leaves start in the middle of the blade and run to the tip. The leaves split in the wind.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves show pale stripes between the veins that begin in the middle of the leaf and run toward the tip. The blades may split and fray in the wind, and the edges can curl upward. In severe cases the whole leaf bleaches and a grey purplish shine shows on the upper surface.
entries.stage: Young cane and early grand growth.
entries.causes: High pH or over limed soils, and some very weathered tropical soils.
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency stripes run from the base to the tip of the leaf. Zinc deficiency gives a broad yellow band with green edges and midrib.
entries.confirm: Send the top visible dewlap leaf blade to a lab: UF IFAS counts below 16 mg/kg Mn as deficient and 20 to 100 mg/kg as the target. Check soil pH. Spray a few stools and watch the new leaves.
entries.fix: Spray Manganese sulfate on the leaves. TNAU gives 1 to 2 percent (10 to 20 g per liter) while KAU gives 5 g per liter. So start with the lower rate on a few stools to check for leaf burn. Stop liming until the pH comes down.
entries.prevent: Lime only to the rate the soil test gives.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in pineapple
entries.hint: Plants look pale yellow green with narrow leaves, and the fruits come out small (batterball).
entries.symptoms: Older, lower leaves turn pale green to light yellow first, often starting at the tips, and then the whole plant looks pale. Leaves stay narrow and the plant grows slowly. Fruits come late, small and less sweet. DA Bicol warns that cutting fertilizer doses gives the small fruits farmers call batterball.
entries.stage: Vegetative growth in the first 8 months, before flower induction.
entries.causes: Skipped or late urea doses, sandy and leached soils, and heavy rain.
entries.confuse: Mealybug wilt turns leaves red then pink, with tips dying and curling down and rotten roots. Look for mealybugs and ants at the base. Nematode damaged roots also make plants look hungry even when fertilized. Sulfur shortage yellows the leaves evenly much like nitrogen, so a leaf test helps.
entries.confirm: Leaf color is the quickest guide: healthy pineapple is an intense green, and pale or yellowish green means low nitrogen. For a lab test, send D leaves (the longest, youngest fully grown leaves) at 6 to 8 months. ICL counts below about 1.7 percent N as low. Pull a plant and check the roots for rot, mealybugs or nematode galls before blaming fertilizer.
entries.fix: Apply Urea 46 0 0 or Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 on a split schedule. DA Bicol advises, per hill for Formosa: 10 g Ammonium phosphate 16 20 0 and 5 g Muriate of potash 0 0 60 one month after planting, then 5 g urea at 3, 5 and 7 months. For a quick fix, spray 1 to 2 percent urea (10 to 20 g per liter) every two weeks. From about 12 months, place fertilizer in the axils of the old leaves.
entries.prevent: Do not cut doses or skip splits. Use the free soil test at the DA regional soils laboratory before planting.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in pineapple
entries.hint: Old leaves get yellow to orange spots and dry tips while young leaves stay dark green. The fruit is small and sour.
entries.symptoms: Older, lower leaves get white, yellow or orange spots and streaks that spread in from the tips and edges, and the tips die. The upper leaf surface turns reddish purple while the young leaves stay dark green. Leaves curl down and lose their firmness. Fruits are small and low in sugar, and the flesh can turn brown.
entries.stage: Grand growth and fruit filling, when potassium need is highest.
entries.causes: Sandy, acid soils low in exchangeable potassium and too little potash in the schedule. Pineapple takes up more potassium than nitrogen.
entries.confuse: Mealybug wilt also reddens the leaves, but it starts about halfway up the plant, turns pink and wilts, and the roots rot. Magnesium shortage yellows the old leaves between the veins without the orange spotting and dead tips.
entries.confirm: Send D leaves at 6 to 8 months. ICL counts below about 2.2 percent K as low. A soil test helps too: Haifa notes that little potash is needed where the soil has over 140 ppm exchangeable K.
entries.fix: Keep potash in the schedule. DA Bicol gives 5 g Muriate of potash 0 0 60 per hill at one month and again at about five months for Formosa. Haifa notes pineapple gives better yield and fruit quality with Sulfate of potash 0 0 50 than with the chloride form. For a quick fix, spray potassium sulfate at 1 percent (10 g per liter) every two weeks.
entries.prevent: Set potash from a soil test, and balance it with magnesium because high potassium holds back magnesium uptake.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in pineapple
entries.hint: The young heart leaves turn pale yellow, often on acid red soils that are high in manganese.
entries.symptoms: The youngest leaves in the heart turn pale yellow first, and later the whole leaf goes yellow. Growth slows. On acid soils rich in manganese, whole blocks of the field can yellow even though the soil holds plenty of iron.
entries.stage: Vegetative growth, worst during fast growth.
entries.causes: Two kinds of soil cause it: acid soils very high in manganese, where manganese stops iron from working inside the plant. High pH or limed soils, where iron is locked in the soil.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency yellows the older leaves first, while iron starts in the young heart leaves. Zinc deficiency gives yellow spots and a bent heart (crookneck).
entries.confirm: Test soil pH and manganese. A test spray of ferrous sulfate on a few plants that greens the new heart leaves confirms it.
entries.fix: Spray Ferrous sulfate at 2 to 3 percent (20 to 30 g per liter) monthly or as needed, best mixed into the urea spray, as Haifa advises. Queensland growers add 3 percent ferrous sulfate to the urea spray. Vikaspedia gives a milder 0.5 to 1 percent spray, so try the lower rate first on young plants. Do not lime to fix it: in Hawaii, lime raised root and heart rot. Without iron sprays no calcium source stopped the yellowing.
entries.prevent: On high manganese soils, plan regular iron sprays from the start of the crop.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in pineapple (crookneck)
entries.local: Kakulangan sa zinc ng pinya (baluktot na puso)
entries.hint: The heart leaves bunch together and the top bends over to one side, called crookneck.
entries.symptoms: In young plants the heart leaves bunch together and then tilt over sideways, which is called crookneck. Leaves are narrow and pale, with yellowing between the veins that starts at the tip and leaves only the midrib green. Older plants get yellow spots and dashes near the edges of older leaves that join into brown, blister like patches that feel rough.
entries.stage: Young plants in the first months after planting.
entries.causes: Old pineapple soils and sandy soils low in zinc, high pH or limed soils, and heavy phosphate use.
entries.confuse: Copper deficiency gives narrow young leaves folded into a U shape with drooping tips, but the heart does not bend over. Mealybug wilt makes leaves curl down and turn red to pink. Heart rot makes the heart leaves pull out easily with a rotten base.
entries.confirm: Look for the bent heart in young plants. Send D leaves for a zinc test. Healthy Queensland plants held about 19 mg/kg Zn. Spray zinc on a few plants and watch whether the new leaves come out straight.
entries.fix: Spray Zinc sulfate at 1 percent (10 g per liter), once or twice, as Haifa advises. Vikaspedia gives 0.5 percent (5 g per liter). Where crookneck keeps coming back, mix Zinc sulfate into the soil before planting. KAU gives about 20 kg per hectare (8 kg per acre). Do not mix zinc with phosphate fertilizer in one application.
entries.prevent: On fields with past crookneck, add zinc sulfate at planting and spray young plants once.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in pineapple
entries.hint: Older leaves turn yellow between the veins, most often where potash is applied heavily.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn yellow between the veins while the young leaves stay green. On fruiting plants, the leaves at the base of the fruit crown can die. Yield drops: in Brazilian trials, plants given no magnesium bore less fruit than fully fed plants.
entries.stage: Grand growth and fruit development.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy soils with exchangeable magnesium below about 70 ppm, and heavy potash, which holds back magnesium uptake.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency also starts on old leaves, but it shows orange spots and dry tips. Nitrogen deficiency yellows the whole leaf evenly rather than between the veins.
entries.confirm: Send D leaves at 6 to 8 months. ICL counts below about 0.25 percent Mg as low. Ask for exchangeable magnesium on the soil test.
entries.fix: Where soil magnesium is low, Haifa gives 50 to 120 kg MgO per hectare from a magnesium fertilizer such as Kieserite or magnesium sulfate, keeping MgO to K2O at about 1 to 2.5. ICL notes foliar magnesium works during fast fruit growth. Use magnesium sulfate at the label rate.
entries.prevent: Do not pile on potash without magnesium, and test the soil before each crop.
