entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in pineapple
entries.hint: Leaves stay small and narrow with a purple or bronze color, and the plant barely grows.
entries.symptoms: Leaves are small and narrow with a purplish or bronze color. Older leaves develop dead patches and drop. New leaves can turn reddish purple and fruits get a reddish skin. Plants are stunted with weak roots, and badly starved plants may bear no fruit at all.
entries.stage: Early growth, from planting to about 6 months.
entries.causes: Acid soils that lock up phosphorus and no phosphate at planting.
entries.confuse: Strong sun and drought also redden pineapple leaves, but the plant keeps growing. Phosphorus shortage comes with small, narrow leaves and poor growth. Mealybug wilt turns leaves red then pink, with wilting and rotten roots.
entries.confirm: Send D leaves to a lab. ICL gives 0.2 to 0.3 percent P as the target. A soil test before planting shows available phosphorus.
entries.fix: Give phosphate early: DA Bicol uses 10 g Ammonium phosphate 16 20 0 per hill one month after planting. For a quick fix, Vikaspedia gives a 2 percent DAP spray (20 g of 18 46 0 per liter).
entries.prevent: Put the phosphate in at or soon after planting, at the soil test rate.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in pineapple
entries.hint: The fruitlets crack and turn corky between the eyes, and the flesh browns inside.
entries.symptoms: The fruit shows corky tissue and cracks between the fruitlets, and fruits come out misshapen. Inside, the flesh browns from the center outward, and brownish black areas can show on the skin. Buds and young growth can die back, and fruit set is poor.
entries.stage: Flowering and fruit development.
entries.causes: Sandy, leached soils low in organic matter, and dry spells during fruiting.
entries.confuse: Fruit borers and fruit rots also make brown spots in fruit. But borers leave holes and gum, while boron gives corky lines and cracks between the eyes. Low calcium also browns the inside of the fruit.
entries.confirm: Send D leaves for a boron test. Haifa lists about 14 mg/kg B as optimum in Red Spanish. Test soil boron.
entries.fix: Spray Borax at 0.3 percent (3 g per liter) two or three times late in grand growth, as Haifa advises. KAU gives 1 g per liter and Vikaspedia 0.5 percent. KAU gives soil borax at about 10 kg per hectare (4 kg per acre). Do not overdo boron, because too much is toxic to the plant.
entries.prevent: Add compost to sandy fields, and give one or two boron sprays before fruiting on fields that showed cracked fruit.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in pineapple
entries.hint: Young leaves go pale and curl down, then turn pinkish red, and the fruit is soft or brown inside.
entries.symptoms: Young emerging leaves turn pale green and curl down, later turning greenish pink or red. Root and leaf tips brown and die, and leaf edges become ragged and brittle. Fruit quality falls: low calcium, often with low boron, gives soft fruit with brown flesh inside and more glassy, translucent flesh.
entries.stage: Fast growth and fruit development.
entries.causes: Very acid, leached soils. Growers keep the pH low to avoid rot, so calcium can run short.
entries.confuse: Mealybug wilt also reddens and curls the leaves, but it starts halfway up the plant and the roots rot. Copper deficiency gives narrow U shaped young leaves with drooping tips.
entries.confirm: Send D leaves to a lab. ICL gives 0.4 to 0.7 percent Ca as the target. Test soil pH and calcium.
entries.fix: Use Gypsum to add calcium without raising the pH. In a Hawaii trial gypsum raised calcium in the leaves and fruit and cut translucent flesh. While lime raised the risk of root and heart rot. ICL notes foliar calcium works during fast fruit growth. Use a calcium foliar product at the label rate.
entries.prevent: Use gypsum rather than lime on pineapple fields, and keep boron and calcium in the program.

entries.name: Copper deficiency in pineapple
entries.hint: Young leaves fold up into a narrow gutter shape and their tips droop, then die.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves are narrow, with the edges folded up so the leaf looks like the letter U in cross section. The leaf tip droops, then dies back. The underside looks waxy because it lacks its normal powdery bloom. Badly affected plants are stunted, with short heart leaves and dead older leaves.
entries.stage: From about a year after planting, on poor soils.
entries.causes: Very acid, sandy soils and fields that never got copper.
entries.confuse: Zinc deficiency bends the whole heart over (crookneck), while copper folds each young leaf into a U with a drooping tip. Mealybug wilt makes leaves curl down and turn red to pink.
entries.confirm: Send the white basal part of D leaves to a lab: in a Queensland trial, deficient plants had about 3 ppm Cu while healthy plants in other studies had 8 ppm or more.
entries.fix: TNAU advises copper sulfate in the soil at 30 kg per hectare, because copper sprays can burn the leaves. Haifa gives Bordeaux mixture carrying 7 to 11 kg copper sulfate per hectare.
entries.prevent: On acid sandy soils, include copper in the basal fertilizer when a soil or leaf test shows it is low.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in tobacco
entries.hint: Lower leaves turn paler than the top leaves and dry up early. The plant stays small and the cured leaf is pale and thin.
entries.symptoms: The lower leaves turn paler than the upper ones and then yellow and dry up early, which growers call burning up. The yellowing moves up the stalk as nitrogen moves from old leaves to the new growth. Plants stay short with small, thin leaves, and the cured leaf comes out pale and slick, so both yield and grade drop.
entries.stage: From two to five weeks after transplanting, when the crop grows fastest, up to topping.
entries.causes: Nitrogen washes out of sandy soils quickly after heavy rain or heavy irrigation. Skipping or delaying the sidedress after off barring brings it on.
entries.confuse: Sulfur shortage looks almost the same, but it starts at the bud and the top leaves pale first. While the lower leaves do not burn up. NC State warns that adding more nitrogen to a sulfur short crop will not green it. Leaves that yellow evenly at harvest time are simply ripening, which is normal for tobacco.
entries.confirm: NC State notes that a soil test does not tell how much nitrogen tobacco needs, because nitrogen leaches. Compare the field with the rate and timing your NTA program gives. Send a leaf sample to a lab if you are unsure whether it is nitrogen or sulfur.
entries.fix: Sidedress with Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 along the row as soon as you see it, then hill up. In the NTA 2025 manual, Virginia neutral flavor tobacco gets 4 bags of 10 18 24 at transplanting, then 4 bags of Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 at 21 to 28 days after transplanting. Native tobacco programs use Urea 46 0 0 as the sidedress. Do not overdo it: NC State warns that too much nitrogen delays ripening, makes curing harder and feeds suckers, hornworms and aphids.
entries.prevent: Follow the NTA rate for your tobacco type and split it between transplanting and the sidedress. NTA advises using only 75 percent of the rate on moderately to highly fertile soils.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in tobacco
entries.hint: The tips and edges of the middle leaves turn yellow, then brown to black, and the cured leaf burns poorly.
entries.symptoms: Leaf tips and edges yellow first on leaves in the middle of the stalk. If not corrected, the yellowing spreads to the upper leaves, and in bad cases the yellow tissue turns black and falls away. Leaf yield, quality and price all drop, and leaf low in potash burns poorly.
entries.stage: Mid season to ripening, often during weather extremes: drought, long wet spells or very hot weather.
entries.causes: Potash leaches from deep sandy soils, and dry soil or waterlogged soil slows its movement to the roots. NC State notes that many cases come from the weather and weak roots, not only from a lack of potash in the soil. K+S notes that the dried leaf needs 3 to 6 percent potassium, and shortage shows below 3 percent.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage also yellows lower leaves, but the yellow runs between the veins, starting near the edge and tip, rather than a scorch on the edge itself. Natural ripening yellows the whole leaf evenly from the bottom up.
entries.confirm: Send a leaf sample and a soil test for potash to a lab. Check the soil moisture and the roots, since NC State notes that many cases clear on their own once moisture and root growth improve.
entries.fix: Use Sulfate of potash 0 0 50, not Muriate of potash 0 0 60. NC State advises avoiding muriate because it is about 40 percent chlorine. Chlorine above about 34 kg per hectare (30 pounds per acre) is toxic to the crop. K+S notes that chloride in the leaf spoils burning, color, aroma and storage. In the NTA 2025 manual every potash dose for Virginia and Burley comes as 0 0 50 or the tobacco grade 10 18 24. For example, Virginia neutral flavor gets 1 bag of 0 0 50 sidedressed at 21 to 28 days after transplanting. Add more potash only in extreme cases where rain has leached it, as NC State advises.
entries.prevent: Follow the NTA potash rate for your tobacco type with sulfate of potash. Split it on sandy soils so rain does not wash it away. Keep the soil evenly moist.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in tobacco
entries.hint: Lower leaves yellow between the veins, starting near the tip and edge, while the top stays green.
entries.symptoms: The lower, older leaves yellow between the veins first, starting at the leaf edge near the tip, while the veins stay green. Dead brown patches can form between the veins later. Magnesium moves from old leaves to the new growth, so the top stays green the longest.
entries.stage: Mid to late season. Worst after heavy rain on sandy soil.
entries.causes: Deep sandy soils under heavy leaching, acid soils that were not limed, and heavy potash use. NC State notes it can show even on limed fields when sandy soil is leached hard.
entries.confuse: Potash shortage starts as a yellow scorch on the tip and edge of middle leaves. Manganese shortage also yellows between the veins, but on the upper leaves. Natural ripening yellows the whole leaf, veins included.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test with pH, magnesium and potash, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: NC State advises keeping soil pH at 5.8 to 6.2 with Dolomite, which supplies both calcium and magnesium. Where soils are sandy and leached, they advise 17 to 22 kg of magnesium per hectare (15 to 20 pounds per acre) in the fertilizer. Sulfate of potash magnesia (K Mag, 0 0 22 with 11 percent magnesium) gives magnesium with the potash. Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) also works. Follow the label for a leaf spray.
entries.prevent: Lime with Dolomite rather than plain lime, based on a soil test. NC State notes that a fertilizer with magnesium does not replace liming when soil pH is too low.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in tobacco
entries.hint: The bud and the top leaves pale first, and the whole plant slowly turns light green from the top down.
entries.symptoms: Yellowing starts in the bud and the youngest leaves, and the leaves slowly pale from the top down. Unlike nitrogen shortage, the lower leaves do not dry up early unless nitrogen is also short. Adding nitrogen does not green the plant and can lower leaf quality.
entries.stage: Early to mid season, after heavy rain.
entries.causes: NC State notes it shows most on deep sandy soils very low in organic matter, after heavy rain. When the fertilizer carries no sulfur. Urea gives no sulfur, while Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 and Sulfate of potash 0 0 50 do.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage gives the same pale color, but it starts on the lower leaves, which dry up early. A leaf test is often needed to tell the two apart, as NC State advises.
entries.confirm: Send a leaf sample to a lab. NC State notes that soil tests for sulfur are not reliable.
entries.fix: NC State advises banding 112 to 168 kg per hectare (100 to 150 pounds per acre) of Sulfate of potash 0 0 50 or sulfate of potash magnesia as soon as it is found, before the last hilling up. Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 as the sidedress also adds sulfur.
entries.prevent: Give about 22 to 34 kg of sulfur per hectare (20 to 30 pounds per acre) every year through the fertilizer, as NC State advises. Ammonium sulfate and Sulfate of potash, which the NTA programs use, both carry sulfur.

sources.title: NC State Extension Tobacco Growers Information: Fertility, nutrients (Vann)
NC State Extension: Potassium fertility for flue cured tobacco, nutrient demand, application rates and deficiency
National Tobacco Administration (DA): Tobacco Production Manual 2025 (Virginia, Burley, Native)

entries.name: Boron deficiency in tobacco
entries.hint: The bud twists and dies, the top leaves are thick, brittle and curled down, and the midribs crack across.
entries.symptoms: Plants are stunted early. The growing point twists, and the youngest leaves get kinks, then turn thick and brittle with a ridged feel. The bud soon dies and may drop off, and suckers grow because the top is lost. Whole leaves curl down and crinkle, older leaves turn darker green. In bad cases the midribs crack across near the stem and the stem shows brown spots.
entries.stage: Early, from a few weeks after transplanting. Once signs start, they move fast.
entries.causes: No Philippine reports were found. In general, boron runs short on sandy soils low in organic matter, on soils limed to a high pH, and in long dry spells.
entries.confuse: Calcium shortage also kills the bud and twists new leaves. But NC State notes that calcium shortage curls the leaf edges down, while boron shortage curls the whole leaf down. Hormone weed killer drift also twists new growth.
entries.confirm: Send young leaves to a lab for a leaf test, and test the soil and its pH.
entries.fix: Apply Borax or Solubor to the soil or as a leaf spray, following the label or a soil test. No tobacco rate from a Philippine source was found. Boron is easy to overdo. NC State also lists boron toxicity, so measure the dose with care.
entries.prevent: Keep organic matter up, do not lime above the pH your soil test calls for. Test the soil for boron before planting.

NC State Extension, From the Field Agronomy Notes: Boron deficiency in tobacco
U.S. Borax crop guide: Boron deficiency in drug, fumitory and masticatory crops (tobacco)

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in tobacco
entries.hint: New leaves bend down like a shepherd's crook, their edges yellow and die, and the bud can rot.
entries.symptoms: The edges of the newest leaves turn yellow, and those edge cells die. Because the dead edges cannot grow, the new leaf bends down at the tip like a shepherd's crook. The edges then tear and brown, and in bad cases the growing tip dies with a dark, spongy bud, the plant stops growing and suckers take over.
entries.stage: Fast growth before topping, mostly during drought or waterlogging.
entries.causes: Acid soils low in calcium. NC State notes that it can show even when soil calcium is enough, because drought or waterlogged soil stops the plant from taking it up.
entries.confuse: Boron shortage also kills the bud, but it curls the whole leaf down and cracks the midribs. While calcium shortage curls the leaf edges down first. Drift from hormone type weed killers also twists new leaves.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test with pH and calcium, and a leaf test of young leaves.
entries.fix: Correct acid soil with Agricultural lime or Dolomite, based on a soil test. NC State keeps tobacco soil at pH 5.8 to 6.2. Where lime does not cover it, they give 45 to 56 kg of calcium per hectare (40 to 50 pounds per acre) through the fertilizer. Gypsum adds calcium without raising pH. Water evenly in dry spells.
entries.prevent: Lime before planting, based on a soil test, and avoid long dry spells or waterlogging.

sources.title: NC State Extension, From the Field Agronomy Notes: Calcium deficiency in tobacco
NC State Tobacco Diagnostic Key: Calcium deficiency
NC State Extension Tobacco Growers Information: Fertility, nutrients (Vann)

entries.name: Manganese deficiency in tobacco
entries.hint: Yellow netting between the veins with small white spots, on fields that were limed too much.
entries.symptoms: The leaves yellow between the veins, giving a white netted look. Small white spots then form and grow larger. NC State's diagnostic key shows it on the upper leaves. While their fertility page notes the flecks can look much like weather fleck from ozone.
entries.stage: Mid season, mostly on soils with high pH.
entries.causes: NC State links it to over liming: it shows on soils at pH 6.2 or higher that are low in manganese. It should be rare on acid soils.
entries.confuse: Weather fleck from ozone gives small flecks too, but soil pH is normal. Magnesium shortage yellows between the veins on the lower leaves instead.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test with pH and manganese, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: Use Manganese sulfate as a leaf spray or banded in the soil. NC State gives about 3.4 kg of actual manganese per hectare banded (3 pounds per acre), 11 kg broadcast, or 0.56 kg as a leaf spray. Warns not to broadcast it on soils above pH 6.1.
entries.prevent: Do not lime above the rate your soil test calls for. Keep soil pH at about 5.8 to 6.2.

NC State Extension Tobacco Growers Information: Fertility, nutrients (Vann)

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in cotton
entries.hint: Lower leaves turn pale yellow, then reddish. Plants stay short with few fruiting branches and shed their squares.
entries.symptoms: The older, lower leaves turn light green, then evenly yellow, often starting at the leaf tip. In bad cases the yellow leaves turn red and then die. Plants stay short and weak, with small leaves, few fruiting branches and few nodes, and they hold fewer squares and bolls.
entries.stage: Squaring to boll filling, when most of the nitrogen goes into the fruit.
entries.causes: Sandy, light soils, heavy rain or irrigation that washes nitrogen down, and a late or skipped sidedress. Applying urea at noon or on dry soil also loses nitrogen to the air, as PhilFIDA warns.
entries.confuse: Sulfur shortage also gives pale plants, but it starts on the young top leaves while old leaves stay green. Magnesium shortage reddens old leaves too, but the veins stay green. Normal reddening of old leaves late in the season, as the crop matures, is not a shortage.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test before planting, as Kerala Agricultural University advises. In season, a leaf test of the most recently matured leaf, about four or five nodes below the top, tells the plant's status, as Bayer notes.
entries.fix: Sidedress Urea 46 0 0 3 to 5 cm from the plant base, hill up and irrigate. PhilFIDA sidedresses cotton at 42 to 47 days after planting, or splits it at 35 to 42 and 55 to 60 days on sandy soil. For cotton after garlic it gives 3 to 4 bags of urea per hectare. For a quick boost, KAU gives a urea leaf spray of 10 grams per liter every 15 days. TNAU gives 1 percent urea (10 grams per liter) or 2 percent DAP.
entries.prevent: Band a basal fertilizer at planting and sidedress on time. PhilFIDA's options give 4 bags of Complete 14 14 14 on light soils or 3 bags of 16 20 0 on heavy soils as the basal. Too much late nitrogen is also harmful, as Yara notes.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in cotton
entries.hint: Yellow white mottling on leaf tips and edges that turns brown. Leaves curl, turn reddish brown and drop early, and bolls stay small.
entries.symptoms: Yellowish white mottling starts at the tips and edges and between the veins, then turns into brown dead spots. The edges and tips curl down and break, and the whole leaf turns reddish brown, dry and brittle. Leaves drop early, the crop cuts out early, and bolls stay small, may not open, and give weak lint. Before bloom it shows on the old leaves. Late in the season it can show on the young upper leaves, as the bolls pull potash from them.
entries.stage: From first bloom to boll filling. About 70 percent of potash uptake comes after first bloom, as Yara notes.
entries.causes: Sandy soils that hold little potash, dry soil (potash moves to roots through soil water), acid soil, hardpans or nematodes that limit roots, and soils high in magnesium. High yielding, early varieties are more prone, as UF IFAS notes.
entries.confuse: Leafhopper damage also yellows and reddens leaf edges and makes them curl down. But you will find the small green insects under the leaves. Alternaria and other leaf spots get worse on potash short plants, so check for both. Magnesium shortage reddens old leaves while the veins stay green.
entries.confirm: UF IFAS advises a petiole test at early bloom from the fourth or fifth fully developed leaf from the top. A soil test before planting.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 by soil test, split: UF IFAS suggests a third at planting and two thirds at squaring to early bloom on sandy soils. For quick help, Georgia research cited by UF IFAS gives two leaf sprays of 5.6 to 11 kg of potash per hectare (5 to 10 pounds per acre) during peak bloom, with potassium nitrate as the usual spray. KAU gives Sulfate of potash at 10 grams per liter, and TNAU gives 1 percent potassium chloride.
entries.prevent: Keep soil pH above 6 with lime or Dolomite, as KAU advises, give potash in splits. Keep the soil moist through boll filling.

Bayer Crop Science US: Identifying nutrient deficiencies in cotton

entries.name: Boron deficiency in cotton
entries.hint: Dark green rings on the leaf stalks, many squares and young bolls dropping, and small, misshapen bolls.
entries.symptoms: Leaf stalks get short, with dark green rings or bands. Young leaves turn thick and brittle, with water soaked spots, and new growth can be misshapen. Many squares and young bolls drop, and the bolls that stay are small, flat sided and dark at the base, and mature late. In bad cases the growing tip dies and many short side branches form.
entries.stage: Squaring to boll development, when cotton needs the most boron.
entries.causes: Sandy soils and heavy rain that leach boron, soils above pH 7.5 or over limed soils. Drought, which cuts boron uptake, as Yara notes.
entries.confuse: Heat, drought and plant bugs also make squares and young bolls drop, and bollworms leave holes in bolls. The dark rings on the leaf stalks point to boron. Calcium shortage also hits the growing tip, but boron shortage shows the ringed stalks and boll shedding.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test, as KAU advises. A leaf or petiole test before or at early bloom, which Yara uses to decide on more boron.
entries.fix: Yara gives a base of about 0.56 kg of boron per hectare (0.5 pound per acre), best given as two leaf sprays of 0.28 kg boron per hectare between first square and first bloom. KAU gives Borax at 4 kg per acre (about 10 kg per hectare) to the soil, or a Borax spray of 1 gram per liter. TNAU gives a 0.2 percent Borax spray. Use Solubor for sprays since it dissolves easily, and never overdo the rate.
entries.prevent: Plan boron every season on sandy or limed soils. Do not mix borax with calcium or ammonium fertilizer in one dose, as KAU warns.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in cotton
entries.hint: Lower leaves turn purple red between green veins, then drop early.
entries.symptoms: The lower, older leaves turn purple red between the veins while the veins stay green. In bad cases whitish to brown spots form and the edges die. Affected leaves age early and fall, and plants may look stunted. TNAU describes cupping and yellowing between the veins starting on young leaves. But most sources, KAU and Bayer included, put it on the old leaves first.
entries.stage: From flowering on, when the bolls take up magnesium.
entries.causes: Acid soils, sandy soils that have lost magnesium to rain, and heavy potash use, which competes with magnesium.
entries.confuse: Potash shortage starts at the tips and edges with yellow white mottling and brown spots. Nitrogen shortage reddens the whole leaf, veins included. Late season reddening of old leaves at maturity is normal.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test for magnesium, potash and pH, as KAU advises, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: KAU gives Magnesium sulfate at 32 kg per acre (about 80 kg per hectare) in bands near the plants. TNAU gives a 1 percent Magnesium sulfate leaf spray (10 grams per liter). Do not apply magnesium and potash fertilizer together.
entries.prevent: Use Dolomite on acid soils. KAU notes that long use of dolomite keeps magnesium shortage away.

Bayer Crop Science US: Identifying nutrient deficiencies in cotton

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in cotton
entries.hint: Dark green, stunted plants with reddish purple old leaves and late flowering.
entries.symptoms: Plants stay short and dark green, with small leaves, weak stems and few side branches. Older leaves can turn reddish purple. Roots grow poorly, flowering and boll set come late, and boll numbers drop.
entries.stage: Seedling to early squaring.
entries.causes: Acid soils, which tie up phosphorus, as Bayer notes. KAU notes cotton takes it up best between pH 6.5 and 7.5. Poor soils with no basal fertilizer bring it on.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage also stunts the plant, but leaves are pale, not dark green. Cold or waterlogged soil also slows early growth and can redden seedlings, and it clears as soil warms or drains.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test for phosphorus and pH before planting, as KAU advises.
entries.fix: For quick correction, KAU advises Superphosphate 0 20 0. For the long term, bone meal or rock phosphate. TNAU gives a 2 percent DAP leaf spray (20 grams of Ammonium phosphate 18 46 0 per liter).
entries.prevent: Band a phosphate basal at planting. PhilFIDA's options use 16 20 0 on heavy soils and Complete 14 14 14 on light soils. Lime acid soils.

Bayer Crop Science US: Identifying nutrient deficiencies in cotton

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in cotton
entries.hint: The young top leaves turn pale green to yellow while the old leaves stay green. Plants are small and spindly.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves at the top turn pale green to yellow while older leaves stay green. Veins stay green for a while, but in bad cases they pale too. Plants are small and spindly with thin stalks, few side branches and small bolls.
entries.stage: Early to mid season, after heavy rain or waterlogging.
entries.causes: Sandy, well drained soils low in organic matter and waterlogged soils, as Bayer notes. Using only urea and phosphate fertilizers that carry no sulfur adds to it, and KAU notes that burning crop waste loses sulfur.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage gives the same pale color, but it starts on the old, lower leaves, as TNAU notes. Iron shortage also yellows young leaves, but with green veins standing out sharply.
entries.confirm: A leaf test of young leaves for sulfur and nitrogen together. A soil test helps.
entries.fix: Use a sulfur fertilizer such as Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 or Superphosphate, as KAU advises. On very short soils, KAU gives sulfur dust at 10 kg per acre (about 25 kg per hectare). TNAU gives a 1 percent Magnesium sulfate leaf spray as a quick fix.
entries.prevent: Use Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 for part of the nitrogen, return crop waste instead of burning it, and add organic matter.

sources.title: Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Cotton nutrient deficiencies
TNAU Agritech Portal: Sulfur deficiency in cotton
Bayer Crop Science US: Identifying nutrient deficiencies in cotton

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in cotton
entries.hint: Young leaves thick, leathery and cupped upward, yellow between the veins, on short, bushy plants.
entries.symptoms: New leaves yellow between the veins, starting from the edge, and turn thick, brittle, leathery and cupped upward. Leaves stay small and may look bronzed, and the space between nodes shortens so plants look bushy. TNAU also notes red coloring on old and young leaves and brown spots. Squares and flowers may drop.
entries.stage: Seedling to early squaring.
entries.causes: Soils outside pH 5 to 7.5, as KAU notes, and heavy phosphate use, which ties up zinc.
entries.confuse: Manganese shortage also yellows young leaves between the veins, but TNAU notes zinc short leaves are more misshapen, with long narrow tips. Leafhopper or mite damage also cups and bronzes leaves, so check under the leaves for insects.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test with pH, as KAU advises, and a leaf test. Spray zinc on a few rows and compare the new leaves.
entries.fix: TNAU gives Zinc sulfate at 5 kg per hectare to the soil, or a 1 percent Zinc sulfate leaf spray (10 grams per liter). KAU gives a milder morning spray of Zinc sulfate at 2 grams per liter with 2.5 grams per liter of calcium carbonate. So start with the lower rate on young plants. Do not apply zinc and phosphate fertilizer at the same time.
entries.prevent: Base zinc on a soil test and do not overuse phosphate fertilizer.

TNAU Agritech Portal: Zinc deficiency in cotton
Bayer Crop Science US: Identifying nutrient deficiencies in cotton

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in abaca
entries.hint: Pale yellow green plants that stay short, with thin stalks and small leaves.
entries.symptoms: Abaca is a close cousin of banana and shows nitrogen shortage the same way. Old leaves turn light green, then yellow, and leaf stalks can redden. Plants stay short with thin stalks, small leaves and little leaf area, so the fiber harvest is light. In a Visayas State University trial, plants without nitrogen were the shortest, had the least leaf area and the lowest leaf green color.
entries.stage: From planting through the first harvest, and in old hills that are never fertilized.
entries.causes: Most abaca farmers do not fertilize at all, and every harvest carries nutrients off the farm. Steep, eroded and sandy soils show it first.
entries.confuse: Potassium shortage also stunts abaca, but it scorches old leaf tips orange brown. Bunchy top and mosaic viruses also give weak, yellowish plants, but with streaks, mosaic patterns or bunched narrow leaves.
entries.confirm: A soil test and a leaf test. The PhilFIDA practice code calls for a soil test before opening a new farm and every five years after.
entries.fix: Apply Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 or Complete 14 14 14 after ring weeding, 60 to 90 cm away from the hill. The PhilFIDA code lists ammonium sulfate at planting and at 8 months, then complete fertilizer at 21 months. Established farms get Complete 14 14 14 once a year before or after the rainy season, about a quarter kilo per hill (12 bags per hectare).
entries.prevent: Fertilize every year, return stripping waste and leaves as compost, and plant cover crops on slopes.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in abaca
entries.hint: Old leaves yellow and scorch orange brown from the tip and edges. Short plants.
entries.symptoms: Signs follow banana, its close cousin. Old leaves yellow from the tip, turn orange, then dry brown along the edges, and the midrib may bend. Plants stay short with thin stalks. In a Visayas State University trial, abaca was most sensitive to nitrogen and potassium shortage. Plants without potassium were among the shortest.
entries.stage: From the first months through harvest, and in old hills that are cut often.
entries.causes: Fiber harvests remove potash every cycle, and most farms never return it. Sandy and leached soils under heavy rain lose it fastest.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage also yellows old leaves, but the leaf edge stays green and leaf stalks show purple mottling. Leaf spot diseases show spots and streaks across the leaf rather than a scorch from the tip.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potash and a leaf test.
entries.fix: Apply Complete 14 14 14 as the PhilFIDA code advises, after ring weeding and 60 to 90 cm from the hill. Where the soil test shows low potash, add Muriate of potash 0 0 60 in split doses.
entries.prevent: Fertilize every year and return stripping waste and old leaves to the field.

sources.title: Rosit and others 2025, Macro nutrient deficiency symptoms of abaca var. Inosa grown in nutrient film culture (VSU)
PNS/BAFS 266:2019 Abaca Code of Good Agricultural Practices (PhilFIDA, DA BAFS)

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in abaca
entries.hint: Short pseudostems and narrow leaves. Old leaf edges yellow and young leaves look bluish.
entries.symptoms: In a Visayas State University trial, abaca without phosphorus had shorter pseudostems and narrower leaves, though plant height was close to normal. As in banana, old leaf edges may yellow and die and young leaves can look dark bluish green. Roots stay weak.
entries.stage: Early growth after planting.
entries.causes: Acid soils that lock up phosphorus, and soils low in organic matter. Abaca does best at pH 5.8 to 7.0, so very acid soils bring it on.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage gives pale, not dark, leaves. Poor drainage and root pests also stunt plants.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: Use Complete 14 14 14 at planting and after, as the PhilFIDA code lists, and lime very acid soils. Where the test shows very low phosphorus, add 16 20 0 or Ammonium phosphate 18 46 0, following the soil test.
entries.prevent: Put a phosphorus fertilizer in the planting hole and add compost.

sources.title: Rosit and others 2025, Macro nutrient deficiency symptoms of abaca var. Inosa grown in nutrient film culture (VSU)
PNS/BAFS 266:2019 Abaca Code of Good Agricultural Practices (PhilFIDA, DA BAFS)
Yara Philippines: Phosphorus deficiency in banana (same genus, used for symptoms)

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in abaca
entries.hint: Old leaves yellow in the middle of the blade, edges stay green, leaf stalks show purple blotches.
entries.symptoms: No abaca particular description was found, so this follows banana. Old leaves yellow in the middle of the blade near the midrib while the edge stays green. Leaf stalks show purple mottling, and dead spots form in the yellow parts.
entries.stage: Older hills, especially after heavy potash.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy, leached soils and heavy potash fertilizer.
entries.confuse: Potassium shortage starts at the leaf tip and edge as an orange scorch. Viral mosaic gives streaks and patterns on young leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium, potash and calcium, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: Apply Dolomite on acid soils, or Magnesium sulfate or Kieserite where pH is fine, following the soil test. Do not apply magnesium and potash on the same day.
entries.prevent: Use dolomite when liming and keep potash and magnesium in balance.

sources.title: Yara Philippines: Magnesium deficiency in banana (same genus, used for symptoms)
National Horticulture Board India: Banana manuring and fertilization
PNS/BAFS 266:2019 Abaca Code of Good Agricultural Practices (PhilFIDA, DA BAFS)

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in abaca
entries.hint: Young leaves narrow with yellow stripes between the veins, but no dark streaks like bunchy top.
entries.symptoms: No abaca particular description was found, so this follows banana, where zinc is the most common micronutrient shortage. Young leaves come out smaller and narrower, with yellow and green stripes between the side veins. A purple tint under the rolled new leaf.
entries.stage: Young plants and new suckers.
entries.causes: High pH or limed soils, organic soils and heavy phosphorus.
entries.confuse: Abaca bunchy top virus, spread by the banana aphid, is the bigger worry: it gives small, narrow, bunched leaves with dark green streaks along the veins and the plant stops growing. Zinc shortage has no dark streaks and new leaves recover after a zinc spray. Remove bunchy top plants. Do not spray them.
entries.confirm: Test spray Zinc sulfate on a few plants and watch the next leaves. A leaf test and soil pH help.
entries.fix: Spray Zinc sulfate on young leaves. Banana guides from India give 2 to 5 grams per liter. Follow the soil test for any soil dose.
entries.prevent: Avoid overliming and very heavy phosphorus.

sources.title: Yara Philippines: Zinc deficiency in banana (same genus, used for symptoms)
National Horticulture Board India: Banana manuring and fertilization
PNS/BAFS 266:2019 Abaca Code of Good Agricultural Practices (PhilFIDA, DA BAFS)

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in rubber
entries.hint: Leaves of the lower storeys turn evenly pale yellow green, worst on leaves in full sun, and the canopy stays thin.
entries.symptoms: The whole leaf turns pale yellow green, then yellow. It shows first on the older leaves of the lower storeys and, when severe, moves up to the young storeys. Leaves in full sun show it more than shaded ones. Young trees grow slowly and the canopy stays small, so trees reach tapping size late.
entries.stage: Young trees in the first years after planting, and trees under tapping that are never fertilized.
entries.causes: Young plantations without fertilizer or cover crops, weedy rows that compete for nitrogen, and leached, eroded soils on slopes.
entries.confuse: Rubber sheds its leaves once a year (wintering), and leaves turn yellow to orange before they drop. That is normal and the whole tree changes together. Corynespora leaf fall gives yellow leaves with dark brown veins that look like a railway track. Magnesium shortage yellows between the veins, not the whole leaf.
entries.confirm: The DA guide advises basing fertilizer on soil and leaf tests. Kerala Agricultural University also advises a soil test to judge how severe it is. Sample leaves from the same storey and age on healthy and pale trees.
entries.fix: Without a test, the DA guide gives Complete 14 14 14 at 125 grams per tree in the first year, 250 grams in the second. 500 grams in the third and fourth years, split into two doses six months apart, spread in a ring 30, 60, 90 and 120 cm from the trunk as the tree grows. For trees under tapping, the Rubber Research Institute of Sri Lanka gives about 200 grams of Urea 46 0 0 per tree per year with potash and rock phosphate. For a quick boost, KAU gives a urea leaf spray of 10 grams per liter.
entries.prevent: Plant a legume cover crop between rows, as the DA guide advises, keep the tree rings weeded, and fertilize every year.

sources.title: DA High Value Crops Development Program: Rubber production guide (rubber plantation establishment)
Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Rubber nutrient deficiencies
Rubber Research Institute of Sri Lanka: Fertilizer recommendations for rubber

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in rubber
entries.hint: Old leaves yellow at the tips and edges, then the edges die brown. Leaves come out smaller.
entries.symptoms: Only the older leaves of the lower storeys show it. The tips and edges turn yellow, and then the edges die and turn brown. Leaves get smaller, and in bad cases yellowing between the veins and dead patches spread, leaf stalks and stems shorten, and the bud at the top can die.
entries.stage: Young trees and trees under tapping.
entries.causes: Sandy and leached soils, heavy rain, and trees fed only nitrogen. The Rubber Research Institute of Sri Lanka lists potassium among the nutrients short in most of its rubber soils.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage also starts on old leaves, but it yellows between the veins inward from the edge, without the brown edge scorch. Leaf diseases such as Colletotrichum leave spots spread over the blade, not a band along the edge. Drought can also scorch leaf edges.
entries.confirm: Soil and leaf tests, as the DA guide and Kerala Agricultural University advise.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 based on a soil test, in split doses, as KAU advises. KAU gives a quick leaf spray of Sulfate of potash at 10 grams per liter. For trees under tapping, the Rubber Research Institute of Sri Lanka gives about 200 grams of Muriate of potash per tree per year on virgin bark. 150 grams on renewed bark.
entries.prevent: Use a complete fertilizer such as 14 14 14 in young trees and straight potash once trees are tapped. Keep cover crops and mulch.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in rubber
entries.hint: Old leaves in the lower storeys yellow between the veins, the yellow moving in from the edge while the veins stay green.
entries.symptoms: Leaves in the lower, older storeys yellow between the veins first. The yellow usually spreads inward from the leaf edge while the veins stay green. In young seedlings and buddings, the yellow patches may sit away from the edge. Leaf size drops only a little, but severe cases bring heavy leaf fall and slow growth.
entries.stage: Young and mature trees. Kerala Agricultural University notes it shows most from September to December in Kerala.
entries.causes: Acid, leached soils low in magnesium, and heavy potash use. Some clones are more sensitive. The Rubber Research Institute of Sri Lanka gives clone RRIC 102 a 25 percent larger magnesium dose.
entries.confuse: Potash shortage also starts on old leaves, but scorches the tip and edge brown. Manganese shortage keeps the midrib and main veins as green bands on a pale leaf, but with no dead tips or edges. Normal wintering yellows the whole leaf before it drops.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test, as KAU advises, and a leaf test of leaves from the lower storey.
entries.fix: KAU gives 50 kg of Magnesium sulfate per hectare for plantations that show the yellowing. The Rubber Research Institute of Sri Lanka adds Dolomite to the yearly fertilizer on low magnesium soils, from 50 to 75 grams per tree in the first year up to 150 to 250 grams per tree from the fifth year to tapping. Warns not to mix dolomite with urea based mixtures. Kieserite is another source. Do not apply magnesium and potash together.
entries.prevent: On acid, low magnesium soils give magnesium every year with the fertilizer. Keep potash and magnesium in balance with a soil test.

Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Rubber manuring
Rubber Research Institute of Sri Lanka: Fertilizer recommendations for rubber

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in rubber
entries.hint: Bronzing under part of the leaf, often on one half and at the far end, with dying leaf tips and early leaf fall.
entries.symptoms: A bronze color shows on part of the underside of the leaf and is hard to see from the top. It is often limited to one half of the leaf and starts at the far end of the blade. The leaf tip often dies back. It shows first on leaves in the middle and upper storeys, and many leaves can fall.
entries.stage: Young trees on poor soils.
entries.causes: Old, weathered acid soils that hold phosphorus tightly, and no phosphate at planting. The Rubber Research Institute of Sri Lanka lists phosphorus among the nutrients short in most of its rubber soils.
entries.confuse: Mites and thrips can also bronze the leaf underside, so check with a hand lens. Potash and magnesium shortage start on the lower, older storeys, not the middle and upper ones.
entries.confirm: Soil and leaf tests, as Kerala Agricultural University and the DA guide advise.
entries.fix: For quick correction, KAU advises Superphosphate 0 20 0. For the long term, rock phosphate or bone meal. The Rubber Research Institute of Sri Lanka uses rock phosphate in its mixtures and about 100 grams per tree per year for trees tapped on virgin bark.
entries.prevent: Put phosphate in the planting hole and use a complete fertilizer such as 14 14 14 in the first years, as the DA guide does.

DA High Value Crops Development Program: Rubber production guide (rubber plantation establishment)

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in rubber
entries.hint: In young plants, new leaflets come small, narrow, hooked like a claw and wavy edged, with yellow between the veins.
entries.symptoms: It shows mostly in young rubber plants in the nursery or the field. New leaves yellow between the veins and come out smaller, both shorter and narrower. Young leaflets look hooked or claw like, the blade can twist, and the edges turn wavy. In bad cases the growing tip dies and side shoots grow from below it.
entries.stage: Nursery and young field plants.
entries.causes: Soils outside pH 5 to 7.5, as Kerala Agricultural University notes, and heavy phosphate use, which ties up zinc.
entries.confuse: Powdery mildew and Colletotrichum leaf disease also twist and spot young leaves. But they leave white powder or dark spots and patches on the leaflets. Manganese shortage pales young leaves too, but they keep their normal shape.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test, as KAU advises. Spray a few plants with zinc to see if the next flush comes out normal.
entries.fix: KAU gives Zinc sulfate at 40 grams per plant (8 kg per acre) to the soil. In severe cases, KAU gives a morning leaf spray of Zinc sulfate at 2 grams per liter with 2.5 grams per liter of calcium carbonate. Do not apply zinc and phosphate fertilizer at the same time.
entries.prevent: Add compost to nursery soil and test nursery and young field soils for zinc.

sources.title: Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Rubber nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in oil palm
entries.hint: Orange spots on the leaflets of old fronds that join into orange patches.
entries.symptoms: Pale green spots appear on the leaflets of older fronds, then turn orange and run together. Old fronds dry early, the middle of the crown yellows, and new fronds stay short. Fruit ripens unevenly and bunches are small and light.
entries.stage: Young and bearing palms. The most common deficiency in oil palm.
entries.causes: Oil palm needs more potash than any other nutrient, and most soils run short unless it is given. Sandy soils and heavy rain make it worse. In an Indonesian smallholder study, potassium shortage was found in over 80 percent of farms, because most farmers relied on cheap NPK and skipped straight potash.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage also hits old fronds, but the whole frond goes bright orange yellow, and shaded parts of a leaflet stay green. Leaf spot diseases leave brown spots with no orange spread.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of frond number 17 is the standard sample. Also a soil test.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 in two splits a year, spread in a 2 meter circle and forked in. TNAU lists 2.7 kg of potash (K2O) per palm per year from the third year, which is about 4.5 kg of Muriate of potash. Follow your soil and leaf test.
entries.prevent: Give straight potash every year, not only NPK, and return empty fruit bunches and pruned fronds to the field.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in oil palm
entries.hint: Old fronds pale yellow green with bright yellow midribs, and slow growth.
entries.symptoms: The older, lower fronds turn pale yellow green first while new fronds stay greener. Midribs can turn bright yellow. Growth slows, fronds stay short, and yields drop.
entries.stage: Young palms after planting, and palms on wet or weedy sites.
entries.causes: Poorly drained or waterlogged soils, weeds and grass competing in the circle, sandy soils and no fertilizer.
entries.confuse: Sulfur shortage also yellows fronds, but starts on the young ones. Waterlogging alone can cause the same yellowing, so check drainage first.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of frond number 17. Check drainage and weed cover in the circle.
entries.fix: Apply Urea 46 0 0 or Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 in the weeded circle in two splits a year. TNAU lists 1.2 kg of nitrogen per palm per year from the third year (about 2.6 kg Urea). Fix drainage on wet sites.
entries.prevent: Keep the circle weeded, keep legume cover between rows, and fertilize every year.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in oil palm
entries.hint: Leaflet tips on new fronds bend into a hook. In bad cases fronds look like a fish bone.
entries.symptoms: The first sign is a hook at the tip of the leaflets on young fronds, with crinkled leaflets. Then leaflets fail to open and break easily, fronds come out short and fan shaped, and the tip ends in bristles. In severe cases fronds carry only tiny leaflets like a fish bone, and the bud can rot dry. Fruit set is poor and bunches can drop early.
entries.stage: Young palms most, and any age after a dry season.
entries.causes: Oil palm removes a lot of boron each year. Sandy soils, heavy rain followed by dry spells, and high pH bring it on. Smallholders often skip boron because it seems costly.
entries.confuse: Hooked or crinkled new fronds can also follow insect damage to the spear or bud rot. But boron shortage shows the same hook on many fronds and returns after dry months.
entries.confirm: Look for hooked and fused leaflets on the newest fronds. Leaf test of frond number 17 for boron.
entries.fix: Apply Borax to the soil around the palm. TNAU gives 50 to 200 grams of Borax per palm depending on age and severity. 100 grams per palm per year as routine. U.S. Borax gives about 50 grams of its Fertibor product per young palm per year, rising to 100 to 200 grams.
entries.prevent: Give a small boron dose every year with the main fertilizer. Too much boron is toxic, so stay within the rates.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in oil palm
entries.hint: Old fronds turn bright orange yellow, but the shaded part of each leaflet stays green.
entries.symptoms: Older fronds turn yellow then bright orange, the so called orange frond. A clear sign is that parts of a leaflet shaded by other leaflets stay dark green while the sunlit parts yellow. In bad cases the leaflet tips and edges die and old fronds dry up. Fruit set and bunch size drop.
entries.stage: Young and bearing palms, often after heavy potash.
entries.causes: Sandy, acid, leached soils, and heavy potash fertilizer, which pushes magnesium out.
entries.confuse: Potassium shortage shows orange spots that join up rather than a whole frond that yellows, and it has no green shaded patches. The two often come together.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of frond number 17 for magnesium and potash, and a soil test.
entries.fix: Apply Magnesium sulfate or Kieserite in the circle. TNAU gives 500 grams of Magnesium sulfate per palm per year. On acid soils Dolomite also works. Do not apply magnesium and potash on the same day.
entries.prevent: Keep magnesium in the yearly program whenever potash rates are high.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in oil palm
entries.hint: Old fronds dull olive green and dying early. A thin, tapering trunk and small bunches.
entries.symptoms: In seedlings, older leaves turn a dull, pale olive green. In older palms, the old fronds dry early, the trunk stays narrow and tapers like a pyramid, and roots are shallow. Flowering drops and bunches stay small.
entries.stage: Seedlings and young palms most.
entries.causes: Acid, weathered soils that lock up phosphorus, and soils low in organic matter. Indonesian smallholder farms showed phosphorus shortage in 40 to 60 percent of fields.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage makes fronds yellow green rather than dull olive. Poor drainage and grass competition also give thin, slow palms.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and a leaf test of frond number 17.
entries.fix: Apply a phosphorus fertilizer in the circle in two splits a year. TNAU names rock phosphate as the best source and lists 0.6 kg of phosphate (P2O5) per palm per year from the third year. Superphosphate acts faster. Follow the soil test.
entries.prevent: Put phosphorus in the planting hole and keep up yearly doses.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in bamboo
entries.hint: The clump turns pale yellow green, older leaves yellow first, and new shoots come few and thin.
entries.symptoms: No bamboo particular description of this shortage was found, so this follows general plant signs for grasses and leafy plants. Older leaves turn pale green to yellow first, then the whole clump looks light green. Few new shoots come up, and the culms that form are thin and short. Bamboo needs nitrogen in larger amounts than phosphorus or potash, as the VSU study notes.
entries.stage: Young plantings and old clumps that are cut every year without feeding.
entries.causes: Yearly harvests of shoots and poles carry nitrogen away, and most clumps are never fertilized. Eroded slopes and sandy riverbanks low in organic matter make it worse.
entries.confuse: Bamboo also drops old leaves in the dry season and while new shoots grow, which is normal. Spider mites leave fine yellow to white specks and webbing under the leaves, and rust leaves orange to brown powdery spots underneath. Gregarious flowering also turns a whole clump yellow, but the clump fills with flower heads and then dies.
entries.confirm: A soil test for nitrogen and organic matter. In the Dumanjug, Cebu study, the most productive kawayan tinik plots had about 0.89 percent soil nitrogen and 4.8 percent organic matter. Clumps that push more and greener shoots after feeding confirm it.
entries.fix: For old kawayan tinik clumps, an MMSU study in Batac found that 2 kg of Complete 14 14 14 per clump per year, together with sanitation cutting, gave more and bigger shoots and culms. For nursery plantlets, a VSU study found 0.25 grams of nitrogen per plant was enough. Ammonium sulfate worked better than calcium nitrate. 0.25 grams of nitrogen is about 1.2 grams of Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0.
entries.prevent: Fertilize clumps every year, keep the leaf litter under the clump, and remove old and dead culms. ERDB trials in Pampanga found that bamboo harvested every year needed fertilizer to keep up shoot and culm production.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in bamboo
entries.hint: Older leaves yellow and scorch brown at the tips and edges.
entries.symptoms: No bamboo particular description of this shortage was found, so this follows general plant signs for grasses and leafy plants. Older leaves yellow and then dry brown at the tips and edges, while the middle of the leaf stays green longer. New shoots and culms stay smaller.
entries.stage: Clumps harvested every year, on sandy or leached soils.
entries.causes: Sandy, leached soils and heavy harvests. In the Dumanjug, Cebu study, exchangeable potassium was one of the soil traits that predicted the number of new shoots. The best plots had about 206 ppm.
entries.confuse: Bamboo also drops old leaves in the dry season and while new shoots grow, which is normal. Spider mites leave fine yellow to white specks and webbing under the leaves, and rust leaves orange to brown powdery spots underneath. Drought and salt spray near the coast also scorch leaf tips, so check where the clump grows.
entries.confirm: A soil test for potash. Compare with the Dumanjug productive plots, which had about 206 ppm exchangeable potassium.
entries.fix: Use a complete fertilizer such as Complete 14 14 14, as in the MMSU study, or add Muriate of potash 0 0 60 where a soil test shows potash is low. No bamboo potash rate from a Philippine source was found, so follow the soil test.
entries.prevent: Return leaf litter and chopped branches to the clump, and fertilize every year.

MMSU Batac: Effects of sanitation cutting and fertilizer application on the rejuvenation of old kawayan tinik stands (Philippine E Journals)
University of Delaware Cooperative Extension: Identifying nutrient deficiencies in ornamental plants (general signs)

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in bamboo
entries.hint: Clumps spread slowly and send up few shoots. Leaves may look dull dark green.
entries.symptoms: No bamboo particular description of this shortage was found, so this follows general plant signs for grasses and leafy plants. The clump spreads slowly and sends up few new shoots and culms. Leaves can look dull dark green and growth is slow, especially in young plantings.
entries.stage: The first years after planting, and on old, poor soils.
entries.causes: Acid, weathered and eroded soils that hold phosphorus. In the Dumanjug, Cebu study, available phosphorus helped explain clump spread, culm numbers and shoot numbers. The best plots had about 13.9 ppm.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage also cuts shoot numbers, but leaves turn pale instead of dark. Root and rhizome damage from digging or waterlogging also slows clumps.
entries.confirm: A soil test for available phosphorus and pH, compared with about 13.9 ppm found in the productive Dumanjug plots.
entries.fix: Put phosphate in the planting hole and feed clumps with a complete fertilizer such as Complete 14 14 14 or 16 20 0. Superphosphate 0 20 0 can be added where a soil test shows phosphorus is low. Follow the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Add compost or manure at planting and keep the leaf litter in place.

MMSU Batac: Effects of sanitation cutting and fertilizer application on the rejuvenation of old kawayan tinik stands (Philippine E Journals)
University of Delaware Cooperative Extension: Identifying nutrient deficiencies in ornamental plants (general signs)

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in bamboo
entries.hint: Older leaves get yellow streaks between green veins. Culms stay thin.
entries.symptoms: No bamboo particular description of this shortage was found, so this follows general plant signs for grasses and leafy plants. Older leaves yellow between the veins, which in a grass leaf shows as yellow streaks along green veins. Culms come thinner and lighter.
entries.stage: Established clumps on acid, leached soils.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy and leached soils. In the Dumanjug, Cebu study, exchangeable magnesium was one of the soil traits that best predicted culm diameter, culm height and culm dry weight. Productive plots had about 1,135 ppm.
entries.confuse: Bamboo also drops old leaves in the dry season and while new shoots grow, which is normal. Spider mites leave fine yellow to white specks and webbing under the leaves, and rust leaves orange to brown powdery spots underneath. Iron shortage also streaks leaves, but it shows on the new leaves at the tips of branches.
entries.confirm: A soil test for magnesium, potash and pH.
entries.fix: On acid soil, apply Dolomite, which supplies magnesium and raises pH. Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) or Kieserite can also be used. No bamboo rate from a Philippine source was found, so follow the soil test.
entries.prevent: Keep potash and magnesium in balance with a soil test and lime acid soils with dolomite.

University of Delaware Cooperative Extension: Identifying nutrient deficiencies in ornamental plants (general signs)

entries.name: Iron deficiency in bamboo
entries.hint: New leaves turn yellow with green veins, on limestone or high pH soils.
entries.symptoms: No bamboo particular description of this shortage was found, so this follows general plant signs for grasses and leafy plants. The newest leaves turn yellow while the veins stay green. In bad cases whole new leaves turn yellow to white and their edges may brown.
entries.stage: New growth, on high pH soils.
entries.causes: Iron is locked up in alkaline soils above about pH 7.5, especially where limestone is plentiful, as Arizona extension notes. Waterlogged or compacted soil makes it worse. It should be rare on the acid soils where most Philippine bamboo grows.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage yellows the older leaves first, not the new ones. Magnesium shortage streaks the older leaves. Mite damage gives speckles, not a clean yellow with green veins.
entries.confirm: A soil test for pH. A test spray of iron on a few branches. Leaves that green up within a few weeks point to iron.
entries.fix: Spray chelated iron or Ferrous sulfate on the leaves, as Arizona extension advises. It shows results within a few weeks but may need repeating each year. On high pH soil, soil sulfur lowers the pH so iron becomes available. Follow the label for rates.
entries.prevent: Do not lime soils that are already near neutral, add organic matter, and keep the soil well drained.

sources.title: University of Arizona Cooperative Extension, Backyard Gardener 232: Iron deficiency (general signs)
University of Delaware Cooperative Extension: Identifying nutrient deficiencies in ornamental plants (general signs)

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in banana
entries.hint: Old leaves turn orange yellow from the tip, the edges scorch brown and the midrib bends.
entries.symptoms: The oldest leaves yellow first, starting at the leaf tip and between the veins. The yellow turns orange, the patches join, and the tissue dries dark brown, often as a scorch along the edges. Leaves get smaller, may split along the side veins, and the midrib can bend and break. Bunches come late and stay short and thin, with small fingers that fill poorly.
entries.stage: Any age, but worst from the fast leaf growth stage to bunch filling, when the plant takes up the most potash.
entries.causes: Sandy or light soils, acid soils and heavy rain that washes potash away. Soils already rich in magnesium, which hold back potash uptake. Long dry spells also cut uptake.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also starts on old leaves. But the yellow band sits between the midrib and the edge while the edge stays green, and the leaf stalk shows purple mottling. Sigatoka leaf spot starts as small streaks and spots spread over the leaf, not as a scorch that moves in from the tip and edge. Salt burn from too much fertilizer can also scorch edges.
entries.confirm: Send a leaf sample and a soil sample to a lab. A soil test that shows low potash, or a high magnesium to potash balance, points to this. Bunches that fill better after potash is added confirm it.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 to the soil around the mat, split into several doses, following the soil test. A quick foliar spray of Sulfate of potash at 1 percent (10 grams per liter) helps leaves while the soil dose works, as Indian extension guides advise. Keep the soil pH above 6 with lime or dolomite on acid soils.
entries.prevent: Give potash every cycle, in splits, from the early vegetative stage up to bunch emergence. Return chopped leaves and pseudostems to the mat.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in banana
entries.hint: Pale green to yellow leaves, pinkish red leaf stalks and a thin, slow plant.
entries.symptoms: The oldest leaves go light green, then yellow, and the veins do not stay green. Leaf stalks, midribs and leaf sheaths take on a pink to reddish color. The pseudostem stays thin, new leaves are small and come slowly, and leaves may crowd together. Bunch weight and fruit quality drop.
entries.stage: From early growth to bunch emergence, most often in fast growing young plants.
entries.causes: Sandy soils with little organic matter, heavy rain or irrigation that washes nitrogen down. Fresh straw or raw manure that ties up nitrogen as it rots. Roots damaged by nematodes or weevils also take up less.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency also gives light green to yellow leaves, but it starts on the young leaves. Iron deficiency starts on young leaves and keeps the midrib and veins green for a while. Weak roots from nematodes give a similar pale plant, so check the roots too.
entries.confirm: A leaf test shows low nitrogen. Check that the roots are healthy. New leaves that green up within a few weeks after urea confirm it.
entries.fix: Apply Urea 46 0 0 or Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 around the mat and water it in. The National Horticulture Board of India gives 300 grams of Urea per plant followed by irrigation. Split it into smaller doses on sandy soil. Add compost or well rotted manure to build the soil.
entries.prevent: Split nitrogen through the crop, from the third month up to bunch emergence. Keep a mulch of old leaves on the mat.

Haifa: Crop guide, banana fertilizer (deficiency symptoms)

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in banana
entries.hint: Old leaves yellow in the middle of the blade while the edge stays green. Purple blotches on the leaf stalk.
entries.symptoms: Old leaves yellow in the middle part of the blade, along the midrib, while the leaf edge stays green. Dead spots form inside the yellow parts. The leaf stalk shows bluish purple mottling, and leaf sheaths may pull away from the pseudostem. Bunch weight and yield fall.
entries.stage: Mostly on older plants and after heavy potash feeding, during the vegetative stage and bunch filling.
entries.causes: Sandy and acid soils, and heavy use of potash, which competes with magnesium. Cold, wet spells make it worse. In Davao plantations the opposite also happens: soils very high in magnesium crowd out potash and calcium.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency also hits old leaves, but it starts at the tip and edge as an orange scorch. Manganese deficiency looks similar but starts on young leaves.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test for magnesium, potash and calcium together, since the balance matters, and a leaf test. Purple mottled leaf stalks with green leaf edges are a strong field sign.
entries.fix: Apply Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) or Kieserite around the mat and water it in. The National Horticulture Board of India gives 25 grams of Magnesium sulfate per plant. On acid soils use Dolomite, which gives both lime and magnesium. Do not put magnesium and potash fertilizer down on the same day.
entries.prevent: Base potash and magnesium on a soil test so one does not crowd out the other. Use dolomite instead of plain lime on acid soils.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in banana
entries.hint: Young leaves narrow and pointed, with yellow and green stripes and a purple tint underneath.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves come out smaller and more lance shaped, with yellow to white stripes between the side veins that give a striped, mottled look. The underside of the rolled new leaf shows a strong purple tint. Leaves may crowd into a rosette. Bunches are small and the fingers short, thin, twisted and light green at the tip.
entries.stage: On young plants and suckers, and in later cycles. Losses often show in the second or third year.
entries.causes: High pH or limed soils, organic soils, heavy phosphorus fertilizer, and cold wet weather. It is the most common micronutrient shortage in banana.
entries.confuse: Bunchy top virus also gives narrow, bunched leaves. But it shows dark green dot and dash streaks along the veins and leaf stalk and the leaves stand stiff and upright. Zinc deficiency has no such streaks and responds to a zinc spray. Herbicide drift can also stripe young leaves.
entries.confirm: A leaf test for zinc and a soil test for pH and phosphorus. Spray a few plants with zinc sulfate. New leaves that come out normal confirm it.
entries.fix: Spray Zinc sulfate on the leaves. Indian guides give 5 grams per liter (0.5 percent), or 2 grams per liter mixed with 2.5 grams of lime per liter on young leaves. On poor soils also apply Zinc sulfate to the soil, following the soil test. Do not apply it on the same day as phosphate fertilizer.
entries.prevent: Avoid overliming and very heavy phosphorus. Include zinc in the program on soils that tested low.

National Horticulture Board India: Banana manuring and fertilization
Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Banana nutrient deficiencies
Haifa: Crop guide, banana fertilizer (deficiency symptoms)

entries.name: Boron deficiency in banana
entries.hint: Young leaves curl and crumple, with white streaks across the veins on the underside.
entries.symptoms: The youngest leaves show it. Leaf edges go pale and curl inward, then brown. White streaks run across the veins on the underside, the side veins thicken, and the blade can be crumpled, misshapen or missing. Plants may be stunted with leaves bunched in a fan. Bunches are light, poorly filled or deformed.
entries.stage: During fast leaf growth and around flowering, often after a dry spell.
entries.causes: Sandy or alkaline soils low in organic matter, drought, and very high nitrogen or calcium. Cold wet spells can also bring it on.
entries.confuse: Calcium deficiency also damages young leaves, but its dead tissue is lighter brown and starts at the tip. The side veins thicken more. Virus diseases and herbicide damage can look alike, so a leaf test helps.
entries.confirm: A leaf test for boron, and a soil test. New leaves that come out normal after a light boron dose confirm it.
entries.fix: Apply Borax to the soil around the root zone. The National Horticulture Board of India gives 25 grams per plant. A foliar spray of Borax at 1 gram per liter also works. Boron is toxic in excess, so do not repeat high doses without a test.
entries.prevent: Keep organic matter up and water during dry spells. Add a small boron dose on soils that tested low.

sources.title: Yara Philippines: Boron deficiency in banana
National Horticulture Board India: Banana manuring and fertilization
Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Banana nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in banana
entries.hint: New leaves come out as a spike with little or no blade. Ripe fruit peel splits.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves fail to open fully, giving a 'spike leaf' with a deformed or missing blade. Leaves pale, then die back light brown from the tip, with thick side veins. Roots are short and thick. The peel splits as fruit ripens, fingers curl, and weak fruit tips let cigar end rot in.
entries.stage: During fast growth and fruit formation.
entries.causes: Acid soils, sandy soils that leach, soils high in sodium or aluminum, drought, and heavy potash or nitrogen that pushes calcium out.
entries.confuse: Boron deficiency also hurts young leaves, but its dead tissue is darker and starts at the leaf edge with white streaks under the leaf. Virus and herbicide damage can also deform new leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for pH and calcium, and a leaf test. Low pH with spike leaves points to calcium.
entries.fix: On acid soils apply Agricultural lime or Dolomite to the mat, following the soil test. Indian guides range from 50 grams up to 1 kg of lime per plant split over the year. On soils with normal pH use Gypsum or Calcium nitrate. Do not overload potash.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soils before planting, keep water steady, and keep potash and calcium in balance.

Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Banana nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in banana
entries.hint: Short plant with weak roots. Old leaf edges yellow in a saw tooth pattern and young leaves look bluish.
entries.symptoms: Growth is slow and the plant stays short, with a thin, woody pseudostem and weak roots. The edges of old leaves yellow in a saw tooth pattern with purplish brown flecks, then die, and the leaves curl. Leaf stalks break easily. Young leaves look dark bluish green, sometimes purple underneath.
entries.stage: Early growth, right after planting and in young suckers.
entries.causes: Acid soils that lock up phosphorus, very alkaline soils, low organic matter, cold or waterlogged soil, and poor roots.
entries.confuse: Too much nitrogen also gives dark blue green leaves. Manganese deficiency also kills leaf edges, but its dead areas are darker and it starts on younger leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: Apply a phosphorus fertilizer near the roots and water it in. The National Horticulture Board of India gives 50 grams of DAP (Ammonium phosphate 18 46 0) per plant. On acid soils correct the pH with lime so the phosphorus stays available.
entries.prevent: Put phosphorus in the planting hole and in the first months, and lime acid soils.

sources.title: Yara Philippines: Phosphorus deficiency in banana
National Horticulture Board India: Banana manuring and fertilization
Haifa: Crop guide, banana fertilizer (deficiency symptoms)

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in banana
entries.hint: Young leaves even pale yellow, veins included, on a small slow plant.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves turn light green to yellowish white, evenly over the whole leaf, veins included. New leaves are small and the side veins can look thick, and in bad cases the edges die. The plant grows slowly and bunches stay small or get stuck in the throat.
entries.stage: During fast vegetative growth.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy soils that leach, low organic matter, waterlogged soils. Years of using only urea and muriate of potash with no sulfur.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency looks the same but starts on old leaves. Iron deficiency also hits young leaves, but it is patchy and keeps green areas near the midrib.
entries.confirm: Leaf test for sulfur and a soil test. Plants that green up after a sulfur fertilizer confirm it.
entries.fix: Use a nitrogen or phosphorus fertilizer that carries sulfur, such as Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 or 16 20 0, in place of part of the urea. The National Horticulture Board of India gives 20 grams per plant of a sulfur containing complex. Gypsum also supplies sulfur.
entries.prevent: Use ammonium sulfate or 16 20 0 for part of the nitrogen every cycle.

sources.title: Yara Philippines: Sulfur deficiency in banana
National Horticulture Board India: Banana manuring and fertilization
Haifa: Crop guide, banana fertilizer (deficiency symptoms)

entries.name: Manganese deficiency in banana
entries.hint: The second or third youngest leaf yellows from the edge inward along the veins, like the teeth of a comb.
entries.symptoms: It shows first on the second or third youngest leaf. Mild cases are just light green. Then yellow starts at the leaf edge and runs in along the veins toward the midrib, giving a comb tooth pattern. In bad cases the yellow areas die and the edges curl down.
entries.stage: During fast growth, more often in cool wet months.
entries.causes: High pH or limed soils, sandy soils, organic soils, and cold wet periods.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency looks similar but starts on old leaves. Iron deficiency yellows the whole young leaf without the comb tooth pattern or dead areas.
entries.confirm: Leaf test for manganese and soil test for pH. Test spray a few plants.
entries.fix: Spray Manganese sulfate on the leaves at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter), as Indian extension guides advise. Repeat if new leaves still show it.
entries.prevent: Avoid overliming. On high pH soils include manganese in the foliar program.

sources.title: Yara Philippines: Manganese deficiency in banana
National Horticulture Board India: Banana manuring and fertilization
Haifa: Crop guide, banana fertilizer (deficiency symptoms)

entries.name: Iron deficiency in banana
entries.hint: Young leaves turn yellow to almost white while the veins stay green for a while.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves turn yellowish green, then yellow or nearly white. The yellow starts between the veins near the base and edges and spreads to the tip, giving a mottled look. The midrib and veins stay green longer but fade in bad cases. Growth slows and bunches stay small.
entries.stage: Young plants and new leaves, especially after flooding.
entries.causes: High pH and limey soils, waterlogged soils, and too much copper, manganese or zinc.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency also yellows young leaves, but evenly with no green veins. Nitrogen deficiency starts on old leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for pH and check drainage. A test spray of iron on a few plants that greens the new leaves confirms it. Leaf iron numbers alone are not reliable.
entries.fix: Spray Ferrous sulfate at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter) mixed with Urea at 1 percent (10 grams per liter), as the National Horticulture Board of India advises. Improve drainage where water stands.
entries.prevent: Drain wet spots and avoid overliming.
