National Horticulture Board India: Banana manuring and fertilization
Haifa: Crop guide, banana fertilizer (deficiency symptoms)

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in papaya
entries.hint: Lower leaves go pale green from the tip, new leaves come small and slow, and leaf stalks are short, thin and pinkish.
entries.symptoms: The older, lower leaves turn pale green to light green first, often starting at the leaf tip. New leaves come out smaller and less often, so the crown looks thin. Leaf stalks stay short, thin and pressed together, and may show a pinkish color. The tree grows slowly and sets fewer fruit.
entries.stage: Any stage, but most often in fast growing young trees and in bearing trees that carry many fruit.
entries.causes: Papaya feeds heavily and fruits all year, so it runs short fast when it is not fed every month or two. Sandy soils, heavy rain that washes nitrogen down, and soils low in organic matter make it worse.
entries.confuse: Papaya ringspot virus also makes trees pale and slow. But it gives a yellow mosaic on young leaves, oily dark streaks on the leaf stalks and stem, and ring spots on the fruit. Magnesium shortage also starts on old leaves, but the yellow sits between the veins with green bands near the edge and midrib. Waterlogged roots also turn the lower leaves yellow, so check drainage.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test to see how short the soil is, as Kerala Agricultural University advises. A leaf test of recently matured leaves, blade and stalk, helps. New leaves that green up within two to three weeks after urea confirm it.
entries.fix: Apply a quick nitrogen fertilizer such as Urea 46 0 0 or Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 around the tree, based on the soil test, and water it in. For a fast boost, Kerala Agricultural University gives a urea leaf spray of 10 grams per liter every 15 days. TNAU gives a stronger 2 percent spray (20 grams per liter), so try the milder rate first. Add compost or well rotted manure as well.
entries.prevent: Feed in small, regular splits. A Central Mindanao University trial on Solo papaya in Bukidnon followed a local grower's program of ammonium sulfate, Complete 14 14 14, superphosphate, muriate of potash and dolomite split into 12 doses from the first to the tenth month after transplanting.

sources.title: Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Papaya nutrient deficiencies
TNAU Agritech Portal: Nitrogen deficiency in papaya
Valleser 2016, Planting densities and nutrient rates on the growth and fruit set of Solo papaya (Central Mindanao University, Bukidnon)

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in papaya
entries.hint: Old leaves get lemon yellow edges that die brown, purplish brown patches show at the base of leaf stalks, and fruit come out misshapen.
entries.symptoms: The older, lower leaves show pale to lemon yellow edges first. The leaf tips and edges then die and turn brown, and new leaves come smaller. Purplish brown patches appear at the base of the leaf stalks. The whole tree can yellow early and grow much less, and the fruit are misshapen, poorly filled and hard to sell.
entries.stage: Mostly in bearing trees, since the fruit pull a lot of potash out of the leaves.
entries.causes: Bearing trees need a steady supply of potash for the fruit. Sandy soils, acid soils below pH 6 (Kerala Agricultural University notes potash is taken up best above pH 6), heavy rain and feeding nitrogen without potash bring it on.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage also hits old leaves, but the yellow runs between the veins and leaves green bands along the edge and midrib. While potash shortage scorches the edge itself. Salt or fertilizer burn also browns leaf edges, but it follows a heavy dose and hits leaves of all ages. Dry spells can scorch edges too, so check soil moisture.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test for potash, and test magnesium and calcium with it since they compete. A leaf test of the leaf stalks helps. Better fruit shape and filling after potash is a strong sign.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 around the tree based on the soil test, split into several doses, as Kerala Agricultural University advises. For quick help, KAU gives a Sulfate of potash leaf spray at 10 grams per liter with a sticker, sprayed in the morning. TNAU gives a 2 percent potassium chloride spray. On acid soil, bring the pH above 6 with Agricultural lime or Dolomite, and add organic matter.
entries.prevent: Give potash in every split along with nitrogen once the tree starts to bear. In the Central Mindanao University trial, the local grower's program gave a little more potash than nitrogen.

Valleser 2016, Planting densities and nutrient rates on the growth and fruit set of Solo papaya (Central Mindanao University, Bukidnon)

entries.name: Boron deficiency in papaya
entries.hint: Bumpy, lumpy fruit that bleed latex, with empty or poorly formed seeds inside.
entries.symptoms: Young fruit start to bleed latex and lose their shape, and the bumps grow worse as the fruit gets older. Parts of the fruit stop growing while the rest keeps swelling, so the fruit turns lumpy. Small cracks may ooze drops of latex, ripening is uneven, and seeds inside are aborted or poorly formed. In bad cases new leaves cup inward and turn brittle, the top bunches up, and the growing point can die.
entries.stage: Fruiting. Signs start on young fruit and show most on mature fruit. It can come and go with the season.
entries.causes: Heavy rain washes boron out of tropical soils. Shallow, rocky soils, dry spells and high pH soils also keep boron from the roots. TNAU notes it is common where papaya is grown on the same land again and again.
entries.confuse: Papaya ringspot virus marks the fruit with dark rings and the leaves with a yellow mosaic. But the fruit stays round, while boron shortage makes real lumps. Fruit fly stings leave small holes and maggots inside. Poor pollination from too few male flowers also gives misshapen fruit. So check the seeds: boron short fruit have aborted seeds and dark strands inside.
entries.confirm: Send leaf stalks from healthy and sick trees of the same age to a lab. Hawaii CTAHR reports that trees with deformed fruit have about 20 ppm boron or less in the leaf stalk. While normal trees have 25 ppm or more. Test the soil and its pH as well.
entries.fix: Hawaii CTAHR reports that a 0.25 percent borax spray (2.5 grams per liter) on the leaves, or 1 to 3 kg of boron (not borax) per hectare on the ground, raised boron and cleared the next fruit. Kerala Agricultural University gives 4 grams of Borax per tree in the soil, or a spray of 1 gram per liter. Fruit set after the treatment comes out normal in about three months. Boron turns toxic easily, so never go above these rates.
entries.prevent: Add compost every season, since boron comes with organic matter. TNAU gives a 0.1 percent boric acid spray every three months from the sixth month after planting. Do not mix borax with calcium or ammonium fertilizers in one dose.

Pacific Pests, Pathogens and Weeds: Papaya and celery boron deficiency (fact sheet 191, from CTAHR PD 91)
Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Papaya nutrient deficiencies
TNAU (Jeyakumar and Balamohan): Micronutrients for horticultural crops

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in papaya
entries.hint: Lower leaves yellow between the veins while green bands stay along the edge and the midrib. Leaf stalks look purple mottled.
entries.symptoms: The bottom leaves yellow between the veins first, while a band of green stays around the edge and beside the midrib. Later the yellow moves in from the edge toward the midrib and brown spots form on the edges. Leaf stalks show purplish mottling, leaves can be misshapen, and trees stay shorter.
entries.stage: Mostly in bearing trees and after heavy potash feeding.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy soils that have lost magnesium to rain, and heavy potash use, which crowds magnesium out.
entries.confuse: Potash shortage also starts on old leaves. But it scorches the edge itself and puts purplish brown patches at the base of the leaf stalk. Manganese shortage also yellows between the veins, but it shows on younger leaves. Papaya ringspot virus gives a mosaic on young leaves, not a banded yellowing of old ones.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test, as Kerala Agricultural University advises, and check magnesium, potash and calcium together. A leaf test helps. Green bands along the edge and midrib of old leaves are a strong field sign.
entries.fix: Kerala Agricultural University gives 32 grams of Magnesium sulfate per tree, laid in a band near the tree. For a quick fix, TNAU gives a Magnesium sulfate leaf spray at 1 to 2 percent (10 to 20 grams per liter). Do not apply magnesium and potash fertilizer at the same time.
entries.prevent: Use Dolomite instead of plain lime on acid soils. KAU notes that long use of dolomite keeps magnesium shortage away. Keep potash and magnesium in balance with a soil test.

sources.title: Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Papaya nutrient deficiencies
TNAU Agritech Portal: Magnesium deficiency in papaya

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in papaya
entries.hint: New leaves pale with curled edges and small dead spots, a bunched top, and soft fruit flesh.
entries.symptoms: The growing tip and the young leaves show it first. New leaves turn pale with curled edges, and small dead spots spread over the blade so the leaves do not grow well. Leaf stalks can twist and fold, the space between leaves shortens so the top looks bunched, and the fruit flesh goes soft.
entries.stage: Fast growth and fruit development.
entries.causes: Acid soils low in calcium, and too much phosphorus. Boron shortage can also bring on calcium shortage, since the plant needs boron to use calcium. Dry soil cuts calcium uptake as well.
entries.confuse: Boron shortage also hits young leaves and the top, and the two often come together. But boron shortage shows most as lumpy fruit that bleed latex. Papaya ringspot virus and herbicide drift both twist and narrow young leaves. Virus leaves show a yellow mosaic and drift damage follows spraying nearby.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test with pH, since acid soils point to low calcium. A leaf test helps, and test boron at the same time.
entries.fix: On acid soil, Kerala Agricultural University gives Agricultural lime at 300 to 500 grams per tree per year. On soil that is not acid, use Gypsum, which adds calcium without raising pH. Correct boron shortage too. Calcium nitrate can also be used. Follow the label.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soil before planting, based on a soil test, and avoid too much phosphate fertilizer. Water evenly in dry months.

sources.title: Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Papaya nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in papaya
entries.hint: Dark bluish green leaves on a tree that stops growing taller, with dead patches on the old leaves.
entries.symptoms: The tree stops growing taller and makes fewer leaves. Leaves take on a dark or bluish green color. The older, lower leaves get uneven dead patches and yellow edges, and they die early. Roots grow poorly.
entries.stage: Young trees after transplanting, and on poor acid soils.
entries.causes: Acid soils and very alkaline soils hold phosphorus tight. Kerala Agricultural University notes it is taken up best between pH 6.2 and 7. Poor, eroded soils and no basal fertilizer at planting add to it.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage also stunts the tree, but its leaves are pale, not dark. Root rot and nematodes also stop growth, so pull a weak tree and look at the roots.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test for phosphorus and pH. A leaf test helps.
entries.fix: For quick correction, Kerala Agricultural University advises Superphosphate 0 20 0. For the long term, bone meal or rock phosphate. Follow the soil test for the rate, as TNAU also advises. Mix organic manure with phosphate solubilizing bacteria to make more of it available.
entries.prevent: Put phosphate fertilizer and compost in the planting hole, and keep soil pH between about 6.2 and 7 with lime.

sources.title: Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Papaya nutrient deficiencies
TNAU Agritech Portal: Phosphorus deficiency in papaya

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in papaya
entries.hint: New leaves come small and yellow between the veins, and the top bunches up.
entries.symptoms: No detailed papaya description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. New leaves come out small and narrow and turn yellow between the veins, while the veins stay green. The space between leaves shortens so the top looks bunched, and fruit stay small. TNAU notes that zinc and boron shortage are common where papaya is grown on the same land year after year.
entries.stage: Young leaves in any stage. Worst in fields that have grown papaya for several crops.
entries.causes: Fields cropped to papaya again and again, high pH soils, sandy soils and heavy phosphate use.
entries.confuse: Papaya ringspot virus also makes young leaves small, mottled and twisted. But it brings a yellow mosaic, oily streaks on the stalks and ring spots on the fruit. Manganese shortage also yellows young leaves between the veins, but leaves stay normal size. Herbicide drift gives narrow, strappy new leaves after nearby spraying.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test with pH and a leaf test. Spray zinc on a few trees and see if the next leaves come out normal.
entries.fix: TNAU reports that a leaf spray of 0.5 percent Zinc sulfate (5 grams per liter) together with 0.1 percent boron, given at the fourth and eighth month after planting, raised yield and fruit quality. Do not mix zinc with phosphate fertilizer in one dose.
entries.prevent: Rotate papaya with other crops where you can, add compost. Use a fertilizer with zinc in fields that have grown papaya before.

University of Delaware Cooperative Extension: Identifying nutrient deficiencies in ornamental plants (general signs)

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in mango
entries.hint: Small, pale yellow leaves over the whole tree, yellowish twigs, weak flushes and small fruit.
entries.symptoms: Leaves come out undersized and turn an even pale green to yellow, older leaves first, until the whole canopy looks yellowish. Even the young twigs take on a yellow color. New flushes are short and few, growth slows badly, and the fruit that sets stays small and matures early.
entries.stage: Any age. Most common in young trees that are never fed and in bearing trees that carried a big crop without fertilizer.
entries.causes: Trees that get little or no fertilizer, sandy soils low in organic matter, and heavy rain that washes nitrogen down. Thick grass and weeds under the canopy also compete for it.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also starts on old leaves. But the veins stay dark green in a fishbone pattern while the tissue between them yellows. Iron deficiency starts on the newest leaves, with a net of green veins. Waterlogged soil and root rot can also make the whole tree pale, so check drainage and the roots.
entries.confirm: Take a leaf test before flower induction: the youngest fully expanded, hardened leaf of a flush (about eight weeks old), four or five leaves per tree from ten trees, as the Australian mango industry guide describes. A soil test taken at the same time helps read the leaf result. A Philippine baseline survey of fruit farms gives local normal leaf levels for mango that labs can compare against.
entries.fix: Feed nitrogen in a ring under the edge of the canopy and cover it with soil. The DA mango GAP code gives Complete 14 14 14 by tree age, for example 500 g to 1 kg per tree at 5 to 6 years, 2 kg at 7 to 8 years, 3 kg at 9 to 10 years and 5 kg at 11 to 15 years, half at the start and half at the end of the rainy season. For quick greening, Kerala Agricultural University gives a Urea spray of 10 grams per liter every 15 days. TNAU gives 80 kg of nitrogen per hectare as its soil rate.
entries.prevent: Fertilize every year in two splits and add compost or manure. Do not overdo nitrogen on bearing trees: too much nitrogen makes soft nose and internal breakdown of the fruit worse.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in mango
entries.hint: Old leaves get grey to brown dead edges and scattered yellow to orange spots. Fruit stays small.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves show it first. Yara describes greyish dead tissue along the leaf edges, after which the leaves die, without a general yellowing of the blade. Indian guides add white, yellow or orange spots scattered over both sides of old leaves, scorch that starts at the tip and edge, and edges that curl up. In bad cases leaves are small, roots are weak, shoot tips burn and die back, and fruit size and yield drop.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, most during fruit growth, and trees on sandy soils.
entries.causes: Acid soils, sandy soils, heavy rain or heavy irrigation that leaches potash, drought, and soils with little potash in reserve. Years of nitrogen only feeding make it worse.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also starts on old leaves. But the tissue between the veins yellows in a fishbone pattern, not a grey brown edge scorch. Fertilizer or salt burn also scorches edges, but it shows soon after a heavy dose and on leaves of all ages. Anthracnose gives dark, sunken spots on young flush in wet weather.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the youngest fully expanded, hardened leaves before flower induction. A soil test for potash, magnesium and calcium together, since their balance matters.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 under the canopy edge in split doses, following the soil test, as Kerala Agricultural University advises. As a quick help, KAU gives a Sulfate of potash spray at 10 grams per liter with a sticker in the morning. TNAU gives a potassium chloride spray at 2 percent (20 grams per liter) every two weeks. Keep the soil pH above 6 with lime or dolomite on acid soils.
entries.prevent: Use a complete fertilizer every year, such as the 14 14 14 schedule in the DA mango GAP code. Add extra potash on sandy soils. Return leaves and prunings to the soil.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in mango
entries.hint: New leaves small, thick, brittle and crowded in a rosette at the shoot tip, pale between green veins (little leaf).
entries.symptoms: The new flush shows it. Leaves come out small, narrow, thick and brittle, with wavy edges that bend up or down and tips that curl back. The tissue between the veins turns pale green to yellow while the midrib stays green. Short internodes crowd the leaves into a rosette, and some twigs die back. Flower panicles on these shoots are small, odd shaped and drooping.
entries.stage: On new flushes, in young trees and in old trees on poor soils. It also cuts flowering.
entries.causes: High pH and limestone soils, sandy soils, and heavy phosphate fertilizer, which holds zinc back. Zinc is most available between pH 5 and 7.5.
entries.confuse: Mango malformation, a disease caused by the fungus Fusarium mangiferae, also shortens shoot internodes into bunches. Its panicles become short, thick and clustered, set no fruit and dry black. Prune and burn malformed shoots. Zinc will not cure them, while a true zinc shortage shows pale tissue between the veins and the next flush recovers after a zinc spray. Iron deficiency also yellows young leaves, but they keep a normal size.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the youngest fully hardened leaves and a soil test for pH and zinc. Spray zinc on a few branches. If the next flush comes out with normal size, green leaves, it was zinc.
entries.fix: TNAU gives Zinc sulfate on the soil at 10 kg per hectare, or a spray at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter). For severe cases Kerala Agricultural University gives a morning spray of 2 grams of Zinc sulfate plus 2.5 grams of fine lime (calcium carbonate) per liter. 8 kg per acre (about 20 kg per hectare) on the soil. Spray when the new flush is expanding. Do not apply zinc and phosphate fertilizer at the same time.
entries.prevent: The DA mango GAP code calls for a foliar fertilizer with zinc, boron, magnesium and calcium 18 to 25 days after flower induction, before bagging. Avoid heavy phosphate and overliming.

DA BAFS Code of Good Agricultural Practices for Mango (PNS/BAFPS 45:2009), Explanatory Manual 2025

entries.name: Boron deficiency in mango
entries.hint: Fruit cracks and shows brown, soft, watery flesh inside. Many flowers drop. New leaves thick and misshapen.
entries.symptoms: It shows at the growing points, in young leaves and in developing fruit. New leaves stay small and turn thick, leathery and uneven in shape. Many flowers drop. Fruit may crack, the yellow flesh shows brown areas. In bad cases the flesh turns soft and watery and splits down to the centre.
entries.stage: Flowering to fruit growth.
entries.causes: TNAU links it to high rainfall areas, high temperature, acid soils and also limestone soils. Sandy soils low in organic matter and dry spells add to it.
entries.confuse: Floral malformation (Fusarium) gives short, thick, crowded panicles that set no fruit and turn black. Boron shortage shows instead as flower drop, thick misshapen young leaves and damaged fruit. Soft nose and internal breakdown from low calcium start at the blossom end of ripening fruit without cracks. Fruit can also crack when heavy rain follows a long dry spell.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron and a leaf test. Boron is a key trace element for mango but is hard to manage, so do not add it on guesswork.
entries.fix: TNAU gives Borax at 5 to 10 kg per hectare on the soil, or a spray of Borax at 0.25 percent (2.5 grams per liter) every 10 days, or Solubor at 3 grams per liter. Kerala Agricultural University gives a lighter Borax spray of 1 gram per liter. Do not mix boron with calcium sprays or put borax down with ammonium fertilizers. Boron is toxic in excess, so keep to low rates.
entries.prevent: On soils that tested low, include boron in the foliar fertilizer the DA mango GAP code calls for after flower induction. Keep organic matter up and water during long dry spells.

Australian Mango Industry Association: Leaf and soil analysis (mango best practice resource)
DA BAFS Code of Good Agricultural Practices for Mango (PNS/BAFPS 45:2009), Explanatory Manual 2025

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in mango
entries.hint: Ripening fruit go soft and watery at the tip (soft nose) or brown and jelly like inside near the seed.
entries.symptoms: The fruit shows it first, from the inside. The flesh turns brown and breaks down (internal breakdown). At ripening the blossom end goes soft and water soaked while the shoulders are still firm (soft nose). Other forms are a hollow at the stem end, over ripe flesh around the seed (jelly seed), or spongy greyish black patches. On the tree, young leaves may yellow, wilt and curl down near the bud, and root and shoot tips brown and die.
entries.stage: Fruit ripening, worse in fruit left to ripen on the tree.
entries.causes: Acid and sandy soils low in calcium, soils high in sodium or aluminium, drought, and too much nitrogen or potash. High phosphorus and a shortage of boron also cut calcium use.
entries.confuse: Fruit fly maggots also rot the flesh, but you will find sting marks on the skin and larvae inside. Stem end rot and anthracnose start as dark patches on the skin. Boron shortage browns the flesh too, but usually with cracks.
entries.confirm: Soil test for pH and calcium, and a leaf test. Cut open a sample of ripe fruit from each block and count how many show breakdown.
entries.fix: On acid soils Kerala Agricultural University gives Agricultural lime at 1 kg per tree per year in four doses of 250 grams. On neutral or alkaline soils use Gypsum. TNAU gives 50 kg per hectare. Cut back nitrogen on trees with soft nose, as UF IFAS advises, and harvest at the mature green stage. Calcium in the foliar spray after flower induction, as the DA GAP code lists, helps the fruit.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soils, keep nitrogen and potash in balance, and water during long dry spells.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in mango
entries.hint: Old leaves yellow between the veins while the veins stay dark green like a fishbone. Edges bronze.
entries.symptoms: Lower, older leaves yellow between the veins while the veins stay dark green, giving a fishbone pattern, often with a green wedge down the middle of the leaf. Bronzing starts at the edge, in the rounded margin between each pair of side veins. The yellow parts later brown and die. Leaves may curl and cup and fall early, and the tree grows less.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, often after heavy potash feeding.
entries.causes: Acid soils, soils rich in potash or given heavy potash, and cold, wet periods.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency also hits old leaves, but as a grey to brown scorch on the edges without the fishbone yellowing. Nitrogen deficiency yellows the whole leaf, veins included. Iron and manganese shortages start on young leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for magnesium, potash and calcium, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU gives Magnesium sulfate at 5 to 10 kg per hectare on the soil, or a 2 percent spray (20 grams per liter) every two weeks. Kerala Agricultural University gives 32 kg per acre in bands near the trees and Dolomite for long term correction. Do not apply magnesium and potash fertilizer together.
entries.prevent: Use dolomite instead of plain lime on acid soils and keep potash in balance with magnesium.

TNAU Agritech: Mango magnesium deficiency
Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Mango nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in mango
entries.hint: Slow growth, old leaves fall early, shoot tips die back and new leaves stay small and dark green.
entries.symptoms: Kerala Agricultural University notes a reddish color on the underside of leaves as the first sign, on older leaves. Leaf tips die, older leaves drop early and branches partly die back from the tip. Small, dark green young leaves sit at the ends of the branches, roots grow poorly, and fruit ripening and quality are delayed.
entries.stage: Young trees and trees on poor, acid soils. Growth and flushing slow down.
entries.causes: Acid soils that lock up phosphorus, and soils low in organic matter. Phosphorus is taken up best at pH 6.2 to 7.0.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency makes leaves pale, not dark. Drought, root damage and twig dieback diseases can also drop leaves and kill shoot tips. So check the roots and look for dark streaks in the wood under the bark.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: Use Superphosphate for a quick fix, or bone meal or rock phosphate for slow, long term correction, as Kerala Agricultural University advises. TNAU also gives a phosphoric acid spray at 0.5 percent three times. On acid soils lime toward pH 6.2 to 7.0. Organic manure with phosphate dissolving bacteria helps free phosphorus.
entries.prevent: Put phosphorus in the planting hole and use the Complete 14 14 14 schedule of the DA mango GAP code every year.

sources.title: Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Mango nutrient deficiencies
TNAU Agritech: Mango phosphorus deficiency
DA BAFS Code of Good Agricultural Practices for Mango (PNS/BAFPS 45:2009), Explanatory Manual 2025

entries.name: Iron deficiency in mango
entries.hint: Newest leaves pale yellow to almost white with a fine net of green veins.
entries.symptoms: The youngest leaves show it first. At first even the smallest veins stay green, giving a net of green veins on a yellow leaf. Later the whole leaf turns pale yellow or bleaches white, and new leaves come out smaller. In extreme cases leaves dry from the tip down and shoots die back.
entries.stage: New flushes, mostly in trees on limey or waterlogged soils.
entries.causes: High pH and limestone soils (lime induced chlorosis), waterlogged soils, and low potash. Many tropical soils hold plenty of iron (Kerala Agricultural University notes this for Kerala soils). So the yellowing often means iron is locked up rather than missing. A soil test finds the real cause.
entries.confuse: Zinc deficiency also hits young leaves, but they are small, thick and crowded in rosettes. Manganese deficiency shows on leaves just reaching full size, is milder, and has grey brown specks. Mango decline, linked in Florida to iron and manganese shortage plus fungi and nematodes, adds dieback and dead leaves that hang on.
entries.confirm: Soil test for pH and iron, and check drainage. The Australian mango guide notes that soil iron is a more reliable measure than leaf iron.
entries.fix: On high pH soils, UF IFAS advises chelated iron (Fe EDDHA works best) as a soil drench two or three times a year. On neutral or acid soils, Ferrous sulfate can go on the soil and be watered in two or three times a year. Kerala Agricultural University gives 6 kg per acre. UF notes that iron sprays on the leaves are generally not effective. Drain wet spots.
entries.prevent: Avoid overliming and keep the soil drained. Keep potash up.

sources.title: TNAU Agritech: Mango iron deficiency
Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Mango nutrient deficiencies
UF IFAS EDIS HS2: Mango growing in the Florida home garden
Australian Mango Industry Association: Leaf and soil analysis (mango best practice resource)

entries.name: Manganese deficiency in mango
entries.hint: Leaves just reaching full size turn yellowish green with a fine net of green veins and grey specks.
entries.symptoms: It shows on leaves that are just reaching full size, in the middle of the canopy. They turn yellowish green between the veins with a fine network of green veins on the upper side. Mature leaves become thicker and blunt, and light grey to greyish brown specks appear. In severe cases the leaves brown and growth slows.
entries.stage: New and maturing flushes. Leaf signs appear late.
entries.causes: High pH and limestone soils, and sandy soils. In Florida it is part of mango decline together with iron shortage.
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency shows on the very newest leaves and bleaches them paler, often to white. Zinc deficiency makes leaves small and crowded. Magnesium deficiency starts on old leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf test and soil test for pH and manganese. Spray a few branches. The next flush should come out greener.
entries.fix: Spray Manganese sulfate on the leaves. Kerala Agricultural University gives 5 grams per liter. TNAU gives 0.2 percent (2 grams per liter) every two weeks. UF IFAS advises yearly sprays that carry manganese, zinc and boron on limey soils.
entries.prevent: Avoid overliming and include manganese in the yearly foliar program on high pH soils.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in coconut
entries.hint: The whole crown is pale yellow green, the fronds taper, and few palms bear nuts.
entries.symptoms: The oldest fronds turn an even light green to yellow first. The yellow moves up until the whole crown is pale except the spear. Fronds look tapered and new ones come slowly. Few palms flower, and those that do set few nuts with thin meat and low copra.
entries.stage: Any age. Very common in old, unfertilized bearing palms.
entries.causes: Nitrogen is short in most Philippine coconut soils, as leaf surveys and PCA research have found. Palms that never get fertilizer, weedy rings, and sandy soils show it most.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency gives the same even yellowing and often comes together with it. Chloride shortage also yellows old fronds early. Cadang cadang disease gives bright yellow spots on the fronds and small round nuts with scars.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of frond number 14 (Philippine trials take the middle part of 24 leaflets from the middle of that frond). A clear greening within a year after ammonium sulfate confirms it.
entries.fix: Apply Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 in a ring around the palm after weeding. In trials on three Leyte soils, 1.5 to 2 kg Ammonium sulfate plus 2 kg Muriate of potash per palm per year, in two equal splits, gave the best nut and copra yields. About 0.66 kg Urea did about as well as the ammonium sulfate. Ammonium sulfate also supplies sulfur.
entries.prevent: Fertilize every year, split in two at the start and end of the rainy season, and keep the ring weeded. Legume cover crops help a little but do not replace fertilizer.

sources.title: Baliad, Effects of organic and inorganic nitrogen on coconut on three soil types in Leyte, Philippines (CORD)
Magat 1997, Coconut yield improvement in farmers' fields through research based fertilization in the Philippines (CORD)
UF IFAS EDIS: Nutrient deficiencies of garden and field grown palms in Florida (Broschat)

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in coconut
entries.hint: Old fronds show see through yellow to orange spots near the tips, then dead leaflet edges.
entries.symptoms: The oldest fronds show small, see through yellow or orange spots, first near the leaflet tips. Later the leaflet edges and tips dry brown, and the old fronds die early. In bad cases only a few live fronds remain and the trunk narrows to a pencil point. Nuts are smaller, with thin shells, less water and lower copra.
entries.stage: Bearing palms, and palms on sandy soils under heavy rain.
entries.causes: Sandy and coral soils, heavy rain that leaches potash, and heavy nitrogen without potash. Salt fertilizer alone can make it worse because sodium competes with potash.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also starts on old fronds. But as a broad yellow band on the leaflet edges with a green centre and no spots. Chloride shortage, common inland, also brings early yellowing of old fronds and small nuts. Muriate of potash fixes both.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of frond number 14, and a soil test for potash.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 in the weeded ring. The Leyte trials used 2 kg per palm per year in two splits together with ammonium sulfate. Inland palms in many provinces are also short of chloride. PCA recommends common salt at 1.5 kg per bearing palm per year. On low potash soils salt should go with potash, not replace it.
entries.prevent: Give potash every year in two splits, and return husks and fronds to the ring.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in coconut
entries.hint: Fronds pale yellow to orange, fewer nuts, and copra that comes out rubbery and shrunken.
entries.symptoms: Leaflets turn from dark green to yellowish orange, most of all on the older, lower fronds, and dry early. The yellowing can spread to younger fronds, which stay thin and brittle. Nut numbers drop, and the copra is rubbery and shrunken instead of white and thick.
entries.stage: Bearing palms.
entries.causes: Sulfur is one of the widespread shortages in Philippine coconut soils. Palms fed only urea and muriate of potash, with no sulfur source, show it most.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency gives the same pale crown. The two often come together, which is why ammonium sulfate works so well on coconut. Rubbery copra is a key sign that points to sulfur.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of frond number 14 for sulfur. In a PCA trial, leaf sulfur matched yield closely.
entries.fix: Use Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 as the nitrogen source, or apply Gypsum. In a PCA Davao trial, gypsum at 0.75 kg per palm per year was the most profitable rate and about 2.5 kg gave the most nuts. Treated palms gave whiter, thicker copra.
entries.prevent: Keep a sulfur source such as ammonium sulfate or gypsum in the yearly program.

Magat 1997, Coconut yield improvement in farmers' fields through research based fertilization in the Philippines (CORD)

entries.name: Boron deficiency in coconut
entries.hint: New fronds stay crinkled and unopened, leaflet tips hook, and young nuts (buttons) fall.
entries.symptoms: Only the young fronds show it. Leaflets stay fused and fail to split or open, tips bend into a hook. Fronds come out small, crinkled, zigzag or with no leaflets at all. New leaves crowd at the top and choke the crown, and in bad cases the bud blackens and the palm dies. Bearing palms shed many buttons, flower clusters abort or carry few female flowers, and some nuts crack or have little meat.
entries.stage: Young palms in the field, and bearing palms after a long dry season.
entries.causes: Sandy and inland soils, dry months with less than about 75 mm of rain, heavy liming, and heavy potash or salt rates. PCA found it on 11 of 37 young plantings in Misamis Oriental.
entries.confuse: Button shedding also comes from drought, poor pollination, pests and other nutrient shortages, so look at the young fronds too. Bud rot also kills the spear, but the spear rots and smells, and the fronds do not show hooks or fused leaflets.
entries.confirm: Look for hooked, fused or unopened leaflets on the newest fronds. A leaf test and a soil test for boron help. A low reading warns of trouble even before signs appear.
entries.fix: Apply Borax in the ring around the palm, split in two doses with the other fertilizer. An Indian coconut research bulletin cured it with 300 grams of borax per young palm and 500 grams per adult palm per year. Damaged fronds stay misshapen, but new fronds come out normal after six to ten months.
entries.prevent: On sandy or inland soils add a small yearly boron dose, avoid heavy liming, and water young palms in the dry season. Too much boron is toxic, so test first.

UF IFAS EDIS: Nutrient deficiencies of garden and field grown palms in Florida (Broschat)
U.S. Borax crop guide: Boron deficiency in coconut

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in coconut
entries.hint: Old fronds show a wide yellow band along the leaflet edges while the centre stays green.
entries.symptoms: The oldest fronds yellow first, as broad bands along the leaflet edges while the centre near the midrib stays green. Younger fronds show less and less of it. In bad cases the leaflet tips die reddish brown and fruit set drops.
entries.stage: Bearing palms, often after years of heavy potash.
entries.causes: Sandy, leached soils, and heavy nitrogen, potash or lime, which push magnesium out. Leaf tests in Leyte found magnesium below the critical level.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency also starts on old fronds. But it shows see through orange spots and dead tips, not a clean yellow edge band. The two can occur together.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of frond number 14, and a soil test for magnesium, potash and calcium.
entries.fix: Apply Kieserite or Magnesium sulfate in the ring, following the soil test. On acid soils Dolomite supplies magnesium and lime together. Do not put magnesium and potash down on the same day.
entries.prevent: Balance potash with magnesium, and use dolomite instead of plain lime on acid soils.

Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Coconut nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in coconut
entries.hint: Old fronds dark or purplish green, small fronds, and flowering comes late.
entries.symptoms: Older, lower fronds show it first. In bad cases they turn dark green or purplish and drop early. Fronds stay smaller than normal, roots are weak, and flowering and fruiting come late.
entries.stage: Seedlings and young palms most. Less common in bearing palms.
entries.causes: Very acid soils that lock up phosphorus and soils low in organic matter. In Leyte leaf tests, phosphorus was above the critical level, so it is less common than nitrogen or potash shortage.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency makes old fronds pale, not dark. Drought and root damage also slow growth, so check the soil and roots.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test of frond number 14.
entries.fix: Apply a phosphorus fertilizer in the ring, following the soil test. Superphosphate acts quickly. Rock phosphate and bone meal work slowly over years. Phosphorus is most available near pH 6.5 to 7.5, so lime very acid soils.
entries.prevent: Put phosphorus in the planting hole and in the first years, and add compost or manure.

Baliad, Effects of organic and inorganic nitrogen on coconut on three soil types in Leyte, Philippines (CORD)

entries.name: Manganese deficiency in coconut
entries.hint: New fronds come out yellow with dead streaks, then wither and frizzle. Leaflet tips drop off.
entries.symptoms: The newest fronds come out yellow with dead streaks along or between the veins, worst near the base. New leaflets wither and curl, giving a frizzled top. On coconut the dead leaflet tips fall off so the crown looks singed. In bad cases growth stops and the bud dies.
entries.stage: Any age, on high pH soils.
entries.causes: High pH soils such as coral and limestone soils near the coast, cold soils. Heavy manure or compost that ties up manganese.
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency also yellows new fronds but without the dead streaks and frizzled leaflets. Boron deficiency also deforms new fronds, but with hooked and fused leaflets.
entries.confirm: Soil test for pH, and a leaf test for manganese.
entries.fix: Spray Manganese sulfate on the fronds at 5 grams per liter, or apply it to the soil, following the soil test. Use the sulfate form.
entries.prevent: On coral and limestone soils include manganese in the program and avoid adding more lime.

Kerala Agricultural University Agri Infotech: Coconut nutrient deficiencies

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in calamansi
entries.hint: The whole tree turns light green to yellow, old leaves drop early and the canopy thins.
entries.symptoms: Leaves turn light green, then yellow, evenly over the whole tree with no clear pattern, starting with the older leaves. Old leaves fall early, so the canopy looks thin and hollow, and new leaves come out small, thin and pale. Twigs may die back, the top looks thin and bushy, and the tree flowers sparsely, with fewer and smaller fruit.
entries.stage: Bearing trees after a heavy crop or heavy rains, and young trees that miss their regular feeding.
entries.causes: Sandy soils with little organic matter, heavy rain or watering that leaches nitrogen, drought, very low or very high soil pH. Fresh straw or raw manure that ties nitrogen up as it rots. Waterlogged soil also loses nitrogen.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency looks alike but starts on the young leaves, with veins that stay green. Late magnesium deficiency also yellows whole leaves, but leaves at an earlier stage show a green V at the base. When only the veins turn yellow, look for a girdled branch or trunk, for example from bark borers. Citrus greening (HLB) gives yellow shoots with a blotchy mottle that is not the same on both sides of the midrib.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of 4 to 6 month old leaves from a flush on twigs without fruit, the way UF IFAS samples citrus, plus a soil test. A tree whose next flush greens up after fertilizer confirms it.
entries.fix: The DA ATI calamansi guide gives 50 to 100 grams of Ammonium sulfate or Urea per tree a month after planting and every four months after, 200 to 300 grams in the second year. From the fourth year a complete fertilizer with potash at 500 grams per tree, rising to 2 to 3 kg per tree three times a year at 8 to 10 years. For quick greening TNAU gives a Urea spray at 2 percent (20 grams per liter) every 15 days. UF IFAS advises low biuret urea for sprays.
entries.prevent: Feed bearing trees three times a year: in the rainy season before flowering, two months after flowering and after harvest, as the ATI guide sets out. Mulch the ring with dry leaves and keep it weeded.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in calamansi
entries.hint: Young leaves with yellow patches between green veins (mottle leaf), small, narrow and standing upright.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves show it first: yellow patches between the veins, with an uneven green band along the midrib and main veins, called mottle leaf. As it gets worse the leaves turn pale yellow to almost white, come out small, narrow and pointed (little leaf), stand upright, and twigs die back. Fruit on these twigs stay small, with a smooth, pale, thin skin and little juice, and the tree flowers and sets less.
entries.stage: New flushes, at any age.
entries.causes: High pH and limed soils, soils high in phosphorus or given heavy phosphate, organic soils, and large, frequent doses of poultry manure. Shortage of magnesium or copper can also cut zinc uptake. UF IFAS prefers a soil pH below 6.5.
entries.confuse: Citrus greening (huanglongbing, HLB) is the big look alike. A UPLB survey in Oriental Mindoro found HLB in 150 of 155 calamansi trees tested, with a blotchy mottle and yellowing between the veins similar to zinc deficiency. Small, narrow, thick, corky, upright leaves with enlarged veins. Do the pen test: draw a circle on each side of the midrib. Zinc deficiency looks the same in both circles, HLB blotches do not match. Manganese deficiency also mottles young leaves but keeps them normal in size.
entries.confirm: Do the pen test, then spray zinc on a few branches: if the next flush comes out green and normal sized, it was zinc. If the blotches stay uneven or the tree keeps declining, send leaves for an HLB laboratory test (the UPLB team used PCR). A leaf test for zinc also helps.
entries.fix: Spray zinc on the young flush when the leaves are two thirds to almost fully expanded, as UF IFAS advises. Repeat on each major flush in bad cases, because zinc does not move on to later flushes. TNAU gives Zinc sulfate at 2 percent (20 grams per liter) mixed with 1 percent lime (10 grams per liter), every two weeks. Zinc on the soil rarely pays on acid soils and does not work on limey ones.
entries.prevent: Keep the pH below 6.5, avoid heavy phosphate and too much poultry manure, and include zinc in regular sprays. Control citrus psyllids and buy planting material from BPI or other trusted nurseries so HLB does not hide behind zinc signs.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in calamansi
entries.hint: Old leaf edges pale yellow to bronze, small wrinkled leaves, and small thin skinned fruit that may split.
entries.symptoms: The edges of older leaves turn pale yellow or bronze, and with time the yellowing spreads over the leaf. Growth slows, leaves drop around flowering, and new leaves are small and wrinkled, with scorched tips and small brown resin spots. Twigs may die back. Fruit stay small with a smooth, thin peel and may split from the blossom end or drop.
entries.stage: Bearing trees during fruit growth, most of all under heavy crops.
entries.causes: Acid and sandy soils, heavy rain or watering that leaches potash, drought, soils rich in magnesium. High nitrogen rates on heavy crops without enough potash.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also starts on older leaves, but it leaves a green V at the base of the leaf. Salt or fertilizer burn scorches leaf edges on leaves of all ages after a heavy dose or salty water. Fruit also split when heavy rain follows a dry spell, and copper deficiency splits fruit around brown gum stains.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of 4 to 6 month old leaves from twigs without fruit. A soil test for potash, magnesium and calcium together.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 or a complete fertilizer in the ring in split doses, following the soil test. From the fourth year the DA ATI guide gives a complete fertilizer with potash at 500 grams per tree, rising to 2 to 3 kg per tree three times a year at 8 to 10 years. For a quick fix TNAU gives a Potassium nitrate spray at 2 percent (20 grams per liter) every two weeks.
entries.prevent: Match potash to nitrogen, especially on heavy bearing trees, and never feed nitrogen alone for long.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in calamansi
entries.hint: Old leaves near the fruit yellow from the sides inward, leaving a green V shape at the leaf base.
entries.symptoms: It shows on mature leaves close to the fruit. A yellowish green blotch starts near the base of the leaf on each side of the midrib and grows until only the tip and a V shaped area at the base, pointing up the midrib, stay green. In bad cases the whole leaf turns yellow to bronze and drops, heavily fruiting branches lose most of their leaves, and those twigs may die. Seedy fruit like calamansi draw more magnesium than seedless kinds.
entries.stage: During fruit growth, on heavily bearing branches. The new flush may look normal while older leaves near the fruit yellow.
entries.causes: Sandy and acid soils, soils rich in potash or given heavy potash, and cold, wet periods. On limey soils, the high calcium also holds magnesium back.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency yellows the whole tree evenly with no pattern. Potassium deficiency bronzes the leaf edges. Citrus greening can look like magnesium deficiency, as Yara warns. In the pen test magnesium yellowing is the same on both sides of the midrib, HLB blotches are not.
entries.confirm: Leaf test and a soil test for magnesium, potash and calcium together.
entries.fix: On acid to neutral soils, Dolomite corrects mild cases and gives lime too. Where the soil test shows low magnesium, UF IFAS gives magnesium at a rate equal to 20 percent of the nitrogen rate. Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) or Kieserite can supply it. On limey soils use magnesium sprays on the leaves.
entries.prevent: Use dolomite when liming and keep potash and magnesium in balance.

UF IFAS EDIS CH142: A guide to citrus nutritional deficiency and toxicity identification
Yara Philippines: Magnesium deficiency in citrus

entries.name: Boron deficiency in calamansi
entries.hint: Fruit small, hard and lumpy with gum spots in the white peel. Leaves curl and shoot tips die, sending out many shoots.
entries.symptoms: Fruit stay small, hard and misshapen with a lumpy surface, many drop. Dark gum spots form in the white inner peel and sometimes in the core. Young leaves wilt early, show water soaked spots, curl, and the veins can split and turn corky. The growing tip dies, so the shoot sends out many side shoots and the tree looks bushy.
entries.stage: Flowering, fruit set and fruit growth, often after a long dry spell.
entries.causes: Sandy and alkaline soils low in organic matter, high nitrogen or calcium, cold wet weather and drought. UF IFAS also sees it where growers use only high analysis fertilizers with no micronutrients.
entries.confuse: Citrus greening also gives corky veins and small, lopsided fruit that color unevenly. Use the pen test on the leaves. Too much boron also hurts: leaf tips yellow or mottle and gum spots form on the leaf underside, then leaves drop.
entries.confirm: Leaf test and soil test for boron. Cut a few fruit: brown or gummy spots in the white peel point to boron.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a Borax spray at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter). UF IFAS advises boron every year where it is needed, either on the soil or as a spray but never both, because citrus is easily burned by too much.
entries.prevent: Use fertilizers that carry micronutrients, not straight high analysis grades only, keep organic matter up and water during long dry spells.

entries.name: Manganese deficiency in calamansi
entries.hint: Young full size leaves pale between the veins with broad dark green bands along the veins. Leaf size stays normal.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves show a fine network of green veins on a lighter green background, less sharp than with zinc or iron. By full size the pattern is clear: dark green bands along the midrib and main veins with light green areas between. In bad cases white spots form between the veins, leaves drop early and the tree looks weak. Leaves keep their normal size and shape.
entries.stage: On young and newly matured flushes. Mild signs on new shoots may fade as the flush hardens.
entries.causes: It happens on both acid soils, where manganese leaches, and on limey or overlimed soils, where it is locked up. Sandy and organic soils and cold, wet periods add to it. It often comes together with zinc shortage.
entries.confuse: Zinc deficiency makes the leaves small, narrow and pointed. Iron deficiency is paler, with a finer net, on the newest leaves. Citrus greening also mottles leaves. Use the pen test. Boron toxicity can also look like it.
entries.confirm: Look at the leaves more than once over several weeks before acting, since mild signs can pass. Then do a leaf test and a soil test for pH and manganese.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a Manganese sulfate spray at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter) every two weeks. Spray the new flush when the leaves are two thirds to fully expanded. UF IFAS notes that a little low biuret urea in the spray helps uptake. On acid soils manganese sulfate can also go on the soil. On limey soils use sprays only.
entries.prevent: Avoid overliming and include manganese with zinc in the regular spray program.

UF IFAS EDIS CH142: A guide to citrus nutritional deficiency and toxicity identification

entries.name: Iron deficiency in calamansi
entries.hint: Newest leaves yellow to ivory with green veins. Worst in wet, poorly drained or limey spots.
entries.symptoms: It always starts on the youngest leaves: yellow green, then pale yellow between veins that stay green, sometimes with even the fine veins green like a net. In bad cases the whole leaf turns ivory, new leaves are small, thin and fragile and drop early. Twigs die back at the top and edge of the canopy while older leaves stay green.
entries.stage: New flushes, especially in the rainy season on wet soils.
entries.causes: High pH and limey soils, too much water, poor drainage, cool soils, salty soils, high phosphorus. Copper built up in old orchard soil. Calamansi does not tolerate waterlogged ground.
entries.confuse: Manganese and zinc shortages often come with it, since all three get worse at high pH. Flood damage to roots and copper toxicity both first show as iron chlorosis, so check the roots and the spray history. Nitrogen deficiency starts on old leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for pH, and for copper on old orchard land, and check drainage and the roots.
entries.fix: Fix drainage first. UF IFAS reports trees helped or cured just by better irrigation and drainage. On high pH soils apply an iron chelate (Fe EDDHA) to the soil. UF does not recommend iron sprays on citrus, because they green the leaf only in specks and can burn. TNAU does give a Ferrous sulfate spray at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter), twice, two weeks apart, as a quick try.
entries.prevent: Plant on well drained ground or raised beds, avoid overliming, and keep the pH near neutral.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in calamansi
entries.hint: Old leaves dull with bronze or purplish freckles. Fruit coarse with a thick peel, and few flowers.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves lose their deep green and turn dull, small and narrow, with a purplish or bronze cast. In bad cases small brown to bronze freckles join up along the main veins. Leaves and fruit drop early, flowering and fruit set are poor, and roots stay short. Fruit are rough, with a coarse, thick peel, a hollow core and more acid.
entries.stage: Young trees and new plantings on land never fertilized. Rare in trees fed regularly for years.
entries.causes: Strongly acid soils where iron and aluminium lock phosphorus up, very alkaline soils, low organic matter, cold wet soil and weak roots.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency gives the opposite fruit: small, with a smooth, thin peel. Nitrogen deficiency gives evenly pale leaves without bronze freckles.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: Apply a phosphorus fertilizer, following the soil test. The DA ATI guide uses ammophos (16 20 0) with potash once trees bear. UF IFAS notes that superphosphate suits soils of any pH and adds sulfur. Warns not to use DAP (18 46 0) on alkaline soils. Lime very acid soils so the phosphorus stays available.
entries.prevent: Put phosphorus in the planting hole and in the first years, and add compost.

entries.name: Copper deficiency in calamansi
entries.hint: Extra large, dark green leaves on long, soft, S shaped shoots, gum blisters at the nodes and twig dieback.
entries.symptoms: The first sign is unusually large, dark green leaves with the midrib bowed up, on long, soft, angular shoots that droop in an S shape. Small blisters of clear gum form at the nodes, and reddish brown gum breaks out on older twigs. Twigs then die back from the tip and push out a bunch of weak buds. Fruit can show brown gum stains and split.
entries.stage: Young trees in new plantings, and trees pushed with heavy nitrogen.
entries.causes: New plantings on sandy or organic soils never farmed before, limey soils, and heavy nitrogen feeding. It is rare where copper fungicides are sprayed.
entries.confuse: Gummosis, which the DA ATI guide describes as dark, sticky gum oozing from branches and trunk, is a bark disease. Copper deficiency gum sits in small blisters on young twigs and as stains on the fruit. Too much nitrogen alone also gives dark, soft growth, and the two often come together.
entries.confirm: Check the spray record: if copper fungicides are used, copper deficiency is unlikely. A soil test on new land helps.
entries.fix: UF IFAS reports near immediate recovery from a copper spray at flowering. TNAU gives Copper sulfate at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter) every two weeks. Try it on a few branches first, since plain copper sulfate can burn soft leaves. Cut back excess nitrogen. Do not overdo copper: it builds up in the soil and below pH 5.5 it can kill roots.
entries.prevent: On new sandy land UF IFAS adds copper to the fertilizer at 2.5 percent of the nitrogen rate. Where copper fungicides are already sprayed, no extra copper is needed. Keep the soil pH near neutral.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in citrus (dalandan, ponkan)
entries.local: Kakulangan sa nitrogen ng dalandan at ponkan
entries.hint: Older leaves pale green to yellow and falling early, so the inside of the canopy goes bare.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves go pale green to yellow, with pale veins, and fall early. Yara notes a leaf can live only about 6 months instead of 1 to 3 years. So the inside of the canopy goes hollow. New leaves are small, thin and light green, and the whole tree looks evenly yellowish with no pattern. Trees bloom sparsely and set a light crop. The fruit peel is smooth and pale and the juice is lower in sugar and acid.
entries.stage: UF IFAS sees it most after flowering and before the rainy season. Trees often green up again in the rains if the crop is light. Heavy crops on unfed trees show it at any time.
entries.causes: Low farm inputs, sandy soils low in organic matter, heavy rain or watering that leaches nitrogen, waterlogging, drought. Fresh straw or raw manure. DOST PCAARRD lists low farm inputs among the causes of low citrus yields in the Philippines.
entries.confuse: Late magnesium deficiency also yellows whole leaves. It shows during fruit growth and does not green again without magnesium. While leaves at an earlier stage show a green V at the base. Sulfur deficiency starts on young leaves. Citrus greening (HLB) gives yellow shoots and a blotchy mottle that does not match on the two sides of the midrib.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of 4 to 6 month old leaves from a flush on twigs without fruit, as UF IFAS samples citrus, and a soil test. Even yellowing all over the tree, with no leaf pattern, points to nitrogen.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a yearly dose of 200 grams of nitrogen, 100 grams of phosphate and 200 grams of potash per tree for citrus, split over the year. That much nitrogen is about 435 grams of Urea. For quick greening TNAU gives a Urea spray at 2 percent (20 grams per liter) every 15 days. UF IFAS notes that sprays of low biuret urea, calcium nitrate or potassium nitrate work fast. Weak or old trees do better with small, frequent doses.
entries.prevent: Split nitrogen over the year and keep potash in step. Do not overfeed: too much nitrogen gives leafy growth at the cost of fruit and quality.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in citrus (dalandan, ponkan)
entries.local: Kakulangan sa potassium ng dalandan at ponkan
entries.hint: Old leaf edges yellow to bronze. Small fruit that split from the blossom end or show sunken creases in the peel.
entries.symptoms: The edges of older leaves turn pale yellow or bronze, and the yellow spreads over the leaf. On mandarins like ponkan, TNAU describes yellowing and bronzing with twisted, wrinkled leaves and spindly twigs. The top of the canopy thins. Fruit stay small with a smooth, thin peel, may split lengthwise from the blossom end, or show creasing, narrow sunken furrows in the peel. More fruit drop and the juice is weaker.
entries.stage: Fruit growth, most of all in heavy crop years.
entries.causes: Acid and sandy soils, heavy rain or watering, drought, soils rich in magnesium, limey soils. High nitrogen on heavy crops without enough potash.
entries.confuse: Creasing can also come from low calcium or boron. Fruit that split around brown gum stains point to copper deficiency. Magnesium deficiency leaves a green V at the leaf base instead of yellow edges. Salt or fertilizer burn scorches leaf edges on all leaf ages.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of 4 to 6 month old leaves from twigs without fruit, and a soil test for potash, magnesium and calcium. Count split and creased fruit per tree before and after feeding.
entries.fix: TNAU gives 200 grams of potash (K2O) a year per bearing tree together with 200 grams of nitrogen and 100 grams of phosphate. 200 grams of potash is about 330 grams of Muriate of potash 0 0 60. Split it into two or three doses. For a quick fix TNAU gives a Potassium nitrate spray at 2 percent (20 grams per liter) every two weeks.
entries.prevent: Keep potash in step with nitrogen every year, more so on heavy bearing trees.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in citrus (dalandan, ponkan)
entries.local: Kakulangan sa zinc ng dalandan at ponkan
entries.hint: Young leaves mottled yellow between green veins, small, narrow and upright. Small, smooth, pale fruit.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves show yellow patches between the veins with an uneven green band along the midrib and main veins (mottle leaf). In severe cases leaves are pointed, narrow, upright and very small (little leaf), twigs thin out and die back. The outer canopy looks dead while the centre stays dense. Fruit on weak twigs are small with a smooth, pale, thin skin and little juice. While water sprouts on the main limbs carry normal leaves and big, coarse fruit. Flowering and fruit set drop.
entries.stage: New flushes. Worse on trees with a heavy crop and weak roots.
entries.causes: High pH and limed soils, soils high in phosphorus or given heavy phosphate, organic soils, heavy poultry manure, and too much nitrogen. Magnesium or copper shortage can also cut zinc uptake.
entries.confuse: Citrus greening (huanglongbing, HLB) also gives a yellow mottle between the veins. DOST PCAARRD names HLB and tristeza as the main causes of low citrus production in the country. In the pen test, zinc deficiency looks the same in circles drawn on both sides of the midrib. While HLB blotches do not match. Manganese deficiency mottles leaves too but keeps them normal in size.
entries.confirm: Do the pen test, then spray zinc on a few branches and watch the next flush. If blotches stay uneven or the tree keeps declining, send leaves for an HLB laboratory test. Nueva Vizcaya mother trees are indexed for HLB by PCR. A leaf test for zinc helps.
entries.fix: Spray zinc on each new flush when leaves are two thirds to almost fully expanded, as UF IFAS advises. TNAU gives Zinc sulfate at 2 percent (20 grams per liter) mixed with 1 percent lime (10 grams per liter) every two weeks. Zinc on the soil rarely pays on acid soils and does not work on limey soils.
entries.prevent: Keep the pH below 6.5, avoid heavy phosphate and poultry manure, and include zinc in the regular spray program. Plant clean, HLB indexed trees and control psyllids.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in citrus (dalandan, ponkan)
entries.local: Kakulangan sa magnesium ng dalandan at ponkan
entries.hint: Mature leaves next to the fruit yellow on both sides of the midrib, leaving a green V at the leaf base (bronzing).
entries.symptoms: Leaves look normal on the new flush, then mature leaves close to the growing fruit show yellow blotches near the base on each side of the midrib. The blotches join until only the tip and a V shaped area at the base, pointing up the midrib, stay green. In acute cases the whole leaf turns yellow or bronze and drops. Heavily fruited limbs can lose nearly all their leaves while lightly loaded limbs stay green. Fruit are lower in sugar, acid and vitamin C, and seedy kinds swing into alternate bearing.
entries.stage: Fruit growth and maturing, on heavily bearing limbs.
entries.causes: Sandy and acid soils, soils rich in potash or given heavy potash, and cold, wet periods. On limey soils high calcium holds magnesium back. Seedy kinds need more magnesium than seedless ones.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency yellows the whole tree evenly and often greens again in the rains. Magnesium yellowing does not, without magnesium. Iron deficiency also yellows between veins but starts on the youngest leaves. Citrus greening can look like it, as Yara warns. Use the pen test.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of 4 to 6 month old leaves from twigs without fruit, and a soil test for magnesium, potash and calcium. Signs worst on the heaviest fruiting limbs point to magnesium.
entries.fix: On acid to neutral soils, Dolomite corrects mild cases. Where the soil test shows low magnesium, UF IFAS gives magnesium at a rate equal to 20 percent of the nitrogen rate, from Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) or Kieserite. On limey soils use magnesium sprays on the leaves.
entries.prevent: Lime with dolomite, keep potash and magnesium in balance, and avoid very heavy crops on weak trees.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in citrus (dalandan, ponkan)
entries.local: Kakulangan sa boron ng dalandan at ponkan
entries.hint: Small, hard, lumpy fruit with gum pockets in the white peel. Many fruit drop. Shoot tips die and branch out.
entries.symptoms: Fruit show it most: small, hard and misshapen with a lumpy surface, with gum pockets and dark spots in the white inner peel (albedo) near the rind and sometimes in the core, and gum on the skin. Many fruit drop, peel can crease, and fruit rot more after harvest. The growing tip dies and the shoot sends out many side shoots. Young leaves wilt early, show water soaked spots, curl, and the veins split and turn corky.
entries.stage: Flowering to fruit growth, often after a long dry spell.
entries.causes: Sandy and alkaline soils low in organic matter, high nitrogen or calcium, cold wet weather and drought. Programs that use only high analysis fertilizers without micronutrients. Poor boron also cuts calcium uptake in the peel.
entries.confuse: Citrus greening also gives corky veins and small, lopsided fruit that color unevenly. Check leaves with the pen test. Potassium shortage also creases the peel, but without gum pockets. Boron toxicity yellows and mottles leaf tips and leaves gum spots under the leaf.
entries.confirm: Leaf test and soil test for boron. Cut open a few fruit to look for gum and dark spots in the albedo.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a Borax spray at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter). UF IFAS advises boron each year where needed, on the soil or as a spray but never both, since citrus is easily burned by excess boron.
entries.prevent: Use fertilizers that carry micronutrients, keep organic matter up, and water in long dry spells.

entries.name: Manganese deficiency in citrus (dalandan, ponkan)
entries.local: Kakulangan sa manganese ng dalandan at ponkan
entries.hint: Young and medium leaves light green between dark green vein bands. Leaves keep their size. Fruit pale and soft.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves show a fine net of green veins on a lighter green background. By full size there are dark green bands along the midrib and main veins with light green to yellow areas between. In bad cases white or grey spots form between the veins and leaves drop early, but leaf size and shape stay normal. The crop is smaller, and fruit are smaller, softer and paler in color. With zinc shortage it forms marl chlorosis: dark veins with dull white and green between.
entries.stage: Young and newly matured flushes. Mild signs can fade as leaves harden.
entries.causes: Acid soils, where manganese leaches, and limey or overlimed soils, where it is locked up. Sandy and organic soils and cold, wet periods add to it.
entries.confuse: Zinc deficiency makes leaves small, narrow and pointed. Iron deficiency is paler, with a finer net, on the newest leaves. Citrus greening and boron toxicity can look alike. Use the pen test for HLB.
entries.confirm: Watch the leaves over a few weeks, since mild signs can pass. Then do a leaf test and a soil test for pH and manganese.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a Manganese sulfate spray at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter) every two weeks. Spray when the new flush is two thirds to fully expanded. UF IFAS notes that a little low biuret urea in the tank helps uptake. On acid soils manganese sulfate can also go on the soil, but not on limey soils.
entries.prevent: Avoid overliming and include manganese with zinc in the regular sprays.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in citrus (dalandan, ponkan)
entries.local: Kakulangan sa iron ng dalandan at ponkan
entries.hint: Newest leaves yellow to white with green veins. Tops of trees die back on wet or limey ground.
entries.symptoms: It starts on the youngest leaves: yellow green, then pale yellow between veins that stay green, sometimes like a fine net. In acute cases leaves are small, very thin and fragile and shed early. The tree dies back hard at the top and outer edge, sometimes with a dead top over normal lower limbs. It may hit only one branch or a few trees. Fruit are small, hard, coarse and light colored, with weaker juice.
entries.stage: New flushes, mainly on wet or limey ground.
entries.causes: High pH and limey soils (lime induced chlorosis), over watering, prolonged wet soil, poor drainage, cool soil, excess salts, high phosphorus. Copper built up in old orchard soils.
entries.confuse: Manganese and zinc shortage often come with it. Flood damage to roots and copper toxicity both show first as iron chlorosis. Nitrogen deficiency starts on old leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for pH, and for copper on old orchard land. Check drainage and look at the roots.
entries.fix: Improve drainage and watering first. UF IFAS reports trees helped or cured by that alone. On high pH soils apply an iron chelate (Fe EDDHA) to the soil. UF does not recommend iron sprays for citrus because they green leaves only in specks and can burn leaves and fruit, though TNAU gives a Ferrous sulfate spray at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter), twice, two weeks apart.
entries.prevent: Plant on well drained ground, avoid overliming, and keep pH near neutral.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in citrus (dalandan, ponkan)
entries.local: Kakulangan sa phosphorus ng dalandan at ponkan
entries.hint: Rough fruit with a coarse, thick peel, a hollow core and sour juice. Old leaves dull with bronze freckles.
entries.symptoms: Leaf signs are weak. Older leaves lose their deep green, partly yellow. May show a dull purplish or bronze cast or small bronze freckles along the main veins. Leaves and fruit drop early and flowering is poor. The clearest sign is the fruit: rough, with a coarse, thick peel, a hollow core and high acid, ripening late.
entries.stage: Young trees and new plantings on land never fertilized. Rare where trees have been fed phosphorus for years.
entries.causes: Strongly acid soils where iron and aluminium lock phosphorus up, limey soils where calcium does, low organic matter, cold wet soil and weak roots.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency gives the opposite fruit: small, with a smooth, thin peel. Nitrogen deficiency gives evenly pale leaves without bronze freckles.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: Apply a phosphorus fertilizer, following the soil test. TNAU's yearly citrus dose includes 100 grams of phosphate per tree. UF IFAS notes that superphosphate suits soils of any pH and adds sulfur. Warns against DAP (18 46 0) on alkaline soils. Lime very acid soils so phosphorus stays available.
entries.prevent: Put phosphorus in the planting hole and in the first years on new land, and add compost.

entries.name: Copper deficiency in citrus (dalandan, ponkan)
entries.local: Kakulangan sa copper ng dalandan at ponkan
entries.hint: Brown gum stains on the fruit peel, fruit that split, and long, soft, S shaped shoots with big dark leaves.
entries.symptoms: On oranges the fruit often show it first: brown stained areas of hard gum on the peel that darken to almost black by half size, fruit splitting across or around the stains, and heavy fruit drop. Leaves come out unusually large and dark green with the midrib bowed up, on long, soft, angular, drooping S shaped shoots. Clear gum blisters form at the nodes, reddish brown gum breaks out on twigs. Twigs die back and sprout bunches of weak buds.
entries.stage: Young trees and new plantings, and trees pushed with heavy nitrogen.
entries.causes: New plantings on sandy or organic soils never farmed, limey soils, and heavy nitrogen (it is also called ammoniation). It is rare where copper fungicides are used.
entries.confuse: Normal splitting starts only at the blossom end. Copper splits also run across the fruit and around gum stains. Potassium shortage splits fruit without gum stains. Gummosis is a bark disease that oozes gum from the trunk and larger branches. Too much nitrogen alone gives dark soft growth without gum blisters.
entries.confirm: Check the spray record. Copper deficiency is unlikely where copper fungicides are sprayed. UF IFAS notes that fruit signs are the most reliable field indicator. A soil test on new land helps.
entries.fix: UF IFAS reports near immediate recovery and normal fruit set from a copper spray at flowering. TNAU gives Copper sulfate at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter) every two weeks. Try a few branches first, since plain copper sulfate can burn soft leaves. Cut back excess nitrogen. Below pH 5.5 built up soil copper can kill roots, so do not overdo it.
entries.prevent: On new sandy land UF IFAS adds copper to the fertilizer at 2.5 percent of the nitrogen rate. Keep pH near neutral and nitrogen moderate.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in pomelo
entries.hint: The whole tree pale green to yellow, old leaves falling early, thin canopy and few flowers.
entries.symptoms: No pomelo particular leaf description was found, so this follows the citrus pattern. Older leaves turn pale green, then yellow, evenly with no clear pattern, and drop early, so the canopy thins. New leaves are small, thin and light green, flushes are short, and the tree flowers sparsely and sets a light crop.
entries.stage: Flowering and after harvest. A leaf survey of Mekong Delta pomelo orchards found nitrogen among the most limiting nutrients at both stages.
entries.causes: Trees fed little or irregularly, sandy or leached soils, heavy rain, waterlogging. Raw straw or manure that ties nitrogen up as it rots.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also yellows older leaves but leaves a green V at the leaf base and is worst next to the fruit. Sulfur deficiency starts on young leaves. Citrus greening (HLB) gives yellow shoots and blotches that do not match on the two sides of the midrib.
entries.confirm: Leaf test: the Mekong Delta study sampled the third and fourth leaves from 3 month old branches. UF IFAS uses 4 to 6 month old leaves from twigs without fruit. The DA Cagayan Valley pummelo guide asks for a soil analysis, through the DA, to set rates.
entries.fix: Apply nitrogen in the weeded ring, split into two equal doses: at the start of the rainy season to build vigour before flowering. Toward the end of the rainy season, as the DA Cagayan Valley pummelo guide sets out. The guide budgets urea, complete fertilizer, muriate of potash and chicken dung every year, with the amount based on the soil analysis. For quick greening, TNAU gives a Urea spray at 2 percent (20 grams per liter) every 15 days for citrus.
entries.prevent: Fertilize every year by the soil test, ring weed before each dose and mulch. Do not overdo ammonium fertilizers: in Chinese pomelo orchards, decades of heavy ammonium nitrogen dropped the soil pH from 5.7 to 4.3 and brought magnesium shortage.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in pomelo
entries.hint: Few flowers and fruit, poor fruit set and light fruit. Older leaf edges yellow to bronze.
entries.symptoms: Leaf signs follow citrus: the edges of older leaves turn pale yellow or bronze, then the yellow spreads, and new leaves are small. In pomelo the cost shows most in the crop. In a UPLB trial on 13 year old Magallanes pomelo in Davao City, trees given more potash flowered about four times as much, set 86 to 117 percent more fruit, carried about seven times as many fruit. Had heavier fruit with thinner peel and more juice.
entries.stage: Flowering, fruit set and the first two months of fruit growth. In the Davao trial peak flowering and fruit set came in April and peak flushing in June.
entries.causes: Sandy or leached soils, heavy rain, soils rich in magnesium, and nitrogen fed without enough potash. While each heavy crop carries potash away.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also starts on older leaves, but leaves a green V at the base. Salt or fertilizer burn scorches edges on leaves of all ages. Poor fruit set also comes from drought at flowering, so check the watering too.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the third and fourth leaves from 3 month old branches, and a soil test for potash, magnesium and calcium.
entries.fix: In the Davao trial the recommended rate was 150 grams of potassium (K) per tree as a basal dose, about 300 grams of Muriate of potash 0 0 60. 225 grams of potassium per tree (about 450 grams of Muriate of potash) gave much more flowering, fruit set and yield. Adding a foliar potash spray to the basal dose helped further. Time the doses before flowering and in the two months after fruit set.
entries.prevent: Give potash every year along with nitrogen, and more on trees carrying heavy crops.
