entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in pomelo
entries.hint: Older and middle leaves yellow between the veins, leaving a green V at the leaf base, worst near the fruit.
entries.symptoms: Older and middle leaves yellow between the veins. As in other citrus, the yellow starts near the leaf base on each side of the midrib and spreads until only the tip and a V shaped area at the base stay green, then the leaf turns yellow to bronze and drops. Limbs carrying heavy fruit show it most. In a Chinese honey pomelo district, about a third of leaves showed this yellowing and most soils were short of magnesium.
entries.stage: Fruit growth, on heavily bearing limbs.
entries.causes: Acid soils, especially soils acidified by years of heavy ammonium fertilizer, high rainfall that leaches magnesium, and heavy potash. Seedy fruit draw more magnesium than seedless kinds.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency yellows the whole tree evenly. Potassium deficiency bronzes the leaf edges. Citrus greening can look like magnesium deficiency. In the pen test magnesium yellowing is the same on both sides of the midrib, HLB blotches are not.
entries.confirm: Leaf test and a soil test for pH, magnesium, potash and calcium.
entries.fix: On acid soils use Dolomite. The DA Cagayan Valley guide wants pH 5.5 to 6.5 and advises liming below pH 5. Where the soil test shows low magnesium, UF IFAS gives magnesium at 20 percent of the nitrogen rate, as Magnesium sulfate or Kieserite. In the Chinese honey pomelo trial, sprays of Magnesium sulfate at 4 percent (40 grams per liter), about 7 liters per tree split over three monthly sprays, together with much less NPK, raised leaf magnesium and cut the yellowing. That is a strong mix, so try a few branches first.
entries.prevent: Lime with dolomite, avoid overusing ammonium fertilizers, and keep potash and magnesium in balance.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in pomelo
entries.hint: Young leaves mottled yellow between green veins, small, narrow and upright.
entries.symptoms: No pomelo particular description was found, so this follows citrus. Young leaves show yellow patches between the veins with an uneven green band along the midrib and main veins (mottle leaf). In severe cases new leaves are small, narrow, pointed and upright, twigs die back. Fruit on weak twigs stay small with low juice.
entries.stage: New flushes.
entries.causes: High pH and limed soils, heavy phosphate, heavy poultry manure, organic soils and cold wet spells.
entries.confuse: Citrus greening (HLB) is the main look alike and, with tristeza, is named by DOST PCAARRD as the main cause of low citrus production in the country. Do the pen test: zinc deficiency looks the same on both sides of the midrib, HLB blotches do not. Manganese deficiency mottles leaves but keeps them normal in size.
entries.confirm: Pen test, then a zinc spray on a few branches and a look at the next flush. If the mottle stays uneven, send leaves for an HLB laboratory test. A leaf test helps.
entries.fix: Spray zinc on each new flush when leaves are two thirds to almost fully expanded, as UF IFAS advises. TNAU gives Zinc sulfate at 2 percent (20 grams per liter) mixed with 1 percent lime (10 grams per liter) every two weeks for citrus. Zinc on the soil does not work on limey soils.
entries.prevent: Keep the pH below 6.5, avoid heavy phosphate, include zinc in regular sprays, and control psyllids.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in pomelo
entries.hint: Few flowers and a light crop. Old leaves dull with bronze freckles. Fruit coarse with a hollow core and sour juice.
entries.symptoms: Leaf signs are weak and follow citrus: older leaves lose their deep green, partly yellow. May show a dull bronze or purplish cast with small freckles along the main veins. Flowering and fruit set are poor, leaves and fruit drop early, and fruit are coarse, with a hollow core and sour juice. A leaf survey of Mekong Delta pomelo found phosphorus the most limiting nutrient at flowering, fruit growth and after harvest.
entries.stage: All through the cycle. Most felt at flowering and fruit set.
entries.causes: Strongly acid soils where iron and aluminium lock phosphorus up, limey soils, low organic matter, cold wet soil and weak roots.
entries.confuse: A thick peel is not proof of phosphorus shortage: in the Davao Magallanes trial, trees given more potash grew a thinner peel. So low potash can thicken it too. Nitrogen deficiency gives evenly pale leaves without bronze freckles.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test of the third and fourth leaves from 3 month old branches.
entries.fix: Apply a phosphorus fertilizer by the soil test. Complete fertilizer is already in the DA Cagayan Valley pummelo budget every year. UF IFAS notes superphosphate suits soils of any pH, and warns against DAP (18 46 0) on alkaline soils. Lime soils below pH 5 so phosphorus stays available.
entries.prevent: Put phosphorus in the planting hole, keep the pH at 5.5 to 6.5, and add compost or chicken dung.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in pomelo
entries.hint: Small, hard, lumpy fruit with gum spots in the thick white peel. Many fruit drop. Shoot tips die.
entries.symptoms: No pomelo particular deficiency description was found, so this follows citrus. Fruit stay small, hard and misshapen, with gum pockets and dark spots in the white inner peel and sometimes in the core, and many drop. The growing tip dies and the shoot branches out. Young leaves curl and their veins split and turn corky.
entries.stage: Flowering to fruit growth, often after a long dry spell.
entries.causes: Sandy and alkaline soils low in organic matter, high nitrogen or calcium, drought, and fertilizers with no micronutrients.
entries.confuse: Too much boron is a real risk in pomelo. In a Chinese field trial, 100 grams of borax per tree per year, split in two doses, caused toxicity: yellowing between the veins that starts at the leaf tip and moves to the base. A 45 percent yield loss. Citrus greening also gives corky veins and lopsided fruit. Use the pen test.
entries.confirm: Soil and leaf test for boron before adding any. The Chinese study treats soil boron below 0.5 mg per kg as short and above 5 mg per kg as toxic.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a Borax spray at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter) for citrus. UF IFAS advises boron on the soil or as a spray, never both. Keep soil doses small and only on soils that test low.
entries.prevent: Use fertilizers that carry micronutrients, keep organic matter up and water during dry spells. Never repeat big borax doses without a test.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in jackfruit
entries.hint: The whole canopy turns pale green, older leaves go yellow and drop, and new shoots stay short.
entries.symptoms: No jackfruit particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The tree first looks light green all over. Then the older, lower leaves turn evenly yellow, veins included, and fall early, while the yellowing slowly moves up to younger leaves. New flushes are short with small leaves, and the tree sets fewer fruits.
entries.stage: Young trees in the first years after planting, and old bearing trees that never get fertilizer.
entries.causes: In the Philippines jackfruit is seldom fertilized, so many trees run short. Sandy or eroded soils low in organic matter, heavy rain that washes nitrogen away. Weeds or grass competing under the canopy make it worse.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also starts on old leaves, but the yellow sits between the veins while the veins stay green. Jackfruit does not tolerate wet soil, and two or three days of standing water can yellow and kill a tree. Check drainage and the roots before blaming nitrogen.
entries.confirm: Send a sample of recently matured leaves for a leaf test and a soil sample for a soil test. A clear greening of new leaves within a few weeks after a nitrogen dose confirms it.
entries.fix: For young trees, the Philippine practice described by Coronel gives 100 to 150 grams of Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 per tree one month after planting and the same again six months later. For fruiting trees it gives 0.5 to 1 kg of Complete 14 14 14 per tree at the start of the rainy season and the same near its end. At least 2 to 3 kg per dose for full grown trees of 15 to 20 years. Spread it in a ring under the canopy edge and water it in.
entries.prevent: Fertilize every year in two splits, raise the amount as the tree grows. Keep a mulch or compost ring under the canopy.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in jackfruit
entries.hint: Edges of older leaves yellow and then burn brown. Fruits stay small with thin flakes.
entries.symptoms: No jackfruit particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The edges and tips of older or newly matured leaves yellow first, then dry brown as a scorch that moves in toward the midrib. Badly hit leaves drop. Fruit and seed production suffers, so fruits are smaller and lower in quality.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, most of all during fruit growth when the fruit pulls potash from the leaves.
entries.causes: Heavy crops remove potash every year, and most trees get none back. Sandy, leached soils under heavy rain and dry spells that cut uptake make it worse.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also hits old leaves but yellows between the veins, not along the edge. Fertilizer burn from too much fertilizer close to the trunk and dry wind can also brown leaf edges. Those show after a dose or a dry spell and on the windward side.
entries.confirm: A leaf test of recently matured leaves and a soil test for exchangeable potassium.
entries.fix: Give potash with the yearly fertilizer, following the soil test. In a Samar and Leyte trial on the EVIARC Sweet variety, trees given 0.83 kg Complete 14 14 14, 3.33 kg Solophos and 0.73 kg Muriate of potash 0 0 60 per tree gave bigger pulp and more flakes per fruit than unfertilized trees. TNAU's schedule rises from 0.1 kg potash per tree in the first year to 0.5 kg from the sixth year, in two splits.
entries.prevent: Include potash every year, split in two doses, and return leaves and fruit waste to the ring as compost.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in jackfruit
entries.hint: A slow, stunted tree whose older leaves turn dull with a purple or bronze tint underneath.
entries.symptoms: No jackfruit particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. Growth is slow and the tree stays small. Older leaves lose their shine and take on a purple or bronze color, most of all on the underside. Roots stay weak and young trees take longer to start bearing.
entries.stage: Young trees after planting, and trees on very acid soils.
entries.causes: Acid soils that lock phosphorus up, soils low in organic matter, and cold or waterlogged soil.
entries.confuse: Cool weather, drought and root damage can also slow growth and redden leaves, so check the soil moisture and the roots. Nitrogen deficiency makes old leaves pale yellow rather than purple or bronze.
entries.confirm: A soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: Apply a phosphorus fertilizer in a ring under the canopy and work it into the topsoil, following the soil test. The Samar and Leyte trial used 3.33 kg Solophos (Superphosphate 0 20 0) per tree with complete fertilizer and potash. TNAU's schedule gives 0.08 kg phosphorus per tree in the first year, rising to 0.4 kg from the sixth year. Lime very acid soils so the phosphorus stays available.
entries.prevent: Mix compost and a phosphorus fertilizer into the planting soil, and add some every year.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in jackfruit
entries.hint: Fruits split or crack with a reddish purple color and gum in the cracks. Young leaves yellow and brittle.
entries.symptoms: Fruits split or crack, and the cracks show a reddish purple color with gum oozing out. Young leaves turn yellow, thin and brittle, and the shoot tips grow poorly. Flowers can drop before they are pollinated, which leaves misshapen fruit.
entries.stage: Flowering and fruit growth, and on new flushes.
entries.causes: Sandy or leached soils low in organic matter, dry spells, and heavy liming. Boron moves little inside the tree, so young tissue and fruit show it first.
entries.confuse: Rhizopus fruit rot makes young fruits go soft and grey black with mould, not dry cracks with gum. Fruit borers leave holes with frass. Uneven watering after a dry spell can also split fruit, so look at the young leaves too.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test, as Kerala Agricultural University advises, and a leaf test for boron. Cracked fruit together with yellow, brittle young leaves points to boron.
entries.fix: Kerala Agricultural University gives Borax at 4 kg per acre (about 10 kg per hectare) to the soil, or a foliar spray of Borax at 1 gram per liter. Do not mix boron with calcium fertilizers or apply it together with ammonium fertilizers. Too much boron is toxic, so do not repeat high doses without a test.
entries.prevent: Keep organic matter up, water during long dry spells, and add a small boron dose on soils that tested low.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in jackfruit
entries.hint: Small leaves on short stalks crowd into a rosette and yellow between the veins. Many fruits drop.
entries.symptoms: New leaves come out small with short stalks and crowd together at the shoot tip in a rosette. They yellow between the veins and can show yellow streaks. Fruits stay smaller and more of them drop, so the yield falls.
entries.stage: New flushes, flowering and early fruit growth.
entries.causes: Zinc is the most common micronutrient shortage of fruit crops. Soils with pH outside about 5 to 7.5, heavy phosphate fertilizer, and sandy or eroded soils bring it on.
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency also yellows young leaves between the veins, but the leaves stay normal in size and do not rosette. Mites and thrips can also stunt new leaves. Look for the pests and for scarred, curled leaves.
entries.confirm: A soil test for zinc and pH, and a leaf test. New leaves that come out normal after a zinc spray on a few branches confirm it.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a foliar spray of 500 grams Zinc sulfate, 250 grams lime and 100 grams urea with 100 ml soap in 100 liters of water (5 grams Zinc sulfate per liter), three times at 20 day intervals, plus 250 grams Zinc sulfate per tree mixed with compost or manure in two equal doses when the tree puts out new growth. Kerala Agricultural University gives 8 kg Zinc sulfate per acre (about 20 kg per hectare) on deficient soils. Do not apply zinc and phosphate fertilizer at the same time.
entries.prevent: Avoid heavy phosphate, keep organic matter up, and include zinc in the program on soils that tested low.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in jackfruit
entries.hint: Older leaves yellow between the side veins, from the edge in toward the midrib, while the veins stay green.
entries.symptoms: Older, lower leaves turn yellow between the side veins on both sides of the midrib while the veins stay green. The yellow starts at the leaf edge and moves in toward the midrib. Later the yellow parts turn reddish with dead patches, and the leaves drop early.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, often after heavy potash fertilizer.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy and leached soils, and heavy potash fertilizer, which competes with magnesium.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency also hits old leaves, but it burns the leaf edge brown instead of yellowing between the veins. Nitrogen deficiency yellows the whole old leaf, veins included. Iron deficiency shows the same green veins but on young leaves.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test for magnesium, potassium and calcium, as Kerala Agricultural University advises, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: Kerala Agricultural University gives 32 kg Magnesium sulfate per acre (about 80 kg per hectare) in bands near the trees. TNAU gives 1.5 kg Dolomite per tree per year to the soil and a foliar spray of Magnesium sulfate at 30 to 50 grams per liter. That is a strong mix, so test it on a few branches first. Do not apply magnesium and potassium fertilizers together.
entries.prevent: Use Dolomite when liming acid soils, and keep potash and magnesium in balance based on a soil test.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in jackfruit
entries.hint: Young leaves turn yellow between green veins. In bad cases the whole new leaf goes yellow.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves yellow between the veins while the veins and midrib stay green. In bad cases the whole young leaf turns yellow, though the midrib can stay green, and growth is stunted. Older leaves usually stay green.
entries.stage: New flushes, mostly on high pH soils or after waterlogging.
entries.causes: Iron is plentiful in most acid Philippine soils, so true shortage is uncommon. It shows on limestone, coralline or overlimed soils with high pH, and in waterlogged soil. Kerala Agricultural University notes that low potassium can also bring on iron yellowing.
entries.confuse: Zinc deficiency also yellows young leaves between the veins, but the leaves are small and bunched. Manganese deficiency shows on fully grown leaves as a mix of green and yellow between the main veins. Nitrogen deficiency starts on old leaves.
entries.confirm: A soil test for pH and iron. Kerala soils are often high in iron. So Kerala Agricultural University advises a soil test to find the real cause before adding iron.
entries.fix: On deficient soils Kerala Agricultural University gives Ferrous sulfate at 6 kg per acre (about 15 kg per hectare). UF IFAS advises chelated iron (EDDHA) as a soil drench on high pH soils, since iron sprays on the leaves generally work poorly. Ferrous sulfate to the soil on acid soils. Improve drainage where water stands.
entries.prevent: Do not overlime, drain wet spots, and keep potash up.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in avocado
entries.hint: Leaves fade from dark green to light green or yellow. Thin canopy of small leaves and few fruits.
entries.symptoms: At first the leaves just fade a little and new shoots grow more slowly. Later the dark green leaves turn evenly light green to yellow, the canopy thins out and new leaves are smaller, narrow and stiff. Trees set and hold fewer fruits.
entries.stage: Young trees, and bearing trees after several years of fruiting with no fertilizer.
entries.causes: Many Philippine avocado trees are grown with no fertilizer at all, which a UPLB review links to the fall in yield and quality after a few years of bearing. Heavy rain on sandy or eroded soils washes nitrogen away.
entries.confuse: Phytophthora root rot also gives small, pale green or yellowish leaves and a thin canopy. But the leaves wilt even when the soil is wet, leaf tips brown, branches die back, and the small feeder roots are black, brittle and dead. Dig and check the roots. Sulfur shortage hits the young leaves first, while nitrogen shortage fades the whole tree.
entries.confirm: Leaf test: University of California advises taking the most recently expanded and matured leaves near the shoot tips, from the last main flush, about 5 to 7 months old. Check roots and drainage. Trees that green up after ammonium sulfate or urea confirm it.
entries.fix: Apply Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 or Urea 46 0 0 in a ring under the canopy at the start and end of the rainy season. Philippine growers give young, non bearing trees 100 to 200 grams of Ammonium sulfate or 50 to 100 grams of Urea per tree twice a year. Bearing trees about 500 grams of Complete 14 14 14 twice a year. Full bearing trees about 2 kg of complete fertilizer a year. Add manure or compost.
entries.prevent: Fertilize every year in two splits and keep a mulch of leaves or compost under the canopy, away from the trunk.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in avocado
entries.hint: Old leaves yellow between the veins and along the edge, turning tan then brown. Leaves curve down.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves show it first. Yellowing starts between the veins and in an uneven band along the edge, then turns tan and brown. Scorched dead patches appear over the leaf. Leaves may curve downward. Fruits stay smaller, and Haifa notes the veins inside the fruit can turn black.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, most of all while fruits fill.
entries.causes: Sandy or leached soils, heavy fruit crops, and fertilizer programs that give nitrogen only.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also starts on old leaves, but the veins stay dark green and bright while the tissue between them pales. Root rot gives brown leaf tips too, but with wilting, a thin canopy and dead black roots.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of recently matured leaves near the shoot tips, 5 to 7 months old, and a soil test for potash.
entries.fix: Give bearing trees a fertilizer richer in potash, following the soil test. University of Florida advises mixes with 9 to 15 percent potash and only 2 to 4 percent phosphate for bearing trees. Add Muriate of potash 0 0 60 or Sulfate of potash 0 0 50 to the complete fertilizer in two splits during the rains.
entries.prevent: Switch from a nitrogen only program to a complete fertilizer once trees bear, and return fallen leaves as mulch.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in avocado
entries.hint: Little leaf: new leaves small, mottled yellow between the veins and crowded in tufts at the twig tips. Fruit small and round.
entries.symptoms: Early on, the leaves yellow between the veins and come out a little smaller. In bad cases the leaves are much smaller and narrower, trough shaped and bent back, yellow or bronzed between the veins. Old leaves get many small dead spots. Twigs grow very short so the leaves crowd into tufts like a feather duster. Fruits stay small and round, sunburn easily and get dead spots on the skin, and twig tips die back.
entries.stage: New flushes, often worst while the crop matures and after long dry spells.
entries.causes: Limestone and high pH soils, long droughts without watering. Years of only chemical nitrogen with no manure or compost, as a Florida study found.
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency also yellows young leaves between green veins, but the leaves keep their normal size and shape and do not tuft. Manganese deficiency starts as yellowing near the midrib that spreads out. Root rot also gives small leaves and dieback, but with wilting and dead black roots.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of recently matured leaves near the shoot tips, and a soil test for pH and zinc. Spray a few trees: small leaves that already formed only green up, but the next flush comes out normal size.
entries.fix: Spray Zinc sulfate with hydrated lime just before a main growth flush. In the Florida trial that cured little leaf, the mix was about 12 grams of Zinc sulfate and 6 grams of hydrated lime per liter of water for severe cases. Half that for mild ones. University of Florida advises 3 to 4 nutrient sprays a year with zinc for young trees.
entries.prevent: Give manure or compost along with chemical fertilizer, water in long dry spells, and keep zinc in the yearly foliar sprays.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in avocado
entries.hint: Dull or bronzed leaves with purple veins underneath and purplish leaf stalks. Slow growth.
entries.symptoms: Signs are often not clear. Leaves look dull and can turn bronze, the veins on the underside turn purple, and leaf stalks may take a purple cast. Older leaves can show uneven dead spots between the veins. Growth is slow, the canopy is thin and leaves drop early.
entries.stage: Young trees after planting, and trees on poor acid soils.
entries.causes: Acid, weathered soils that lock up phosphorus and soils low in organic matter.
entries.confuse: Potassium and magnesium deficiency also mark old leaves, but with yellowing between the veins rather than a dull purplish cast. Root rot also slows growth and thins the canopy, so check the roots.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test of recently matured leaves near the shoot tips.
entries.fix: Use a complete fertilizer for young trees, following the soil test. University of Florida advises mixes with 6 to 10 percent phosphate for young trees and 2 to 4 percent for bearing trees. Where the soil test is very low, add 16 20 0 or Superphosphate 0 20 0 in the ring, and lime very acid soils.
entries.prevent: Put phosphorus and compost in the planting hole and use a complete fertilizer in the first years.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in avocado
entries.hint: Tip growth discolored and burnt, leaves twisted with corky split veins. Lumpy, misshapen fruit.
entries.symptoms: The shoot tips discolor, young leaves burn and twist, and their veins split and turn corky. Twigs may swell. Haifa adds small holes between the veins with a pale ring around each. In bad cases dead patches on branches and the trunk. Fruits can be lumpy, curved or misshapen, with sunken corky patches.
entries.stage: New flushes, flowering and fruit set.
entries.causes: No avocado particular causes were found in the sources. In other tree crops such as coffee it comes with soils low in boron, heavy liming, heavy potash and long droughts. The same likely holds here.
entries.confuse: Calcium deficiency also distorts young leaves with dead tips and uneven edges, but without split corky veins. Copper deficiency kills the growing tips after the internodes shorten, with dark green leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of recently matured leaves near the shoot tips, and a soil test for boron.
entries.fix: University of Florida includes boron in 3 to 4 nutrient sprays a year for young trees, and possibly later. No avocado particular rate was found, so use Solubor or Borax at the label rate and retest. Too much boron is toxic.
entries.prevent: Add organic matter, mulch and water in dry spells. Keep a small boron dose in the foliar program where tests run low.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in avocado
entries.hint: Young leaves yellow with narrow dark green strips along the veins. Later the veins pale too and leaves drop.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves turn yellow between the veins while narrow strips along the veins stay dark green. Later the veins yellow as well and the leaves may fall. Leaves keep a normal size and shape.
entries.stage: New flushes, on limestone soils and after waterlogging.
entries.causes: Alkaline, high pH soils such as limestone soils, overliming, and waterlogged soils. University of Florida notes that wet, poorly drained soils bring on nutrient deficiency signs and dieback in avocado.
entries.confuse: Zinc deficiency also yellows young leaves between the veins, but the leaves are small, narrow and crowded in tufts. Manganese deficiency starts near the midrib and turns dull. Phytophthora root rot also yellows leaves on wet soils, but the trees wilt and the feeder roots are black and dead.
entries.confirm: Soil test for pH and check drainage. Look at the roots. A test treatment of iron chelate on one or two trees that greens the next flush confirms it.
entries.fix: University of Florida advises iron chelate made for high pH soils, drenched into the soil under the canopy from late spring through summer, because foliar iron sprays are generally not effective on avocado. Its table gives about 15 to 20 grams of chelate per tree a year in the first year, rising to about 55 to 110 grams for trees five years and older. Improve drainage where water stands.
entries.prevent: Plant on a mound where water stands, avoid overwatering and overliming.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in guava
entries.hint: Old leaves pale green to light yellow from the tip. Slow, thin tree with few fruits.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn pale green to light yellow, usually starting at the tip, and in bad cases they die and drop. The tree grows slowly and stays small, with few new shoots, so it flowers and fruits less.
entries.stage: Young trees, and bearing trees after heavy crops.
entries.causes: Trees that get little fertilizer, sandy soils low in organic matter, and heavy rain that washes nitrogen away.
entries.confuse: Root knot and other nematodes also cause stunting, yellowing, wilting and dieback, as University of Florida notes. So check the roots for galls. Magnesium shortage on old leaves shows yellow, bronze or reddish patches between green veins rather than an even pale color.
entries.confirm: Soil test and a leaf test of the third pair of leaves from the shoot tip. New growth that greens up after urea confirms it.
entries.fix: DA Caraga advises Complete 14 14 14 at 100 to 150 grams at planting and 200 to 300 grams per young tree. For bearing trees 300 grams to 1 kg of complete fertilizer plus 300 grams each of Muriate of potash 0 0 60 and 16 20 0, in a shallow furrow around the canopy edge, together with compost. India's National Horticulture Board gives 300 to 400 grams of nitrogen per bearing tree a year. For a quick lift, TNAU gives a Urea spray at 1 to 2 percent (10 to 20 grams per liter) every two weeks.
entries.prevent: Fertilize every year in splits during the rains and add compost or manure under the canopy.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in guava
entries.hint: Older leaves dark blue green or bronzed with purple to red specks. Weak, slow tree and poor fruit.
entries.symptoms: Growth is slow, weak and stunted. Older leaves turn dark or blue green, and in bad cases leaves and stems take a purple color. Fruit matures late and develops poorly. In India this shows as leaf bronzing: purple to red specks scattered over the leaves, a bronze or copper color on older leaves, heavy leaf fall in bad cases. Brown patterns on the fruit skin.
entries.stage: Young trees, and bearing trees once fruiting begins, when the tree pulls nutrients from old leaves into the fruit.
entries.causes: Poor, acid soils. In bronzed guava orchards in India, soils were low in fertility and pH. The leaves were low in nitrogen, phosphorus and zinc. Indian course notes tie bronzing to soils that are marginal in phosphorus and potash.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also gives bronze or reddish patches between the veins of old leaves, but the veins stay clearly green. Potassium deficiency scorches the leaf edges. A leaf test separates them.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH. A leaf test of the third pair of leaves from the shoot tip for nitrogen, phosphorus, potash and zinc together.
entries.fix: In an Indian study, bronzing was largely overcome by spraying 0.5 percent DAP (Ammonium phosphate 18 46 0, 5 grams per liter) together with Zinc sulfate every week for two months. TNAU gives DAP at 2 percent every two weeks. For the soil, DA Caraga gives bearing trees 300 grams of 16 20 0 plus complete fertilizer and potash. Lime very acid soils, following the soil test.
entries.prevent: Use a complete fertilizer with phosphorus and potash every year from the time trees start to bear, plus compost, and correct acid soils.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in guava
entries.hint: Older leaves yellow and scorch at the edges. Weak stems, small and few fruits.
entries.symptoms: The edges of older leaves turn yellow and then scorch brown. Growth is slow, stems are weak, and fruits stay smaller and fewer. Shortage of potash, with phosphorus, is also linked to leaf bronzing once trees start to fruit.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, during fruit growth.
entries.causes: Sandy and leached soils, heavy crops, and programs that give nitrogen only. Indian course notes tie bronzing to soils marginal in phosphorus and potash.
entries.confuse: Phosphorus shortage and bronzing give purple to red specks over the leaf rather than a scorched edge. Salt damage also browns leaf tips and edges, with leaf drop and dieback, as University of Florida notes. So check the water and fertilizer history.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potash and a leaf test of the third pair of leaves from the shoot tip.
entries.fix: DA Caraga gives bearing trees 300 grams of Muriate of potash 0 0 60 with complete fertilizer and 16 20 0. India's National Horticulture Board gives 250 to 350 grams of K2O per bearing tree a year. Notes that Sulfate of potash sprays at 1 to 2 percent raised yield and fruit quality. TNAU gives a 2 percent spray every two weeks.
entries.prevent: Raise the potash share once trees bear. University of Florida advises 9 to 15 percent potash in mixes for bearing trees.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in guava
entries.hint: Newest leaves small, narrow and pointed, strongly yellow between bright green veins, with tiny brown dots.
entries.symptoms: The youngest leaves come out small, narrow and pointed, with raised veins. The blade cups up or down along the midrib, with the edges turned in. Leaves yellow strongly between the veins while the veins stay bright green, and small brown dots spread over the blade. Shoots stay thin and the tree stays dwarfed.
entries.stage: New flushes, and orchards on poor soils where bronzing also shows.
entries.causes: High pH soils, heavy phosphate fertilizer, and poor, acid soils low in zinc and organic matter, where bronzed Indian orchards had low leaf zinc.
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency also keeps green veins on yellow young leaves. But the leaves keep a normal shape, turn fully yellow and then whitish, and lower leaves stay normal. Manganese deficiency starts as a faint yellowing on the shaded middle leaves, best seen against the light.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the third pair of leaves from the shoot tip. In a Brazilian trial deficient seedlings held 9 ppm zinc against 14 ppm in healthy ones. A soil test for pH and phosphorus helps. Spray a few trees and watch the next flush.
entries.fix: Spray Zinc sulfate with DAP every week for two months, as the Indian bronzing study did (DAP at 0.5 percent). Indian guides also give a spray of 0.3 percent Zinc sulfate (3 grams per liter) with 0.4 percent boric acid before flowering, which raised yield and fruit size. Course notes give 100 grams of Zinc sulfate per tree to the soil on bronzed trees.
entries.prevent: Avoid heavy phosphate and overliming, add compost, and include zinc in a pre flowering spray where leaf tests run low.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in guava
entries.hint: Old leaves get yellow, bronze or reddish patches between the veins while the veins stay green.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves develop yellow, bronze or reddish patches between the veins while the veins stay green. In bad cases younger leaves show it too and leaves fall early.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, mostly on acid soils.
entries.causes: Acid soils, and heavy potash or calcium fertilizer, which compete with magnesium.
entries.confuse: Bronzing from low phosphorus and zinc also gives purple to red specks on the leaves. A leaf test tells them apart. Potassium shortage scorches the leaf edges instead.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the third pair of leaves from the shoot tip, and a soil test for magnesium, potash and calcium together.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a foliar spray of Magnesium sulfate at 2 percent (20 grams per liter) every two weeks. On acid soils use Dolomite, following the soil test. University of Florida advises 4 to 6 percent magnesium in the mix for young trees.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soils with Dolomite and keep potash and magnesium in balance.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in guava
entries.hint: Newest leaves narrow, thick and brittle, bent down as if the stalk were broken. Shoot tips die back.
entries.symptoms: The youngest leaves come out narrower than normal, pale, with a dark net of veins on a light background. They thicken, turn brittle and curl or twist downward as if the leaf stalk were broken. The top pairs drop while older leaves stay. Later the growing points die and branches dry from the tip down.
entries.stage: New flushes and before flowering.
entries.causes: No guava particular soil causes were found in the sources. The Brazilian trial notes that boron interacts with calcium and phosphorus in the leaf.
entries.confuse: Aphids feeding on young growth also curl the leaves, as DA Caraga notes. But you can see the insects and the leaves are not thick and brittle. Zinc deficiency also gives small, narrow new leaves, but with brown dots and no dying tips.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the third pair of leaves from the shoot tip. In the Brazilian trial deficient seedlings held 7 ppm boron against 43 ppm in healthy ones. A soil test for boron helps.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a foliar spray of Borax at 0.5 percent every two weeks. Indian guides also give boric acid at 0.4 percent with zinc sulfate before flowering. Boron is toxic in excess, so do not repeat high doses without a test.
entries.prevent: Add organic matter and include a small boron dose in a pre flowering spray where tests run low.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in lanzones
entries.hint: Pale yellow green trees with few, small new leaves, and the older leaves yellow and drop.
entries.symptoms: No lanzones particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The whole tree turns light green, then the older leaves yellow evenly and fall, and the yellowing moves up the tree. Young trees put out few new leaves, and the leaflets stay small. Bearing trees flower and fruit poorly.
entries.stage: Young trees under coconut or banana shade, and old trees after a heavy crop.
entries.causes: Trees that get little or no fertilizer show it most. In a long PCA trial in Davao, leaf nitrogen of bearing trees fell below the normal level after a heavy fruiting year, because the fruit takes up so much. Sandy, eroded soils and competing intercrops make it worse.
entries.confuse: Heavy shade also gives thin, pale trees. Check how much light the tree gets. Bark borer attack on the trunk and branches weakens the tree and can yellow the canopy. Scrape the bark and look for larvae and frass.
entries.confirm: Leaf test using the third leaf from the top of a tertiary branch, as in the PCA trial. PCA gives about 2.7 percent nitrogen as the normal level for bearing lanzones. A soil test helps set the rate.
entries.fix: For young trees, a Southern Mindanao University trial found that two doses of 25 to 100 grams of nitrogen per tree (about 55 to 220 grams of Urea 46 0 0) gave more and bigger leaves. Bearing trees in the PCA Davao trial got a complete fertilizer with chlorine, sulfur and boron (14 5 20) plus organic fertilizer or coconut husks every year. Apply in a ring under the canopy after weeding, and water it in.
entries.prevent: Fertilize every year, with an extra dose after a heavy crop. Keep litter and husks as mulch to build soil organic matter.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in lanzones
entries.hint: Older leaflets scorch brown at the tips and edges. Bunches carry small, sour fruits.
entries.symptoms: No lanzones particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The tips and edges of older leaflets yellow and then dry brown, and the scorch moves inward. Fruit set and fruit quality drop, so bunches carry fewer, smaller fruits.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, most of all during and right after fruit growth.
entries.causes: Fruit carries a lot of potash away. In the PCA Davao trial, leaf potassium of lanzones dropped below normal in a heavy fruiting year as the nutrient moved into the developing fruit. Leached, acid soils under heavy rain lose potash fast.
entries.confuse: Dry wind and drought also brown leaf edges, mostly on the exposed side of the tree. Fertilizer burn from a heavy dose close to the trunk shows soon after application.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the third leaf from the top of a tertiary branch. PCA gives about 2 percent potassium as normal for bearing lanzones. A soil test for exchangeable potassium.
entries.fix: Give potash every year, following the soil test. The PCA Davao trial used a 14 5 20 fertilizer and, in some years, 80 grams Muriate of potash 0 0 60 with 400 grams rock phosphate per tree, split between June and October. A Philstar farm column describes growers using 17 0 17 and Muriate of potash 0 0 60 at about 1 kg per 10 kg of expected fruit, with the last dose at least two months before ripening.
entries.prevent: Add potash after each harvest and again before flowering, and keep a mulch ring of leaf litter.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in lanzones
entries.hint: Slow, stunted trees with dull older leaves tinged purple or bronze underneath, and poor flowering.
entries.symptoms: No lanzones particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. Growth is slow and the tree stays stunted. Older leaves turn dull with a purple or bronze tint, most of all on the underside. In the PCA trial, trees with more leaf phosphorus flowered and bore better.
entries.stage: Young trees, and bearing trees on very acid soils before flowering.
entries.causes: Very acid soils that hold phosphorus tightly. Soil under lanzones in the PCA Davao trial ranged from about pH 4.1 to 5.8. Heavy inorganic fertilizer made it more acid.
entries.confuse: Cold, drought and root damage also slow growth and tint leaves, so check the roots and soil moisture. Nitrogen deficiency makes old leaves pale yellow, not purple.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test. PCA gives about 0.2 percent phosphorus as normal for bearing lanzones.
entries.fix: Apply a phosphorus fertilizer in the ring under the canopy, following the soil test. The PCA Davao trial added 400 grams of rock phosphate per tree in split doses in some years, together with a complete fertilizer and organic matter. Lime very acid soils so phosphorus stays available.
entries.prevent: Mix compost and phosphorus into the planting hole. Keep adding organic matter, which raised available phosphorus over 15 years in the PCA trial.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in lanzones
entries.hint: New leaflets come out small, narrow and bunched, yellow between the veins.
entries.symptoms: No lanzones particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. New leaves come out small and narrow, yellow between the veins. Bunch together at the shoot tip because the shoot fails to lengthen. Flowering and fruit size suffer.
entries.stage: New flushes on bearing trees, especially after a heavy crop.
entries.causes: In the PCA Davao trial, leaf zinc of lanzones fell below normal in fruiting years. Langsat grows poorly and turns chlorotic on limestone and other alkaline soils. Heavy phosphate fertilizer can also bring on zinc shortage.
entries.confuse: Iron or manganese deficiency also yellow young leaves between the veins, but leaves keep their normal size. Mites and thrips can stunt and curl new leaves. Look for the pests.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the third leaf from the top of a tertiary branch. PCA gives about 32 ppm zinc as normal for bearing lanzones. Spray a few branches with zinc and watch the next flush.
entries.fix: No lanzones particular rate was found. A soil dose of 50 grams Zinc sulfate per tree in the PCA trial did not raise leaf zinc of young trees. So a foliar spray is the surer route. Spray Zinc sulfate on new flushes, following the label. TNAU sprays for other fruit trees use 3 to 5 grams Zinc sulfate per liter.
entries.prevent: Avoid very heavy phosphate, keep organic matter up, and check leaf zinc every few years in bearing orchards.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in lanzones
entries.hint: Shoot tips stunt and die back, flowers and young fruits drop, and some fruits crack or come out misshapen.
entries.symptoms: No lanzones particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. Boron moves little in the tree, so the shoot tips, young leaves and young fruit show it first. Growing tips stunt and can die, young leaves are small and brittle, flowers and fruitlets drop. Fruits may crack or grow out of shape.
entries.stage: Flowering and early fruit set, and after a heavy crop.
entries.causes: In the PCA Davao trial, leaf boron of lanzones fell below normal after heavy fruiting. Sandy or leached soils low in organic matter, long dry spells and heavy liming bring it on.
entries.confuse: Fruit drop also comes from drought at flowering, bark borer damage and poor care. PCAARRD notes that watering during flower bud emergence in dry months improves fruiting. Heavy rain after a long dry spell can crack fruit without any boron shortage.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the third leaf from the top of a tertiary branch. PCA gives about 54 ppm boron as normal for bearing lanzones. A soil test helps, since boron is easy to overdo.
entries.fix: No lanzones particular rate was found. Use a fertilizer that carries a little boron, as the PCA trial did with its 14 5 20 blend, or spray Solubor or Borax on the leaves before flowering, following the label. Do not repeat high doses without a test, because too much boron is toxic.
entries.prevent: Keep organic matter up, water during flowering in dry months, and test leaf boron every few years.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in rambutan
entries.hint: Pale canopy, yellow older leaves that drop, and weak, short flushes after harvest.
entries.symptoms: No rambutan particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The canopy turns light green, then the older leaves yellow evenly and drop, and the yellowing moves up. New flushes after harvest come out short with small leaves, so the tree has less leaf to carry the next crop.
entries.stage: After harvest, when the tree should flush, and in young trees.
entries.causes: Rambutan removes a lot of nitrogen with its fruit and the twigs cut at harvest. Trees fed only organic matter or nothing at all, sandy soils and heavy rain show it most.
entries.confuse: Glyphosate sprayed under the canopy edge causes severe yellowing and drop of lower leaves, as the ICRAF tree database warns. Ask what was sprayed. Magnesium deficiency yellows old leaves between green veins. Waterlogged roots also yellow the canopy.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the last fully mature leaflets on branch tips, taken before flowering. Queensland researchers suggest 2.0 to 2.5 percent nitrogen as the target range.
entries.fix: For young trees in the third and fourth year, the DA Cagayan Valley guide gives 1 to 2 kg of complete fertilizer per tree with 300 grams of Muriate of potash. For bearing trees it gives 25 kg of organic fertilizer per tree after ring weeding, then 2 to 3 kg of Complete 14 14 14 or 16 20 0 one to two months later. The ICRAF tree database gives about 200 grams of nitrogen per tree for each year of age, up to 12 years, with half of the yearly amount right after harvest. Too much nitrogen can delay flowering and make fruit drop.
entries.prevent: Feed the tree right after harvest to push a good flush, and return pruned twigs and leaves as mulch.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in rambutan
entries.hint: Older leaflets scorch brown at the edges. Fruits stay small and less sweet.
entries.symptoms: No rambutan particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. Edges and tips of older leaflets yellow, then dry brown, and the scorch moves inward. Fruit set is poorer and fruits stay small and less sweet.
entries.stage: Fruit growth, when the crop pulls the most potash.
entries.causes: Rambutan removes a lot of potassium with its fruit. Leached, sandy soils under heavy rain, and trees fed mostly nitrogen, show it most.
entries.confuse: Rambutan is very sensitive to chloride. Queensland researchers link leaf edge burn and leaf drop mostly to too much chloride, for example from Muriate of potash. So a scorch after potash may mean chloride burn, not potash shortage. Dry winds also brown leaf margins.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the last fully mature leaflets on branch tips before flowering, for both potassium and chloride. Queensland researchers suggest 0.7 to 0.9 percent potassium and chloride below 0.2 percent.
entries.fix: The DA Cagayan Valley guide gives 300 grams of Muriate of potash with the complete fertilizer before flowering. A second potash dose in water during fruit growth for bigger, sweeter fruit. Because rambutan dislikes chloride, Queensland researchers advise Sulfate of potash or potassium nitrate instead. Switch to those where leaf edges burn. The ICRAF tree database gives about 130 grams of potash per tree for each year of age for fruiting trees, up to 12 years.
entries.prevent: Split potash between before flowering and fruit growth, and choose a chloride free source on trees that show edge burn.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in rambutan
entries.hint: Slow growth, dull older leaves with a purple or bronze tint underneath, and weak flowering.
entries.symptoms: No rambutan particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The tree grows slowly and stays stunted, and older leaves turn dull with a purple or bronze tint, mostly underneath. Flowering is weak.
entries.stage: Young trees, and the weeks before flowering in bearing trees.
entries.causes: Very acid soils that hold phosphorus tightly, and soils low in organic matter. Rambutan needs less phosphorus than nitrogen and potash, but leaf surveys in Queensland still found some trees below the suggested range.
entries.confuse: Drought, cold and root damage can also slow growth and tint leaves. Nitrogen deficiency gives pale yellow, not purple, old leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the last fully mature leaflets on branch tips before flowering. Queensland researchers suggest 0.2 to 0.3 percent phosphorus. A soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: The DA Cagayan Valley guide uses Complete 14 14 14 or 16 20 0 before flowering, which supply phosphorus. In a Thai trial, a leaf spray of monopotassium phosphate at 5 grams per liter, three times a week apart once the last flush matured, followed by a 7 13 34 foliar feed with zinc, gave the most flowering, about 10 days earlier than unsprayed trees. Follow the soil test and lime very acid soils.
entries.prevent: Put phosphorus and compost in the planting hole and keep some in the yearly program.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in rambutan
entries.hint: New leaflets small, narrow and bunched, yellow between the veins. Few, short flower panicles.
entries.symptoms: No rambutan particular leaf description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. New leaflets are small and narrow, yellow between the veins, and crowd at the shoot tip. In a Thai trial, trees with more leaf zinc made more flower panicles per shoot. So a shortage shows up as weak flowering and fewer fruits.
entries.stage: The last flush before flowering, and flowering.
entries.causes: Sandy or eroded soils, high pH or overlimed soils, and heavy phosphate fertilizer. Queensland leaf surveys found some orchards below the suggested zinc range.
entries.confuse: Iron and manganese deficiency also yellow young leaves between the veins, but the leaves keep their size. Mites and thrips can stunt and curl new leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the last fully mature leaflets on branch tips before flowering. Queensland researchers suggest 30 to 35 ppm zinc. Spray a few branches and compare the next flush.
entries.fix: Spray zinc on the mature last flush before flowering. In the Thai trial, a 7 13 34 foliar fertilizer containing zinc, at 1.5 grams of product per liter and sprayed three times a week apart, gave the biggest panicles. Zinc sulfate also works. TNAU sprays for other fruit trees use 3 to 5 grams Zinc sulfate per liter. Follow the label.
entries.prevent: Avoid very heavy phosphate and overliming, and check leaf zinc every few years.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in rambutan
entries.hint: Older leaflets yellow between green veins. In bad cases lower leaves drop.
entries.symptoms: No rambutan particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. Older leaflets yellow between the veins while the veins stay dark green. In bad cases growth slows, new leaves are smaller and lower leaves drop.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, often during and after fruit growth.
entries.causes: Acid, leached soils and heavy potash fertilizer, which competes with magnesium. Queensland leaf surveys found some orchards below the suggested magnesium range.
entries.confuse: Potassium shortage or chloride burn scorches the leaf edges brown rather than yellowing between the veins. Nitrogen deficiency yellows the whole old leaf, veins included.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the last fully mature leaflets on branch tips before flowering. Queensland researchers suggest 0.25 to 0.35 percent magnesium. A soil test for magnesium, potassium and calcium.
entries.fix: The ICRAF tree database gives Dolomite at 0.4 kg per tree for each year of age, up to 10 years, applied in the slow growing months. Where the soil pH is already fine, use Magnesium sulfate or Kieserite, following the soil test.
entries.prevent: Use Dolomite when liming and keep potash and magnesium in balance.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in durian
entries.hint: Pale canopy, older leaves yellow and fall, and the flush after harvest comes out short and thin.
entries.symptoms: No durian particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The canopy turns light green, the older leaves yellow evenly and drop, and the yellowing moves up. The flush after harvest is short with small leaves, and young trees grow slowly and take longer to bear.
entries.stage: Young trees before bearing, and bearing trees after harvest when the new flush should come.
entries.causes: Native soils in many Mindanao durian areas are low in nutrients. A University of Southern Mindanao trial found even small fertilizer doses sped up growth of pre bearing trees for that reason. Trees that get little fertilizer and weedy rings show it most.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency yellows old leaves between green veins. Phytophthora root and trunk rot also yellows and thins the canopy. Look for dark, wet bark cankers near the base and rotten feeder roots.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the second and third leaves from the shoot tip of the first flush after harvest, taken at flowering. In a Philippine study on Chanee trees, the best yields came with leaf nitrogen of 2.22 to 2.35 percent at flowering.
entries.fix: Where no soil test is done, the DA guide gives fertilizer with an NPK ratio of 12 4 7 at 100 grams per tree for the first five years, raised step by step to 4 kg per tree by the twelfth year. A Southern Mindanao trial on pre bearing trees found 400 grams Urea and 445 grams superphosphate per tree, with a small dose of Muriate of potash, enough to speed growth. Haifa puts the yearly need of bearing trees over six years old at about 1.0 to 1.8 kg nitrogen per tree, split through the season.
entries.prevent: Fertilize right after harvest to push a strong flush, keep the ring weeded, and mulch in the dry season.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in durian
entries.hint: Older leaf edges burn brown. More young fruits drop and the flesh is less sweet.
entries.symptoms: No durian particular leaf description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. Edges and tips of older leaves yellow and then dry brown, and the scorch moves inward. Fruit set and fruit quality fall. In a BPI Davao trial, trees that got only soil fertilizer dropped about twice as many young fruits as trees also sprayed with a high potash foliar feed.
entries.stage: Fruit growth up to harvest, when the fruit takes the most potash.
entries.causes: Potash is the biggest nutrient need of bearing durian, so heavy crops drain it. Sandy and leached soils, heavy rain and long dry spells make it worse.
entries.confuse: Fertilizer burn from a heavy dose near the trunk, and drought, also brown leaf edges. Magnesium deficiency yellows between the veins instead of along the edge.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the second and third leaves from the shoot tip of the first flush after harvest. A soil test for exchangeable potassium.
entries.fix: In a BPI Davao trial, trees given 5 kg Complete 14 14 14 per tree before flowering plus a 20 5 30 foliar feed from flower emergence to fruit growth bore 158 fruits per tree against 41 with soil fertilizer alone. A 4 0 48 foliar feed gave the sweetest flesh. A Thai orchard program used 1 kg Sulfate of potash 0 0 50 per tree during fruit growth and another 1 kg before ripening. Haifa puts the yearly need of bearing trees at about 2.1 to 4.0 kg potash per tree. Follow the soil test.
entries.prevent: Split potash between flowering, fruit growth and before ripening, and return husks and leaves to the ring.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in durian
entries.hint: Slow growing trees with dull older leaves, a purple or bronze tint underneath, and weak flowering.
entries.symptoms: No durian particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The tree grows slowly and older leaves turn dull with a purple or bronze tint, mostly on the underside. Flowering is weak and fewer flowers set fruit.
entries.stage: Young trees, and bearing trees in the months before flowering.
entries.causes: Acid soils that hold phosphorus tightly, and low organic matter. Leaf tests found phosphorus below the standard range in a Thai orchard. A survey of 90 Vietnamese orchards listed phosphorus among the limiting nutrients.
entries.confuse: Drought and root damage also slow growth and tint leaves. Nitrogen deficiency makes old leaves pale yellow, not purple.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of mature leaves from the last flush. Thai standards put leaf phosphorus at 0.15 to 0.25 percent. A soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: The Southern Mindanao trial on pre bearing trees used 445 grams superphosphate per tree with urea and potash. The Thai program gave 1 kg of a 9 25 25 fertilizer per tree before flowering. Haifa adds a leaf spray of monopotassium or ammonium phosphate at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter) two months before flowering, three to five times two weeks apart. Lime very acid soils.
entries.prevent: Put phosphorus in the planting hole and give a high phosphorus dose before each flowering.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in durian
entries.hint: Poor fruit set, small or lopsided fruits, cracked husks, and hard, leathery flesh inside.
entries.symptoms: Flowering and fruit set are poor because pollination fails. Fruits come out small, misshapen or lopsided, the husk can crack or split, and the flesh can be corky and dry. Some fruits ripen unevenly, with hard, leathery, whitish flesh that lacks smell and taste, which shows only when opened. Leaves yellow along the edges, then brown, and can be brittle or deformed.
entries.stage: Flowering, fruit set and fruit growth.
entries.causes: Every crop removes boron from the tree. Sandy or leached soils low in organic matter and dry spells make it worse. Large fleshed varieties such as Monthong (D159), Musang King (D197) and D24 show uneven ripening more often.
entries.confuse: Phytophthora fruit rot gives brown, wet patches on the husk that spread, not dry cracks. Uneven ripening can also follow a new leaf flush or heavy rain during fruit growth. Poor fruit set also comes from rain at flowering and poor pollination by bats.
entries.confirm: Leaf test and soil test for boron. The U.S. Borax guide advises basing rates on both, because boron is easy to overdo.
entries.fix: U.S. Borax advises a leaf spray of Solubor mixed with calcium at 0.5 to 1 gram per liter from flowering through fruiting. A boron fertilizer to the soil based on tests. In a Bukidnon farm trial, foliar boron with calcium and fermented goat urine gave the most fruits per tree. Boron raised the edible portion and sweetness. Too much boron is toxic, so do not repeat high doses without a test.
entries.prevent: Add a small boron dose each season on sandy or low boron soils, keep organic matter up, and water during dry spells.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in durian
entries.hint: New leaf tips burn and shoot tips die back on acid soils. Fruit quality drops.
entries.symptoms: No durian particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs and keeps claims modest. Calcium does not move from old leaves to new ones. So the newest leaves, shoot tips and root tips suffer first: tips and edges of young leaves brown, and growing tips can die. Fruit quality falls. Leaf tests in a Thai orchard showed calcium well below the standard range.
entries.stage: New flushes and fruit growth.
entries.causes: Very acid, leached soils, heavy potash or ammonium fertilizer that crowds out calcium. Dry spells that slow calcium flow to the fruit. A survey of 90 Vietnamese orchards listed calcium among the limiting nutrients.
entries.confuse: Boron deficiency also hurts young tissue and fruit, and the two often come together, which is why sprays mix them. Leaf tip burn can also come from fertilizer or salt burn.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of mature leaves from the last flush. Thai standards put leaf calcium at 1.7 to 2.5 percent. A soil test for pH and calcium.
entries.fix: On acid soils apply Agricultural lime or Dolomite in the ring, following the soil test. Where pH is fine, Gypsum adds calcium without raising pH. During flowering and fruit growth, U.S. Borax advises Solubor mixed with a calcium spray. In the Bukidnon trial foliar calcium with boron gave the best yield and return. Follow the label for calcium spray rates.
entries.prevent: Test and lime acid soils before planting and every few years, keep potash and calcium in balance, and water during dry spells.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in durian
entries.hint: Older leaves yellow between green veins. Lower leaves may drop.
entries.symptoms: No durian particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. Older leaves yellow between the veins while the veins stay dark green. In bad cases growth slows, new leaves are smaller and lower leaves drop.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, often after heavy potash feeding and in the months before flowering.
entries.causes: A leaf survey of 90 Vietnamese durian orchards found magnesium and sulfur the most deficient nutrients two months before flowering. Heavy potash, acid leached soils and heavy rain bring it on.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency browns the leaf edges instead of yellowing between the veins. Nitrogen deficiency yellows the whole old leaf, veins included.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of mature leaves from the last flush, and a soil test for magnesium, potassium and calcium together.
entries.fix: On acid soils apply Dolomite. Where pH is fine, use Magnesium sulfate or Kieserite, following the soil test. Haifa advises a magnesium leaf spray at 0.4 to 0.5 percent (4 to 5 grams per liter) two months after harvest, two or three times two weeks apart, to support the new flush.
entries.prevent: Use Dolomite when liming and keep potash and magnesium in balance.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in mangosteen
entries.hint: Pale, slow trees whose older leaves yellow evenly and drop, with few new flushes.
entries.symptoms: No mangosteen particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The tree turns light green, the older leaves yellow evenly, veins included, and fall early. Mangosteen is slow growing anyway, but a short tree puts out even fewer and smaller flushes and takes longer to bear.
entries.stage: Young trees in the years before bearing, and bearing trees after harvest.
entries.causes: Trees that get no fertilizer, poor sandy soils and weedy rings. Leaf nitrogen of mangosteen drops during flowering and fruiting and climbs again during leaf growth. So it runs short after a heavy crop.
entries.confuse: Young mangosteen trees need partial shade, and seedlings in full sun yellow and scorch even when well fed. Iron shortage yellows the young leaves, not the old ones. Poor drainage also yellows the tree.
entries.confirm: A leaf test of mature leaves from the last flush and a soil test. Leaves that green up within weeks after a nitrogen dose confirm it.
entries.fix: The DA guide, based on BPI practice, gives 200 to 250 grams of complete fertilizer per tree at planting. Young trees get 300 to 500 grams of Complete 14 14 14 or 12 24 12 plus 200 to 300 grams of urea per tree per year, in two equal doses at the start and end of the rainy season, in four to six holes around the canopy edge. An Indonesian study found nitrogen raised both growth and yield.
entries.prevent: Fertilize every year in two splits, increase the dose as the tree grows, and add organic fertilizer, which mangosteen responds to well.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in mangosteen
entries.hint: Slow growth, dull older leaves with a purple or bronze tint, and many flowers and young fruits dropping.
entries.symptoms: No mangosteen particular leaf description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The tree grows slowly and older leaves turn dull with a purple or bronze tint, mostly underneath. In an Indonesian study, more phosphorus raised flower and fruit set and cut flower and fruit drop. So a shortage shows as poor set and heavy drop.
entries.stage: Flowering and fruit set, and young trees.
entries.causes: Very acid soils that hold phosphorus tightly. Leaf tests in Indonesian orchards found phosphorus at a very low status, lower than nitrogen or potassium.
entries.confuse: Flower and fruit drop also follow drought or heavy rain at flowering. Nitrogen deficiency makes old leaves pale yellow rather than purple.
entries.confirm: A leaf test of mature leaves and a soil test for available phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: Use a high phosphorus complete fertilizer such as 12 24 12, as the DA guide lists: 1.5 to 3.0 kg per bearing tree per year with potash, in two equal doses at the start and end of the rainy season. On very acid soils add lime, following the soil test, so the phosphorus stays available.
entries.prevent: Mix phosphorus and compost into the planting hole, and keep a high phosphorus grade in the yearly program.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in mangosteen
entries.hint: Older leaf edges yellow and burn brown. Fewer flowers set fruit.
entries.symptoms: No mangosteen particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. Edges and tips of older leaves yellow, then dry brown, and the scorch moves inward. Growth slows and fewer flowers set fruit. In an Indonesian study potash raised growth and the share of flowers and fruits that set.
entries.stage: Bearing trees during flowering and fruit growth.
entries.causes: Heavy crops remove potash, and leached, acid soils under heavy rain lose it. Leaf tests in Indonesian orchards found potassium at a low to medium status.
entries.confuse: Sun scorch on exposed young trees and dry wind also brown leaf edges, mainly on the sunny or windward side. Fertilizer burn shows soon after a heavy dose near the trunk.
entries.confirm: A leaf test of mature leaves and a soil test for exchangeable potassium.
entries.fix: The DA guide gives bearing trees 1.5 to 3.0 kg of Complete 14 14 14 or 12 24 12 plus 200 to 300 grams of Muriate of potash 0 0 60 per tree per year, in two equal doses at the start and end of the rainy season, in holes around the canopy edge. Increase it each year as the crop grows.
entries.prevent: Give potash every year once the tree bears, and return leaf litter and husks to the ring.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in mangosteen
entries.hint: Glassy, water soaked flesh inside the fruit, and yellow gum (gamboge) in the flesh or oozing on the rind.
entries.symptoms: The two main fruit disorders of mangosteen, translucent flesh and gamboge, are linked to calcium. With translucent flesh, some segments look glassy and water soaked, and it shows only when the fruit is opened. With gamboge, yellow gum appears in the flesh and the rind and can ooze onto the skin. The two often come together and cut the share of fruits fit to sell.
entries.stage: Fruit growth, from about six weeks after bloom to harvest.
entries.causes: Very acid soils low in nutrients. The Thai orchards in the calcium trial had soil pH of about 3.9 to 4.9. Calcium moves poorly into fruit, so a short supply during fruit growth shows in the flesh first.
entries.confuse: Heavy rain during fruit growth is also tied to these disorders, so they can show even with fair calcium. Insect bites and knocks on the rind also make yellow gum ooze, but only at the wound.
entries.confirm: Cut open a sample of fruits to count glassy and gummy ones. A soil test for pH and calcium, and a leaf test. Researchers found total calcium in affected flesh can be high, so a fruit test alone may mislead.
entries.fix: In a Prince of Songkla University trial, spraying Calcium chloride at 10 percent (100 grams per liter) on the fruit at 6, 7 and 8 weeks after bloom raised the share of normal fruit. Adding a little boron made it work better. This is a strong salt, so test it on a few branches first. Calcium put on the soil also lowered the disorders in earlier trials. On acid soils use Agricultural lime or Dolomite, following the soil test for the rate.
entries.prevent: Lime very acid soils, keep water steady during fruit growth, and drain wet spots.

sources.title: Pechkeo, Sdoodee and Nilnond 2007, Calcium and boron sprays and translucent flesh and gamboge disorder in mangosteen (Agriculture and Natural Resources)

entries.name: Iron deficiency in mangosteen
entries.hint: Seedlings in the nursery whose young leaves turn more and more yellow while old leaves stay green.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves turn progressively yellow, first between the veins, while the older leaves stay green. A Brazilian study saw this on mangosteen seedlings after 12 months in a shaded nursery, with low iron and manganese in the leaves.
entries.stage: Nursery seedlings and young trees in pots.
entries.causes: Mangosteen is poor at taking up iron, even from a potting mix rich in iron. High pH or overlimed mixes and soggy pots make it worse.
entries.confuse: Manganese deficiency also yellows young leaves, but in the Brazilian trial a manganese spray did not bring the green back while an iron spray did. Nitrogen deficiency starts on the old leaves.
entries.confirm: Spray a few seedlings with iron and see if the next leaves come out green. A leaf test for iron and manganese.
entries.fix: Spray Ferrous sulfate mixed with a little urea on the leaves, following the label. In the Brazilian trial this greened the seedlings again. The authors also advise adding iron to the potting mix or spraying it during the nursery stage.
entries.prevent: Use a slightly acid, well drained potting mix, do not overlime it, and add iron to the nursery program.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in chico (sapodilla)
entries.hint: Small, yellow green mature leaves, amber to red new leaves, thin shoots and few small fruits.
entries.symptoms: Growth slows and the tree looks thin. Mature leaves stay small and turn yellow green. While young leaves on growing shoots come out amber to bright red and the bark of young shoots turns reddish brown. Leaves fall early, and the tree carries fewer and smaller fruits. TNAU describes these signs for sapota (chico).
entries.stage: Young trees in fast growth, and bearing trees after heavy crops, mostly during flushing and fruit set.
entries.causes: Trees that get no fertilizer or manure, sandy or eroded soils low in organic matter, and heavy rain that washes nitrogen down. Grass and weeds under the canopy compete for it.
entries.confuse: New chico leaves are normally pinkish when they first open (UF IFAS). So judge by the mature leaves: in nitrogen shortage they stay small and yellow green. Young chico trees also drop leaves in drought, so check soil moisture first. Potassium shortage leaves brown specks and dead patches between the veins instead of an even pale color.
entries.confirm: A leaf test of mature leaves from recent growth shows low nitrogen. A soil test shows organic matter. New flushes that come out green and full sized after urea confirm it.
entries.fix: For a quick lift, spray Urea 46 0 0 at 2 percent (20 grams per liter). TNAU found this spray effective and reports that 250 grams of nitrogen per tree raised fruit weight and yield. Then feed the soil: TNAU gives 0.2 kg of nitrogen per tree in the first year, rising by 0.2 kg each year to 1 kg from the sixth year, with farm manure. While PROSEA gives 1.5 kg of nitrogen or more per year for mature trees. One kg of nitrogen is about 2.2 kg of Urea 46 0 0. Spread it in a ring under the drip line at the start of the rainy season and again before the rains end.
entries.prevent: Feed every year in a ring under the canopy edge, add compost or manure, and keep grass away from the trunk. In 25 years of trials at Gujarat Agricultural University, nitrogen alone raised chico yield by about 70 percent over unfed trees.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in chico (sapodilla)
entries.hint: Light brown specks over the leaf that join into dead patches between the large veins.
entries.symptoms: Light brown specks appear scattered over the leaf blade. They grow and join into dead patches between the large veins, the underside of the leaf browns. Yellow areas form between the veins. TNAU describes these signs for sapota (chico). As in other fruit trees, fruit size and quality drop when potash runs short.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, most of all while fruits are growing, since fruits draw heavily on potash.
entries.causes: Sandy and leached soils, heavy cropping year after year with no potash returned, and long dry spells that cut uptake.
entries.confuse: Chico leaf spot diseases (Phyllosticta, Pestalotia, Septoria and others listed by UF IFAS) make separate spots scattered on any leaf, not patches that join between the veins. Magnesium shortage also yellows between the veins, but the midrib and big veins stay deep green. Salt spray near the sea burns leaf tips and margins rather than the blade between the veins.
entries.confirm: A soil test for potash and a leaf test. New leaves that stay clean after potash is applied confirm it.
entries.fix: Apply potash to the soil under the canopy and water it in. TNAU gives Muriate of potash at 80 kg per hectare and also advises Sulfate of potash in place of muriate for sapota. TNAU's tree schedule gives 0.3 kg of K per tree in the first year, rising each year to 1.5 kg from the sixth year. PROSEA gives about 0.5 kg of potash (as K2O) per mature tree per year. Split the yearly dose between the start and the end of the rainy season.
entries.prevent: Give potash every year together with nitrogen. In the Gujarat trials, nitrogen plus potash raised yield by about 128 percent over unfed trees, the best of the combinations tested.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in chico (sapodilla)
entries.hint: Older leaves take on a dull purplish tint and leaves come out smaller than normal.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves show a purplish pigment and leaf size gets smaller. TNAU gives only this short description for sapota. So the rest follows general signs of phosphorus shortage: growth is slow, flushes are weak and the tree stays small for its age.
entries.stage: Young trees in the first years after planting, while roots build up, and trees on poor acid soils.
entries.causes: Acid and eroded soils low in organic matter, and trees that never get manure or a fertilizer with phosphate.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage gives small yellow green leaves, not a purplish tint. Normal new chico leaves are pinkish, so judge the color on old leaves. Waterlogged roots also slow growth (UF IFAS), so check drainage.
entries.confirm: A soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU advises a leaf spray of DAP at 2 percent (20 grams of Ammonium phosphate 18 46 0 per liter) every two weeks until new leaves look normal. In the soil, give phosphate with the yearly feeding under the canopy: TNAU's schedule gives 0.2 kg of P per tree in the first year, rising each year to 1 kg from the sixth year. PROSEA gives about 0.5 kg of phosphate (as P2O5) for mature trees. Superphosphate 0 20 0, 16 20 0 or Complete 14 14 14 can carry it. Mix in manure or compost.
entries.prevent: Put phosphate in the planting hole and in each yearly feeding, and lime very acid soils according to the soil test.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in chico (sapodilla)
entries.hint: Yellowish green leaves with burnt tips and edges, and split midribs on the leaf underside.
entries.symptoms: Leaves turn yellowish green. Older leaves burn at the tips and along the edges and drop early, the tips of young leaves burn too. The midrib and large veins split or crack on the underside of the leaf. Boron shortage also upsets pollination, so many flowers fail to set fruit. TNAU describes these signs for sapota (chico).
entries.stage: Flowering and fruit set, and during new flushes.
entries.causes: Sandy, leached soils and soils low in organic matter. Long dry spells make it worse because roots take up less boron from dry topsoil.
entries.confuse: Salt spray or salty soil also burns leaf tips and margins and makes leaves drop (UF IFAS). But it does not split the midrib. Poor fruit set can also come from poor pollination, since some chico cultivars need another variety nearby to set fruit. Potassium shortage gives brown specks and patches between the veins rather than a tip and edge burn.
entries.confirm: A leaf test for boron and a soil test. Look under the leaves for split midribs and veins. A boron spray at flowering on a few branches that then set more fruit supports the diagnosis.
entries.fix: TNAU gives Borax at 5 kg per hectare to the soil, spread evenly under the canopy and mixed in. For flowering trees, TNAU advises a 0.3 percent boron spray at flowering and again 15 days later to help pollination and fruit set. Use Solubor or Borax and follow the label for the exact amount. Do not overdose, because too much boron also burns leaf tips and edges.
entries.prevent: Add compost every year and give a small boron dose before flowering on sandy soils.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in chico (sapodilla)
entries.hint: Young leaves come out small and pale, crowded at the shoot tip.
entries.symptoms: Signs show on young leaves, which stay small. TNAU gives only this short description for sapota. So the rest follows general fruit tree signs of zinc shortage: young leaves turn pale or yellow between the veins, and shoots stop lengthening so that small leaves crowd at the tip in a rosette.
entries.stage: During new flushes, when shoots grow fast.
entries.causes: Sandy and leached soils, high pH or overlimed soils, and heavy use of phosphate fertilizer, which can hold back zinc uptake.
entries.confuse: Iron shortage also yellows young leaves between green veins, but the leaves keep their normal size. UF IFAS notes that chico seldom shows iron shortage even on high pH limestone soils. Manganese shortage leaves wide green bands along the veins with pale spots, and the leaves are not much smaller.
entries.confirm: A leaf test for zinc and a soil test for pH and zinc. Spray a few branches with zinc and see whether the next flush comes out normal sized.
entries.fix: TNAU advises a leaf spray of Zinc sulfate at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter) on the new flush. Repeat on later flushes if the small leaves return. On soils proven low in zinc, add Zinc sulfate to the soil following the soil test.
entries.prevent: Avoid heavy phosphate alone. UF IFAS advises 2 to 3 minor element leaf sprays a year for chico during the growing season. Include zinc in them.
