entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in chico (sapodilla)
entries.hint: Older leaves turn greenish yellow between the veins while the midrib and big veins stay deep green.
entries.symptoms: Leaves go lighter green, then greenish yellow, while the midrib and larger veins stay deep green. The yellow leaves then show scattered brown spots. On older leaves the yellowing between the veins is followed by dying of the leaf edge toward the tip. TNAU describes these signs for sapota (chico).
entries.stage: Bearing trees, most often during fruit growth and after heavy potash feeding.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy and leached soils, and heavy potash fertilizer, which competes with magnesium.
entries.confuse: Potassium shortage gives brown specks and dead patches between the veins without the clear deep green band along the veins. Manganese shortage shows first on young leaves. Leaf spot diseases make separate spots on green leaves without the yellowing between the veins.
entries.confirm: A soil test for magnesium, potash and calcium together, since their balance matters, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU advises Dolomite on the soil or a 1 percent magnesium nitrate leaf spray. On acid soils, Dolomite supplies both lime and magnesium. Take the amount from the soil test. Where the soil pH is already fine, spread Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) or Kieserite under the canopy and follow the label.
entries.prevent: Use a fertilizer that carries magnesium, as UF IFAS does for young chico trees (a 6 6 6 2 mix with magnesium). Balance potash with magnesium according to the soil test.

entries.name: Manganese deficiency in chico (sapodilla)
entries.hint: Pale yellow between the veins with wide green bands along the veins, light spots and early leaf drop.
entries.symptoms: Light colored spots appear on the leaves and some turn into dead spots. Green bands of varying width run along the midrib and veins, with yellow areas between them. Leaves drop early and the shoot tips can die back. TNAU describes these signs for sapota (chico). In fruit trees in general the signs start on the younger leaves.
entries.stage: New flushes, mostly on high pH or overlimed soils.
entries.causes: High pH and limestone soils, and overliming of light, sandy soils, which locks up manganese. TNAU notes that acid soils, which most fruit orchards are planted on, usually hold plenty of manganese. So this is less common than the other troubles.
entries.confuse: Iron shortage yellows young leaves more evenly between fine green veins, without the wide green bands. Zinc shortage makes young leaves clearly small. Magnesium shortage starts on old leaves.
entries.confirm: A leaf test for manganese and a soil pH test. A spray on a few branches that greens the next flush supports it.
entries.fix: TNAU advises Manganese sulfate sprays at 0.3 percent (3 grams per liter) every two weeks until new leaves green up. Soil doses often fail on limed or high pH soils because the manganese gets locked up, so spraying works better there.
entries.prevent: Do not overlime. Lime only to the level the soil test calls for.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in atis (sugar apple)
entries.hint: Older leaves fade to an even pale green, then yellow and drop early. The tree grows slowly and sets few fruits.
entries.symptoms: No atis particular description was found in TNAU or UF IFAS. So this follows its close cousin guyabano, where a Brazilian study notes the same signs were seen in atis. Older leaves near the base lose their green evenly, blade, stalk and veins alike. As it gets worse all leaves turn yellow and dull, the old ones drop early. The tree stays short with a thin stem. Fewer and smaller fruits follow.
entries.stage: Young trees in their first years of growth, and bearing trees from flowering to fruit fill.
entries.causes: Light, sandy soils, trees that get no manure or fertilizer, and heavy rain that washes nitrogen down.
entries.confuse: Atis naturally drops many leaves in the dry or cool season (UF IFAS), and drought makes it shed more. So yellowing before a dry spell is not always hunger. Waterlogged roots also yellow and stunt atis, with wilting and browning leaves. Check drainage first. Sulfur shortage looks like nitrogen shortage but starts on the young leaves (TNAU).
entries.confirm: A leaf test shows low nitrogen. New leaves that come out green and full sized after a nitrogen dose confirm it.
entries.fix: Give nitrogen in small, frequent doses while the tree is growing, spread under the canopy and watered in. TNAU gives 250 grams of nitrogen, 125 grams of phosphate and 250 grams of potash per bearing tree a year, with 10 kg of farm manure and 1 kg of neem cake. In a Brazilian field trial, urea at rates up to 400 grams of nitrogen per tree raised atis yield and fruit number. Use Urea 46 0 0, Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 or Complete 14 14 14.
entries.prevent: UF IFAS feeds young trees about 100 grams of a complete fertilizer every 6 to 8 weeks in the growing season, then cuts the number of nitrogen doses once trees start bearing so the tree puts its strength into flowers and fruit. Add manure or compost every year.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in atis (sugar apple)
entries.hint: Yellowish spots along the leaf edges that spread and turn brown, starting on older leaves.
entries.symptoms: Signs start on the older leaves. Yellowish spots form along the leaf margins, then spread over the blade and turn brown. Leaves first go greyish at the margin and later between the veins. TNAU describes these signs for custard apple (atis). Fruit set and fruit size drop when potash runs short.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, most of all while the fruits are filling.
entries.causes: Sandy and leached soils, heavy rain, and years of cropping with no potash returned.
entries.confuse: Salt in the soil or water also burns leaf margins and tips and makes leaves drop. UF IFAS notes atis does not tolerate saline soil. Magnesium shortage yellows between the veins while the leaf margin stays green, the opposite of the potash pattern. Leaf diseases after heavy rain give scattered spots and leaf drop over the whole canopy.
entries.confirm: A soil test for potash and a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU gives Muriate of potash at 300 to 500 grams per tree to the soil, spread under the canopy and watered in. Split it into two doses on sandy soil. Sulfate of potash 0 0 50 or a complete fertilizer such as 14 14 14 can also be used.
entries.prevent: Feed potash every year with nitrogen and phosphate. Morton reports that a fertilizer with 3 percent nitrogen and 10 percent each of phosphate and potash clearly raised flowering, fruit set and yield of atis.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in atis (sugar apple)
entries.hint: Bluish green or purplish trees with small mature leaves that later yellow with purple veins.
entries.symptoms: The tree looks bluish green or purplish. Mature leaves stay small, first with purplish tints and scorched patches, later turning yellow with purple veins before they die and fall early. Growth is slow. TNAU describes these signs for custard apple (atis).
entries.stage: Young trees after planting, and trees on poor acid soils at any age.
entries.causes: Acid and eroded soils low in organic matter, and trees that never get manure or a fertilizer with phosphate.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage makes leaves pale and yellow without the bluish or purple tint. Cool weather and the normal dry season leaf drop of atis can also make leaves dull before they fall. So look at the new flush after the rains.
entries.confirm: A soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU advises Superphosphate to the soil. Its yearly schedule for bearing annona trees gives 125 grams of phosphate per tree, with farm manure. Take the exact amount from the soil test. Superphosphate 0 20 0, 16 20 0 or Complete 14 14 14 can carry it, worked into the soil under the canopy.
entries.prevent: Put phosphate and manure in the planting hole and give phosphate every year. Lime very acid soils according to the soil test.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in atis (sugar apple)
entries.hint: Young leaves yellow between the veins, bend downward and crowd on short shoots.
entries.symptoms: Leaves turn yellow between the veins, shoots grow short between the leaves, and the leaves bend downward. TNAU describes these signs for custard apple (atis). In fruit trees in general the newest leaves are hit first and stay small and narrow.
entries.stage: New flushes after the dry season rest, when shoots grow fast.
entries.causes: Sandy and leached soils, and heavy phosphate fertilizer, which can hold back zinc. A Brazilian review notes that zinc and boron matter most for annonas on acid tropical soils below pH 6.5. TNAU names custard apple among the fruit crops that zinc shortage commonly affects.
entries.confuse: Iron shortage also yellows young leaves, but a fine net of green veins stays and the leaves keep their size and shape. Manganese shortage gives orange yellow mottling and small brown spots.
entries.confirm: A leaf test for zinc and a soil test for pH. Spray a few branches with zinc and see whether the next flush comes out normal.
entries.fix: TNAU advises a leaf spray of Zinc sulfate at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter) on the young flush. Repeat on the next flush if needed. UF IFAS notes that on acid sandy soils zinc can also go on the soil. While on high pH soils leaf sprays work better.
entries.prevent: UF IFAS gives 2 to 4 micronutrient sprays a year with zinc, manganese and magnesium during the growing season. Avoid heavy phosphate alone.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in atis (sugar apple)
entries.hint: Few fruits set, misshapen or cracked fruits, and shoot tips that stop growing.
entries.symptoms: No atis particular description of boron shortage was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. Growing tips and young leaves suffer first: shoot tips stop growing and may die, and new leaves stay small and misshapen. Pollination and seed development fail, so few fruits set and fruits can be lopsided or cracked. A Brazilian field trial showed that boron, given to the soil or the leaves, raised atis yield and fruit number.
entries.stage: Flowering, fruit set and early fruit growth.
entries.causes: Sandy, leached and acid soils low in organic matter, and long dry spells. A Brazilian review notes boron and zinc matter most for annonas on acid soils below pH 6.5.
entries.confuse: Poor fruit set in atis often comes from pollination: the flower is female first and male the next day. Dry air below about 70 percent humidity at flowering cuts fruit set (UF IFAS). Lopsided fruits also come from poor pollination. Calcium shortage burns the edges of upper leaves and can cause blossom end rot of fruit (TNAU).
entries.confirm: A leaf test for boron and a soil test. Spray a few branches with boron before flowering and compare fruit set with untreated branches.
entries.fix: Apply Borax to the soil under the canopy or spray Solubor on the leaves before flowering, following the soil test and the label. The Brazilian trial used boric acid on the soil or the leaves. Do not overdose, because too much boron burns leaf tips and edges.
entries.prevent: Add compost every year, and on sandy or acid soils include boron in the micronutrient sprays before flowering.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in atis (sugar apple)
entries.hint: Leaves yellow or greenish yellow between the veins while the leaf margins stay green.
entries.symptoms: Leaves lose color, and the areas between the veins turn yellow or greenish yellow while the leaf margins stay green. TNAU describes these signs for custard apple (atis). As in other fruit trees, magnesium shortage shows first on the older leaves.
entries.stage: Bearing trees during fruit growth, and trees fed heavy potash.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy and leached soils, and heavy potash fertilizer, which competes with magnesium.
entries.confuse: Potassium shortage starts at the leaf margin with yellow spots that turn brown, while magnesium shortage keeps the margin green. Iron and zinc shortage start on young leaves.
entries.confirm: A soil test for magnesium, potash and calcium together, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU advises Dolomite on the soil. On acid soils it supplies both lime and magnesium, and the soil test gives the amount. Where the pH is already fine, Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) or Kieserite can go on the soil, following the label. UF IFAS notes that on high pH soils magnesium works better as a leaf spray.
entries.prevent: Use a fertilizer that carries magnesium. UF IFAS lists mixes such as 6 6 6 3 and 8 3 9 5 with magnesium for atis. Balance potash with magnesium according to the soil test.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in atis (sugar apple)
entries.hint: The newest leaves turn yellow with a fine net of green veins, and later go fully yellow.
entries.symptoms: Signs start on the youngest leaves. At first even the smallest veins stay green, which leaves a fine net of green veins on a yellow leaf. Later the whole leaf turns yellow, but it does not die or scorch. Older leaves stay green. TNAU describes these signs for custard apple (atis).
entries.stage: New flushes, mostly on limestone or high pH soils.
entries.causes: High pH, limestone (calcareous) soils, where iron is locked up. TNAU notes custard apple is more sensitive to this than most fruit crops. Too much phosphate also brings it on (TNAU). On the acid soils common in the Philippines it is less frequent.
entries.confuse: Zinc shortage also yellows young leaves, but the leaves bend down and crowd on short shoots. Manganese shortage leaves wider green bands along the veins with small brown spots. Waterlogging yellows the whole tree and leaves wilt and brown.
entries.confirm: A soil test for pH (iron trouble is likely above pH 7). Leaf tests for iron are not reliable. So a soil drench of iron on a few trees that greens the next flush is the better check.
entries.fix: TNAU gives Ferrous sulfate at 0.5 kg per tree to the soil. UF IFAS advises iron sulfate on low pH sandy soils. But on limestone and high pH soils a chelated iron made for high pH soils, mixed with water and drenched under the canopy. It notes that drenches, not sprays, prevent the deficiency.
entries.prevent: Do not overlime, avoid heavy phosphate, and plant atis on well drained ground, since waterlogging also yellows and weakens it.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in guyabano (soursop)
entries.hint: Lower leaves fade evenly to pale green, then the whole tree turns dull yellow and stays short.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves near the base slowly lose their green and turn an even pale green over the blade, stalk and veins. As it gets worse all leaves turn yellow and lose their shine, the old leaves drop early. The plant stays short with a thin stem. In a Brazilian nutrient trial on guyabano, leaving out nitrogen hurt growth the most of all nutrients, cutting plant dry weight by 94 percent.
entries.stage: Seedlings and young trees in fast growth, and bearing trees during fruit growth.
entries.causes: Sandy or eroded soils low in organic matter, trees that get no manure or fertilizer, and heavy rain that washes nitrogen down.
entries.confuse: Guyabano drops leaves during long droughts (CTAHR), so check soil moisture before blaming nitrogen. Sulfur shortage also gives pale, small leaves, but it shows on the young leaves while the lower leaves look normal. Waterlogged roots also yellow the tree. Guyabano does not tolerate waterlogging (PROSEA).
entries.confirm: A leaf test shows low nitrogen. For guyabano, Brazilian work found the best leaves to sample are from the middle of branches in the middle third of the canopy. New leaves that come out green after a nitrogen dose confirm it.
entries.fix: Give nitrogen in small doses a few times a year, spread under the canopy and watered in. CTAHR gives a 10 10 10 fertilizer four times a year: about 0.23 kg per tree in total in the first year, 0.45 kg in the second. 1.4 kg a year after that. In the Philippines, Complete 14 14 14 is the usual complete fertilizer. Add Urea 46 0 0 or Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 when leaves are pale. Mix in manure or compost.
entries.prevent: Feed in several small doses through the year rather than one big dose, keep a thick mulch over the shallow roots, and add manure every year.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in guyabano (soursop)
entries.hint: Older leaves yellow from the tip and edges inward, then the edges brown and die.
entries.symptoms: At first the foliage turns a deep green and the young leaves come out a little smaller. Then older leaves yellow along the margin, starting at the tip. The yellow moves inward between the veins, from yellow green to brown as the tissue dies. Other studies saw the edges turn orange yellow before browning. In severe cases the lower leaves fall and growth stops. These signs come from guyabano trials in Brazil and Venezuela.
entries.stage: Bearing trees during fruit growth, and young trees on sandy soil.
entries.causes: Sandy, leached soils and heavy rain, and years of fruiting with no potash returned. A Brazilian review notes that guyabano seedlings take up potash and nitrogen in the largest amounts of all nutrients.
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage also starts on older leaves, but it yellows along the midrib while the leaf margins stay green. Salt or fertilizer burn scorches margins quickly after a heavy dose. Anthracnose, the main guyabano disease in humid places, rots or shrivels flowers and fruits and also damages leaves and stems, rather than giving a steady scorch from the tip and edge (PROSEA).
entries.confirm: A soil test for potash and a leaf test of leaves from the middle of branches in the middle third of the canopy.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 or Sulfate of potash 0 0 50 under the canopy in split doses, following the soil test. A fertilizer with 3 percent nitrogen and 10 percent each of phosphate and potash has been used for guyabano in Cuba and Queensland (Morton). In the Philippines a Complete 14 14 14 plus Muriate of potash does the same job.
entries.prevent: Give potash in every feeding of bearing trees, and return fallen leaves and prunings as mulch.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in guyabano (soursop)
entries.hint: Narrow, small leaves with edges curled and tips bent down. Lower leaves pale and held close to the stem.
entries.symptoms: In a Brazilian trial the upper leaves showed it first: they came out narrower and smaller, with curved edges and tips pointing down. The lower leaves turned light green and were held close against the stem. Growth slowed sharply. Earlier trials saw the signs start on the lower leaves and move up. Leaving out phosphorus was the third most damaging omission for guyabano, after nitrogen and calcium.
entries.stage: Seedlings and young trees, and trees on poor acid soils.
entries.causes: Acid and eroded soils low in organic matter, and no phosphate at planting. In a survey of guyabano orchards in Nayarit, Mexico, phosphorus was low in every orchard. In a quarter of them it was the most limiting nutrient.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage gives an even pale yellow without the narrow, curled leaves. Mealybugs and scale insects, listed as guyabano pests by CTAHR, also weaken new growth. Look for the insects on stems and the leaf underside. Calcium shortage burns and rolls the tips of the youngest leaves.
entries.confirm: A soil test for available phosphorus and pH. A leaf test of leaves from the middle of branches in the middle third of the canopy.
entries.fix: Work Superphosphate 0 20 0, 16 20 0 or Ammonium phosphate 18 46 0 into the soil under the canopy, following the soil test, together with manure or compost. CTAHR's 10 10 10 program and the 3 10 10 mix used in Cuba and Queensland both carry a good share of phosphate. Complete 14 14 14 can be used in the Philippines.
entries.prevent: Put phosphate and manure in the planting hole and give phosphate in the yearly feeding. Lime very acid soils according to the soil test. CTAHR notes guyabano does best at pH 5 to 6.5.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in guyabano (soursop)
entries.hint: The tips of the youngest leaves burn dark brown and roll up while the rest of the leaf stays green.
entries.symptoms: The youngest leaves show it first: the leaf tip and the upper edge die and turn a burnt dark brown. While the rest of the leaf stays normal green. The burnt part rolls over on itself with the edges turned up. Later leaves drop early and the shoot tip stops growing. Earlier trials also saw yellowing around the edges and between the main veins before the tissue died. Leaving out calcium was the second most damaging omission after nitrogen.
entries.stage: Young trees and new flushes, most often on acid soils.
entries.causes: Strongly acid, leached soils low in calcium, which are common under heavy rainfall. Dry spells that slow calcium flow to the growing tips. In the Nayarit orchard survey, leaf calcium was low in every orchard.
entries.confuse: Potassium shortage burns the edges of older leaves first, not the newest leaves. Boron shortage also damages growing tips, but young leaves come out small and misshapen and fruit set fails. Salt or fertilizer burn scorches leaves of all ages at once.
entries.confirm: A soil test for pH, calcium and magnesium. A leaf test of leaves from the middle of branches in the middle third of the canopy.
entries.fix: On acid soils apply Agricultural lime or Dolomite under the canopy to raise the pH toward 5 to 6.5, the range CTAHR gives for guyabano. Take the amount from the soil test. Where the pH is already fine, Gypsum supplies calcium without changing the pH. TNAU gives Gypsum at 50 kg per hectare for custard apple, a close cousin. A Calcium nitrate spray on young flushes helps while the soil dose works. Follow the label.
entries.prevent: Test the soil every few years and lime before the pH drops too low. Keep the soil moist with mulch during dry spells.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in guyabano (soursop)
entries.hint: Many flowers but few fruits set, lopsided or cracked fruits, and shoot tips that stop growing.
entries.symptoms: No guyabano particular description of boron shortage was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. Young tissues suffer first: shoot tips stop growing and may die, and new leaves come out small and misshapen. Pollination and seed development fail, so fruit set is poor and fruits can grow lopsided or crack. A survey of guyabano orchards in Nayarit, Mexico found leaf boron low in every orchard.
entries.stage: Flowering, fruit set and early fruit growth.
entries.causes: Sandy, leached and acid soils low in organic matter, and long dry spells. A Brazilian review notes boron and zinc matter most for annonas on acid tropical soils below pH 6.5.
entries.confuse: Poor pollination is the main cause of low yield in guyabano (PROSEA), and it also gives lopsided fruits. So do not blame boron for every misshapen fruit. Very high or very low air humidity at flowering also cuts fruit set. Anthracnose rots or shrivels flowers and young fruits in humid weather (PROSEA). Calcium shortage burns the tips of the youngest leaves.
entries.confirm: A leaf test for boron of leaves from the middle of branches in the middle third of the canopy, and a soil test. Spray a few branches with boron before flowering and compare fruit set.
entries.fix: Apply Borax to the soil under the canopy or spray Solubor on the leaves before flowering, following the soil test and the label. Do not overdose, because too much boron burns leaf tips and edges.
entries.prevent: Add compost every year, and on sandy or acid soils include boron in the micronutrient sprays before flowering.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in guyabano (soursop)
entries.hint: A yellow to orange band along the midrib of older leaves while the leaf margins stay green.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves in the middle of the plant show it first, with light yellowing along the midrib. The midrib and the side margins of the leaf stay green. As it gets worse the yellow band turns orange, the leaves drop early, and the plant grows less. Earlier trials described the same yellowing between the veins, starting beside the midrib and moving out to the edges. These signs come from guyabano trials in Brazil and Venezuela.
entries.stage: Bearing trees and trees fed heavy potash, during fruit growth.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy and leached soils, and heavy potash fertilizer, which competes with magnesium.
entries.confuse: Potassium shortage also starts on older leaves, but the yellow and brown start at the tip and margin and move inward. Nitrogen shortage yellows the whole leaf evenly, veins included. Normal leaf fall in a long dry season yellows whole leaves without the green margins.
entries.confirm: A soil test for magnesium, potash and calcium together. A leaf test of leaves from the middle of branches in the middle third of the canopy.
entries.fix: On acid soils apply Dolomite, which supplies both lime and magnesium. Take the amount from the soil test. Where the pH is already fine, spread Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) or Kieserite under the canopy and follow the label.
entries.prevent: Balance potash with magnesium according to the soil test, and use Dolomite rather than plain lime on acid soils.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in santol
entries.hint: A pale, light green tree with yellowing older leaves, short new shoots and a light crop.
entries.symptoms: No santol particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The whole tree turns light green, and the older leaves turn yellow, then brown, and fall. New shoots are short and thin, growth is slow, and the tree flowers and fruits less.
entries.stage: Young trees in the first years after planting, and bearing trees after a heavy crop.
entries.causes: Trees that get no fertilizer or manure, sandy or eroded soils low in humus, and heavy rain that washes nitrogen down. Grass and weeds close to the trunk compete for it.
entries.confuse: Santol leaves normally turn red or yellow just before they fall. The tree is partly deciduous, sometimes dropping most of its leaves at one time (ITFnet, PROSEA). A few colored old leaves are normal. Hunger shows as a pale canopy with small new leaves all over the tree. Gall mites, the worst santol pest, make bumps and galls on the leaves and stunt young trees, which is not a color change.
entries.confirm: A leaf test of mature leaves from recent growth shows low nitrogen. New leaves that come out greener and bigger after a nitrogen dose confirm it.
entries.fix: PROSEA gives 100 to 200 grams of Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 per tree in the first year, a month after planting and again before the rainy season ends. Young bearing trees get 200 to 500 grams of a complete fertilizer twice a year. Full grown trees need at least 2 kg of complete fertilizer per application. Use Complete 14 14 14, spread in a ring under the canopy edge and watered in or put on moist soil.
entries.prevent: Keep a weed free circle about 50 cm around young trees (ITFnet), mulch, add manure. Feed every year at the start and near the end of the rainy season.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in santol
entries.hint: Older leaflets scorch brown along the edges and tips. Fruits stay small and poor.
entries.symptoms: No santol particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The edges and tips of older leaflets look burnt, and the scorch moves inward. Fruit size and quality drop, and the tree may suffer more from disease.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, most of all during fruit growth.
entries.causes: Sandy, leached soils under heavy rain, and years of fruiting with no potash returned.
entries.confuse: Pink disease (Corticium salmonicolor), common on santol, forms cankers on branches. Fungal blights wilt and kill leaves on whole twigs and branches (PROSEA, ITFnet). Potash shortage instead scorches the edges of old leaves across the tree. Salt spray near the sea also burns leaf edges. Normal old leaves turn red or yellow before they drop.
entries.confirm: A soil test for potash and a leaf test.
entries.fix: Feed bearing trees with Complete 14 14 14 at the PROSEA rates (200 to 500 grams twice a year for young bearing trees, 2 kg or more per application for full grown trees). Where the soil test shows low potash, add Muriate of potash 0 0 60 in split doses under the canopy, following the soil test.
entries.prevent: Give a complete fertilizer every year from the first crop on, and return fallen leaves and prunings under the tree.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in santol
entries.hint: Slow, stunted growth with a purplish tint on older leaves, most on the underside.
entries.symptoms: No santol particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. Growth is slow and the tree stays small for its age. Older leaves take on a purple color, most of all on the underside.
entries.stage: Young trees after planting, and trees on poor acid soils.
entries.causes: Acid and eroded soils low in humus, and trees that get no phosphate at planting or later.
entries.confuse: Santol leaves turn red before they fall as a normal habit. So look for the purplish tint on leaves that are still firmly attached and on a tree that is also growing slowly. Nitrogen shortage gives an even pale color without the purple.
entries.confirm: A soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: Work Superphosphate 0 20 0, 16 20 0 or Ammonium phosphate 18 46 0 into the soil under the canopy, following the soil test, with manure or compost. For bearing trees, the complete fertilizer that PROSEA advises (Complete 14 14 14) also supplies phosphate.
entries.prevent: Put phosphate and manure in the planting hole, and lime very acid soils according to the soil test. Santol grows best in loose, friable soils with plenty of humus (PROSEA).

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in santol
entries.hint: New leaflets come out small, pale between the veins and crowded on short shoots.
entries.symptoms: No santol particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. TNAU names zinc as the most widespread micronutrient shortage in fruit crops. Young leaves turn yellow between the veins and come out small, narrow and sometimes distorted. Shoots stay short so the leaves crowd in a rosette. Flowering and fruit size drop.
entries.stage: New flushes, when shoots grow fast.
entries.causes: Sandy, leached soils, high pH or overlimed soils, and heavy phosphate fertilizer, which can hold back zinc uptake.
entries.confuse: Gall mites (Eriophyes sandorici), the most serious santol pest, cause galls, bumps on the leaves, and stunted young trees (PROSEA). Zinc shortage gives small pale leaves without galls. Iron shortage yellows young leaves between green veins but the leaves keep their normal size. Manganese shortage leaves green bands along the veins.
entries.confirm: A leaf test for zinc and a soil test for pH and zinc. Spray a few branches and see whether the next flush comes out normal sized.
entries.fix: No santol rate was found. TNAU uses a 0.5 percent Zinc sulfate spray (5 grams per liter) on several fruit trees, for example guava before flowering. So try it on a few branches of the new flush first. On soils proven low in zinc, add Zinc sulfate to the soil following the soil test.
entries.prevent: Avoid heavy phosphate alone, and add compost or manure every year.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in kaimito (star apple)
entries.hint: The upper side of the leaves turns pale, older leaves yellow and drop, and new shoots stay short.
entries.symptoms: No kaimito particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The shiny upper side of the leaves loses its deep green, the older leaves turn yellow, then brown, and fall. Growth slows, new shoots are short, and the tree flowers and fruits less.
entries.stage: Young trees in the first years after planting, and bearing trees during fruit growth.
entries.causes: Trees that are never fed (Morton notes most kaimito trees in tropical America never get fertilizer), sandy or limestone soils low in organic matter. Heavy rain that washes nitrogen down.
entries.confuse: In a long dry season kaimito sheds many leaves and its fruits shrivel (PROSEA), which is drought, not hunger. The underside of a kaimito leaf is normally golden brown (UF IFAS), so judge the color on the upper side. Red algae (Cephaleuros) attack leaves, stems and limbs and cause twig and limb dieback (UF IFAS).
entries.confirm: A leaf test of mature leaves from recent growth shows low nitrogen. New leaves that come out deep green after a nitrogen dose confirm it.
entries.fix: PROSEA gives 150 to 200 grams of Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 per tree twice a year for young trees not yet bearing. At the start of fruiting, 500 grams of complete fertilizer go on twice a year. Full grown trees may need 3 kg or more of complete fertilizer a year. Apply at the start of the rainy season and again near its end, in a ring or in shallow holes under the canopy.
entries.prevent: Feed every year and mulch the root zone. Morton notes that a complete, well balanced fertilizer greatly improves kaimito on limestone and other poor soils.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in kaimito (star apple)
entries.hint: Edges and tips of older leaves scorch brown. Fruits stay small and poor in quality.
entries.symptoms: No kaimito particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The edges and tips of older leaves look burnt, and the scorch moves inward. Fruit size and quality drop.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, most of all while fruits are growing. UF IFAS raises the potash share of the fertilizer once trees bear.
entries.causes: Sandy and leached soils, heavy rain, and years of fruiting with no potash returned.
entries.confuse: The golden brown underside of kaimito leaves is normal (UF IFAS). Phomopsis and Phyllosticta leaf spots make separate spots on the blade rather than a scorch along the edge. Salt spray near the sea also burns leaf edges.
entries.confirm: A soil test for potash and a leaf test.
entries.fix: For bearing trees, UF IFAS raises potash in the fertilizer to 9 to 15 percent and cuts phosphate to 2 to 4 percent. Mixes such as 8 3 9 with magnesium are used. In the Philippines, give the PROSEA rates of Complete 14 14 14 and add Muriate of potash 0 0 60 where the soil test shows low potash, in two doses at the start and near the end of the rainy season.
entries.prevent: Give potash every year once the tree bears, and return fallen leaves under the canopy.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in kaimito (star apple)
entries.hint: Young trees grow slowly and older leaves take on a purplish tint, most on the underside.
entries.symptoms: No kaimito particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. Growth is slow and the tree stays small. Older leaves take on a purple color, most of all on the underside, though on kaimito this can be hard to see against the natural golden brown underside.
entries.stage: Young trees in the first years, before bearing.
entries.causes: Acid and eroded soils low in organic matter, limestone soils, and no phosphate at planting.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage gives an even pale color without the purple tint. Drought stress slows growth and makes leaves drop (PROSEA). Red algae (Cephaleuros) attack leaves and stems and cause dieback (UF IFAS).
entries.confirm: A soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: UF IFAS uses 6 to 10 percent phosphate in the fertilizer for young trees. Work Superphosphate 0 20 0, 16 20 0 or Complete 14 14 14 into the soil under the canopy, following the soil test, with manure or compost.
entries.prevent: Put phosphate and manure in the planting hole and feed young trees with a complete fertilizer every 1 to 2 months in the first year, as UF IFAS advises. PROSEA notes kaimito prefers fertile, well drained, slightly acid soils.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in kaimito (star apple)
entries.hint: Older leaves yellow between the veins while the veins stay green.
entries.symptoms: No kaimito particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. Older leaves turn yellow between the veins while the veins stay green, and growth slows. UF IFAS includes 4 to 6 percent magnesium in the fertilizer for young kaimito trees as part of its regular feeding.
entries.stage: Bearing trees during fruit growth, and trees fed heavy potash.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy and leached soils, and heavy potash fertilizer, which competes with magnesium.
entries.confuse: Iron shortage also yellows between the veins, but on the young leaves at the shoot tip. Potassium shortage scorches the leaf edges.
entries.confirm: A soil test for magnesium, potash and calcium together, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: On acid soils apply Dolomite, which supplies both lime and magnesium. Take the amount from the soil test. Where the pH is already fine, spread Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) or Kieserite under the canopy and follow the label.
entries.prevent: Use a fertilizer that carries magnesium, such as the 6 6 6 2 and 8 3 9 mixes with magnesium that UF IFAS lists. Balance potash with magnesium according to the soil test.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in kaimito (star apple)
entries.hint: New leaves turn pale yellow with green veins, mostly on limestone or high pH soil.
entries.symptoms: UF IFAS notes kaimito is prone to iron shortage on alkaline, high pH soils but gives no detailed description. So this follows general fruit tree signs. The newest leaves turn light green to yellow between the veins while the veins stay green, making a net pattern. In bad cases the new leaves bleach almost white and may burn, while older leaves stay green.
entries.stage: New flushes on limestone or high pH soils.
entries.causes: Alkaline, limestone (calcareous) soils, where iron is locked up. Too much phosphate also brings it on. It is less likely on the slightly acid soils kaimito prefers (PROSEA).
entries.confuse: Magnesium shortage yellows between the veins of older leaves, not the newest ones. Zinc shortage makes the new leaves small and crowded. Manganese shortage leaves wider green bands along the veins.
entries.confirm: A soil pH test. Trouble is likely on limestone soils. Leaf tests for iron are not reliable. So a soil drench of iron on one tree that greens the next flush is the better check.
entries.fix: On alkaline and high pH soils, UF IFAS advises regular soil applications of an iron chelate made for high pH soils. On low pH soils, regular soil doses of Ferrous sulfate can be used. Follow the label for the amount.
entries.prevent: Do not overlime, avoid heavy phosphate, and plant on well drained ground. UF IFAS also gives 3 to 4 micronutrient sprays a year (copper, zinc, manganese and boron) during the first 4 to 5 years.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in tamarind (sampalok)
entries.hint: Pale, thin crowns with yellowing older leaflets, slow growth and few pods.
entries.symptoms: No tamarind particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The crown turns light green, older leaflets turn yellow, then brown, and drop. Young trees grow slowly with thin shoots, and bearing trees set fewer pods.
entries.stage: Grafted trees in the first years after planting, and bearing trees that are never fed.
entries.causes: Poor, eroded and gravelly soils low in organic matter, where tamarind is often planted, and trees that get no manure or fertilizer. PROSEA notes tamarind trees generally receive minimal care.
entries.confuse: Powdery mildew coats leaflets with a white powder and leaf eating caterpillars strip leaves (TNAU), which is not a color change from hunger. Few pods can also come from climate rather than hunger: PROSEA notes tamarind does not flower in very wet areas. Wet weather late in pod growth harms the crop.
entries.confirm: A leaf test of mature leaflets from recent growth shows low nitrogen. New leaves that come out greener after a nitrogen dose confirm it.
entries.fix: TNAU gives 200 grams of nitrogen, 150 grams of phosphate and 250 grams of potash per tree each year, along with 25 kg of farm manure and 2 kg of neem cake. 200 grams of nitrogen is about 430 grams of Urea 46 0 0 or about 950 grams of Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0. Spread it in a ring under the canopy edge when the soil is moist, early in the rainy season.
entries.prevent: Feed every year, add manure, and keep the circle under young trees free of weeds. Legume intercrops in the first four years, as TNAU suggests, also help the soil.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in tamarind (sampalok)
entries.hint: Tips and edges of older leaflets scorch brown. Pods stay small and poorly filled.
entries.symptoms: No tamarind particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. The tips and edges of older leaflets look burnt, and the scorch moves inward. Pod filling and pulp quality drop.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, most of all during pod filling.
entries.causes: Sandy, leached and eroded soils, and years of pod harvests with no potash returned.
entries.confuse: Salt in the soil or water also scorches leaflet edges. Tamarind seedlings are fairly salt tolerant, and in a Berlin greenhouse trial high salt mainly yellowed the leaves without dead patches. A bacterial leaf spot of tamarind is reported from India (PROSEA). It makes spots on the leaflets rather than an edge scorch. Powdery mildew leaves a white powder.
entries.confirm: A soil test for potash and a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU's yearly dose for tamarind gives the largest share to potash: 250 grams per tree, with 200 grams of nitrogen and 150 grams of phosphate. 250 grams of potash (K2O) is about 420 grams of Muriate of potash 0 0 60. Spread it under the canopy with the farm manure, in split doses on sandy soils.
entries.prevent: Give potash every year once the tree bears, and return fallen leaflets and prunings under the tree.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in tamarind (sampalok)
entries.hint: Seedlings and young trees grow slowly, with a purplish tint on older leaflets.
entries.symptoms: No tamarind particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. Growth is slow and stunted, and older leaflets take on a purple color, most of all on the underside. Seedlings in the nursery show it most.
entries.stage: Nursery seedlings and rootstocks, and young trees in the first years.
entries.causes: Low phosphorus tropical soils. A Brazilian nursery study calls phosphorus the most important nutrient for tamarind seedlings for that reason. Eroded and gravelly soils add to it.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage gives an even pale color without the purple. Leaf eating caterpillars thin the canopy but do not change the leaf color.
entries.confirm: A soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test.
entries.fix: TNAU gives 150 grams of phosphate per tree each year with manure. 150 grams of phosphate (P2O5) is about 750 grams of Superphosphate 0 20 0. In the nursery, the Brazilian study found that cattle or goat manure in the potting mix already supplied enough phosphorus for good seedling growth. While added superphosphate raised the phosphorus in the shoots. 16 20 0 or Complete 14 14 14 can also carry it.
entries.prevent: Fill planting pits with manure and topsoil, as TNAU advises, and add phosphate there and in the yearly feeding.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in tamarind (sampalok)
entries.hint: New leaflets come out small and pale, bunched on short shoots.
entries.symptoms: No tamarind particular description was found, so this follows general fruit tree signs. TNAU names zinc as the most widespread micronutrient shortage in fruit crops. Young leaflets turn pale or yellow between the veins and come out small and sometimes distorted. Shoots stay short so the leaves bunch in a rosette.
entries.stage: New flushes after the dry season.
entries.causes: Tamarind is often grown on poor, eroded, saline or alkaline soils (TNAU). Zinc is harder for roots to take up on high pH soils. Heavy phosphate fertilizer can also hold back zinc.
entries.confuse: High salt yellows the leaves of tamarind seedlings (Gebauer and others), which is not the same as small new leaves. Iron shortage yellows young leaves on alkaline soils too, but leaf size stays normal. Mealybugs and scale insects on shoots can also weaken new growth (PROSEA). Look for the insects.
entries.confirm: A leaf test for zinc and a soil test for pH and zinc. Spray a few branches and see whether the next flush comes out normal sized.
entries.fix: No tamarind rate was found. TNAU uses a 0.5 percent Zinc sulfate spray (5 grams per liter) on several fruit trees, for example guava before flowering. So try it on a few branches of the new flush first. On soils proven low in zinc, add Zinc sulfate to the soil following the soil test.
entries.prevent: Add manure every year, avoid heavy phosphate alone, and test the soil pH before planting on alkaline or saline ground.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in cashew
entries.hint: Old leaves pale from the tip, then yellow and droopy. Small leaves, small nuts.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves turn pale green from the tip, then yellow and droop. The tree grows slowly, with smaller leaves and smaller fruits and nuts that mature early. In bad cases the young leaves pale too.
entries.stage: Young trees in the first five years, and bearing trees that are never fertilized.
entries.causes: Most Philippine cashew trees get no fertilizer at all, as a review of cashew production in the Philippines notes. A study of cashew soils in coastal India found nitrogen only low to medium.
entries.confuse: Tea mosquito bug damage also makes trees look poor. But it leaves dark dead lesions on young shoots and flower stalks, and the shoots and flower clusters dry up. Nitrogen shortage is an even pale color without lesions. Magnesium shortage yellows old leaves between the veins while the veins stay green.
entries.confirm: Soil test, and a leaf test: a Brazilian study on dwarf cashew recommends the fifth or sixth mature leaf, counted from the flower cluster down the branch, taken at the start of flowering. New flushes that come out greener after urea confirm it.
entries.fix: Apply Urea 46 0 0 or Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 in a ring under the canopy and water it in, following the soil test. Kerala Agricultural University gives a full yearly dose of 750 grams of nitrogen per tree from the fifth year, with one fifth of that in the first year and one fifth more each year after. For a quick lift it gives a foliar spray of Urea at 10 grams per liter every 15 days.
entries.prevent: Fertilize young trees every year as they grow, split the dose over the rainy season, and mulch the basin.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in cashew
entries.hint: Leaves dark green, then dull red, green or purple. Slow tree with some dying branch tips.
entries.symptoms: Young mature leaves first turn darker green, then take on a dull red, green or purple tint. The tree stays small with less leaf area, leaves fall early, and some branches die back with dead leaf tips.
entries.stage: Young trees after planting and trees on poor acid soils.
entries.causes: Acid, weathered upland soils that lock up phosphorus and soils low in organic matter. A study of cashew soils in coastal Karnataka, India found phosphorus highly deficient in every soil profile.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency also brings purple spots, but on the underside of leaves, together with yellow, browning leaf edges. Tea mosquito bug causes shoot dieback too, but with dark lesions on the shoots.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test of mature leaves taken at the start of flowering.
entries.fix: Kerala Agricultural University advises Superphosphate for a quick fix and rock phosphate or bone meal for the long term, applied after a soil test. Its full yearly dose for trees from the fifth year is 325 grams of P2O5 per tree. Phosphorus is taken up best near pH 6.5 to 7.5, so lime very acid soils.
entries.prevent: Put phosphorus in the planting hole, add organic manure each year, and lime acid soils.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in cashew
entries.hint: Old leaf edges turn pale yellow then brown. Purple spots under the leaf. Light nuts.
entries.symptoms: The edges of older leaves turn pale yellow, then brown and die, and the damage moves up to younger leaves. In bad cases the whole leaf browns. Purple spots can show on the underside of leaves. Trees grow poorly and give smaller, lighter nuts.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, most of all during nut filling.
entries.causes: Sandy and leached soils, acid soils, and years of harvest with no potash returned. Potash is readily available above about pH 6.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also starts on old leaves, but it yellows between the veins rather than scorching the edge. Drought can also brown leaf edges, but over the whole tree at once.
entries.confirm: Soil test for potash and pH, and a leaf test of mature leaves at the start of flowering.
entries.fix: Kerala Agricultural University advises Muriate of potash 0 0 60 in split doses following the soil test. Lime or dolomite to keep pH up. Its full yearly dose for trees from the fifth year is 750 grams of K2O per tree. For a quick fix spray Sulfate of potash at 10 grams per liter in the morning. TNAU gives a 1 percent potassium chloride spray.
entries.prevent: Give potash every year with nitrogen, add organic matter, and keep the soil pH near 6.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in cashew
entries.hint: Newest leaves small, long and pale with green veins, on short shoots with few side branches.
entries.symptoms: The youngest leaves come out small and long, green to pale green with the veins staying green. Sometimes show small dead spots. Internodes stay short and the tree makes few side branches.
entries.stage: New flushes, mostly before flowering.
entries.causes: Soils naturally low in zinc, heavy phosphate, and pH outside 5 to 7.5. The coastal Karnataka cashew soil study found zinc highly deficient in every soil profile.
entries.confuse: Manganese deficiency also bunches the leaves into a rosette. But the leaves are pale green to greenish yellow and the tree makes more side branches, not fewer. Iron deficiency bleaches young leaves to a pale, see through yellow, but the leaves are not narrow.
entries.confirm: Soil test for zinc and pH, and a leaf test of mature leaves at the start of flowering. Spray a few trees and watch the next flush.
entries.fix: In bad cases Kerala Agricultural University gives a morning spray of Zinc sulfate at 2 grams per liter mixed with 2.5 grams per liter of lime (calcium carbonate). TNAU gives Zinc sulfate at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter). Do not apply zinc and phosphate fertilizer at the same time.
entries.prevent: Avoid heavy phosphate and overliming, and spray zinc before flowering where tests run low.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in cashew
entries.hint: Growing buds and young leaves die, flowers drop, apples split and nuts stay empty.
entries.symptoms: It hits the growing points. Buds and young leaves die, and root tips stop growing, lose color and die. Flowers drop, the fruits split, and nuts stay small and poorly filled.
entries.stage: Flushing and flowering, and during nut setting.
entries.causes: No cashew particular causes were found in the sources. In other tree crops such as coffee, it is linked to soils low in boron, heavy liming, heavy potash and long droughts. The same conditions likely apply here.
entries.confuse: Tea mosquito bug also dries flower clusters and kills young shoots, but it leaves dark lesions where it fed. Calcium deficiency also kills growing points, but the young leaves ripple, turn brittle and cup with scorched edges.
entries.confirm: Soil test for boron, and a leaf test of mature leaves at the start of flowering.
entries.fix: After a soil test, Kerala Agricultural University gives Borax to the soil at 50 grams per tree, or a foliar spray of Borax at 1 gram per liter. Do not mix borax with calcium or ammonium fertilizers. Too much boron is toxic, so do not repeat high doses without a test.
entries.prevent: Add organic matter, mulch the basin in the dry season. Give a small boron dose before flowering on soils that tested low.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in dragon fruit
entries.hint: Stems turn pale green to yellowish all over, new shoots come slowly and thin, and few flowers form.
entries.symptoms: No dragon fruit particular description of this shortage was found in an extension source. So this follows general plant signs, read on the green stems that do the work of leaves. The older stem segments turn pale green to yellowish evenly, without spots. New shoots come slowly, stay thin and short, and the plant fills its post slowly. Fewer flowers and smaller fruit follow.
entries.stage: Young plants growing up the post in the first two years, and bearing plants that are not fed after harvest.
entries.causes: Sandy soils low in organic matter, heavy rain that washes nitrogen down, and plants left without fertilizer or manure. Dragon fruit is a heavy feeder even though it is a cactus.
entries.confuse: Sunburn bleaches the sun facing side of stems yellow to white in patches, while nitrogen shortage pales the whole plant. Stem canker shows small orange to brown spots that sink and crack. Root rot from waterlogged soil also yellows stems, so check that the soil drains. Too much nitrogen, on the other hand, gives lush stems with few flowers.
entries.confirm: Do a soil test before planting, as Wikifarmer advises. A tissue test of a mature stem section helps. The UC South Coast trial sampled a 5 cm (2 inch) section of fully matured growth. New shoots that green up and lengthen after feeding confirm it.
entries.fix: UF IFAS gives young plants about 118 grams of a complete fertilizer every two months in the first year, 136 to 182 grams every two months in the second and third years. 227 to 341 grams three to four times a year after that, with manure or compost around the base. In the Philippines, Wikifarmer reports growers giving about 2 kg of organic fertilizer plus 25 grams of Urea 46 0 0 and 75 grams of Complete 14 14 14 per plant every three to six months.
entries.prevent: Feed in small, regular doses with plenty of compost or manure, kept a little away from the stem base, as UF IFAS advises. Once plants bear, give less nitrogen and more potash around flowering.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in dragon fruit
entries.hint: Older stems yellow and dry at the edges, and fruit come small, light and less sweet.
entries.symptoms: No dragon fruit particular description of this shortage was found in an extension source. So this follows general plant signs, read on the green stems that do the work of leaves. Older stem segments yellow and may dry at the edges and tips. Stems get weaker, and fruit come small, light and less sweet.
entries.stage: Flowering and fruit filling, when the fruit pull the most potash.
entries.causes: Dragon fruit takes out much more potash than nitrogen. In a UC South Coast trial, harvested fruit and pruned stems removed about two to three times as much potash as nitrogen. Sandy soils and heavy rain add to it.
entries.confuse: Sunburn scorches the sun facing side of the stems. Stem canker and anthracnose leave sunken brown spots spread over the stem, not a drying that starts at the edges of old segments. Drought also wrinkles and yellows stems, so check soil moisture.
entries.confirm: A soil test and a tissue test of a mature stem section. Bigger, heavier fruit after potash is added point to it.
entries.fix: Give more potash than nitrogen once plants bear, using Muriate of potash 0 0 60 or Sulfate of potash 0 0 50 with a complete fertilizer. In a Claveria, Misamis Oriental trial on red fleshed dragon fruit, 60 60 120 kg of NPK (N, phosphate, potash) per hectare gave a higher return on investment than 120 120 120, as less nitrogen and phosphorus and more potash paid best. Follow a soil test for the exact rate.
entries.prevent: Return pruned stems as compost only if they are healthy, and add potash at every feeding of bearing plants.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in dragon fruit
entries.hint: Plants grow slowly with weak roots and few new shoots, and flower poorly.
entries.symptoms: No dragon fruit particular description of this shortage was found in an extension source. So this follows general plant signs, read on the green stems that do the work of leaves. Shoots and roots grow slowly, so the plant climbs its post late and makes few new shoots. Stems may look dull dark green. Flowering is poor and fruit numbers drop.
entries.stage: Young plants after planting, and bearing plants that flower poorly.
entries.causes: Acid, weathered soils that hold phosphorus tightly and soils with no phosphate at planting. The Claveria researchers note that phosphorus shortage cuts the growth of shoots and roots.
entries.confuse: Waterlogged or rotting roots also stunt the plant, so check the roots and drainage. Nitrogen shortage stunts too, but the stems turn pale, not dark.
entries.confirm: A soil test for phosphorus and pH. A tissue test of a mature stem section helps.
entries.fix: Put Superphosphate 0 20 0 or Ammonium phosphate 18 46 0 in the planting hole and at feedings, following a soil test. In a 2019 Claveria, Misamis Oriental trial, 60 300 60 kg of NPK per hectare gave the most flowers, the most fruit per post, the highest yield and the best return, compared with lower phosphorus rates.
entries.prevent: Add phosphate and compost at planting, and keep soil pH in the range the UC South Coast trial gives, about 5.3 to 6.7, with lime on very acid soils.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in dragon fruit
entries.hint: Older stem segments turn yellow while the young shoots stay green.
entries.symptoms: No dragon fruit particular description of this shortage was found in an extension source. So this follows general plant signs, read on the green stems that do the work of leaves. Since dragon fruit has no true leaves, look at the older stem segments: they lose color and turn yellowish while the young shoots stay green. Fruit quality can drop.
entries.stage: Bearing plants, especially after heavy potash feeding.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy soils that have lost magnesium to rain, and heavy potash use, which competes with magnesium. UF IFAS recommends a fertilizer that carries 2 to 3 percent magnesium.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage pales the whole plant, young shoots included. Sunburn bleaches only the sun facing side. Old segments also yellow naturally before they die back, so look for many segments at once.
entries.confirm: A soil test for magnesium, potash and pH, and a tissue test of an older stem section.
entries.fix: UF IFAS uses a complete fertilizer with 2 to 3 percent magnesium at every feeding. Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) can be added to the soil or sprayed. Follow the label. On acid soils, use Dolomite, which supplies magnesium and raises pH.
entries.prevent: Use a fertilizer or mix that contains magnesium, and keep potash and magnesium in balance with a soil test.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in dragon fruit
entries.hint: New shoots come out pale yellow on high pH or limestone soils.
entries.symptoms: No dragon fruit particular description of this shortage was found in an extension source. So this follows general plant signs, read on the green stems that do the work of leaves. New shoots and young segments come out pale yellow, while older stems stay green. Growth of new shoots slows. UF IFAS notes that pitaya shows minor element shortages on poor, high pH soils.
entries.stage: New growth flushes, in the warm rainy season.
entries.causes: High pH, limestone or coral soils, and soils limed too heavily. Waterlogged soil also cuts iron uptake.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage pales older stems first. Young shoots are often lighter green for a short time and darken as they mature. Iron shortage keeps them yellow.
entries.confirm: A soil test with pH. A small test drench of iron on a few plants, watching whether the next shoots come out green.
entries.fix: On high pH soil, UF IFAS drenches each plant with 7 to 15 grams of chelated iron in the first year, rising to 22 to 29 grams per plant in later years. On neutral or acid soil, apply small amounts of Ferrous sulfate at the base. UF IFAS also gives four to six minor element sprays through the warm, rainy season.
entries.prevent: Do not over lime, add plenty of organic matter, and keep the soil well drained.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in coffee
entries.hint: The whole tree turns pale yellow green, leaves lose their shine and new shoots barely grow.
entries.symptoms: Leaves turn an even pale green, then yellow green, until the whole tree looks pale. In the Hawaii trial the young leaves paled first in full sun and the old leaves followed. Indian guides say the older, lower leaves go first. Leaves lose their normal glossy shine, old leaves may show whitish veins and drop early. Shoot growth falls by half or more. Flowering comes late and beans fill poorly.
entries.stage: Any age, worst during new leaf growth and flowering, when uptake peaks, and on heavy bearing trees.
entries.causes: Trees that get little or no fertilizer, sandy or eroded soils with little organic matter, heavy rain that washes nitrogen down. Coffee grown in full sun, which uses nitrogen fast.
entries.confuse: Sulfur deficiency also yellows young leaves, but those leaves keep their shine and the yellow sits along the midrib. Coffee leaf rust gives round pale yellow spots on top of the leaf with orange powder underneath, starting on the lower branches, not an even pale color. Brown eye spot (Cercospora) gives brown spots with a light centre and a yellow ring, and it is worst on poorly fed trees. So the two often come together.
entries.confirm: Send a leaf sample: on a lateral branch about halfway up the tree, pick the most recently matured leaf, usually the third or fourth pair back from the tip, from at least 15 trees, at or just before flowering, as the University of Hawaii coffee guide advises. Healthy leaves in the Hawaii trial held 3.0 to 3.7 percent nitrogen and deficient ones 1.5 to 1.9 percent. Leaves that green up within weeks after urea confirm it.
entries.fix: Apply Urea 46 0 0 or Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 in a ring under the canopy and work it in, following the soil test. For a quick boost, Kerala Agricultural University gives a foliar spray of Urea at 10 grams per liter every 15 days. Yara puts the yearly nitrogen uptake of mature coffee at 150 to 250 kg per hectare. So split the soil dose over the rainy season.
entries.prevent: Fertilize every year in splits at the start and middle of the rains, keep a mulch and organic matter on the soil. Keep some shade over the trees.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in coffee
entries.hint: Old leaves go mottled yellow or take a pink to purple tint. Roots and new growth stay weak.
entries.symptoms: It develops slowly. Older leaves first show a faint mottled yellowing, then a soft yellow between the veins, and in bad cases dead spots. Indian guides also note a pink or purple tint on old leaves. Roots stay small, the tree grows slowly, and flowering and fruit set come late.
entries.stage: Nursery and young trees after planting, and before flowering in bearing trees.
entries.causes: Acid soils that lock up phosphorus, and soils low in organic matter. A study of 22 coffee farms in Pigtauranan, Bukidnon found soil phosphorus very deficient on moderately acid soils (pH 5.6 to 6).
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency makes the whole tree pale, not mottled or purplish. Magnesium deficiency also yellows old leaves between the veins. But it brings a wide band of sunken light brown spots along the leaf edges. Cold or waterlogged soil and root damage also slow a tree, so check the roots.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH, plus a leaf test of the third or fourth leaf pair on a fruiting branch. Healthy leaves in the Hawaii trial held 0.14 to 0.18 percent phosphorus and deficient ones 0.05 to 0.08 percent. The University of Hawaii notes that on acid soils a soil test can look fine while the leaf test shows low phosphorus.
entries.fix: Apply a phosphorus fertilizer near the roots, following the soil test. Superphosphate 0 20 0 acts fast. Rock phosphate and bone meal work slowly, as Kerala Agricultural University advises. The Bukidnon study suggests 16 20 0 and Ammonium phosphate 18 46 0. TNAU gives a foliar spray of DAP (Ammonium phosphate 18 46 0) at 2 percent (20 grams per liter) for a quick fix. Lime very acid soils, since phosphorus is most available near pH 6.5.
entries.prevent: Put phosphorus in the planting hole, add compost or manure every year, and lime acid soils based on a soil test.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in coffee
entries.hint: Old leaves get a yellow band at the edge, then dark brown dead spots that join into a burnt edge. The centre stays green.
entries.symptoms: Only the older leaves show it. A yellow band forms along the leaf edge, then dark brown dead spots appear on the edge and grow until the whole edge is dark brown while the area along the midrib stays green. Young leaves stay normal. Badly hit leaves fall early and branches can die back.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, most of all while the berries grow and fill, when potash demand peaks.
entries.causes: Sandy or porous soils and heavy rain that leach potash, heavy crops that carry potash away in the pulp. Heavy liming or magnesium that crowd out potash. Long dry spells also cut uptake.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also starts on old leaves. But its spots are sunken and light brown in a wide band, with yellowing between the veins near the midrib. Coffee leaf rust gives round yellow spots with orange powder on the underside, not a burnt edge. Sun scorch and drought can also brown edges, but on the most exposed leaves at any age.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the third or fourth leaf pair on a fruiting branch, at or before flowering. Healthy leaves in the Hawaii trial held 2.6 to 3.9 percent potassium and deficient ones 0.4 to 1.1 percent. Add a soil test for potash, calcium and magnesium.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 to the soil under the canopy in split doses, following the soil test, as Kerala Agricultural University advises. For a quick fix spray Sulfate of potash at 10 grams per liter with a sticker in the morning. Yara puts the yearly potash uptake of mature coffee at 150 to 250 kg per hectare, about the same as nitrogen.
entries.prevent: Give potash every year together with nitrogen, in splits during the rains, and return pulp and prunings to the field.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in coffee
entries.hint: New leaves come out small, bent and misshapen with dead tips, and the shoot tip dies.
entries.symptoms: The youngest leaves come out light green, small, curved and leathery, mottled with small dead spots and with dead tips and uneven edges. The tip bud grows abnormally and can die, and the side branches show the same on their newest leaves. Older leaves stay normal. Flowers drop, fruit set is poor and beans can be hollow.
entries.stage: New flushes and flowering, often after a long dry season.
entries.causes: Soils low in boron, heavy liming, high rates of muriate of potash, and long droughts or very heavy rain. A Yara survey of about 16,000 coffee leaf samples found 29 percent below the critical boron level.
entries.confuse: Calcium deficiency also damages young leaves and kills the tip bud, but the leaves turn bronze along the edges and cup downward. Zinc deficiency gives narrow, strap like leaves with green veins on a yellow background and short internodes, without dead spots and tips.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the third or fourth leaf pair on a fruiting branch. In the Hawaii trial deficient leaves held 9 ppm boron and healthy ones 31 to 52 ppm. A soil test for boron and pH also helps.
entries.fix: Kerala Agricultural University gives Borax to the soil at 4 grams per tree, or a foliar spray of Borax at 1 gram per liter. TNAU gives a 0.2 percent Borax spray (2 grams per liter). Do not mix borax with calcium or ammonium fertilizers in the same tank. Boron is toxic in excess, so do not repeat high doses without a test.
entries.prevent: Keep organic matter up, do not overlime, and add a small boron dose before flowering on soils that tested low.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in coffee
entries.hint: New leaves narrow and strap like, yellow between dark green veins, bunched at the branch tip.
entries.symptoms: The youngest leaves yellow between the veins, at first just like iron deficiency. Later new leaves stay small and narrow, often strap like, with dark green veins, mostly along the midrib, on a yellow green background. Internodes stay short so leaves bunch into a rosette. Older leaves look normal. Berries can be misshapen and fruit develops poorly.
entries.stage: New flushes before and around flowering.
entries.causes: High pH or overlimed soils, heavy phosphate fertilizer, and soils low in organic matter. Zinc is most available between pH 5 and 7.5.
entries.confuse: Iron deficiency also yellows young leaves between green veins, but the leaves grow to normal size and shape and do not bunch. Boron deficiency also deforms new leaves, but with dead spots, dead tips and a dying tip bud.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the third or fourth leaf pair on a fruiting branch. Healthy coffee leaves held 18 to 25 ppm zinc in the Hawaii trial. Below about 10 to 15 ppm is deficient. A soil test for pH and phosphorus helps. Spray a few branches with zinc sulfate and watch the next flush.
entries.fix: In bad cases Kerala Agricultural University gives a morning spray of Zinc sulfate at 2 grams per liter mixed with 2.5 grams per liter of lime (calcium carbonate). TNAU gives Zinc sulfate at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter). Do not apply zinc on the same day as phosphate fertilizer.
entries.prevent: Avoid overliming and very heavy phosphate, and spray zinc before flowering where leaf tests run low.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in coffee
entries.hint: Old leaves yellow along the edges and between the veins, with a wide band of sunken light brown spots.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves first go pale along the edges, then sunken, yellow brown to light brown dead spots form in a wide band along the edge. The leaf also yellows between the veins, most of all near the midrib. Leaves can curl or cup and drop early after a long shortage. Young leaves stay normal.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, mostly as the berries mature.
entries.causes: Acid, sandy, leached soils and heavy use of potash or lime, which compete with magnesium.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency also starts at the edge of old leaves. But its spots are dark brown and join into a solid burnt edge, without yellowing between the veins. Coffee leaf rust gives round yellow spots with orange powder underneath.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the third or fourth leaf pair on a fruiting branch. Healthy leaves in the Hawaii trial held 0.30 to 0.35 percent magnesium and deficient ones 0.04 to 0.11 percent. Test the soil for magnesium, potash and calcium together.
entries.fix: Kerala Agricultural University gives Magnesium sulfate at 32 grams per tree, placed in a band near the tree after a soil test. On acid soils Dolomite gives magnesium and lime together and keeps the problem away over time. Do not apply magnesium and potash fertilizer at the same time.
entries.prevent: Use Dolomite instead of plain lime on acid soils and keep potash and magnesium in balance.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in coffee
entries.hint: Young leaves turn bronze at the edges and cup downward. The shoot tip dies back.
entries.symptoms: Young leaves turn bronze, mostly along the edges, while the area along the midrib stays green. They do not open fully and cup downward. Later the newest leaves die and the tip bud dies back. Roots stay short and weak, and berries can be misshapen.
entries.stage: New flushes and while berries fill.
entries.causes: Very acid soils, sandy soils that leach, and heavy potash or phosphorus, which push calcium out.
entries.confuse: Boron deficiency also hits young leaves and the tip. But leaves are small, curved and spotted, with dead tips, not bronzed and cupped. Magnesium deficiency starts on old leaves.
entries.confirm: Soil test for pH and calcium, and a leaf test of the third or fourth leaf pair. Healthy leaves in the Hawaii trial held 0.94 to 1.16 percent calcium and deficient ones 0.36 to 0.55 percent.
entries.fix: On acid soils Kerala Agricultural University gives 340 grams of lime per tree per year. Use Dolomite if magnesium is also low. On soils that are not acid use Gypsum. TNAU gives a calcium chloride spray at 1 to 2 percent for a quick fix on leaves.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soils based on a soil test and keep potash and phosphorus in balance.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in coffee
entries.hint: Young leaves pale yellow, a little more along the midrib, but they keep their shine.
entries.symptoms: The youngest leaves turn evenly pale, with a faint yellow between the veins that is strongest along the midrib. Unlike nitrogen shortage, the leaves keep their glossy shine. New leaves stay small, internodes are short and shoots grow slowly. In long cases older leaves pale too. Fruit set drops and ripening is late.
entries.stage: New flushes and berry maturing.
entries.causes: Soils low in organic matter, sandy soils that leach, burning of prunings and weeds. Years of urea and muriate of potash with no sulfur source.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency also gives pale leaves, but the tree loses its shine and the old leaves yellow too. Iron deficiency gives a sharp net of green veins on a yellow or cream young leaf.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the third or fourth leaf pair on a fruiting branch. Healthy leaves in the Hawaii trial held 0.12 to 0.17 percent sulfur and deficient ones 0.04 to 0.05 percent. Trees that green up after ammonium sulfate confirm it.
entries.fix: Use a sulfur carrying fertilizer such as Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 or Superphosphate 0 20 0 in place of part of the urea. Kerala Agricultural University gives sulfur dust at 10 grams per tree on sulfur deficient soils, and Gypsum on alkaline soils.
entries.prevent: Keep ammonium sulfate in the yearly program, return prunings as mulch instead of burning them, and build organic matter.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in coffee
entries.hint: Young leaves light yellow to creamy white with a sharp net of green veins. Old leaves stay green.
entries.symptoms: The youngest leaves turn light green between the veins, then yellow and finally almost creamy white. While every vein stays green and stands out as a clear net. The leaves grow to near normal shape but can be thin and small. Older leaves stay green. In bad cases leaf tips and edges brown, leaves drop and fruits stay small.
entries.stage: New flushes, most often after waterlogging or on limed spots.
entries.causes: High pH or overlimed soils and waterlogged soils. Kerala Agricultural University notes that low potash can bring it on. That many tropical soils already hold plenty of iron, so test before treating.
entries.confuse: Zinc deficiency starts the same way, but the leaves turn narrow and strap like and bunch into a rosette. Sulfur deficiency gives an even pale leaf without the sharp green vein net.
entries.confirm: Soil test for pH and check drainage. Leaf test of the third or fourth leaf pair: the Hawaii trial found 1 to 25 ppm iron in deficient leaves and 43 to 61 ppm in healthy ones. Spray a few branches with ferrous sulfate and watch the next flush.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a foliar spray of Ferrous sulfate at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter). Kerala Agricultural University gives 6 grams of Ferrous sulfate per tree to the soil where a test shows low iron. Fix drainage where water stands.
entries.prevent: Do not overlime, drain wet spots and keep potash in balance.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in cacao
entries.hint: Small, evenly soft yellow green leaves on a slow tree. New leaves come out almost white.
entries.symptoms: Growth slows and the leaves harden early, so they stay small. Full grown leaves turn an even soft yellow green, and the oldest leaves of each flush die back from the tip. New leaves come out yellow to almost white. Internodes are short and the leaf stalks stand at a sharp angle to the stem. Fewer flushes mean fewer flowers and pods.
entries.stage: Young trees in the first years after planting, bearing trees that get no fertilizer, and trees grown without shade. BPI notes nitrogen is most needed at the start of the rainy season and three months later.
entries.causes: Trees that get little or no fertilizer, cacao grown in full sun (BPI notes that proper shade lowers the nutrient need), low organic matter, and leaching rains. In a leaf survey of 63 cocoa farms in Papua New Guinea, a nearby growing area with similar smallholder farming, 95 percent of farms were below the critical nitrogen level.
entries.confuse: Vascular streak dieback also yellows leaves, but it shows scattered green spots on a yellow leaf on one or two leaves about a meter behind the shoot tip, the leaves drop. Three small dark dots show in the leaf scar with a brown streak inside the twig. Nitrogen shortage is an even pale color over the whole tree with no streak. Sulfur shortage is rare and yellows only the newest leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf test: take the second or third leaf of the last flush that is just maturing, four or five leaves from around the canopy of at least 10 trees, skipping damaged leaves, as Yara advises. A soil test for organic matter helps. New flushes that come out green after ammonium sulfate confirm it.
entries.fix: Apply Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 or Urea 46 0 0 in a ring under the canopy after weeding, in two splits at the start and end of the rainy season. The PCA Davao technology guide puts a mature planting of 1,241 trees per hectare yielding 1 tonne of dry beans at about 108 grams of Ammonium sulfate per tree per year. TNAU gives much more, 100 grams of nitrogen per tree per year, doubled for trees bearing over 50 pods. Use the soil and leaf test to choose.
entries.prevent: Fertilize every year in splits, mulch with prunings and composted pod husks. Follow the PCA schedule of Complete 14 14 14 for young trees.
