entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in cacao
entries.hint: Old leaves blotchy pale between the veins, then die back from the tip with a sharp edge. New leaves small and narrow.
entries.symptoms: Growth slows early. New leaves keep a normal color but come out smaller and narrower. Older leaves of the previous flush lose color between the veins in blotches, then die from the tip toward the base, with a sharp line between dead and living tissue. Some leaves turn greyish purple before the dead patch forms. Badly hit leaves fall, and flowering and pod setting drop.
entries.stage: Young trees after planting, and bearing trees at the start of the rainy season, when BPI says phosphorus is most needed for flowering.
entries.causes: Acid soils low in organic matter. A study of eight cacao farms in Davao de Oro found phosphorus generally deficient, on moderately to slightly acid soils with low organic matter.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency starts the same way, but at the advanced stage the dead patch has a wavy, zigzag yellow border instead of a sharp edge. Magnesium deficiency shows small blackish pinpoints with yellow halos first.
entries.confirm: Soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test of the second or third leaf of the last maturing flush.
entries.fix: Apply a phosphorus fertilizer in the ring under the canopy, following the soil test. The PCA Davao guide gives about 49 grams of Solophos superphosphate per mature tree per year for a 1 tonne per hectare crop. Complete 14 14 14 for young trees. Yara notes that on low phosphorus soils, rates up to 200 kg P2O5 per hectare raised yields. That the response is best when nitrogen is also enough.
entries.prevent: Put phosphorus in the planting hole, add compost or composted pod husks every year, and lime very acid soils.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in cacao
entries.hint: Old leaves get reddish yellow patches between the side veins that die from the tip and edge, with a wavy yellow border.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves show it first. A dull reddish yellow color runs along the midrib, wider at the base, or larger reddish yellow patches form between the side veins near the edge. The patches join and die, usually starting at the tip and edge, and the dead part has a wavy, zigzag yellow border. Leaves fall early. New leaves come out long and narrow.
entries.stage: Bearing trees under heavy pod loads. BPI says potash is most needed before flowering and while pods grow.
entries.causes: Every harvest carries potash away, mostly in the pod husks: the PCA Davao guide counts about 72 kg of potassium removed per tonne of dry beans, 63 kg of it in the husks. Sandy, leached soils and husks that are never returned bring it on.
entries.confuse: Phosphorus deficiency looks the same at first, but its dead patches have a sharp edge. Magnesium deficiency begins with blackish pinpoints between the veins. Vascular streak dieback gives green spots on a yellow leaf near the shoot tip, leaf fall and a brown streak inside the twig.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the second or third leaf of the last maturing flush, from at least 10 trees, plus a soil test for potash, calcium and magnesium.
entries.fix: Apply Muriate of potash 0 0 60 in the ring in two splits. The PCA Davao guide gives about 86 grams per mature tree per year for a 1 tonne per hectare crop. Yara puts 70 to 100 kg K2O per hectare as enough for yields under 1 tonne of beans. TNAU gives 140 grams of K2O per tree per year, doubled for trees bearing over 50 pods.
entries.prevent: Return composted pod husks to the trees, give potash every year in splits, and keep potash and magnesium in balance.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in cacao
entries.hint: Sickle leaf: new leaves narrow, curved and lopsided, with wavy edges and pale bands between prominent veins.
entries.symptoms: On young leaves the small veins stand out sharply and the tissue between them is pale, which is easy to see against the light. Leaves grow long and narrow with wavy, fluted edges and may twist. Many show a waist near the base or grow more on one side of the midrib, so they curve like a sickle. In bad cases leaves stay tiny, internodes shorten into rosettes, leaves fall early and shoot tips die back, with many small side twigs.
entries.stage: Young trees in the field and new flushes, often after a drought.
entries.causes: Old, leached, sandy soils low in zinc, high pH, heavy phosphate. Roots damaged by drought or waterlogging, which take up less zinc.
entries.confuse: Boron deficiency can also give sickle leaves. But it also brings brittle leaves with dead tips, a dying top and cracks on the trunk. Iron deficiency gives yellow leaves with green veins and a bumpy surface, but normal shaped leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the second or third leaf of the last maturing flush. Spray zinc on a few trees: leaves that have already hardened stay misshapen, but the next flush comes out normal.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a foliar spray of Zinc sulfate at 0.3 to 0.5 percent (3 to 5 grams per liter) every two weeks, three times. In a field trial in New Guinea, young trees sprayed with zinc sulfate every ten days had almost fully recovered after seven months, while unsprayed trees stayed sick.
entries.prevent: Avoid overliming and heavy phosphate, mulch to protect roots in the dry season, and include zinc where leaf tests run low.

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency in cacao
entries.hint: Old leaves get tiny black pinpoints with yellow halos between the veins, then a marbled dead edge.
entries.symptoms: Older leaves first show a faint yellowing between the side veins with small blackish pinpoints. Yellow spots form around the pinpoints, join toward the tip and edge, and the tissue dies, giving a blotchy, marbled leaf. A bright yellow zone borders the dead parts. In bad cases the dead tissue turns almost white with the green veins standing out like ribs, and leaves fall early.
entries.stage: Bearing trees, after years of potash without magnesium. BPI lists calcium and magnesium as most needed at the start of the rainy season.
entries.causes: Acid, leached soils and heavy potash. In the Papua New Guinea survey most farms had enough magnesium, but in one province 64 percent were short.
entries.confuse: Potassium deficiency also kills old leaf edges, but without the black pinpoints, and with a wavy yellow border. Calcium deficiency shows white spots, seen against the light, on the newest full grown leaves.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the second or third leaf of the last maturing flush. A soil test for magnesium, potash and calcium together.
entries.fix: TNAU gives Dolomite at 100 grams per tree per year from the third year after planting. The PCA Davao guide uses about 40 grams of Dolomite per mature tree for a 1 tonne per hectare crop. Where soil pH is fine, use Magnesium sulfate or Kieserite, following the soil test. Do not put magnesium and potash down on the same day.
entries.prevent: Lime with Dolomite instead of plain lime and keep potash and magnesium in balance.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in cacao
entries.hint: Many chupons, new leaves twisted and falling before they harden, brittle old leaves with dead tips.
entries.symptoms: Early signs are many chupons (water shoots) and a few curled leaves. New leaves come out pale, twisted and bent backward, harden while still small and often fall before they mature. Some curve into a sickle. Older leaves turn brittle and rough with dead tips, the most typical sign. The tip bud and then side shoots die so the tree turns bushy, and the trunk and branches may crack and bleed. Flower cushions swell, and pods can be misshapen with brown streaks inside.
entries.stage: New flushes and flowering, often after a dry spell.
entries.causes: Drought and shallow roots. U.S. Borax notes that fast growing, high yielding trees show it more readily.
entries.confuse: Zinc deficiency also gives sickle leaves, but without brittle dead tipped leaves, a dying top or trunk cracks. Sucking bugs can also deform pods, so check the leaves and shoots too. Vascular streak dieback also kills shoots, but it shows green spots on a yellow leaf and a brown streak inside the twig.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the second or third leaf of the last maturing flush, and a soil test for boron.
entries.fix: No cacao particular rate was found in the sources. Yara notes that boron applied with calcium helps flower set and cuts pod drop. Spray Solubor or apply Borax to the soil at the label rate, then retest. Boron is toxic in excess.
entries.prevent: Mulch and keep the soil moist in the dry season. Keep a small boron dose in the program on soils that tested low.

entries.name: Calcium deficiency in cacao
entries.hint: Small yellow green leaves with tiny white spots seen against the light, and dead tips and edges.
entries.symptoms: Growth nearly stops and leaves stay small and strong yellow green. Full grown leaves of the last flush show many small white spots near the tip and edge when held against the light, and the tip dies. The spots turn reddish yellow, join, and the tip and edge die further, sometimes leaving an oak leaf shape of green tissue. TNAU also notes dead patches near the edge that join into a dead margin on older leaves.
entries.stage: Young trees on acid soils. BPI lists calcium and magnesium as most needed at the start of the rainy season.
entries.causes: Acid, leached soils and heavy potash. Most cacao soils in the Davao de Oro study were moderately to slightly acid, below pH 6.5.
entries.confuse: Magnesium deficiency also kills leaf edges, but it starts with blackish pinpoints on older leaves. Potassium deficiency gives reddish yellow patches with a wavy border.
entries.confirm: Soil test for pH and calcium, and a leaf test of the second or third leaf of the last maturing flush.
entries.fix: TNAU gives Dolomite at 100 grams per tree per year from the third year. On very acid soils apply Agricultural lime or Dolomite following the soil test. On soils that are not acid use Gypsum. Superphosphate in the PCA program also supplies calcium.
entries.prevent: Lime acid soils based on a soil test and keep potash in balance.

entries.name: Iron deficiency in cacao
entries.hint: Leaves dull yellow green with sharp green veins and a bumpy surface between them.
entries.symptoms: Leaves turn a dull yellow green while the veins stay green and sharply outlined. The blade between the side veins bulges up, so the leaf looks bumpy, and the edge can look slightly toothed. TNAU describes it on young leaves, which turn pale yellow, with stunted growth.
entries.stage: Young trees and new flushes, mostly on wet or limed spots.
entries.causes: High pH or overlimed soils and waterlogged soils. A leaf survey in Papua New Guinea found 89 percent of farms below the critical iron level. But the authors warned that the critical level used was uncertain.
entries.confuse: Zinc deficiency also gives a bumpy leaf, but much stronger, and leaves are narrow, waisted or sickle shaped. Nitrogen deficiency yellows the whole leaf including the veins.
entries.confirm: Soil test for pH and check drainage. Since leaf iron numbers are hard to read, a test spray of ferrous sulfate on a few trees is the best check.
entries.fix: TNAU gives a foliar spray of Ferrous sulfate at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter) every two weeks. Fix drainage and stop liming where pH is high.
entries.prevent: Drain wet spots and do not overlime.

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency in cacao
entries.hint: The newest mature leaves evenly yellow green on a very short last flush.
entries.symptoms: It comes on slowly. The last three mature leaves turn evenly yellow green and the internode of the last flush stays very short. Older leaves look patchy from yellowing between the veins, and some yellow at the tip or edge. No field description from cacao farms was found, so this follows a pot trial.
entries.stage: Young trees, after a long time without any sulfur source.
entries.causes: Soils low in organic matter and fertilizer programs that use only urea and muriate of potash.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen deficiency also yellows leaves evenly, but it hits the whole tree and the old leaves die back from the tip. Iron deficiency keeps the veins sharply green.
entries.confirm: Leaf test of the second or third leaf of the last maturing flush for sulfur. Trees that green up after ammonium sulfate confirm it.
entries.fix: Use Ammonium sulfate 21 0 0 as the nitrogen source, as the PCA Davao program does, or add Gypsum, following the soil test.
entries.prevent: Keep a sulfur source in the yearly program and build organic matter.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency in malunggay
entries.hint: The whole plant turns light yellow, new leaves come small, and plants stay thin and weak.
entries.symptoms: In a seedling study from Yunnan, nitrogen shortage gave the earliest and clearest signs of all nutrients: the whole plant turned light yellow and stayed small and weak. The older leaflets pale first, as in other plants. New shoots are short and few, so leaf harvests are light.
entries.stage: Any stage, but worst in plants cut often for leaves, since every harvest takes nitrogen away.
entries.causes: Frequent leaf harvests without feeding, sandy soils low in organic matter, and heavy rain. A Brazilian study found nitrogen and potassium were the nutrients moringa seedlings took up most.
entries.confuse: Red mites, the worst pest in a Tarlac malunggay trial, speckle leaves pale and yellow. Look for tiny mites and webbing under the leaflets. Cercospora leaf spot leaves brown spots scattered over the leaflets. Drought and cool, dry spells also make moringa drop yellow leaves, but new shoots come back green once it rains.
entries.confirm: A soil test before planting. Plants that green up and push new shoots within two weeks after urea or manure confirm it.
entries.fix: TNAU gives 15 kg of compost per pit at planting, then 45 grams of nitrogen per pit 3 months after sowing (as part of 45:15:30 grams of NPK) and another 45 grams of nitrogen at 6 months. 45 grams of nitrogen is about 100 grams of Urea 46 0 0. After cutting back, TNAU gives 45:15:30 grams of NPK per plant with 25 kg of manure. Water after feeding.
entries.prevent: Add compost or manure after every few leaf harvests and feed in small, regular doses.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency in malunggay
entries.hint: Older leaflets yellow and scorch at the edges, and pods stay short and thin.
entries.symptoms: No clear malunggay description was found: in the Yunnan seedling study, plants short of potassium showed no obvious signs, only slower growth. So this follows general plant signs. Older leaflets yellow at the tips and edges, then the edges dry brown. In pod crops, pods stay short and fill poorly.
entries.stage: Bearing trees and plants cut often for leaves.
entries.causes: Sandy, leached soils and heavy harvests. The Brazilian study found potassium was the second most taken up nutrient after nitrogen.
entries.confuse: Red mites, the worst pest in a Tarlac malunggay trial, speckle leaves pale and yellow. Look for tiny mites and webbing under the leaflets. Cercospora leaf spot leaves brown spots scattered over the leaflets. Drought scorch dries leaf edges too, so check soil moisture first.
entries.confirm: A soil test for potash. A leaf test helps.
entries.fix: TNAU gives 30 grams of potash per pit at 3 months as part of 45:15:30 grams of NPK, and again after cutting back. 30 grams of potash is about 50 grams of Muriate of potash 0 0 60. For drip, TNAU applies nitrogen and potash as urea and muriate of potash.
entries.prevent: Use a complete fertilizer such as 14 14 14 or add potash with every feeding. Return pruned twigs and leaves as compost.

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency in malunggay
entries.hint: Slow growing young plants with dull dark green leaves, sometimes purplish, and weak roots.
entries.symptoms: No clear malunggay description was found: the Yunnan seedling study saw no obvious signs, only slower growth. So this follows general plant signs. Young plants grow slowly and root poorly. Leaves stay dull dark green and older ones may turn purplish. Branching and flowering are poor.
entries.stage: Seedlings and young plants after planting.
entries.causes: Acid soils that hold phosphorus and planting without manure or phosphate. TNAU notes moringa does best on deep sandy loam soil at pH 6.5 to 8.
entries.confuse: Nitrogen shortage also slows growth, but leaves turn pale instead of dark. Cold and waterlogged soil also slow young plants and can purple the leaves.
entries.confirm: A soil test for phosphorus and pH.
entries.fix: Mix phosphate into the pit at planting. TNAU gives 15 grams of phosphate per pit at 3 months as part of 45:15:30 grams of NPK. Applies phosphorus to the soil at planting. 15 grams of phosphate is about 75 grams of Superphosphate 0 20 0 or 33 grams of Ammonium phosphate 18 46 0. Lime very acid soils.
entries.prevent: Add compost and a phosphate fertilizer to every planting pit.

entries.name: Boron deficiency in malunggay
entries.hint: Few flowers and few pods set on trees that look healthy, with new shoots that may twist.
entries.symptoms: No malunggay particular description was found, so this follows general plant signs. New leaves and shoot tips grow twisted or stunted and the tip can die. Flowers drop and few pods set. A TNAU trial at Periyakulam found that a 0.2 percent boric acid spray gave the most panicles, flowers per panicle and pods per panicle, which suggests boron limits pod set.
entries.stage: Flowering and pod setting in trees grown for pods.
entries.causes: Sandy, leached soils, soils of high pH, and dry spells. In general, boron is less available at high pH, as the University of Delaware guide notes.
entries.confuse: Pod fly and bud worms also cause flower and pod drop. Look for maggots in pods and caterpillars in buds, as TNAU lists these as main moringa pests. Drought also makes flowers drop.
entries.confirm: A soil test with pH and boron. Spray a few trees and compare pod set.
entries.fix: Spray boric acid at 0.2 percent (2 grams per liter) at the vegetative, flowering and pod setting stages, as in the TNAU Periyakulam trial. Borax or Solubor can also be used. Follow the label. Boron is toxic in excess, so do not raise the rate.
entries.prevent: Add compost every season, and give a boron spray before flowering where pod set is poor.

entries.name: Zinc deficiency in malunggay
entries.hint: New leaflets come small and pale between the veins, and shoots stay short.
entries.symptoms: No malunggay particular description was found, so this follows general plant signs. New leaflets come out small and yellow between the veins while the veins stay green, and the shoots stay short and bunched. In the TNAU Periyakulam trial, a mixed micronutrient spray did best and a ferrous sulfate plus zinc sulfate spray came second for plant growth and pods.
entries.stage: New flushes after cutting back, and young plants.
entries.causes: High pH soils, which hold zinc, as the University of Delaware guide notes, and heavy phosphate use. TNAU notes moringa is often grown on soils up to pH 8, where zinc is less available.
entries.confuse: Iron shortage also yellows new leaves between the veins, often on the same high pH soils. The two are often sprayed together. Red mites leave fine pale speckles and webbing, not a clean pattern between the veins.
entries.confirm: A soil test with pH and a leaf test. Spray a few plants and compare the next flush.
entries.fix: Spray Zinc sulfate at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter) at the vegetative, flowering and pod setting stages, as in the TNAU Periyakulam trial. It was used together with Ferrous sulfate at 1 percent plus 0.1 percent citric acid. Do not mix zinc with phosphate fertilizer in one dose.
entries.prevent: Add compost and avoid overusing phosphate fertilizer.
